I rented this movie primarily due to the director, who has a track record of creating intriguing films (if you haven’t seen *Waxwork*, you’re missing out on a fun experience). From the start, I was skeptical, but I decided to push through and give it a chance. Spoiler alert: It’s terrible—really terrible. If you’re okay with spoilers and haven’t seen the film, keep reading. First off, the adage “You can’t judge a book by its cover” fits perfectly here. The box portrays Jill as an attractive, stylish woman with highlighted hair, while the back shows a cool image of her in red leather. The description makes the movie sound appealing, but once you start watching, you discover it inexplicably takes place in 1977. To your surprise, Jill turns out to be far from the glamorous figure on the cover. Surprisingly, the plot isn’t as straightforward as expected—and that’s definitely not a positive. Characters consistently make baffling decisions without any apparent motivation, making the viewing experience cringeworthy. About 10 minutes before the end, you’ll realize just how flawed the entire production is.

This lesser-known gem from De Sica more than delivers. As the saying goes, "the meek shall inherit the earth," and this story,表面上关于阶级，实则是对战后欧洲流浪人群的隐喻。他们是无家可归者，却保持着乐观的态度，在一个贫穷且自私的社会中被忽视，成为意大利投机者的牺牲品。德·西卡选择用童话的形式来讲述，如同灰姑娘的故事。我未读过原著，因此无法判断结局中的意外转折是作者的构思还是维托里奥的创意。电影以“很久以前……”开头，意在展现故事的永恒性，因为这个故事可以发生在任何地方、任何时间。对贵族阶层的讽刺刻画入木三分，流浪汉们的幽默与想象力尤其动人，尤其是在他们许愿时展现出的童趣，以及结尾处那种极具斯皮尔伯格风格的情节，让这部电影成为一部令人愉悦的作品。这是德·西卡最易被接受的作品之一，也是他最好的作品之一。他摒弃了新现实主义的束缚，始终在这两者之间游走，最终创造出一部既令人心碎又充满魅力的经典之作。

Wes Craven, you’re having a laugh… at our expense. The premise of *Red Eye* is absurd. We’re introduced to a guy who supposedly spent eight weeks stalking a woman, then somehow tracks her down at an airport, flirts with her, strikes up a conversation, manages to score a seat right next to her in a two-seat row (no middle seat in a five-seat row? What are the chances?), and maintains this odd charm throughout an excruciatingly slow buildup. Once aboard, in the cramped confines of an airplane filled with strangers, he wastes no time threatening the sharp-witted yet seemingly dim-witted Rachel McAdams, spouting nonsense about “we’ve got your dad, do what I say, or else.” Seriously, though—if they had her father under their control long before she even boarded the plane, wouldn’t it have been far easier to just grab her off the street and terrify her into making the call from a safe, private location? That way, they could skip all this unnecessary hijinks involving planes and dads. And hey, since this *is* a movie, couldn’t they have added some extra unrealistic twists while they were at it?

I adore horses and appreciate hand-drawn animation, so I had high expectations for DreamWorks' new animated film, *Spirit: Stallion of the Cimarron*. To be honest, I was somewhat let down. The animation is stunning, and the story initially appears flawless — focusing solely on a horse navigating the wild. The animals neither sing nor speak, which is a definite advantage. Unfortunately, the movie includes an unnecessary narration by Matt Damon, a saccharine soundtrack by Bryan Adams, and action sequences reminiscent of a Jerry Bruckheimer production. Had the filmmakers stuck to simplicity, they might have created a true masterpiece. While not a great film, it offers enjoyable entertainment for young children. I’d recommend it to families since it’s harmless and stands out as one of the few child-friendly options available right now. It's decent, but it could have been far better. Still, the visuals are breathtaking.

The first (and only) time I watched "Shades," it was during a sneak preview before the film had officially premiered. There was a member of the director’s team present, though I don’t recall who it was. It was a Belgian movie, completely unknown to us, so we approached it with no expectations. Mickey Rourke delivered a stellar performance, clearly surpassing everyone else in the cast. He portrayed an actor whose career had begun to fade, assisting with the production of a film titled "Shades" in Belgium.

From the very beginning, we noticed the excessive amount of profanity. While occasional swear words aren’t necessarily bothersome, this went far beyond that. When Rourke used curse words to emphasize emotion, it felt organic. But when other actors, especially those who weren’t native English speakers, threw around the F-word or S-word, it came off as pretentious and abrasive.

It didn’t take long for us to lose track of how many times these curses were uttered. By the end, everyone in the audience was relieved to leave the theater. Even giving our feedback was challenging since the scale only went from 0 to 10, and we were tempted to give it a -10.

I absolutely adore this movie, and I could watch it endlessly without getting bored. The only line that bothers me is when Riff refers to herself as a "teenage lobotomy," but aside from that, everything else is fantastic. I’ve never been particularly fond of PJ Soles, and it didn’t help knowing she wasn’t familiar with the Ramones until filming began, but I can overlook her snarky demeanor for the most part. People who repeatedly watch this film are usually Ramones enthusiasts, and that’s honestly the main reason I love it so much. I never tire of seeing Dee Dee botch his pizza lines or Joey repeatedly mispronounce the teacher's name—it’s hilarious! One of the best moments in the film is when they perform "Do You Wanna Dance?" in the high school hallways; it’s pure genius. The special edition DVD includes an insightful retrospective, though surprisingly, PJ Soles doesn’t appear in it. Maybe she had another project going on at the time (*laughs*). Overall, it’s a great film, and it’s even better if you’re a Ramones fan.

This is the finest science fiction I've watched in my 29 years of enjoying sci-fi. I also think "Dark Angel" will gain a devoted cult following. The action sequences are superb, but Jessica Alba stands out as the most captivating star on television today.

It’s commendable that *Vintage Film Buff* has appropriately labeled their outstanding DVD release as a "musical," because that’s precisely what this film is—unadulterated entertainment. Similar to its unofficial remake, *Murder at the Windmill* (1949), the murder mystery here serves merely as a pretext for an extravagant girlie show. Kitty Carlisle and Gertrude Michael lead a visually stunning ensemble featuring Ann Sheridan, Lucille Ball, Beryl Wallace, Gwenllian Gill, Gladys Young, Barbara Fritchie, Wanda Perry, and Dorothy White. Carl Brisson adds his vocal prowess to “Cocktails for Two,” which remains the film’s standout tune, playing no fewer than four times. However, it’s Gertrude Michael who truly commands attention—not only through her memorable performance of “Sweet Marihuana” but also in her compelling portrayal of the jilted love interest. On the other hand, the comedic performances by Jack Oakie and Victor McLaglen are forgettable at best. While Oakie does offer a mild chuckle with his weak interaction with cult figure Toby Wing, much of the humor feels forced and contrived. Even Inspector McLaglen’s bumbling incompetence seems excessive, as he inexplicably fails to apprehend the culprit despite...

I’ve just finished watching this movie. While it wasn’t awful, I’m deeply disappointed by it. I can’t quite figure out why anyone would choose to make a film like this. It managed to be somewhat entertaining, but it feels as though the people involved had constant disagreements about its direction. On Monday, the writer seemed to be in control; Tuesday belonged to the director; Wednesday, maybe the intern got a say; and so on. It’s almost like they intended to create multiple movies but only had enough time and resources for one—and even then, they couldn’t decide which one.

Someone else mentioned that the acting was excellent, but I don’t agree. If the actors could maintain their composure throughout filming, maybe they’re more skilled than I assume—but I doubt it. 

The back of the DVD led me to believe this would be a mystery, something akin to a historical *Law & Order* or *National Treasure*. At first, it does resemble that genre, but then, out of nowhere, it veers toward a terrible episode of *The Twilight Zone*, or maybe *The Outer Limits*—you know, the less impressive one.  

All in all, I’m left feeling... well, let’s just say I won’t be recommending this movie anytime soon.

"Slither" is a horror comedy that falls short in both genres, lacking the necessary scares and laughs to fully satisfy either category. While the film boasts one standout scene and a handful of clever lines, it struggles to deliver genuine frights or sustained comedic moments. Additionally, the script veers off course at several points, failing to keep the focus on its protagonists.

One of the film's biggest shortcomings is its treatment of the hero (played by Fillion). Instead of centering the story around him, the narrative shifts to follow Grant Grant (Michael Rooker), who transforms into the monster. This segment feels sluggish because Rooker's character lacks depth, and his actions as the monster don't hold much intrigue unless the film were reimagined as a psychological study of transformation rather than a horror-comedy. Ultimately, the movie’s issues lie in its script—it matters less to audiences how the monster behaves and reproduces. The true goal of a horror-comedy should be to put the heroes in peril, cornered with shotguns.

Gus Van Sant has directed several outstanding films, and I’m genuinely a fan of his work. However, I can’t help but feel that the intellectual depth of Tom Robbins' novel *Even Cowgirls Get the Blues* doesn’t translate effectively to the big screen. Individually, both Tom Robbins and Gus Van Sant are remarkable visionaries and talents, but unfortunately, this adaptation falls short.

It’s not that the characters lacked depth or the plot failed to engage; rather, it’s that the imaginative power of reading a book like this is far more impactful. When we read, our minds are transported to another time and place, where we envision possibilities—both hopeful and unsettling—that enhance the emotional journey laid out by the author. In contrast, movies often rely on visual storytelling, which can sometimes leave less room for imagination and emotional resonance, diminishing the overall experience. That’s what happened here, in my opinion.

If you haven’t already, I highly recommend reading the book!

What a dreadful piece of nonsense! Who are all these people raving about how great this is? Sure, it’s “artsy” and “foreign,” but that’s simply not enough. The plot is dull and disjointed, resembling a poorly executed reality show. 

The characters are utterly unengaging, lacking any real depth or complexity to evoke sympathy. If these are meant to be representations of real people, then I pity them deeply. 

The violence, which is quite graphic in parts, feels excessive and unnecessary. It’s as though the director is trying to emulate Quentin Tarantino, whose work I’m not particularly fond of anyway. 

Oh, and one more thing—if my neighbors were anything like those in this film, I’d pack up and leave immediately!

This is a straightforward B-movie science fiction flick, and the director doesn't shy away from its genre roots. The story revolves around a dragon brought back to life by a scientific team. Every plot point feels familiar, and the script is underwhelming, lacking depth or compelling characters. Instead, it's packed with clichéd personas and predictable scenarios. The director seems to embrace the formulaic nature of the film, which lends it a modest charm but fails to leave a lasting impression. It’s the kind of movie best enjoyed during mundane tasks like cooking, cleaning, or working out—mindless yet mildly entertaining. While it holds a niche in pop culture, it’s not the type of film you’d watch with friends unless you're in a particularly lighthearted mood. With an average rating of 3.2, I find it reasonable but can’t understand why some viewers praised it so highly. To me, there’s no effort here to craft anything remotely memorable.

I was living in Rawlins when this movie was produced, and I was fortunate enough to have the opportunity to work on it—both as an extra and alongside Eddie Surkin on special effects. It was fascinating to witness all the behind-the-scenes action, from the barbed wire that came alive to the electric chair rising through the warden's office floor. It was also incredibly enjoyable to meet all the actors, from Viggo to Tiny. Interestingly, the gate that was cut into the prison wall for the film is still referred to by locals as the "Disney Gate." For those who are curious and happen to visit Rawlins, many of the movie sets remain intact and can be explored during the self-guided tour. Working with R. Harlin was a blast, and I wish I'd had the chance to be involved again.

I believe the scene that best encapsulates the sheer pointlessness, stupidity, and absurdity of this movie occurs during its climactic moments. Dr. Ted Nelson and his unmarried friend, the Sheriff, have finally cornered the Melting Man on a staircase landing inside an electrical generating plant. By this point, Nelson has spent most of the film searching for the MM, who has already killed and consumed several people (including his own boss). Nelson is fully aware that the MM is not only violently insane but also ravenous for human flesh and blood.

As the Sheriff points his gun at the horrifying creature—credit where it’s due; both the movie and Rick Baker deserve praise for making the Melting Man such a disgustingly terrifying sight—he shouts a crucial question to Dr. Ted Nelson: “WHAT DO WE DO NOW?!?!?” 

The camera shifts to Nelson, and it’s painfully clear that he has no idea how to proceed. Evidently, Nelson was so focused on locating the Melting Man that he neglected to plan what to do afterward.

It’s baffling how Francis Veber, one of the world’s premier comedy directors (especially within his native France), delivered a film so entirely unwatchable. It’s not merely that the characters are unlikable or that the movie lacks even the slightest hint of humor; it’s genuinely agonizing to view. The film is an interminable procession of poor writing, subpar acting, and amateurish filmmaking, making it hard to believe it came from seasoned professionals. The lengthy time spent in editing and storage before its fleeting theatrical release says it all. What were they thinking?

As someone mesmerized by the stunning visuals of *Hero*, I was eager to watch this film, advertised as a superior version of the same genre. Plus, it starred Ziyi Zhang, an actress I admire. Unfortunately, I was let down on both fronts. I blindly purchased the DVD, and that turned out to be a poor decision—this film was not better.  

I understand that these gravity-defying martial arts movies are pure fantasy, but this story stretches credibility to such an absurd degree that it left me shaking my head in disbelief. A blind woman taking down hundreds of opponents? That’s pushing it a bit too far. To make matters worse, the main male character, Jin (played by Takeshi Kaneshiro), was so irritating with his repetitive dialogue, vacant expression, and obnoxious laugh that he single-handedly ruined the movie for me.  

Even with its vibrant colors and thrilling action sequences, this story lacked the charm or depth to make it a must-own film. For me, this wasn’t even close to being another *Hero*.

This movie was terrible—plain and simple. It was so awful that I created an IMDb account just to warn you about its pitfalls.

As someone who’s well-versed in campy horror flicks, let me assure you, I’ve seen my fair share of B-movies like “Redneck Zombies,” “House of the Psychotic Women,” and “Slumber Party Massacre II.” I know schlock when I see it, and this movie is bottom-of-the-barrel trash.

Three-quarters of the runtime consists of terrified characters running back and forth across the screen. When they’re not running, they deliver random, unmotivated lines devoid of any real emotion or purpose. Just as the performances start to improve, the direction tanks. The film is riddled with jarring low-angle shots—I swear Leif Jonker must’ve been using a three-foot-tall tripod. He employs what I call the “Leif Maneuver” constantly: zooming out from something important like an amateur. Clearly, the crew couldn’t manage to wake up early enough for a sunrise, so instead, they shot a sunset and played it backward. Given how lazy the direction is, you almost appreciate the final, gory scene. You can only assume that the last five minutes were filmed before the first eighty-five.

This movie didn't delve into the humanity of the animals, leaving me with a hollow sensation. [Spoilers ahead] I wasn’t persuaded that Dr. D had a strong enough motivation to turn down the lucrative buyout deal just to aid his furry companions. While Babe (the original) defied the norm of big-budget successes by highlighting the human-like qualities of the animals compared to their human counterparts, every creature in this film was merely a comedic stereotype—ones you’d happily toss into a grinder (especially if you could comprehend their senseless chatter). Without Eddie Murphy’s eccentric performance, this film would be a complete failure.

THE2 is amusing because you’ll likely laugh a lot, cringe, and maybe exclaim “oh sh*t!” or “get your face away from the goddamn hole, you dumb**s,” but I’m not sure it’s worth watching. I was consistently annoyed by the entire film due to the terrible military characters, who seem clueless about combat.

While it does have more violence, gore, and a higher body count than the first, I’m still undecided if that outweighs my overall impression of how absurd it feels (and not in a fun way, like *Dead Alive* or *Feast*). I’d have been better off watching Aja’s remake for the fifth time.

So go for some laughs or some gore, but don’t expect to leave feeling satisfied.

(Rating: 21 by The Film Snob.) (Visit our blog What-To-See-Next for insights into our rating system.)  

This is the kind of film that might drive you to claw at your own face in a desperate bid for relief from the overwhelming boredom. It’s not just the eye-rolling or heavy sighs over popcorn that this movie deserves; no, for such a mediocrity, nothing less than frantic face-clawing will suffice.  

When you inevitably reach for your face to claw at it—trust us, you will—start from the bottom. Save the upper half, with its convenient tear ducts, for the heartstring-tugging third act, which may leave you sobbing uncontrollably. If you manage to endure that long, you’ll likely be clawing your way out of the theater before the credits roll.  

In a season where Joe Six-Pack and Hockey Moms are celebrated as the new benchmarks for leadership and diplomacy, perhaps this insufferable film will be hailed as something anyone could make. Watching it, however, is an entirely different matter—a torturous exercise in masochism.  

Now, here’s the story…  

Sidney Young, the hapless editor of a low-rent celebrity rag in London, stands on the brink of watching his publication go under when fate thrusts him into the glitzy world of New York City’s high-stakes book publishing.

Before *The Toxic Avenger* put Troma Films on the map, the studio’s self-proclaimed kings of lowbrow cinema attempted to elevate their game by producing straightforward slasher films. I’d like to believe that watching the end result here was what spurred them to abandon all pretense and fully embrace self-aware parody instead.

*Splatter University* is yet another endurance test for the masochistically inclined among the audience. As it meanders between two separate casts and an endless array of pointless subplots, it eventually becomes painful to sit through. Let me attempt a summary.

Following news of a dangerous psychopath’s escape from a nearby asylum, the story shifts to a Catholic university—whose name escapes me, so let’s humorously refer to it as St. Splatter. The students are lethargic and irritable, bickering over petty issues and embodying the quintessential slackers of yesteryear. Meanwhile, the new professor, Julie Parker, proves hilariously inept at her job. The students navigate romance, infidelity, unplanned pregnancies, predatory clergy, and dodging academic responsibilities, while Julie contends with a creepy boyfriend, rigid university administrators, counseling unwed mothers, and the blank stares of her uninterested pupils. None of it amounts to much of anything.

Certainly! Here's the rewritten version:

---

A woman wrote it, and another directed it. Great. Are we in for a full-on feminist journey? Buckle up, ladies, because we're diving into a world of cruel men and virtuous, well-meaning women. 

In this melodrama, Trish meets a character at an employment agency who acts, looks, and dresses like a stereotypical pimp (!) and hires her, hoping to pursue a romantic relationship down the line. In his office, he even grabs her chin in a manner reminiscent of a villain from a Bond movie—just after capturing her and moments before planning her demise alongside Bond. Later, this so-called pimp/employment agent follows Trish into a women’s changing room, harasses her, and nearly assaults her. Oh, these awful men. They’re all terrible, aren’t they? Can’t even look for work without being assaulted, right, ladies? Well, here’s our chance to fight back. The film features a divorced women’s club led by Janet Leigh, who voices the collective frustration of the female characters when she declares that “men are all s**t.” She goes on to complain...

Frailty—8/10: Despite its nonsensical title and the distracting "Bill Paxton Directs" tagline, this is a solid, old-school biblical horror thriller. In the end, it might just be the Southern Gothic equivalent of Kubrick’s *The Shining*—and that’s a thrilling thought. The film delivers an unexpected plot twist and leaves viewers with a morally ambiguous message. Years from now, people will stumble upon this late at night on basic cable and get thoroughly spooked by it. Too bad Bill Paxton decided to cast himself in addition to directing—oh well, it’s still a darn good rental.

*The Sopranos* is widely regarded as the most celebrated television series in history, so naturally, my anticipation was sky-high. Yet, the show exceeded even those lofty expectations. I’m a fan of the mafia and crime genre in film, and I relish the intricate narratives set within these worlds. However, *The Sopranos* transcends genre conventions. With over 86 hours of content, the series doesn’t just deliver one of the most gripping and unpredictable mafia/action tales; it also unfolds as a profound family drama, a stunning character study, a hilariously comedic take, a brilliant psychological exploration of good and evil, and an intellectually stimulating blend of dreamlike symbolism and hallucinatory artistry—all rolled into one. David Chase’s magnum opus achieves all of this and more, solidifying HBO as the closest TV gets to cinematic perfection, and setting a precedent for countless other series to follow.

While the show remains rooted in realism where necessary, Chase’s occasional departures from it—such as “dream episodes”—add further depth and complexity. Working alongside a formidable writing team that includes Matthew Weiner and Terrence Winter, future architects of *Mad Men*, Chase crafts an unparalleled masterpiece.

Frequently eliciting laugh-out-loud humor with its playful takes on sex, family dynamics, and class distinctions, this Beverly Hills-set comedy wrings more chuckles from the 90210 area code than it has since the heyday of Granny and Jed Clampett. The story revolves around two chauffeurs who wager on which of them can sleep with their respective employers—a pair of alluring, single (or soon-to-be-single) women (played by Bisset and Woronov). If Manuel wins, his pal will settle his debt with a brutal Asian street gang; but if he loses, he’ll have to serve as his friend’s submissive partner! 

Packed with crude dialogue and outrageous physical humor, much of the comedy lies subtly beneath the surface. Bartel shines as an eccentric older family member with a strong sensual side, ultimately embarking on a year-long “missionary trip” to Africa with his attractive teenage niece. 

A riotously entertaining gem!

Despite being remade multiple times, this film is considered a classic for those experiencing it for the first time. With its creative dialogue and a uniquely brilliant finale, it merits greater recognition than it has received from critics. Strongly recommended—it’s one of the finest comedies in recent memory.

Despite having no particular attachment to any genre of filmmaking and appreciating documentaries in general, I must admit I was frustrated with myself for enduring the entirety of *20 Dates*. I won’t bother detailing the plot—other reviews can cover that. However, I will mention that Berkowitz’s overly energetic, Woody Allen-esque narration was incredibly irritating. One couldn’t help but wish he’d cut back on caffeine or take something to calm down. It’s also clear to Berkowitz himself that this project wasn’t his strongest effort, as portions of the film delve into his struggles to secure funding. Please excuse me if my praise feels faintly sarcastic, but I’ll acknowledge Berkowitz for convincing someone to finance this dreadful mess. While I respect the film’s intentions and boundaries, even by his own standards, he falls short across every dimension. To wrap up, I suspect many of these women weren’t entirely comfortable dating a jittery aspiring filmmaker, which makes me doubt the film’s authenticity. Hey Myles, I really enjoyed your earlier work—it reminded me of your previous film...

When I was a kid, I absolutely adored both Bill & Ted movies. The other night, "Bogus Journey" came on, and since it had been at least five years since I last watched it, I decided to check it out. And guess what? I loved it just as much as before! This film remains hilarious after all these years. While "Excellent Adventure" is the better movie, "Bogus Journey" is still a blast. Some performances may feel a bit dated, but that’s part of its charm—it’s cheesy in the best possible way. Oh, and let's not forget: it features the coolest portrayal of Death in cinema history! In conclusion, this is a totally awesome movie, dude! Super excellent! ROCK ON!

CRY FREEDOM offers a compelling introduction to the harsh realities of apartheid, providing a comprehensive overview in just a few hours. Directed by the renowned Richard Attenborough (known for GANDHI), the film benefits from the authentic portrayal of the real-life Woods couple—central white characters in both the book and the movie. The version currently available runs slightly over two and a half hours, as 23 additional minutes of footage were added to expand it into a two-part TV miniseries following its initial theatrical release. Although the extended runtime amplifies some forgivable shortcomings, such as uneven character development and broad stereotypes, it also transforms what could be seen as a flaw into a strength. By focusing more on the experiences of white characters than their African counterparts, the film may resonate more effectively with its intended audience. As an educational tool addressing political and historical themes, CRY FREEDOM remains particularly impactful for white viewers, aiming to raise awareness and provoke reflection among those who need it most. For the younger generation of Black Africans, watching the film provides a vivid depiction of struggles they may already be familiar with, while reinforcing the message for audiences who have yet to fully grasp these injustices.

This movie feels like real life—except that means not much happens in its two-hour runtime, and the plot is elusive thanks to the often indiscernible performances. The actors seem to vanish under the "experimental" lighting that critics have noted, making their presence feel more theoretical than actual. 

It’s painfully dull, and yet it’s not surprising given its director, Altman, whose work can be wildly inconsistent (yes, “Gosford Park” was brilliant, but what about “Pret-a-Porter,” “Kansas City,” or “Dr. T and the Women”? Yikes). Even more baffling is that this adaptation comes from a John Grisham story, and despite an impressive ensemble cast, they’re barely visible as the credits roll and you drift into sleep. This is undoubtedly a masterpiece of bad filmmaking—and not in the fun, campy way. It’s just plain bad.

I have watched *Miracles Still Happen* at least four times, and I never grow tired of this incredible film. From the very start, it captivates your attention. As the story unfolds and the plane crash occurs, the tension rises dramatically as we witness a young girl struggling to survive alone and afraid in the Amazon jungle. The loss of her mother in the crash adds an extra layer of emotion, highlighting the challenges she faces over the course of her ten days there. It’s hard to believe that such an event actually occurred, and even harder to imagine anyone surviving it, as the film portrays the wild animals, snakes, reptiles, dense forests, wildlife, and countless insects she encounters. As the narrative progresses, we see the various dangers she must overcome while attempting to follow a river, hoping it will lead her to a town. She recalls her father’s advice—that streams lead to rivers, which lead to larger rivers, ultimately connecting to civilization.

I’m not sure if it’s available worldwide, but if anyone responsible for selecting movies to be distributed to video clubs is reading this—please, please buy it! (To clarify: Get the movie into video stores!) It can’t be adequately explained—it has to be seen!

A year or so ago, while watching the TV news, I came across a report about a zombie movie being filmed in my area. Since then, I’ve kept an eye on this film, titled *Fido*, as it completed production and started making appearances at festivals. Two weeks ago, *Fido* premiered at my local theater. Just yesterday, I read a newspaper article stating that *Fido* isn’t drawing large crowds in its limited release—except at our local theater. Surprisingly, it’s currently outperforming every other show at The Paramount Theater, even beating *300*. This isn’t surprising, given how many locals want to see their hometown onscreen or spot themselves in zombie makeup. For anyone else in the area who hasn’t seen *Fido* yet but is curious, rest assured—it’s filled with recognizable landmarks, from the school to the city park to the forbidden zone, showcasing the Okanagan Valley in a surprisingly beautiful light. Yes, beautiful scenery in a zombie movie! Moreover, *Fido* is a genuinely excellent film. Despite its flaws, it surpasses most of the 20 other movies currently playing at my local theater.

I saw this at a test screening, and my reaction was: What...the...hell? The movie unfolds as smoothly as Mickey Mouse attempting to read the script for "Scarface." It’s so bizarre that it fails to make the tiniest bit of sense. Even if you leave your critical thinking skills in the parking lot, the film remains so strange that it doesn’t even qualify as amusing.

The plot revolves around crocodile hunter Steve Irwin attempting to "rescue" a crocodile containing a CIA surveillance device. The CIA then goes after Irwin to retrieve their probe, but Irwin mistakes them for poachers and decides to "stop" them.

That’s essentially all the story there is. The rest of the film is a series of over-the-top parodies of Australian culture (think phrases like "Didja see dat?" and "Crikey!") and oddly staged action scenes. At one point, Irwin climbs onto a speeding recreational vehicle and engages in a knife fight with a CIA agent on top of it. Yes, you read that correctly: Steve Irwin knife fights a guy on an RV. Take that as your litmus test for how hilariously bad this movie truly is.

In my view, this is a solid celebrity sketch show. I loved watching Greg Kinnear as the host, and there are several reasons for that. Although Hal Sparks did an adequate job, I sometimes wish Greg Kinnear had stayed on longer. As far as I'm concerned, it seems like no one sticks with a TV show from start to finish anymore. Nonetheless, I thoroughly enjoyed seeing the different hosts and others lampooning celebrities—it was genuinely hilarious. Before I conclude, I have to admit that I miss this show quite a bit. To sum up, I strongly recommend this show to all you dedicated sketch comedy fans—you won’t be disappointed!

My enduring fascination with Italian actress Lucianna Paluzzi, whose performance in the 1965 film "Thunderball" played no small part in igniting my adolescent curiosity, has taken me to some rather unusual spots. One such example is this quirky 1959 British production, "Carlton-Browne of the F.O.," where Lucianna appears in one of her earliest roles. Here, she portrays a princess, though the movie primarily serves as a platform for the comedic brilliance of Terry-Thomas and Peter Sellers, both of whom were ascending rapidly to stardom. This charming, frequently hilarious film introduces us to Gaillardia, an island nation reminiscent of Madeira, which was a British colony until 1916 before being all but forgotten. Decades later, however, it finds itself thrust into the global spotlight—and the realm of international intrigue—when significant cobalt deposits are unearthed. Her Majesty dispatches the hapless Carlton-Browne from the Foreign Office to oversee matters. Terry-Thomas delivers a subtle yet effective performance, as does Sellers as Prime Minister Amphibulos of the diminutive nation. (This was Sellers' second 1959 film centered around a small country tangling with the world, the first being "The Mouse That Roared," naturally.) Ian Bannen nearly steals the show as Gaillardia’s debonair king.

What's Good About It: This indie horror film boasts some inventive and genuinely unsettling effects that will resonate with even veteran horror enthusiasts. It avoids relying on clichéd sound cues for its惊悚 moments. Despite potential familiarity with similar themes, the movie still manages to deliver surprising twists that will leave viewers in awe.

What Could Have Been Better About It: While the film has its strengths, the acting occasionally felt flat and unconvincing. Certain scenes carried a low-budget, "shot-on-video" aesthetic, though this didn't always detract from the intended atmosphere. Camera work is marred by excessive close-ups focusing on inconsequential actions. Although the effects are unsettling, some were reused too frequently. The ending felt hurried and glossed over potentially powerful moments. Viewers are left piecing together significant details without intentional depth or subtlety from the filmmakers.

Despite these shortcomings, it remains a solid indie horror gem, surpassing the average production. Definitely worth renting.

"Bloodsuckers" has the potential to be a mildly entertaining film, as the premise of military personnel hunting and fighting vampires in space holds some charm within the campy sci-fi genre. The notion of the universe teeming with diverse vampire species, each possessing unique traits and many still unknown to the characters, also adds an intriguing layer. However, the idea of nearly all extraterrestrial life being vampire-like is perplexing—how these beings sustain themselves when most of the population shares their same nature remains unclear. Overall, the movie feels like a low-budget mash-up of "Firefly/Serenity" and vampire films, with a sprinkle of "Aliens."

The action sequences are fairly standard and unoriginal, especially compared to "Serenity," but they are competently executed. There's sufficient vampire-themed gore, including some exaggerated, comedic spurts of blood. While there’s plenty of character development, much of it is tiresome, stemming from petty conflicts among characters who come off as whiny and immature.

I've seen movies that put me to sleep, but none have ever done it twice. This one required three sittings to finish. The dialogue was atrocious—women delivered their lines stiffly, while the men came off as caricatures. Two actresses labeled as Japanese had Chinese names, spoke with Chinese accents, and even looked Chinese. I’m still puzzled by the romantic entanglements between the Emmenthal men. Subtracting 8 1/2 from 10 leaves me with a difficult decision: should I rate this movie a one or a two?

Clearly, this movie is illegal. Pedophiles exploit scenarios just like the one depicted here. How was this film even allowed to be made? In a single word, this movie is SICK. What kind of people make and watch this sort of content? While watching, I never thought they’d actually go so far as to show a child—likely around 12 years old—sleeping with an adult woman. I apologize if this is a spoiler, but I wish I hadn’t seen it. Where has the sanity of these individuals gone? Perhaps the filmmakers themselves are pedophiles? Our society already grapples with various sexual predators targeting children, yet filmmakers create movies that only encourage such behavior. On a previous comment, someone even asked if there’s a version showing nudity. This is a child we’re talking about, and someone is asking something like that? What is wrong with this picture?

I’m a big fan of the comic book series, but this movie failed to meet even my lowest expectations. I was hoping for a Heavy Metal 2000 kind of vibe—slow-moving, cheesy dialogue, plenty of gore—but what I got was far worse than anything I could have anticipated. 

While the basic plot follows the comic, that’s about where the positives end. The characters lack the charisma and energy that made the comic series so engaging. The film only scratches the surface of the comic’s story, focusing on tedious and unimportant details rather than the compelling overarching narrative. Even worse, the sections they chose to adapt are some of the slower, more tedious parts of the comic.

With the right creative team behind it, this adaptation could have been incredible. Unfortunately, that didn’t happen, leaving us with yet another forgettable movie destined to be ignored by most and loved by even fewer. My copy will likely gather dust on the shelf for years before I eventually toss it out.

If you're a fan of gangster movies, this is the first one you should definitely buy or at least rent. Al Pacino's performance is exceptional, and the story is timeless! 10/10! How is this movie not on the TOP 250 list?

Despite the impressive 3-D animation, which was undoubtedly the highlight of the show, many of the other elements failed to deliver. It seemed as though the filmmakers relied too heavily on the 3-D aspect, assuming they could skimp on the plot and character development. The fact that it’s a children’s movie is no justification—audiences are just as invested in three-dimensional characters (like Shrek or Nemo’s dad) as they are in three-dimensional visuals. Unfortunately, none of the main characters rose above two-dimensional status; even Scooter, who occasionally livened things up by compulsively eating everything in sight, lacked depth.

But here’s where it gets worse: after spending an excruciating hour and a half watching a wooden, robotic cartoon version of Buzz Aldrin, he finally appears onscreen at the very end. Instead of adding excitement or closure, he ruins the mood entirely by labeling the film’s protagonists as “contaminants” and declaring the entire scenario on screen scientifically impossible. 

Wait… WHAT?! Was this some kind of convoluted way to break the hearts of every kid in the audience by revealing that the Easter Bunny and Santa Claus don’t exist?

Ariauna Albright is undoubtedly a talented actress, yet her involvement in this poorly written project remains puzzling. What had potential for entertainment ends up as uninspired monotony. What sets Ariauna apart is her ability to deliver compelling performances while exuding undeniable charisma. In contrast, her co-star Lilith Stabs appears visually appealing but seems to have prioritized grooming over honing her acting skills. This production sorely needed tasteful nudity and tantalizing moments, which an imaginative screenwriter could have seamlessly integrated. Despite the limitations, Ariauna does her best and somewhat preserves her reputation. Tempe Company should recognize that dressing attractive women in revealing fetish outfits creates viewer expectations for more suggestive content. Enough said.

It’s peculiar to watch a film where certain scenes feel somewhat weak, particularly when compared to others within its series, while secondary or supporting storylines deliver unexpectedly powerful and thought-provoking moments. *Sudden Impact* exemplifies this dichotomy, as Clint Eastwood, in his dual roles as star, producer, and director, showcases both his strengths and limitations when handling a crime/mystery/detective narrative tied to his *Dirty Harry* persona. The iconic "make my day" line makes an appearance, but unlike in the first film, where the "do I feel lucky" speech was initially playful and later hardened, here the dynamic is reversed. Eastwood’s character once again clashes with the police department while attempting to tackle crime his own way—such as during a diner robbery (perhaps inspiring Quentin Tarantino’s *Pulp Fiction*?) and a high-speed chase involving a senior citizen bus. He’s advised to “take a vacation,” though it’s the last thing on his mind. Unfortunately, the central plot feels unconvincing beyond the anticipation built by its dialogue, contributing further to the frustration. However, the film takes a turn as the main storyline converges with the compelling subplot crafted by Eastwood...

"THE SUNSHINE BOYS" is a hilariously endearing 1975 screen adaptation of Neil Simon's play, focusing on a retired vaudevillian duo—played by Walter Matthau and George Burns—who had a bitter falling-out and are now being asked to reunite for a TV special. Despite their mutual animosity, neither wants anything to do with the other. Richard Benjamin plays Matthau's nephew, a theatrical agent tasked with orchestrating this reunion. This heartwarming and delightful comedy pays homage to the bygone world of vaudeville, succeeding largely due to one of Neil Simon’s strongest screenplays and standout performances from Matthau, Burns, and Benjamin. Burns earned an Oscar for Best Supporting Actor, but it's Matthau's flawless, side-splitting portrayal of Willy Clark that truly steals the show. Though Matthau received a Best Actor nomination, he was overshadowed by Nicholson's iconic role in "ONE FLEW OVER THE CUCKOO'S NEST." In any other year, Matthau's performance would have been Oscar-worthy. He dominates the screen with impeccable timing, delivering every line with precision. A standout moment occurs during the audition scene.

Here’s the rewritten version:

This is a review of *The Wizard*, not to be mistaken for *The Wiz* or Mr. Wizard. *The Wizard* is an '80s film centered around a largely mute boy's talent for playing video games, accompanied by his ability to walk throughout the entire opening credits. Meanwhile, *The Wiz* is a needless remake of *The Wizard of Oz*, while Mr. Wizard is the guy who once connected 100 straws and challenged a kid to drink Tang through them.

With that clarified, here’s my take: there’s absolutely no compelling reason to watch this movie. It’s essentially a 100-minute Nintendo advertisement, leveraging the Power Glove, *The Legend of Zelda*, and *Super Mario Bros. 3*. When I say "advertisement," I mean it loosely, as this film appears to have been written over a weekend by a group of people unfamiliar with gaming, and directed by someone whose sense of style rivals that of my grandmother. If the writer and director had spent even a few minutes playing these games together, they might’ve realized they were making something truly dreadful and opted for a more practical career path—like installing car stereos.

—I

This movie begins with some humorous jokes about Frank’s fantasies, like when he travels with a staircase or finds himself in business meetings. However, after watching for an hour, you’ll notice the same scenarios and gags repeated over and over. It becomes monotonous and feels more suited to a TV format, where viewers can step away and return without losing the plot. 

While I enjoy Felix Herngren’s portrayal of Frank, that isn’t enough. Even comedies need more variety and should offer some sort of meaningful message for their audience.

"Ruby in Paradise" is a poignant coming-of-age tale centered on a young woman named Ruby Lee Gissing, who seeks to break free from her suffocating origins and discover her true self. While the titular character is skillfully portrayed by the striking Ashley Judd—arguably marking what could be her breakout role—this film diverges from the conventional narrative of striving to become "somebody." Unlike stories focused on achieving fame or emulating figures like Madonna, it instead highlights the importance of trusting one’s instincts and engaging in self-reflection to evolve into one's ideal adult self.

This is not your typical action movie; it employs subtle elements such as occasional voice-over narration (delivered by Judd as Ruby writes in her journal). I can already hear some male readers clicking away, but give this beautiful film a chance. You’ll discover that personal fulfillment can be found in the simplest things—like carrying water or chopping wood.

Co-starring alongside Ashley Judd is actor/director/writer Todd Field, known for his role as Nick Nightingale in "Eyes Wide Shut." He plays Ruby Lee's compassionate love interest, someone who assists her in healing the skewed perceptions of relationships she inherited from her upbringing. Yet, even he isn’t presented as the ultimate savior for Ruby Lee. The film deliberately avoids imposing an external hero on its protagonist, emphasizing instead her internal journey toward self-discovery.

This is at least the third remake of this film, so if you feel a sense of déjà vu while watching it, don’t be surprised. The filmmakers simply changed the setting and retold the story, but the changes aren’t significant. Unfortunately, it doesn’t improve the movie, as the plot is flawed from the start and never quite works. As with its predecessors, the acting is merely average.

The plot does offer a unique twist at the end, which might surprise viewers unfamiliar with the story. However, the conclusion feels out of place and doesn’t align well with the rest of the narrative. If the movie had ended ten minutes earlier, it could have been both satisfying and far more impactful. Spoiler alert: the ending implies that crime pays, as the perpetrator goes unpunished. I’ve never appreciated this message in a film, as it undermines the moral foundation of the story.
At the very least, it doesn’t充斥着无意义的暴力或空洞的情节。然而，它也缺乏深思熟虑和流畅的故事线。这个故事本可以有所作为，但导演似乎迷失了方向。故事情节支离破碎，偏离主线走向奇怪的方向，最终毫无结论。此外，我怀疑导演对高尔夫球俱乐部并不熟悉，因为其中一些描写显得荒诞不经。整体而言，这部电影不够吸引人。

"Who me? No, I’m serious. That’s exactly what it says on the video case."  

**Plot (short version):** A pretty woman stands around smiling, and for some inexplicable reason, this causes all the men to start killing each other. "Find Ariel… Where’s Ariel… Can’t find Ariel…" She’s right behind you, you idiot…  

Unfortunately, most of what needs to be said about this dreadful little space opera has already been covered.  

A group of corny actors—mostly playing convicts—shows up after the initial batch of actors gets killed off almost immediately. Then they meet the same fate. Every scene feels like it was filmed fifteen minutes ahead of schedule. Maybe it was just a matter of drawing straws to decide who got the most screen time and bigger paycheck. Meanwhile, the alien virus/hologram/VR entity/glitch seems completely harmless and never actually does anything. Why does she keep teleporting around like a “vampire” when staying in the computer would’ve been far more intriguing? (In fact, it would’ve been better if she’d been a proper vampire or done something more than just stand there staring at people, which is all she ever does. Apparently, that’s enough to drive men to murder. Who knew?)  

To be honest, this isn’t even much of a space movie.

While not one of John Cleese's most successful television projects, "Strange Case" carries the unmistakable vibe of a hastily produced first draft, lacking the polish of subsequent revisions. Despite containing some amusing concepts and a sprinkling of clever moments, the narrative ultimately fails to amount to much as a cohesive whole. 

That said, Arthur Lowe shines as Dr. Watson, bionic elements and all, delivering his lines with delightful flair and memorable quips like, "Good Lord."

I absolutely adored the original *Scary Movie*. Parody is my favorite genre of humor, and it’s often considered by many to be one of the smartest forms of comedic expression. The Wayans brothers seemed to fully understand this in their initial film but momentarily lost their way while crafting its sequel. Despite being far from perfect, the Wayans family remains a collection of comedic innovators. Even geniuses aren’t immune to missteps, however.

The movie starts off with some promise. I particularly enjoyed the “Exorcist” parody, especially the "come on out, ma" joke—it was classic Wayans-quality material. Beyond that, though, there were only two instances where I genuinely laughed: 1) When Tori Spelling’s character gets overly attached after a supposed “booty call,” leading to awkward declarations about marriage while the ghost insists, “It was just a hookup!” That moment brought a chuckle. 2) The "Save the Last Dance" spoof where Cindy accidentally knocks someone out with her dance moves. Even these fleeting moments of amusement pale in comparison to the belly laughs elicited by the first *Scary Movie*.

Unfortunately, the remainder of the film is disappointing, packed with lazy gross-out jokes. Some of the subtler gags from the original feel forced here, making them feel more like an uninspired rehash than clever satire.

What's wrong with you if you weren't captivated by the thrilling car chase scenes or Jessica Simpson's stunning presence? If so, you might need to reevaluate your perspective. This film wasn't trying to be a cinematic masterpiece; instead, it aimed for pure entertainment, and it succeeded. I didn’t grow up watching the show, but after seeing an episode, I understood the vibe the movie was going for. It was lively and amusing. During the screening, I could feel the energy—my seat practically vibrated during the action sequences. Unlike *2 Fast 2 Furious*, these scenes kept my attention without becoming monotonous. Jessica Simpson was undeniably attractive, and I hoped they'd given her more action-packed moments. Overall, I thoroughly enjoyed this film and would happily watch it again or purchase the DVD. So, take it as it is—fun, entertaining, and unpretentious.

This movie was utter trash, plain and simple. The opening scene had potential, but any promise it held was quickly shattered once the audience grasped where the plot was headed.  

The wooden statue, Morty, who was unsettling in the original film, now looks ridiculous in this version. It’s painfully obvious that it’s just some guy in a cheap plastic suit. And honestly, who else finds “Morty” one of the least intimidating names ever? It’s right up there with “Jimmy” or “Fred” for horror credibility. Why not call the statue Henry-freakin’-Kissinger instead? At least that would add some unintentional humor to the fear factor.  

Then there’s the scene where the so-called “hero” takes out his aggression on his father’s tombstone—not with a sledgehammer or even a two-by-four—but with a twig. Yes, you read that right. A twig. But wait, it gets worse. After the characters leave, the tombstone inexplicably starts bleeding. Facepalm moment right there.  

Oh, and let’s not forget the Native American guy who lives with the protagonist’s grandparents. His sole purpose seems to be Morty maintenance: sharing eerie Morty legends, warning skeptics, and even fixing Morty’s detached arm. Talk about wasted screen time.

"Brokedown Palace" tells the story of two close friends, Alice and Darlene, who embark on an impromptu trip to Thailand only to find themselves imprisoned after being falsely accused of carrying drugs hidden in their luggage. While the film had the potential to explore weighty themes similar to "Return to Paradise," it instead shifts its focus toward the dynamics of the girls' friendship. 

Claire Danes and Kate Beckinsale deliver strong performances, with the narrative emphasizing the evolving tensions between them—suspicions, jealousies, and the trials that test their bond. The movie avoids delving deeply into political or prison-related issues, opting instead to highlight the complexities of their friendship and the sacrifices made for one another. 

Despite its engaging performances, the film suffers from some plot inconsistencies and moments that lack credibility. The stakes of their dire situation don’t resonate as strongly as they could have, and there’s minimal exploration of life beyond the prison walls, particularly in Bill Pullman's portrayal of a potentially shady character.

It’s hard for me to imagine that the talented Alan Ball had any involvement with this series. After watching the first two episodes, I’m fairly certain it won’t make my “must-see” list. There are just too many issues holding it back.

None of the actors seem particularly strong in their roles. Anna Paquin, who plays the lead character Sookie, delivers a disappointing performance. While I’ve seen her do better in other projects, it feels like the writing might be to blame here. She’s also not visually striking; at times, she appears almost unattractive. Her co-star Stephen Moyer, who plays Bill, fares slightly better, though his character is intentionally stiff and distant, which makes his performance somewhat easier to accept. The rest of the cast tries their best, but the overused character tropes and challenging regional accents they’re given make it a tough challenge. Tara’s scenes are particularly painful to watch, with Rutina Wesley struggling badly with her accent—it’s cringe-worthy. Nelsan Ellis is nearly as problematic; his dialogue is often hard to decipher due to his delivery. Both his character and...

I adore this film, with its standout performances by Jouvet, Arletty, Blier, and Carné. Much has already been said about it, but there’s one detail I want to highlight: no actual footage of the real, still-standing Hôtel du Nord (assuming it still exists—rumor had it slated for demolition) was used in the movie. Instead, the entire setting was meticulously reconstructed on a studio set. The primary reason for this was the inability to halt traffic along the St. Martin canal for an extended period.

"Presque rien" tells the story of two young boys who fall in love during their summer stay by the seaside. While I won’t reveal the plot, rest assured that it is both intriguing and unique. However, the true highlight of this film lies in its cinematography. The visual aspect of "Presque rien" is so breathtaking that it deserves top marks, leaving viewers enchanted by its beauty.

The narrative unfolds in an unconventional manner, without adhering to a straightforward chronological order or providing clear answers to every question it raises. Yet, this complexity adds to the film’s allure. I highly recommend "Presque rien" to those who prioritize the artistic elements of cinema—it will not disappoint.

Films like *Chocolat*, *Beau Travail*, and others have elevated French director Claire Denis to the upper echelons of the world’s most distinctive and accomplished filmmakers, and her 2004 work *The Intruder* (*L'Intrus*) further enriches her acclaimed body of work. A cinematic poem exploring feelings of enduring loneliness and loss, the film offers a window into the mind of a man whose physical and mental decline leads him to journey across the globe in search of redemption and solace, yet finds them elusive. Loosely inspired by Jean-Luc Nancy's memoir about a heart transplant, *The Intruder* is so densely enigmatic that even after multiple viewings, it remains challenging to articulate beyond subjective, impressionistic terms.  

Louis Trebor (played by Michael Subor), a septuagenarian likely suffering from a terminal heart condition, resembles the protagonist of Ingmar Bergman's *Wild Strawberries* as he grapples with the errors of his past while there is still time. Despite being physically robust and financially affluent, he appears emotionally spent, his expression marked by quiet acceptance. Although we encounter only...

I have seen this movie twice, and I intend to watch it again. It is a film that immerses you in the director's perspective on their romantic relationships and the political climate in Israel. It also moves me to tears as it brings back the美好 times it portrays and the devastating murder depicted. It is undoubtedly worth watching.

This isn't your average vampire tale—no Bram Stoker or Anne Rice here. It's a genuinely unique vampire story. These vampires are genetic mutants who aren’t affected by sunlight and are purely malevolent.

The movie isn’t flawless; many of the actors seem amateurish. However, the two main leads—the ones playing Van Helsing and the vampire woman—are quite solid. The film is extremely violent, which might unsettle some viewers. Plus, it’s packed with scientific jargon that could confuse and bore some audiences. I found myself drawn in by the clever plot and a few strong performances. Who knows how successful this could have been with a larger budget and wider release.

The film initially sounds like it might be a biography of Claude Monet, but it’s actually an intensely focused narrative about the complex relationships among three teenage girls on a French synchronized swimming team. Parents and teachers are virtually absent, school plays no role, and boys are scarcely present beyond one recurring character—Francois, the attractive but perpetually befuddled hunk who occasionally enters the scene only to leave just as confused as before.

Pauline Aquart is the youngest of the trio, still striving to become part of the team she idolizes. She’s somewhat unconventional in appearance—still in her awkward adolescent growth phase with long, angular limbs, oversized feet, and little in the way of curves. Her protruding jaw and pouty, full lips add to her distinctive look, which takes some getting used to. Yet, from certain angles, her uniqueness becomes strangely captivating.

Adele Haenel is the older, more physically mature member of the group. She looks effortlessly glamorous in her swimsuit, strutting confidently, teasing the boys, and tossing her flowing blonde hair. But beneath her polished exterior lies a mystery—what exactly is she hiding? I found myself unsure, much like Francois, who remains perpetually puzzled. The French have a knack for embracing contradictions and eschewing straightforward explanations, so perhaps that explains Francois’s confusion.

Critics who dismiss this film likely harbor deep-seated bitterness due to unreciprocated affection. For those who can appreciate Johnny Mathis's music—or similarly timeless pieces like Bobby Darin's "Beyond the Sea" or Stan Getz's "The Girl From Ipanema"—this is a remarkable cinematic experience.

When evaluating films, I gauge how often I need to revisit them to feel fulfilled. *Chances Are* has drawn me in multiple times. 

I also pay attention to the chemistry among actors; here, I found their interactions compelling and natural.

Let your guard down and allow the comedic charm of this movie to sweep you away.

—Alan

You can tell they spent only $5 on this movie. It's a complete waste of time... ugh. There’s absolutely nothing worthwhile about it. I don’t even know why I stuck with it. The lead actress isn’t attractive, the acting is terrible, and doing pretty much anything else would’ve been a far better use of my time—watching trashy TV or playing horrible video games feels more productive. I feel completely ripped off, not just financially, but of my time. I’ve never written a movie review before, but this one made me feel obligated to warn others who might check IMDb to see if it’s worth watching. Spoiler alert: there’s no action, no attractive women, no budget, and absolutely atrocious acting. It screams “bad movie.” Oh, and by the way, the **entire film takes place in a single room**.

It’s challenging to classify the film—perhaps it qualifies as an avant-garde spy thriller? *Mother Night* is a strong Vonnegut novel and arguably one of his most straightforward works for adaptation into a feature film. The movie stays true to the source material. The “indie” approach to its production likely contributed to its effectiveness more than if a major Hollywood studio had funded it. Nowadays, I doubt an intelligent novel like *Mother Night* would receive backing from the big studios. Typically, that would be unfortunate, but not in this instance. The film boasts sharp direction and a reliable cast. Nick Nolte, whose roles seem to improve with age, retains his “everyman” charm, enabling him to portray a diverse array of characters. Sheryl Lee is as beautiful and出色的 as ever. I’ve always felt she deserved greater recognition from the entertainment world. Starting out as a deceased character (*Twin Peaks*) with limited screen time isn’t exactly ideal, even if the show became a cult hit. Still, this film is thoroughly enjoyable and doesn’t require prior reading to appreciate.

After reviewing the extensive comments on this movie, it becomes evident that there are two distinct types of science fiction enthusiasts. On one side are those who are well-versed, highly literate, and intellectually inclined. These individuals understand the genre’s history and recognize the potential for greatness when gifted authors are involved. For many years, science fiction was relegated to the lower echelons of literature, dismissed by critics as simplistic tales of ray guns and aliens catering only to pre-pubescent audiences. Modern, well-read fans are keenly aware of this past and acknowledge the pivotal role played by celebrated authors like Asimov, Heinlein, Bradbury, and Ellison, who elevated the genre from its lowly status. Through their efforts, they crafted thought-provoking, intelligent narratives that expanded boundaries and redefined humanity’s place in the cosmos. These informed fans approach every Hollywood offering with a critical yet fair perspective—not merely to nitpick but because they hold high expectations based on the industry’s inconsistent track record. While their critique is not born out of cynicism, they scrutinize new releases skeptically. To them, the strength of the story remains paramount; they remain unimpressed by dazzling CGI or relentless action sequences. When the emperor is...

This film was truly eye-opening. I’ve watched it multiple times—first when I was four, and surprisingly, I still remember it vividly. Then again when I was 12. The central message from the director is a wake-up call for everyone: don’t leave God out of our daily lives, and certainly don’t go out of your way to disrespect Him. 

A fantastic movie for both non-believers and believers!

A soulless film follows a drifter who accepts a job to kill a man for a mobster, only to be double-crossed. While falling for the victim's wife, he hides his involvement in the murder and moves in with her. In an accidental twist, he ends up killing her after she discovers the truth. Later, he seeks revenge against the mobsters who betrayed him, showcasing a WALKING TALL-style heroism. The primary issue arises when the drifter, by agreeing to commit the hit, forfeits any semblance of empathy, morality, or heroism. His actions make it impossible for viewers to see goodness in him, leaving the story morally adrift. As a result, we struggle to invest emotionally in his journey. Similarly, the wife—a compassionate woman running a shelter for the homeless, played charmingly by Kari Wuhrer—loses some sympathy by hastily entering a relationship with the drifter despite her grief over losing her husband. When she learns the truth about him, her response is bizarre: she locks him in her house, as though every home comes equipped with such security measures.

Twenty years ago, a five-year-old boy named Michael Hawthorne witnessed his father murder his mother with an axe on an empty road and later commit suicide. In the present day, Michael (played by Gordon Currie) invites his girlfriend Peg (Stacy Grant) and his closest friends—Chris (Myc Agnew), Jennifer (Emmanuelle Vaugier), Lisa Ann (Kelly Benson), Ned (Brendon Beiser), Mitch Maldive (Phillip Rhys), and Trish (Rachel Hayward)—to celebrate Halloween at his grandparents' farm in the countryside. Michael asks everyone to dress as their deepest fears and, alongside his Native American friend Crow (Byron Chief Moon), they plan to perform an ancient Indian ritual using a carved wooden dummy named Morty (Jon Fedele) to banish these fears forever. For Michael, his greatest fear is becoming a serial killer like his father, but things go awry when Morty transforms into his father, killing his friends.

"The Fear: Resurrection" is a lackluster and uninspired slasher film that squanders an intriguing concept—the idea of confronting and eliminating people's greatest fears before they manifest—but delivers it through a convoluted screenplay riddled with clichés. Some performances are over-the-top, such as Ms. Betsy Palmer's, while others feel weak and underdeveloped.

There have been several difficult moments in my life when I've felt utterly confused and disheartened. Watching *Rancid Aluminium* was one such instance.  

From the start, there were clear red flags—no premiere (not even the actors wanted to attend) and a complete absence of reviews in major magazines. The only reason I endured the film was in the faint hope of catching up on some sleep.  

Nothing in the movie made sense. The narration was absurd, and I found myself cheering when it appeared that the protagonist had been shot. My relief, however, was short-lived as it was quickly revealed that he hadn’t actually been injured, leaving me thoroughly disheartened. I can only hope those responsible for this disaster face consequences for their actions.  

That said, there were unintentionally humorous moments, though they did little to redeem the film. For instance, there’s a scene where the main character inexplicably decides to use the restroom manually while instructing someone in the adjacent stall to plug their ears.  

Words fail to capture the depth of my frustration. To conclude:  

*Rancid Aluminium* is recommended only for masochists, individuals with questionable taste, and those who enjoy self-inflicted misery.

I watched this movie around five years ago, and its memory still haunts me to this day. I went into it fully expecting it to be terrible, so I can only blame myself. Like most people, I didn’t completely buy into all the negative hype. As a Sandler fan, it seemed unimaginable that one of his films could truly be that bad. I figured it was just the work of Sandler detractors. How wrong I was.

What we have here is a comedy that doesn’t contain a single moment of humor—not even for one second. This is quite an achievement in its own right. You’d think that over 90 minutes, they might accidentally hit upon something remotely amusing. But no, it’s just relentlessly awful. It’s not “so bad it’s good”; it’s just bad. You can’t even laugh at how terrible it is—you can only feel despair. You wait hopefully for a joke that might elicit at least a chuckle, but those moments never arrive.

Have you ever seen the movie *The Ring*? In that film, people watch a cursed videotape and die seven days later. If this movie were on that videotape, viewers would drop dead instantly—likely by their own hands.

Most American war films produced during World War II were highly entertaining but lacked significant realism due to their primary focus on boosting morale at home through propaganda rather than accuracy. While I don’t dismiss these movies—they remain enjoyable to this day—their frequent lack of authenticity prevents them from achieving greatness. A prime example is *Air Force*, the John Garfield film where a single B-17 bomber supposedly decimates half the Japanese air force! In contrast, *Pride of the Marines* stands out as a refreshing departure. It earns high praise for its relatively accurate portrayal of a true story. When I first watched it, I assumed it wasn’t based on reality—it seemed far too implausible. Yet, upon further investigation, I discovered that it was indeed inspired by the remarkable true story of two men who earned the Medal of Honor. In this instance, truth proved stranger than fiction!

I came across this film after reading the book that inspired it. While it isn’t strictly biographical, it takes its cues “loosely” from the facts. Despite this, I found it to be a gripping and haunting examination of evil and madness, with Michel Serrault delivering an unforgettable portrayal of Dr. Petiot.  

The movie is filled with striking visuals; one particularly iconic scene shows Petiot gliding through the night, his black cloak billowing behind him like a vampire. Additionally, the film incorporates elements of expressionism, such as Petiot’s crooked shadow ascending the staircase from the cellar, where the butchered remains of his victims lie waiting to be burned. This moment evokes scenes from *Nosferatu*.  

However, the film’s primary allure for me was auditory. The soundtrack is brimming with ominous sounds, beginning with the unsettling music during the opening credits, accompanied by wordless cries. Petiot operates his medical practice within a building housing numerous small shops, and the soundtrack consistently features the sharp ring of knives being honed in the background, along with a peddler playing eerie melodies on a saw. Animal noises permeate the atmosphere too—there’s the concierge’s goat, unseen cats wailing, and later in the film...

This movie holds no artistic merit and doesn't warrant any awards, nor does it deserve an audience. Surprisingly, one of the awards it was nominated for is for cinematography, but honestly, the camera work is unsettling at best. Each frame feels like your view is being deliberately restricted, as if someone is cropping the scene from the edges without reason. The story is abysmal. To be honest, I couldn't make it through the entire film. The worst part was when I watched the soldiers celebrating in their barracks, with one of them being pressured into drinking alcohol. These scenes, along with several others, reminded me far too much of Steven Seagal's work. 

My advice? Avoid this worthless mess entirely.

To create a film like this, one must be entirely oblivious to Nietzsche's writings and character, psychoanalytic methods, and the history of Vienna. Select a renowned genius whose work you haven’t explored, portray them as insane, introduce erratic doctors attempting to treat them, add a pair of reasonably attractive women, cast an actor with an exaggerated mustache as the protagonist, ensure all characters speak with overly thick accents, depict absurd dreams, throw in another prominent figure unrelated to the first (like Freud), sprinkle in a few phrases from the genius’s texts, and exaggerate every element—especially the soundtrack. And there you have it. Audiences, please avoid this at all costs.

I happen to be the director's nephew. It took me years to obtain a copy of this film, and I can assure you it truly ranks among the worst movies ever made. Even my uncle no longer has a copy (I checked). I’m eager to give him one.

At present, the film holds an average rating of 1.9/10. Based on what I’ve seen, that would place it around the mid-30s on the IMDb "bottom 100," but with only 206 votes, it hasn’t reached that distinction yet.

It’s unfortunate that the film hasn’t even earned the recognition of being part of the bottom 100.

That said, I plan to gift copies of the movie to my family this holiday season. Best or worst gift ever?

Although I was initially hesitant to join the "Lost" fan frenzy, I stumbled upon one episode at the start of Season 1—the polar bear episode—and it captured my full attention from then on. I’m talking about the show, of course—not the polar bear. So humor me as I attempt to articulate my scattered yet heartfelt admiration.

"Lost" begins with a straightforward concept: a group of passengers crashes onto a deserted island after their plane goes down. What sets it apart is how it gradually deepens this premise by delving deeply into each character—uncovering what motivates them, who they truly are, and where their stories began. It quickly becomes apparent that the island serves as a focal point for unresolved issues in their lives. Some characters are running from their pasts (like Sawyer and Kate), while others seek spiritual enlightenment (such as Locke and Claire). Yet, the series doesn’t stop there—it also focuses on the island itself and the eerie mysteries lurking within its boundaries, all of which appear oddly interconnected.

Though TV actors aren’t typically celebrated for their subtlety or acting prowess, the ensemble cast of "Lost" delivers exceptional performances for their roles, skillfully portraying complex emotions and nuances...

I stumbled upon this movie late one Saturday night/Sunday morning while hanging out with my brother. We were already tipsy, and boy, did this film deliver some epic material for mockery! It’s hands down one of the worst movies I’ve ever seen—but in a strangely fascinating way. From the “luxury” ocean liner that looks suspiciously like a roll-on, roll-off ferry (complete with cheap cast-iron everything) to the doors labeled "staff" that inexplicably morph into something else between scenes, this movie is pure gold for nitpickers. The continuity errors are so glaring they practically scream at you, pointing out every plot hole like a relentless teacher. In the final scene, the protagonist leaps off a lifeboat as the ferry looms far behind him. Fast-forward to his son and his new girlfriend—the ship’s PR director, who happens to know kung fu and was mysteriously fired from the police force for doing things her way—and they’re aboard the speeding ferry fleeing an explosion. Next thing you know, Dad shows up out of nowhere, embracing them. HOW?! Who cares? It’s pure cinematic magic. There isn’t a single redeeming quality here. The casino is the size of a small bedroom with just one gaming table. When pursued by villains, there’s literally only ONE place to hide—your brain will finish the sentence before you even think about it.

A series of murders unfolds in a small Texas desert town, leaving the question of responsibility wide open. With only minor twists involving mystery and racial tensions (the latter of which feels out of place), this film primarily caters to slasher enthusiasts, who will likely enjoy its emphasis on gore and nudity—staples of the genre. Dana Kimmell, infamous for her role in *Friday the 13th Part 3*, plays the bratty, quasi-detective teenager at the heart of the story. 

*1/2 out of ****

MPAA Rating: Rated R for strong violence and gore, nudity, and some language.

While it's an R-rated film, I highly doubt you'll enjoy it unless you're a teenager.  

The reason? There’s no substantial plot, no character development, and no genuinely funny jokes. The movie is essentially just packed with nudity—lots and lots of naked or semi-naked women (which, I admit, are quite attractive).  

I don’t get why this movie carries the *American Pie* name because it’s nothing more than a poor mix of an erotic film and a comedy that fails at being either.  

If you're looking to watch this movie, my advice is to do so only if you want to see some nudity but feel too awkward to rent or buy an actual adult film.  

I gave it a 1/10 for the two moments that made me smile throughout the whole experience and another 2/10 for the attractive actresses.

Another cult strikes again. This isn’t a spoiler since the real conclusion lies beyond researching the people behind this overlong, pseudo-scientific infomercial—Ramtha’s School of Enlightenment. Whenever any belief system hides behind an Oz-like veil of deception, I step back.庆幸的是，我是在朋友的推荐下看了借来的版本。要是浪费宝贵的资源在这件新时代的“脑白金”上，那可真是悲剧。我希望他们“真信自己能走钢丝”，并把这种信念推向它的“逻辑”终点——要么成功走过去，要么沉下去……或者干脆闭嘴算了！作为一部电影，它娱乐价值勉强得个“1分”。尤其值得一提的是，它创造了电影史上最令人讨厌的角色（摄影师的室友……可怕！）。如果你非要看这部电影，请从那些被洗脑而推荐的人那里借来看吧。

This early Adam Sandler movie mirrors his comedic persona from 1989, with his character frequently referencing an unrecognized comic genius and expressing frustration over humor-related issues—qualities that seem to stem more from Sandler himself than the script. Compared to his later blockbusters like *Big Daddy* or even *Billy Madison*, this film feels underwhelming. At the time of its release, Sandler hadn’t yet mastered a consistent, effective, or genuinely funny approach, much like the character he plays here. Most of the "jokes" revolve around Sandler talking to himself, typically lamenting his lack of recognition as a comedian or berating himself for being unattractive and single. Watching the film is uncomfortable because it doesn’t take itself seriously—it’s filled with Sandler breaking the fourth wall to address the camera and audience, often poking fun at the film's limited budget or questionable decisions. The result is an awkward, cringe-worthy experience. By the end, I was eager to put it out of my mind, worried that others might discover it and tarnish Sandler’s reputation. Skip this one entirely.

Anyone who can sit through this movie and walk away thinking it’s good simply doesn’t value quality cinema. Watching this film was an insult, with direction and cinematography that felt like they belonged in a high school film class. Even *The Blair Witch Project*, which I loathe, had better cinematography. The story had promise—it could have been intense and compelling—but it failed miserably from the opening moments and throughout its runtime. Some might argue that the film is about a child’s imagination, which is fine in theory, but the script could have been executed much better. Seriously, the scene with the Indian in the store—did the kid just randomly conjure up this entire story about an Indian spirit named Wendigo after looking at a small idol? When they mention this to the store employee, she dismisses it by saying no one else works there. At that point, you think maybe it’s a spooky ghost scenario, but then she casually negotiates the price of the idol, and the whole thing is forgotten. It’s as if the filmmakers didn’t even care whether their own plot made sense.

To all of you who think 1) this telecast was boring or 2) Halle Berry and Denzel Washington didn’t deserve their Oscars, SHUT THE F**K UP!! This was one of the best Academy Awards shows ever. Here’s why:
