1) It was a historic moment for a Black actress—yes, a BLACK ACTRESS—to win the Oscar for Best Actress. So many talented Black actresses have been overlooked by the academy for years. Honestly, I stopped watching the Oscars because there was a serious lack of diversity among winners and nominees. It felt like a bunch of white people congratulating themselves. The academy had numerous opportunities to recognize incredible performances from Black actresses like Alfre Woodard, Whoopi Goldberg, Diana Ross, and Mary J. Bland, but they never did. 

2) Halle Berry absolutely deserved that Oscar. There was no competition. The academy was under immense pressure to finally honor her after so many deserving actresses were consistently ignored. Most of the academy voters are white, and while Nicole Kidman’s performance in *Moulin Rouge* was lovely, it was about time Black performers were given their due recognition at these awards shows. And as for Mr. Washington, the academy owed him BIG TIME after the unfair treatment he received in the past.

If you enjoyed *Deep Cover*, you’ll likely appreciate this film too. Many of the poetic monologues Laurence Fishburne delivers in *Deep Cover* originate from the lyrical screenplay of *"Once In the Life"*, a screen adaptation of a play he penned. If you’re as big a fan of Larry as I am, you’ll adore this film—raw, intense, and deeply immersive. While it features gunplay and illicit substance use, as any gangster movie would, the script is stunning, and the story poignant, leaning into chick-flick territory at times.

This is an AMAZING film—dark, thrilling, sexy, and exhilarating. If you’ve ever felt the thrill of sneaking out at night or bonded with friends in a cramped clubhouse, the confined sets will resonate, symbolizing the claustrophobia of the underworld. Packed with clever foreshadowing and intricate relationships, every detail—from the set design to the cinematography—is deliberate and impactful. Kudos to the filmmakers for creating such a memorable experience!

May 1938: Hitler in Italy, preparing for his historic rendezvous with Mussolini. Emotions, tensions, and acts of self-affirmation ripple through an empty town. A housewife, a journalist, and the silent resonance of two disparate worlds collide. Here lies refuge for a grieving mother, a brief sanctuary for a classical victim. A tale unfolds about solitude, silence, and the hidden crevices of life where desire becomes a form of resistance. The narrative unfolds like a book gifted on a spring afternoon—a poetic film that captures the nuanced hues of everyday loneliness.

This movie is a lament, pleading for an ineffable connection with reality and one’s inner world. Through the looming images of Il Duce, Antonietta’s awkwardness, Gabriele’s quiet patience, and the director’s masterful touch, the film transcends into something sublime. It is a delicate foretaste, a celebration of subtlety and artistry, exploring hypocrisy, arbitrary judgments, and the raw essence of life amidst the repulsion of tyranny.

Loren and Mastroianni deliver performances of profound intelligence, their mastery elevating the story to cinematic greatness. A clear masterpiece, this film is a haunting exploration of the human condition, wrapped in the elegance of poetry.

Despite the numerous negative reviews, I decided to watch this film and was pleasantly surprised by how enjoyable it turned out to be as a horror movie. The acting wasn’t exceptional, except for Alice Krige’s outstanding performance, but some of the lines, like "Just consider yourself lunch," were surprisingly funny. All in all, it’s an above-average Stephen King adaptation, earning a 7/10.

Out there somewhere, surely exists a definitive list of the worst gay films ever made—movies filled with excruciatingly long shots of actors staring vacantly into space or painfully extended scenes of characters watching cats eat spaghetti. This nausea-inducing movie tells the story of two boys who fall in love, swim, and become trapped in underwater caves. One has a depressed mom, the other lacks one entirely. They talk, walk, swim, have sex, drink, break up, and one ends up in the hospital for what feels like forever before getting released. The film is peppered with excessive fast-forward and rewind sequences, interspersed with interminable, brooding shots of one of the protagonists gazing into the void or simply sitting idly. It’s either an intentionally quirky stylistic choice or proof that the filmmakers were desperate to pad out a script so thin it could fit on the back of a napkin. And yet, here I am—a devoted fan who’s now seen my thirtieth gay flick.

If there was any misstep Akira Kurosawa made in creating *Dodes'ka-den*, it was forming a partnership with the "four knights" (Kobayashi, Ichikawa, and Konishiya being the others). Hoping to launch their collaboration with a major box office success, Kurosawa—arguably the leading figure among them—instead delivered an abstract, humanist art film set in a devastated slum. Many of its characters faced grim tragedies, a far cry from the blockbuster they envisioned. Had he worked independently or sought out another studio, the outcome might have been different. However, this decision, along with other financial and creative struggles, contributed to his suicide attempt in 1971. Despite these challenges, as an artist, Kurosawa never wavered in showcasing what made his dramas unforgettable: the resilience of the human spirit in the face of hardship. While the film’s unusual setting may stand out, it is hardly a failing on Kurosawa’s part.

The story of *Dodes'ka-den* is compelling, though not in the ways audiences typically associate with the director. Its focus lies more on character development than on plot progression. There are elements...

As a Pokémon enthusiast, I thoroughly enjoyed this movie. It introduces a new legendary Pokémon, as is typical for each film in the series, while also deepening the connections between its characters. However, I don’t believe those outside the Pokémon fandom will appreciate it (which includes most adults). Some of the dialogue was cringeworthy, but that’s somewhat inevitable when translating from Japanese to English. The animation was visually stunning, though a few scenes appeared subpar. While the villain may come across as cheesy, the movies have consistently featured diverse and evolving antagonists, ensuring not all are alike. To those who didn’t enjoy it, I respect differing opinions, but Pokémon fans will undoubtedly love it.

When an army of derogatory stereotypes—wetbacks, towelheads, and Godless Eastern European communists—amass their forces south of the border, Gary Busey naturally takes them down. Another laughably forgettable relic of Reagan-era cultural attitudes, *Bulletproof* squanders a decent supporting cast led by L.Q. Jones and Thalmus Rasulala.

This is the definitive Lars von Trier film for me, my absolute favorite, and I rate it above "Breaking the Waves" or his more recent "Dancer in the Dark." The sheer beauty of the cinematography takes my breath away—every frame is so uniquely composed. The acting is superb as well. It’s an absolute must-see!

I believe the criticism labeling the show as overly cheesy is somewhat exaggerated. When someone tunes into a TV program, their primary goal is typically to have fun and relax. Unless they’re a professional critic or someone focused on dissecting the narrative, most viewers simply seek entertainment. *Full House* is an excellent choice for unwinding after a long day at work or school. It’s designed to make you laugh, and its charm goes beyond mere humor.

While the Tanner family represents an idealized version of perfection, which may feel unrealistic, it’s important to remember that this is a fictional construct meant to inspire rather than imitate. If such a family were real, it would indeed serve as a worthy example for us to aspire to. However, since this is a television show, there’s nothing inherently wrong with portraying a hypothetical family. The fact that the series ran successfully for years speaks volumes about its widespread appeal, regardless of subsequent critiques.

Another strength of *Full House* is its universal appeal across all age groups. Viewers can enjoy the show while still taking away a lesson—no matter how simple or "childish" it might seem. For instance, Jesse’s...

Forced to endure this adaptation at least 10 times per Christmas over the last two years thanks to my children, I feel justified in critiquing this take on Dr. Seuss's beloved story—and unfortunately, it falls flat. Following in the footsteps of Chuck Jones’s iconic animated TV special is no easy task, but this version is so overly heavy-handed and padded that it becomes tedious. While there are a few clever jokes scattered throughout, the movie feels like a blatant attempt to capitalize on its premise while simultaneously bemoaning the commercialization of Christmas. Jim Carrey, predictably, goes full throttle, but his manic energy clashes horribly with the measured, cunning nature of the Grinch as originally portrayed by Boris Karloff. The original character was a slow-burning force of mischief; Carrey’s performance lacks any subtlety or method, making it the most glaring misstep. Even talented actors like Jeffrey Tambor and Christine Baranski are criminally underutilized. What were you thinking, Universal? Anthony Hopkins may take nearly any role, much like his British counterpart Michael Caine, but this particular casting choice should have raised red flags. This version deserves to be filed away and forgotten.

This was not only the most expensive Canadian film ever shot in British Columbia, but also one of the worst, failing to see the light of day. What's baffling is that the director isn’t even Canadian—he’s British—and it shows. The movie portrays us all as over-sexed drug addicts and imbeciles. The essence of what it means to be Canadian is entirely missing, which is supposedly the justification for funding such drivel. Naturally, the British character comes across as normal, while the rest are reduced to sitcom stereotypes—can we say “Norm!!”? The cinematography oscillates between picturesque postcard-like scenes and murky indoor silhouettes. The actors seem perpetually restless, as if they're as disengaged as the audience—or is this the director's vision of cinema? Skip this mess and explore some of Bruce McDonald’s films instead. A genuine Canadian artist, he has something unique to offer cinematically, and his work won’t leave viewers itching to walk out within the first 10 minutes.

This ranks among the worst films I’ve ever watched. I caught its debut at SXSW, and I was thoroughly let down. The director admitted to knowing very little about John Lennon during the premiere, which didn’t bode well for the film’s authenticity. Intended as a drama, it instead had audiences chuckling throughout due to its overly schmaltzy tone—never a good indicator of quality. The only highlights were Dominic Monaghan and Jason Leonard portraying Livien’s comedic roommates/bandmates; their performances provided some levity in an otherwise overly serious movie. The forced inclusion of Beatles lyrics felt contrived, and the narrative fell flat. On the plus side, the soundtrack was exceptional and stood out as the film’s strongest element. Unless you’re a die-hard Dominic Monaghan fan, this isn’t worth your time.

"Fear of a Black Hat" is an exceptionally well-made film. I found myself laughing almost nonstop from beginning to end. If you have the opportunity, I strongly suggest watching this movie—it’s easily the funniest film I’ve ever had the joy to see. Get ready to laugh!

Why should you dive into the captivating nature documentary "Earth"? How long do you have to spare so I can convince you of its brilliance? Fine, I won’t ramble on forever, but I need to make one thing crystal clear—this is a documentary you simply must watch. Following the migratory journeys of three animal families, the film highlights a resilient female polar bear and her cubs, navigating their icy world while the male bear battles to find food. There’s also a mother whale guiding her calf through an epic journey in search of sustenance, and an elephant matriarch leading her herd across the African plains. Directors Alastair Fothergill and Mark Linfield deliver breathtaking visuals while spotlighting the survival instincts of countless other species. Behind the lens, cinematographers Richard Brooks Burton, Mike Holding, Adam Ravetch, and Andrew Shillabeer capture awe-inspiring natural landscapes and intimate animal behaviors, including those mesmerizing slow-motion sequences of predators in action.

The movie's central theme of romance is well-executed and effectively portrayed. Nonetheless, the context surrounding the love story feels overly sentimental, stylized, and far removed from reality. Worse still, the protagonist's psychological depth is puzzling and difficult to grasp, a flaw that extends to the film's conclusion. If the premise intrigues you, feel free to watch it, but don’t set your expectations too high.

I’m not shocked that cowgirls might feel downcast after watching this film. Uma Thurman’s involvement led me to expect more, which is why I endured this disappointing experience. A terrible movie, with the music being its sole亮点. It’s a pity we can’t rate this 0 out of 10; this film truly deserves it.

This film runs quite long at two hours and twenty minutes, but it covers a significant portion of Pearl Buck's renowned novel. Despite its length, it manages to tackle a lot of ground. While some parts feel overly melodramatic, akin to a soap opera, the movie also features several visually striking moments. One standout scene involves a locust attack near the end, which is visually breathtaking. Given that this film is around 70 years old, the special effects team did an impressive job.

Paul Muni and Luise Rainer, both highly acclaimed actors of their time, deliver strong performances that are hard to fault. However, one issue stands out: the casting choice to have Asians portrayed by Caucasian actors, including Walter Connolly, who doesn’t come across as believable. For the sake of authenticity rather than political correctness, I believe a remake featuring all-Asian actors would enhance the film's credibility and make the storytelling more convincing.

Thomas Clay has been associating with the wrong crowd, which highlights the problem with today’s youth—they lack respect. 

This movie should be avoided at all costs. The action in the main part of the film feels sluggish and heavy-handed, meandering toward its drug-fueled conclusion as though even its director couldn’t find a more interesting destination. We’re introduced to the protagonist, who’s somewhat of an outcast, showing him struggling to fit in at school and at home, feeling uncomfortable in his own skin—something many teenagers experience. Robert gets involved with the wrong group of friends, starts skipping school, experimenting with drugs, and soon enough becomes a psychopathic rapist.

The film essentially revolves around Clay's complete misunderstanding of the connection between violent imagery and violent behavior. He seems to believe that a generation of troubled youths turns evil due to scenes of warfare on television. Yet, he has directed one of the most nauseating pieces of simulated violence ever. Is this guy serious?

Perhaps if Clay hasn’t seen YouTube, he might genuinely be naive or unaware of what audiences will make of the brutal final scene.

In Emily Watson's portrayal of Natalia, she embodies the most loving and romantic leading character I’ve ever encountered on screen. Without question, she reigns supreme as the heart of this film. Or perhaps she transcends traditional gender roles to become the "king" in this narrative? The intricate interplay between the chess games and the familial struggles for dominance, power, and supremacy is nothing short of masterful. Much like the chess grandmasters in the story, the director skillfully plays multiple games with our minds simultaneously, all converging into cohesive patterns—whether major or minor. The film beautifully captures the atmosphere, costumes, and visual motifs of early 20th-century Italy’s lakes region, leaving no detail overlooked or space wasted.

The abundance of memorable scenes is staggering, so much so that watching it twice—perhaps a week apart—would allow you to fully absorb its poetic depth within the confines of its 64-square yet multidimensional framework. 

Though I haven’t read Nabokov’s original novel, this film evokes memories of another romantically triumphant work: Barry Levinson’s *The Natural*. Like that adaptation, this film forgoes a bleak conclusion in favor of a poetic, romantic vision.

This movie apology is utterly meaningless! Rachel Griffiths probably needed the money. It’s clear the film had a tiny budget since the lighting was practically nonexistent. I swear, if I ever encounter Pete Postlethwaite, I might just give up on life. I wonder if there was even a plot or a script. The biggest shame is that I wasted my time watching this nonsense.

Could you describe it as "all shock, no plot"? This movie had countless unexplored paths. Beyond the deaths, there was no backstory provided about the room or why it was malevolent. What turned it evil? What caused its specific nature? And what was the significance of the "one-hour" countdown? Additionally, several elements were teased but never followed through on—for instance, the camera seen in the air vent, which mysteriously vanished when the protagonist checked it out.

Then there’s the curious digital aesthetic of the ghosts and the odd "static flicker" effect whenever objects disappeared mid-air. Taken together, these details suggest Room 1408 might be some kind of futuristic haunted house. Yet, none of this was ever explained or built upon.

Oh, and let’s not forget the bizarre inconsistencies with technology: Electronics fail to function in Room 1408—except for the TV. The cell phone shows no signal, but Wi-Fi works perfectly. How many continuity errors can one film contain?

This movie relied entirely on cheap scares: reflections in mirrors, shadowy figures lurking just out of sight, shifting paintings, bleeding walls, and the classic twist ending where it’s revealed as "just a dream"… or is it? At its core, this film offered nothing new—it was simply one shocking moment after another, lacking any real substance or cohesive narrative.

We came across this movie while flipping through TV channels and decided to watch it with my girlfriend, expecting a heartwarming, family-friendly Christmas tale. Instead, we were thoroughly let down.

The actor portraying the soldier appears completely devoid of emotion. His expression remains static—whether he’s cutting down a Christmas tree, witnessing the woman he loves kissing her boyfriend, or reacting joyfully upon seeing her again. He gives a truly terrible performance, prompting us to laugh at him rather than engage with his character.

Then there’s the blonde protagonist, who seems capable only of counting dots and cheating on her partner. What a charming catch she is! Her life goal apparently involves living with her parents and continuing to count dots. 

In essence, the film revolves around an emotionally vacant man falling for a shallow woman who cheats on her boyfriend. The plot is incredibly predictable, and the entire experience feels like a colossal waste of time. Watching it provides little beyond awkward amusement due to its overly sentimental nature. One particular moment that stood out was when her father jokingly mentioned eating only french fries...

I might just be one of the少数几个who genuinely connected with this film. When it first premiered, I watched it too, and I concur with the previous comment that *Up The Academy* was far ahead of its time. The humor in the movie is straight out of MAD Magazine. I can’t understand why MAD chose to distance themselves from this project. It was also one of the few '80s films to feature an incredible soundtrack, showcasing the emerging punk and new wave bands coming out of LA back then. I own the soundtrack, and I still listen to it all the time. What can I say? There are certainly worse movies out there. *Porky’s* doesn’t strike me as being as funny as *Up The Academy*. The film has its moments, with plenty of good laughs—though the jokes often rely on stereotypes or themes of getting laid. Let’s not expect this to be *The Maltese Falcon*, though.

I’m not a die-hard John Cleese completist (though I thoroughly enjoyed “Fawlty Towers”), but I’m definitely a fan. When I spotted this gem, overlooked and gathering dust on the shelf at my local Blockbuster, I decided to take a chance. What followed was an absolute delight—a hilariously entertaining 50-minute experience that left me thoroughly impressed. The writing leans into classic English “goon show” humor, reminiscent of something you might find on a “Firesign Theater” album. While it works beautifully as an audio sketch, the impeccable execution and flawless timing elevate “Strange Case” into a performance that could inspire a lifelong love for British comedy.

The Brits excel at blending broad satire with nuanced character quirks and precise comedic timing, and the creators skillfully employ both elements here. Cleese’s portrayal of Holmes draws inspiration from the likes of Arkin and Sellers’ Inspector Clouseau, but his natural flair for physical comedy ensures he stands out. However, the true standout is Arthur Lowe, who portrays Watson as an affable yet bewilderingly obtuse simpleton. His impeccable timing and delivery make Watson the highlight of the piece.

Do you recall the early days of Pay-Per-View? I sure do, and I can almost dial up the number we used to call to rent movies on our TV. As a kid, my friends and I were always tempted to order Playboy, but that meant actually picking up the phone and requesting it from PPV. When you finally mustered the courage to do it, you’d end up watching four hours of soft-core, no-angle nonsense. I bring this up because this movie also aired on PPV, and I remember nearly every scene from its trailer. Over the past few years, I’ve made it my mission to track down all the great films I grew up watching, and this was definitely one of them. It’s the kind of movie that’s hard to turn off once it starts. An all-star cast tries to pull off the perfect bank heist, but chaos ensues at every turn. While there are plenty of parody bank caper movies out there, this one deserves to be in that category—it’s packed with action and just the right amount of humor to keep you entertained. Give it a watch if you’re feeling bold!

I mean, seriously. This type of film isn't going to benefit the Australian film industry; it lacks any kind of value. Sure, if you're闲得没事干and don’t mind wasting time, maybe it could be entertaining. But filmmakers here should aim to showcase the incredible talent we have to the rest of the world, and this movie isn't the right way to do that. Honestly, this film is just cheap and tasteless.

To start with, I don’t consider myself an Uwe Boll hater because I don’t think I’ve ever seen one of his films. However, after watching the low-budget mess titled "Seed," which takes its name from the serial killer at the center of the story, I’m nearly ready to join the ranks of the detractors. This movie makes absolutely no sense whatsoever; the plot is laughable, and despite Boll’s obvious attempts to shock viewers, 90% of the film is painfully boring. Here's a brief summary of what unfolds:

1. The killer, who wears a hood, watches real-life footage of animals being tortured on TV, claiming it’s a “statement about humanity” and providing a PETA address. Given that the film lacks any coherent message and is essentially the worst kind of exploitation, you’ll likely despise it from the very first scene.

2. A death scene involving electrocution features a blatantly obvious warning printed on-screen, spoiling key details early on.

3. The police watch disturbing videos of abused animals, starving women, and infants, further emphasizing the gratuitous nature of the film.

John Carpenter's *Halloween* is, without question, a horror masterpiece. It masterfully retells the timeless tale of an escaped mental patient, Michael Myers, who returns to his hometown on Halloween night to terrorize and murder a group of babysitters.

This film stands as the first—and arguably the finest—entry in the *Halloween* series. Carpenter expertly controls the pace of the story, unfolding it slowly while crafting relatable characters, which is rare for a horror film. Even more striking is its lack of blood and gore, yet it remains one of the scariest installments to date. Can you believe it?

*Halloween* launched the career of Jamie Lee Curtis and marked a pivotal moment in the late Donald Pleasance's illustrious career. A true classic.

Last night, while watching this film on video, I continually experienced a sense of excitement, knowing this movie would stand the test of time. I have a feeling I’ll revisit it numerous times over the coming years.

It possesses every enduring quality one could hope for in a story or film. Despite some cultural references being unclear to me, a Western viewer, at its heart lies a universally relatable tale.

Richard C. Sarafian disowned this cinematic disaster, which initially bombed in Japanese theaters before crossing the Pacific to land straight on U.S. video shelves, unseen again until Turner networks needed filler for their early morning infomercial gaps and stumbled upon this forgotten tape. The Smithee credit is typically reserved for instances where a studio ruins a film so thoroughly that the director disassociates themselves from it. However, I fear Sarafian can’t pin all the blame on the studio alone. The cast—mostly fresh out of "Overacting 101"—spouts one cringeworthy line after another. The plot twists and turns into oblivion, while the special effects fail to impress. What isn’t laughable is simply dull. The source material must have been promising—why else would actors like Palance, Matheson, Boyle, and Heston sign on? Yet somehow, the magic vanished between the page and the screen. In short: steer clear. It’s not even so bad it’s entertaining.

In the traditional framework of the four humors—concepts unrelated to humor or entertainment—Altman’s *H.E.A.L.T.H.* humorously and entertainingly embodies them all. There’s Phlegm, embodied by Lauren Bacall’s deliberate, guarded, and protective Esther Brill, whose life seems centered on maintaining appearances, guarding her age and beauty rather than her well-being. Then there’s Paul Dooley’s Choleric Dr. Gil Gainey, who moves frantically like a fish out of water, shouting and rallying the crowd to embrace his aquatic fixation. Glenda Jackson’s melancholic Isabella Garnell channels Shakespeare’s tormented and self-righteous Hamlet, even delivering a soliloquy or two. Don’t overlook Henry Gibson’s Bile character, Bobby Hammer, with his infamous line, “The breast that feeds the baby rules the world.” Meanwhile, James Garner’s Harry Wolff and Carol Burnett’s Gloria Burbank play relatively grounded characters trying to restore balance among the assembled extremes of humor, akin to a World Trade Organization focused on H.E.A.L.T.H.—a term synonymous with everything but actual health.

I was in France around March 5th, and I absolutely love attending film festivals. I had heard about the Cinémas d'Amérique Latine de Toulouse, but I had never been able to attend it. This time, I decided to go, and that’s when I watched *Cero y van 4*.

The movie is incredible. While it didn’t hit me as strongly as it did for Mexican viewers—likely due to the French subtitles—it was still incredibly shocking.

This film is a satire about urban violence, focusing on kidnappings and street crime in Mexico. It offers a raw depiction of the city and its metropolis. *Secuestro Express*, starring the remarkable Mia Maestro, was another satirical take on kidnapping, though with a more serious tone, and I believe there’s some kind of connection between it and *Cero y van 4*. Both tell redemption stories, asking how far one will go. Movies like *Man on Fire*, which was intensely powerful, or *The Brave One* similarly shocked audiences with their unflinching portrayals of life in Mexico’s streets. Like *The Usual Suspects*, this film has unexpected twists and turns, but those make the experience all the more compelling.

Was *Rolling Thunder* the most misogynistic film ever made? And by 1968, shouldn’t filmmakers have stopped using white actors in brownface to portray Native Americans? My favorite moments? When the women giggle and blush as the bikers kidnap them to gang-rape them. Because apparently, rape is a barrel of laughs. Moving on, there’s the obvious借鉴 from *The Hustler*—a portly boss character even plays pool while plotting against the protagonist—and the atrocious performances. The score hits you over the head with its messaging so hard you might as well read a script aloud instead. Oh, and not a single actor in the movie seems remotely Native American. Who are we supposed to root for here? It’s no surprise Quentin Tarantino loves this film, given how much he champions strong female characters in his own work. But apparently, in real life, he’s a misogynistic jerk. So, why did I watch it? Honestly, don’t ask.

SPOILERS  

Jean-Paul Sartre once said, “Hell is other people.” In *The Odd Couple*, Jack Lemmon and Walter Matthau bring this statement to life as they portray two friends who decide to move in together. As Felix Ungar and Oscar Madison, Lemmon and Matthau gradually become increasingly irritated with one another, leading to a series of hilarious moments. Eventually, Felix leaves, leaving Oscar transformed into a cleaner version of himself.  

Lemmon delivers a stellar performance as the neurotic, cleanliness-obsessed divorcé navigating单身生活. Meanwhile, Matthau shines as the slovenly sportswriter focused on earning money for child support through poker.  

Both actors excel in their roles, partly due to Neil Simon’s brilliant script and partly because of their incredible chemistry. Despite their contrasting lifestyles—Ungar meticulous and orderly, Madison messy and carefree—they share common ground in their past relationships with ex-wives and children. This dynamic creates a partnership that feels nearly impossible to replicate, resonating so deeply with audiences that the world couldn’t help but cheer them on.

To start, there’s zero flirting in this film—no romantic tension whatsoever between Anthony or any other character. These individuals simply act without subtlety or charm. Your initial challenge is enduring over 15 minutes of relentless violence and sexual deviance. While I’m no stranger to such content, it lacks meaningful context, making it unsettling rather than engaging. After surviving the brutality, you’re introduced to Donna, and the movie shifts into an entirely different—and not necessarily improved—experience: a hollow road trip narrative. Any comedic attempts, bolstered by cameo appearances, fall flat due to poor writing and hammy performances from actresses like Judy Tenuta and Mink Stole, alongside some stereotypical portrayals of prostitutes and drag queens. It’s all cringe-worthy. The cinematography is deliberately disorienting, which might trigger motion sickness or leave you feeling unwell. Honestly, I can’t imagine who this movie would appeal to, except perhaps fans of poorly made indie films centered around gay and bisexual S&M themes.

What an incredible fall for Sean Ellis.

You gather a group of friends at your place, all eagerly anticipating the follow-up to Sean Ellis's work. With a vague idea of the plot in mind—no spoilers, of course—you head into it with sky-high expectations.

It’s late at night, the perfect ambiance for a film like this.

Fifteen minutes in, you reassure yourself that it will get better. At twenty-five minutes, you’re questioning whether you should just call it quits and save it for another time when you might actually enjoy it. Past the half-hour mark, you notice half your enthusiastic crowd has dozed off, and you decide to wrap things up.

A few days later, after exhausting every other option, you return to it midday, hoping a change of setting will help you stay engaged. Ten minutes in, you’re fast-forwarding through the painfully drawn-out transitional scenes and visuals. Normally, I’d have bailed by now, but the promise of cashback and its legacy keeps me going. Still, even that legacy has its limits.

This may very well be one of the worst films I’ve ever watched. Regardless of what the critics claim, it’s terrible. I believe the issue lies with Kundera’s novel. It’s not impossible to adapt, but much like 99% of his other works, it feels pretentious and overly drawn-out. He seems excessively preoccupied with himself, and his characters appear self-obsessed, while his novels are generally misogynistic. I’ve read numerous of his works, including his Socialist Realist poetry—which was genuinely awful—but I still don’t get the hype. Traits such as self-absorption make his novels frustrating to read. In the film adaptation, all the aspects I dislike about Kundera were amplified. Perhaps I missed something, but I doubt it. By the way, I can’t fathom why this is part of the Criterion Collection. There’s no way this movie is that significant.

Reunion shows come in various forms. One type brings back veteran actors to reprise roles they last played two or three decades ago. The outcomes vary. "Return to Mayberry," while somewhat silly, was passable; "Return to Green Acres" was dreadful (Eddie Albert reportedly used a colorful term for the script, one I won’t repeat, but both the script and the film are undeniably bad). "Rescue from Gilligan's Island," on the other hand, provided closure for fans of the stranded characters, even if the original show itself was absurd by its own standards. Generally, the writing in these reunions is weak, and an overly self-aware humor often undermines their effectiveness. New characters are frequently added without fitting into the original dynamic. Overall, these reunion shows tend to fall flat.

Another category involves the cast setting aside the show’s legacy to share anecdotes, reminisce, and reflect, often accompanied by archival footage from the series. There are also films directly inspired by the shows, which are seldom successful. Additionally, there are documentaries about the shows’ histories, such as those centered around "The Brady Bunch."

I gave *Timecop* a perfect 10, but I’d give this one a 1.  

The story is incredibly boring, and it barely relates to the original *Timecop*. Many elements from the first film were discarded, replaced with pointless new additions. This sequel takes place in 2060 (as far as I can recall), yet for some reason, time travel has become even more dangerous—go figure!  

The action scenes are lackluster, with only the first one being remotely enjoyable. There aren’t many action sequences, and those that exist are brief and forgettable. At one point, the protagonist travels through time around five times in a few minutes… or maybe it was two times—it’s hard to keep track.  

In summary: Skip this movie. It’s not worth your time.

This feels like the kind of movie we think we ought to enjoy, but I didn’t. It appeared to be straining too hard to come across as 'artsy.' Full of style but lacking substance. There are some breathtaking scenes, and each one is pleasant to look at individually, but string them together, and it becomes a challenging experience just to get through the film. I rented it due to the glowing praise on the video box and because I’m a huge Shakespeare fan, but I was thoroughly disappointed. I found it somewhat pretentious and, at times, dull.

Following the rape of his teenage girlfriend by Zebbedy Colt (The Night-Walker), Harry Reems falls into despair and seeks solace in intimate encounters with some lesbians. Meanwhile, Colt, who sports a cane and dresses like a magician, continues his violent assaults on more women. Eventually, Reems resolves to confront and stop Colt's criminal rampage. Despite its grainy 70's porn aesthetic and a mild attempt at grittiness, the film feels amateurishly made. The scenes of abuse and rape are relatively tame compared to what could have been expected, and the film's effort to capitalize on the success of "Death Wish" comes across as silly. R. Bolla ("Cannibal Holocaust") portrays a cop. While Colt typically overacts, his extreme moments feel subdued, which isn't satisfying enough. This exploitation flick could have been far more intense.

D'oh! My Brain Hurts! Honestly, it’s no surprise after enduring this taxing film. I can’t fathom how I resisted hitting the fast-forward button; honestly, only divine intervention could explain it. 

Perhaps it's me—I might be missing the point of the movie or failing to grasp its supposed mystical vibe. But, in my modest opinion, this film feels about as mystical as a visit to McDonald's. 

On top of that, the characters were atrocious, with less depth than a Tom & Jerry cartoon. Ugh! Why do I subject myself to this nonsense? It’s enough to make me want to flee and join a monastery or the Foreign Legion! Argh! This film is abysmal in practically every way. Except for that, it’s not too shabby.

This is an excellent film that I’ve thoroughly enjoyed watching multiple times. Michael Caine delivers another outstanding performance as always. Despite his reputation for accepting diverse roles, regardless of quality, he shines in his portrayal of Sidney. The writing is top-notch from the very beginning. Who would have guessed that Ira Levin, known for chilling works like *The Boys from Brazil* and *Rosemary's Baby*, could craft something so witty? Let’s face it—Michael Caine, Christopher Reeve, Dyan Cannon, Henry Jones… with a cast this talented, directed by Sidney Lumet, it’s hard to go wrong.

I’m hesitant to say too much because revealing anything about the film would be a travesty. Just watch it and let yourself fall in love with it.

Goodness me! It's rare for a "horror" film to both bore me and make me laugh as much as this one does. Starting off with an engaging concept, it quickly devolves into little more than a slasher movie, sprinkled with supernatural and sexual subplots. The typically brilliant Alice Krige is underutilized here, and the plot twists are utterly ridiculous. Save your time unless you're absolutely desperate. Rating: 3/10.

I saw this movie during one of Joe Bob Briggs' broadcasts on Monstervision over at TNT. Even he couldn’t salvage its entertainment value. The only reason I stuck with it until the end was because I teach video production, and I wanted to ensure my students would never produce anything this terrible. Still, it took every ounce of determination I had just to make it through. It’s like watching your great-grandmother flirt with a 15-year-old boy—agonizingly painful. 

If you took the actual film, soaked it in paint thinner, and then tried to watch it, it might actually be more engaging. Honestly. 

If you come across this movie in the bargain bin at S-Mart, step away from it as if it were a rattlesnake.

Sure! Here's the rewritten version:

I don’t typically watch movies by the Farrelly brothers, and I can’t remember ever seeing one before. The same goes for Jimmy Fallon’s films. To be honest, the only Farrelly brothers movie I’ve seen is *Taxi*, but I earned forgiveness for that. However, this film featured Drew Barrymore, and I have to admit—I find her absolutely adorable. There’s just something about her that makes me grin the entire time I’m watching. She has this magnetic quality that draws me in. In fact, I even sat through an Adam Sandler movie just to catch her in *50 First Dates*. Can you believe how obsessed I am? 

This wasn’t your typical baseball movie—it wasn’t meant to be. Instead, it was a heartfelt love story centered around a loyal puppy who clung to the only constant in his life until he found something worth prioritizing more. While the ending was predictable, the journey was full of moments that made it enjoyable.

Embarrassingly, it took me 13 years after its release to watch this movie for the first time. It’s a story that every father or brother will find relatable— one brother is a bit ‘reckless,’ while the other embodies the classic older sibling. Craig Sheffer comes across as slightly too detached as the eldest brother, but Pitt delivers an incredible performance, and Skerritt is perfectly suited to the role of the father. The fishing scenes shot in Montana are absolutely stunning—I had no idea fly fishing could be so captivating. The film stays true to the book, with only minor adjustments made to suit the cinematic format. Unlike most adaptations, this one holds up remarkably well. It’s the ideal movie for anyone seeking a quiet evening with a thought-provoking and emotionally charged film.

This movie features the funniest jokes of all the Cheech & Chong films. It was the first one I watched with these两位演员, and I thought it was really well done. My dad actually suggested I get it. WHAT A GREAT ROLE MODEL! And my grandma even bought it for me, knowing exactly what it was like. Talk about having a supportive family. Anyway, this film is solid and makes for a great rental if you're in the mood for a classic comedy. Just a heads-up—it’s not laugh-out-loud hilarious throughout, though it does have its moments. It’s not as funny as *There’s Something About Mary*, but give it a try anyway. You’ll probably find yourself laughing. Unless you’re some kind of anti-drug activist or something.

Wasting my time on this film left me wondering how the director could face audiences without embarrassment. The idea that anyone would invest resources into such a worthless movie remains baffling to me. When the protagonist died at the end, I couldn't help but laugh—not in a good way. I frequently changed channels throughout the film due to the sheer embarrassment of witnessing such poor acting. I hope the actor who portrayed Heath never works in entertainment again, and I doubly hope the director is barred from making another film. In fact, I think the studio should demand its money back for this mess. {0.02 out of 10}

This film is rather dull, with brief scenes of nudity thrown in as a weak effort to keep viewers engaged, but they fail to make a difference. 

The highlight of the movie is Lena Olin—her portrayal of the character is exceptional, but Daniel Day-Lewis’s delivery is muddled, with many of his lines nearly incomprehensible. 

Clearly, Kaufman lacked a clear vision for filming this story. The transition between domestic marital issues and political crises feels mismatched and poorly executed. Characters' attitudes shift inexplicably throughout, leaving the narrative disjointed and confusing.

I didn’t approach *"Still Crazy"* with much excitement. It seemed like just another rock 'n' roll movie—nostalgia for the baby boomers. While it delivers on that front, it’s so much more than that. Brian Gibson, who previously directed a Tina Turner biopic, proves adept at capturing the essence of this story. Perhaps it’s fitting that this was his final film.

The casting is spot-on. Bill Nighy shines as the band’s charismatic frontman. Bruce Robinson, transitioning from acting to directing, plays the band’s once-great but now washed-up guitarist. His performance is excellent, despite his long hiatus from acting since the 1970s. If you’re searching for a heartfelt and humorous film packed with great music, look no further.

7.4 out of 10

For my 8th birthday, I received the book version of *Kazaam*, and people often claim that book adaptations are superior to their cinematic counterparts, but this instance proved them wrong. At least with the movie, it ends quickly.  

The acting is abysmal, which wasn’t surprising considering Shaq’s involvement as a magical, rapping genie emerging from an old ghetto blaster (likely a result of being stuck in there for a reason). The child actor playing Max is whiny and atrocious, and frankly, I don’t blame the neighborhood kids for bullying him—he’s insufferable.  

The plot is sheer nonsense and painfully clichéd: a boy whose workaholic father rarely spends time with him meets a new “friend” who improves his life and somehow reunites him with his dad. Even at eight years old, I found this concept ridiculous. It’s baffling how anyone involved in this project managed to continue their career afterward, as it’s an absolute disgrace and never should have seen the light of day. There’s so much more I could say about how terrible this movie is, but...

A truly terrible film! It must have been competing against some really糟糕的作品 just to receive a Golden Globe nomination. The filmmakers took the inspiring true story of the first renowned female Renaissance painter and completely distorted it. My issue isn’t that they altered historical facts—had the narrative been compelling, that would have been acceptable. However, this movie is bizarrely dull; the actual events of this artist’s life would have made for a far more engaging film. So why did they opt for such a lifeless script? Perhaps the factual version lacked enough nudity. The film awkwardly wraps up with a rushed summary of the artist's life, leaving viewers wondering why they wasted two hours on something so tedious when brevity would have sufficed.

In reality, it’s practically the same film. They couldn’t even get the timeline of events right. Maybe that was purposeful laziness or indifference. Either way, this is an absolute mess. It doesn’t even deserve to be called a movie. I watched this supposed "second feature" on the disc that included the original *The Boogeyman*, and I thought my head might explode. I implore you to steer clear of this at all costs if you ever encounter it. It should carry a warning label like: *"Caution—may reduce your IQ by several points if you're near it."* For me, there’s no question: this is a resounding 0/10.

In my opinion, this is a rather odd movie with a lot of humor. I wouldn't call it particularly scary, but it's more entertaining, I suppose, especially if you enjoy horror films. It reminded me somewhat of "Children of the Corn," though they're not really similar. Compared to that movie, this one is much more enjoyable to watch! 😊

Alright, alright, calm down. I was just kidding. "Bustin' Out" might actually be a better and more fitting title overall.

Our X-rated animator buddy Ralphie takes aim at racism and crime dramas, giving them a satirical twist. And he pulls it off pretty well here.

In terms of crime, it highlights how they create something, protect it, and eventually lose it due to boredom or stronger competition. Watch it to see the story unfold.

Racist? I’m not so sure. With Scatman (RIP) and the love walrus (also RIP) as black characters and the central perspective, I interpreted it more as a critique of racism. The fact that Richard Pryor loved it speaks volumes too. Plus, seeing the younger Phil Mike Thomas (before "Miami Vice") was a nice bonus.

It’s like an animated "Blaxploitation" film—definitely a positive thing when done right. Some scenes, like the lynching sequence, might make people uncomfortable, but unfortunately, those moments are rooted in reality.

Still, Ralphie really should have reconsidered that title.

I finally got around to watching "Starlight" on TV last night, and my reaction can be summed up in one word: wow! It’s challenging to know where to start — the painfully cheesy special effects (seriously, check out the laser beams shooting out of Willie's eyes!), the dreadful acting, the overly pompous dialogue, the awkward use of stock footage, or the self-important aura that permeates the entire production. This is undoubtedly a singular experience, and for that, we should all be grateful. I hereby crown Jonathon Kay the rightful successor to Ed Wood!

What can I say? I dismissed the reviews and decided to see it for myself. Boy, was I proven wrong—the reviews were spot on. Such a waste of money given its budget. 

Thankfully, I watched *Kill Bill* right after this disaster.

If you're looking for a truly terrifying movie, *Crossroads* takes the prize.

In short, I prefer *Girl in Gold Boots* over this trash.

I wholeheartedly agree with jamrom4. This was hands down the worst movie I’ve ever seen. Seriously, it was atrocious. I was explicitly told not to watch it, but I ignored the advice and regretted it immensely. By the 10-minute mark, I stopped trying to enjoy it entirely and simply endured it out of morbid curiosity, determined to make it to the end. Spoiler alert: I did—and immediately wished I hadn’t. It was grotesque, uneventful, and the ending was unbearably preachy. No movie this bad deserves to exist. To everyone reading this, please avoid "Fatty Drives the Bus" at all costs. If only I’d listened to the warnings! I can’t help but suspect that anyone who rated this positively was somehow connected to its production—and they probably shouldn’t exist either. Save yourselves the misery.

This is my all-time favorite movie. I've watched it at least 10 times, and I cry every single time. My family often begs me not to watch it because they know I'll end up in tears. What I love just as much as the film itself is knowing it's a true story written by Antwone Fisher himself. The acting is exceptional, and each actor perfectly embodies their character. Denzel Washington is one of my favorite actors, and this is easily my favorite performance of his so far. 

I once cared for a little boy who was also born in jail. He was the sweetest child I'd ever met. He's since been adopted by a wonderful family who fought tirelessly for him for nearly two years. While I was watching this movie, the fight for his future was still ongoing, and his fate felt uncertain. I'm overjoyed that he’s safe, loved, and thriving. And I’m equally thrilled that Antwone found happiness and his own family.

I’d love to learn more about him and what life has been like since he reunited with his family. There’s simply no way to express how much I adore this movie!

I’ve never been particularly drawn to Farrah Fawcett… until now. Her performance in this film was genuinely remarkable. The emotional toll she must have endured while filming take after take is almost unimaginable. This movie was incredibly difficult to watch, as its subject matter is deeply unsettling, leaving you feeling powerless as you witness a woman enduring abuse seemingly endless. I found that the tension somewhat dissipated once her friends arrived back at the house, and I found the ending unconvincing. The director clearly had a fascination with incorporating height into his compositions and frequently used mirror reflections, but I believe he could have focused more on maintaining a stronger pace in the film’s latter half. While this undoubtedly works well as a powerful theatrical piece, the movie, despite having merits, ultimately fell short for me.

Don't bother wasting your time, let alone spending money to rent this mess! I’ll never understand how it even got made. (Honestly, I’ve already summed up this terrible film, but what can I do about the 10-line requirement?) The performances were atrocious—every single actor seemed like they needed training. The plot was flimsy, and the ending? Forget it. At least the cinematography wasn’t completely abysmal, though the sound quality was barely passable. On the bright side, if this garbage turned a profit, there’s hope for screenwriters with actual ideas. Take courage, aspiring writers! And actors, too—if these folks got paid, so can you!

POTENTIAL SPOILERS:

This movie was truly dreadful. Touted as a Catholic/superstitious/suspense thriller, it regurgitates themes and ideas that have been explored numerous times in previous films.

A doubting priest, sexual relationships within the priesthood, the intertwining of politics and religion, church hypocrisy, conspiracies involving the institution, the emergence of a new evil era, and epic battles between dark magic and good versus evil—all of these elements are present but feel trite and uninspired.

The plot is weak and predictable. At its core, the story revolves around two central concepts: absolution, or the Sacrament of Anointing the Sick—the final rites offered to cleanse sins before death—and excommunication, which bars someone from receiving absolution. Enter the Sin Eater, and I’ll stop there to avoid further spoilers. Combine all these tired tropes, and you get "The Order."

The sex scene featuring the priest, interspersed with images of the Virgin Mary, came across as deeply disrespectful to Catholic sensibilities. It culminates with Heath Ledger’s character delivering lines like (paraphrased), "I am the judge and savior of sins, living without love," followed by his silhouette walking into the darkness.

HAH! So this is the movie that the "Next Action Stars" were competing for. Well, I’m glad I didn’t participate and didn’t win… 

Isn’t it funny how you can form an opinion about a movie just by looking at the first 10 seconds?! I mean, seriously! Just glance at those titles—enough said! I watched this movie (or more accurately, parts of this “teleplay,” since it was made for TV and we couldn’t bring ourselves to finish it) one evening during my military service. The audience with me was your standard mix of average guys who occasionally tuned into shows like *Las Vegas* just for the eye candy. So the expectations weren’t exactly sky-high. The most-watched movie in our group was *The Girl Next Door*, and not because of its brilliant screenplay (wink). But this movie’s complete lack of originality, acting, scripting, and basically everything else that makes a film enjoyable made it super easy to flip channels to *Las Vegas* (or maybe *CSI*—I don’t even recall) without anyone complaining. Can you believe it? That’s rare! For heaven’s sake, don’t buy this movie! If it’s on TV…

I’m concerned that you’ll discover the vast majority of people giving this movie a rating of 10 are strongly Christian. I am not. If you’re seeking a Christian-themed film, I’d recommend this one. However, if you’re looking for a solid general movie, I regretfully suggest you look elsewhere.

I found the characters and their illogical actions irritating. The film’s premise suggests that teaching morality without attributing it to Jesus as its foundation is flawed. In one scene, the protagonist tells a boy that stealing is wrong and then adds that it was Jesus who established this principle. This struck me as offensive—should we assume “Thou shalt not steal” originated with Jesus? Did he write the Ten Commandments? Was stealing acceptable beforehand? I rented the movie from Netflix, but I should have anticipated its nature based on the reviews. Oh well.

This film is not only entertaining, featuring outstanding comedic performances, but also offers thought-provoking political commentary. Created towards the end of the Soviet Union, it satirizes the Soviet mindset from start to finish. Set during the early days of the USSR, the story challenges the logic of the revolution, examining its cultural and practical implications. By the late 1980s and early 1990s, the rigid structures of Soviet society had softened, yet its ideology and mentality persisted, ripe for dismantling. Fortunately, all this profound philosophical exploration is presented within a humorous and engaging framework!

I absolutely adored this movie! As a dedicated Tom Hanks fan, I’ve always been blown away by his incredible range and talent, from his powerful performances in *Cast Away*, *The Green Mile*, *Saving Private Ryan*, *Forrest Gump*, *Apollo 13*, and *Philadelphia* to his comedic gems in *A League of Their Own*, *Turner and Hooch*, *Catch Me If You Can*, *The Ladykillers*, *Big*, and even *Toy Story*. In this film, though, Hanks isn’t the only standout actor gracing the screen. Tyler Hoechlin, an emerging Hollywood star with immense potential, plays Hanks' son and gives a stellar performance that’s nothing short of exceptional. I’m confident he’ll go on to achieve great things in his career. Paul Newman, as always, delivers a masterful performance, cementing his status as a legendary actor. And let’s not overlook the supporting cast, like the breathtakingly talented Jennifer Jason Leigh, whose unforgettable roles in *Bastard Out of Carolina* and *Single White Female* showcase her brilliance. In this film, she brings elegance and grace to her role as Hank's wife and delivers a remarkable performance.

The movie is simply a blast... possibly even more enjoyable for those of us who were teenagers and fans of "The Ramones" when the film first came out. I’ve watched it countless times, both alone and with friends, and it remains fresh and hilarious. Avoiding excessive seriousness, the idea of being deeply devoted to a particular band is universal, and the monotony of certain high school classes resonates just as strongly today as ever.

The film also boasts some memorable lines and scenes—like the reference to the mythical “permanent record” that supposedly follows you throughout life (spoiler alert: mine hasn’t caught up with me yet). Then there’s the classic exchange about “static” (“I’m getting some static”..."Not as much as you're going to get," says Principal Togar), the frail school board member tended to by nurses, the hall monitor's obsession with conducting “body searches,” and Principal Togar’s dramatic proclamation, “I give you the final solution,” followed by his ceremonial burning of the Ramones records (for context, records were the predecessors to CDs). And, of course, Joey Ramone’s quip, “Things sure have changed since we got kicked out of high school,” swiftly followed by Togar’s retort.

I really enjoyed this show—on Channel 4 in the UK, it aired as the only series available here. The characterizations were spot-on, reminiscent of *The Simpsons* in how they captured all the diverse aspects of small-town life.

There was no laugh track, which was unusual for an American comedy at the time (apart from *Larry Sanders*). This approach worked beautifully, making the eccentric cops feel more authentic and less like they were overacting for the camera.

Overall, it was a charming and quirky gem that struck just the right chord with me. I sometimes wonder if it didn’t quite connect with some viewers. I believe it could have become a cult favorite in the UK if it had been scheduled at a more suitable time.

To wrap up, my usual question: Where can I find this show to watch again? Any suggestions?

It may be hard to believe, but this film drew more denunciations from pulpits than any other movie made before the introduction of the restrictive Hayes Code. In fact, some priests went so far as to declare that watching it amounted to committing a mortal sin.

This isn’t an exaggeration. They had several reasons for their condemnation:

For one thing, Jane unabashedly enjoys sex. In one scene, after waking up in their treetop shelter, she stretches languidly and playfully tells Tarzan, “You’ve been a bad boy!” The implication being that they’ve engaged in not just sex, but unconventional or "kinky" sex. Later, under the Hays Code, such depictions of sexual pleasure—especially for women—were frowned upon.

Another issue was Jane’s preference for the untamed, instinctive Tarzan over the polished, "civilized" Holt. At first, Holt dazzles her with a fancy London dress, and she shows some interest. But when Holt tries—and fails—to kill Tarzan, her loyalty to the jungle and its protector remains unshaken. Once she learns Tarzan is still alive, the allure of civilization fades entirely. Why wouldn’t it? After all, Tarzan...

"THE BRAIN THAT WOULDN'T DIE" was deemed so controversial in 1959 that multiple edits and a delay of three years were necessary before its release in 1962. It’s hard to fathom now how anyone could have taken it seriously even at the time; while lurid and lewd, it’s also absurdly comical in a thoroughly over-the-top manner.

The plot revolves around a doctor with a penchant for experimenting with limb transplants. When his girlfriend meets a tragic end in a car accident, he frantically rushes her severed head to his hidden laboratory. Using some telephone wires, clamps, and something resembling a shallow baking pan, he manages to keep her head alive. However, instead of gratitude, her reaction is pure indignation—especially when she learns that the doctor intends to reattach her head to a new body. 

To complicate matters further, the doctor has specific criteria for the perfect body: he seeks one designed for speed. As a result, he begins stalking disoriented women on urban sidewalks, frequenting strip clubs, attending bodybuilding competitions, and pursuing cheesecake models.

That fleeting, magical moment in life—suspended between the innocent wonder of childhood and the chaotic uncertainty of adulthood—is the heart of this film.

Danni (played with charm by Reese Witherspoon) finds herself at this pivotal juncture as the story begins. At 15, she’s obsessed with Elvis, spins his records on the phonograph, and dreams of romance. Her older sister, Maureen, is即将步入 college, effortlessly attracts attention from boys, and exudes confidence—but beneath her seemingly perfect exterior lies confusion and insecurity. Maureen longs for a decent guy who’ll sweep her off her feet, while her relationship with a local ne’er-do-well proves complicated and dangerous. Meanwhile, Danni, like so many teenagers, feels inadequate, wishing she could trade places with her sister despite her own undeniable beauty.

It’s during a chance encounter with Court Foster that Danni's world begins to shift. Court, whose father recently passed away, has moved into their family’s old farm with his mother and two younger brothers. His arrival sets Danni’s life on a new path, introducing her to challenges and emotions she’s never known.

"Emma" is my favorite Jane Austen novel because Emma, despite her imperfections, is well-intentioned, making readers both forgiving and loving of her. Her relationship with Mr. Knightley is particularly endearing—warm, familiar, respectful, yet playful, creating a romantic excitement that’s both heartwarming and exhilarating. Mr. Knightley embodies the ideal man, while Emma comes across as one of the most independent, intelligent, and self-assured women of her time—despite being just 21, she clearly has the potential to grow beyond her flaws. Who wouldn’t want to be Emma? Or wouldn’t enjoy being gently reprimanded by Mr. Knightley? This version of "Emma," however, completely misses what I adore about the story. I couldn’t even finish watching it—it felt so disappointing. I couldn’t see the kind, patient side of Emma that makes readers love her, like her compassion toward her father or her willingness to prioritize her friend Mrs. Weston’s happiness over her own when she supports Miss Taylor’s marriage. Even Mr. Woodhouse’s character seemed odd instead of charmingly quirky in this adaptation.

I genuinely attempted to enjoy this program. In fact, I even purchased the pilot episode, initially on VHS and later on DVD. Despite my efforts, I struggled to connect with the storyline due to its two central characters: "David" (played by Bruce Willis) and "Maddie" (Cybill Shepherd). For one thing, they appeared overly self-absorbed. While there was indeed some clever dialogue throughout the series, which was undoubtedly a significant factor in its TV success, I found myself appreciating much of that banter. 

In essence, this show resembled the classic screwball comedies of the 1930s and '40s, with its dynamic of male versus female. There were plenty of arguments, accusations, shouting, and screaming. Many people seem to adore this kind of verbal sparring, but it left me cold, so I never became a fan of "Moonlighting."

The only truly enjoyable character for me was Allyce Beasley, who played the hapless assistant "Agnes." It was unfortunate that she had such limited screen time. Shepherd was visually appealing, and I imagine men might say the same about Willis. Nonetheless, the constant bickering between the two ultimately deterred me from fully engaging with the show.

This movie has terrified me ever since the very first time I saw it.  

My mom had watched it on TV back in '92, and I remember being woken up in the middle of the night by her tearful ramblings as my dad helped her up the stairs. She kept saying things like, “Don’t let her get me,” or something similar. I asked what had upset her so much, and she told me she’d been watching *The Woman in Black*.  

Naturally, I had to see it too. Even though I was only eleven, she let me watch it. It scared the living daylights out of me. Ever since then, I haven’t been able to handle horror movies!

This feels less like a film and more like big-budget children’s television. From what I gather, the villain is essentially a massive swarm of chocolate-covered espresso beans. The subtitles seem to confirm this, referring to it as “Insomnia.” Initially, when I heard that an entire civilization had been destroyed by insomnia, I thought, “Wow! A nihilistic martial arts movie!”—but alas, that wasn’t the case. Even considering it experimental cinema when the villain is ultimately killed by an elderly man’s long, white eyebrows doesn’t change things. *Zu Warriors* makes just as little sense with or without the subtitles, which isn’t a great sign. The special effects fall somewhere between Ray Harryhausen’s work and *Xena: Warrior Princess*—primitive, to say the least.

I have always admired Woody Allen and will continue to appreciate much of his earlier work, but even a devoted fan must acknowledge the shortcomings of this film. It is dull, pointless, pretentious, and—above all—poorly acted. A vacuous exercise in self-indulgence built on shaky foundations, it fails to engage or resonate. The decision to create an artificial "Allen clone" in Will Ferrell was a calamitous choice. Attempting to replicate Allen’s mannerisms and style through Ferrell resulted in something laughably absurd. And as for the dialogue, what was meant to pass as philosophical musings devolved into an unintentional parody of intellectual contemplation, completely oblivious to its comedic impact. It's truly disheartening.

This underappreciated film is a slow-paced and relaxed take on the giallo genre, steering clear of many of the genre's clichés in favor of a more casual approach. The story follows a woman searching for her missing lover, a psychiatrist who has vanished inexplicably. Her investigation leads her to a villa inhabited by a quirky group of characters. As expected in a giallo, death lurks around every corner.

The cast is impressive, featuring notable actors such as Adolfo Celi ("Thunderball"), Alida Valli ("Suspiria"), Horst Frank ("Cat o' Nine Tails"), and a young Sybil Danning, known for her roles in 1980s horror films. Leading the film is Rosemary Dexter, whose performance, though unfamiliar to me, is solid and effective.

One of "Eye of the Labyrinth's" standout elements is its music. Unlike most gialli, it boasts a jazz-rock fusion soundtrack composed by Roberto Nicolosi, evoking the style of Miles Davis, particularly his album *In a Silent Way*. This exceptional score adds a unique tone to the film, enhancing its leisurely ambiance and complementing the bright, seaside setting. The blend of jazz and rock perfectly matches the movie's unhurried pace and picturesque locales.

An actor's debut film is typically something you can afford to skip—often, it’s that initial gig where the absence of film experience by everyone involved becomes glaringly apparent, and this movie is no different. 

But worse still, even by 1982 standards, this film is atrocious to the point of being hilariously so. Shot entirely around the Chicago area on what’s clearly a tight budget, the acting across the entire cast feels stiff, wooden, and cartoonish—somewhere between a high school play and subpar community theater. Traffic noise frequently drowns out the dialogue, which is painfully bad, overly declarative in a way that seems forced and convenient rather than authentic and natural. The scenes are awkwardly constructed and disjointed, and despite the characters spanning several years, neither the kids nor the adults appear to age.

I genuinely believe it’s possible to create a Christian film that appeals to a broad, secular audience. However, all too often, filmmakers focus so intently on “The Message” or their personal autobiographical connection to the project that they neglect essential film production values. (I’m sure it’s...)

"The Unborn" is a solid low-budget horror film that taps into fears related to pregnancy. It features strong performances from the reliably talented Brooke Adams and B-movie veteran James Karen, though the supporting cast is somewhat lackluster for its genre. The score, surprisingly composed by Gary Numan, is quite effective. Henry Dominic’s screenplay is commendably smart for this type of film, though it carries a subtle undercurrent of misogyny. Rodman Fender’s direction is competent but unremarkable, and the film includes a few gratuitous cheap thrills. If you’re a fan of Adams, whose career deserves more recognition, it’s worth watching—she delivers her usual出色的 performance.

*The BFG* is among Roald Dahl's most beloved books, yet this animated adaptation falls short of capturing its enchantment. While the film stays largely true to Dahl's original narrative—credit to John Hambley's script—it stumbles due to uninspired animation, a sluggish pace, and uninspiring voice performances. One might anticipate this tale to translate into a cheerful, lively, and entertaining cinematic experience, but instead, the movie proves painfully dull and monotonous. Young viewers unfamiliar with the story would be better served reading the book first; the film risks dissuading them from engaging with what is, in fact, a timeless children's classic.

The story follows young orphan Sophie (voiced by Amanda Root), who resides in an unfriendly orphanage under the harsh rule of Miss Clonkers. One night, while gazing out the window, she spots a towering figure moving surreptitiously through the village. Realizing it has been seen, the giant reaches into the room, plucks Sophie from her bed, and places her in its vast pocket, fleeing into the darkness. Sophie soon learns she’s been taken captive by a giant...

What a travesty...

You neglected to brush your teeth... let’s stretch this into a 30-minute episode where a couple of kids make unnecessary noise, and then the dad delivers one of his trademark lectures, because clearly, that’s the highlight of his existence.

Oh, but don’t miss Uncle Joey adding his bizarre sound effects and goofy facial expressions, or Uncle Jesse sauntering in with his signature black leather jacket and jeans, striking poses while everyone reminisces about how Mother would handle things if she were still around.

Yes, because life’s greatest mysteries revolve around these absurdly trivial moments wrapped in an overstuffed narrative that amounts to absolutely nothing.

*Full House* won’t just put you to sleep—it’ll shave decades off your lifespan with its relentless saccharine overload.

This is one of the most famous films of the French sexual empowerment movement in the 1970s, featuring Gérard Depardieu and Patrick Dewaère in highly sarcastic roles. It is also one of the many dark psychological dramas from the late 1970s and 1980s, alongside "Série Noire," "Buffet froid," and "Beau-père," all directed by Blier. 

That said, I would like to clarify a point regarding a previous comment about the film's title translation. The English title deviates significantly from the French original. While it’s true that the protagonists are "going places," the French title can be literally translated as "the waltz dancers," a metaphor for the movement of the testicles.

Stunning to behold, but imagine this: the instant you uncover Atlantis, what’s the first thing you’d do? Explore it, of course! This was a golden chance to transport viewers to an extraordinary place. Yet, Disney resorted to the same old storytelling formula.

This was the worst movie I’ve ever seen, yet it might just be the best. That’s the magic of original sci-fi films—they’re supposed to be bad, and that’s what makes them so much fun! The line, “I like my dinosaur meat well done!” is possibly the greatest quote in cinematic history. Plus, the plot sounds like it came straight out of a pot-induced dream. Picture this: the writers waking up after a night of getting high and playing Dance Dance Revolution, then tossing together ideas like this: Space marines land on an alien planet teeming with dinosaurs and dotted with medieval-style houses to protect a science team studying the place. It’s the ultimate sci-fi original concept! And it ticks every box on the genre’s checklist: guns, dinosaurs, medieval vibes, space travel, and hilariously bad acting. 

So go watch this movie, but don’t bother buying it.

The lack of likable characters was glaring—the protagonist was an amalgamation of the worst traits from Woody Allen, Paul Provenso, and Reiser. The forced scenes, like the predictable moment with the kid on rollerblades knocking someone over, were simply cringe-worthy.

The film was simple yet incredibly charming. It delicately portrayed the societal issue of gender segregation, which can often be harsh, with a subtle touch. Its bitterness carried a certain poignant humor. The fact that most of the cast were non-professionals added to the movie's authenticity and realism, giving it almost a documentary feel. The most compelling scenes were when the girls, forbidden from watching the match, listened intently as the soldier meant to supervise them broadcasted the game. For Iranians, the familiar cheers and street celebrations after a victory evoke immense national pride. But even for those who aren’t Iranian, the experience remains equally enjoyable.

As the celebration of Christmas has changed over the years, regardless of whether one focuses on religious or secular traditions, it is a time when people are expected to treat each other with a bit more kindness. Somehow, this idea has eluded Ebenezer Scrooge, a 19th-century London merchant and moneylender.

His nephew points out to Scrooge that he doesn’t celebrate Christmas at all, as Scrooge views the entire affair as nonsense. Scrooge’s humanity seems to have vanished long ago; he is stubborn and unyielding—a character very similar to Mr. Potter from 20th-century Bedford Falls.

Yet, as Charles Dickens recounted this story, redemption remains possible for everyone. A lonely ghost and three spirits appear to Scrooge, showing him the path forward.

_A Christmas Carol_ is such an enduring holiday classic that we sometimes overlook its role as a social critique of 19th-century Britain, just like _Oliver Twist_. The characters in this film represent the middle and lower classes. The Cratchits are a step above the street folk in _Oliver Twist_, yet they still struggle to maintain their position.

This film is impeccably crafted! From the set design and lighting to the sound and storyline, there are no flaws. The script invites viewers to engage in a intricate game with characters on a straightforward mission. 

Paxton delivers a standout performance in this role, his every gesture and inflection flawlessly executed. Every scene is meticulously composed. As the movie progresses beyond its first hour, unexpected twists unfold one after another. While it may not be the best film of the year, it’s a finely polished gem, not meant for those with simpler tastes.

Growing up, my babysitter was a big fan of "Scooby-Doo," so I ended up watching many of the older episodes. Oddly enough, I never considered myself a fan, yet I left the TV on when this series premiered. Much to my surprise, I found it entertaining. For me, Shaggy and Scooby have always been the most compelling characters—sorry if that throws shade at the other fans! It’s refreshing that this show zeroes in on just those two. That said, it might rub devoted fans of the originals the wrong way. The voice acting is solid; I particularly enjoy Dr. Phinius Phibes, whose performance I appreciated even before discovering it was Jeff Bennett. Jim Meskimen brings a lot of fun to his role as Robi, clearly relishing every moment. I also find the techie duo amusing, with their quirky personalities and obsessions like playing pretend versions of Dungeons & Dragons or enacting scenes from "Star Wars" (though they’re never named as such in the show).

"The Crush" is a reasonably enjoyable romantic comedy aimed at adult audiences for the first two-thirds of its runtime, attempting to capture the spirit of a British "Sex and the City." 

I found the transformation of the attractive young man, whose character isn’t deeply explored, to be particularly engaging. Thinking back, we didn’t actually see much of his physique either, but Kenny Doughty is certainly worth watching more often. 

It's interesting how this film places a significant emphasis on younger men being paired with older women, unlike either version of "Sabrina," which I didn’t care for, or the pairings in "Douglas/Zeta-Jones" or "Dion/Svengali." 

Andie MacDowell’s expat character is surrounded by familiar faces from British dramas and comedies, including the sharp-tongued Anna Chancellor. 

As the story progresses toward its conclusion, the plot twists seem overly convenient, almost like a deus ex machina. It wasn’t until the credits rolled that I realized what might truly be amiss. Much like "Sex and the City," the writer and director of "The Crush," first-timer Scot John McKay, seems to have originally intended to write a script about three gay men, likely focusing on their journey of coming out.

I initially watched this movie on MST3K, and while I found myself laughing uncontrollably at the jokes, I don't think the film was as terrible as some might claim. Admittedly, it’s somewhat challenging to follow due to its low-budget nature, but it boasts a plot reminiscent of Hitchcock's work. In fact, when I later saw the unmocked version, I was genuinely entertained. This movie really deserves a Hollywood remake.

"Redline" is a blatant rip-off of "Fast & Furious" without any of the charm or appeal. It doesn’t need a complex, twist-filled plot, but it does need *something* to make it watchable. This is like a porn film where the story and dialogue amount to just 60 seconds at the start and another 60 at the end. Worse still, unlike a porn film, this offers no entertainment value. It’s mind-numbingly dull, features unrealistic race sequences, and squanders expensive, beautiful cars, which somehow manage to earn negative points for their involvement. Yes, the lead actress is attractive, but is anyone really that desperate for a token on-screen female presence? It feels as though the director used a hat filled with random lines of dialogue and plot snippets, consulting an eight-ball each time they changed scenes. No one serious about racing or knowledgeable about the subject could possibly enjoy the race scenes in this film.
