Kirstie Alley appears slightly slimmer in this film, though only marginally so, alongside a man who bears a striking resemblance to a younger MacGyver, complete with bleached-blond hair. The movie’s premise revolves around an older woman (yes, 50 years old!) struggling to get her screenplay produced because of ageism. She enlists her younger nephew to pose as the author instead. This concept isn’t particularly fresh, and the execution leaves much to be desired, featuring subpar acting, uninspired dialogue, and an absurd storyline. Another subplot involves a writer harboring affection for Kirstie’s character, a narrative inclusion that feels inexplicable. The actor playing Kirstie’s brother delivers such a stiff, ill-fitting performance that their scenes were painful to watch. What can be said about this film? Simply avoid it.

This is quite possibly the worst movie I have ever seen. Once again, I made the mistake of purchasing it because the synopsis on the back sounded intriguing, and the front cover looked appealing as well (after buying this film and "Malevolence," which I also reviewed here, I’ve since sworn off judging by covers). I enjoy horror movies set in the woods, desert, or on farms, so I was excited when this one claimed to take place in the woods of Texas. However, it probably wasn’t filmed any farther than the director’s backyard. The production quality was among the worst I’ve ever encountered. The acting was atrocious—absolutely the worst I’ve seen in a film. The story bore no resemblance to what was described on the back cover. When I tried to sell it to F.Y.E. and a local used DVD store, neither would accept it. That’s how terrible this movie truly was. I’ve seen some bad films before, like "Troll 2," but this surpasses them all. I never thought there could be a worse movie than "Troll 2"—boy, was I wrong! Do not buy this movie unless someone gives it to you for free, and even then, proceed with caution.

This visually innovative game unfolds as "a story within a story." The central character, scriptwriter Bart Klever, grapples persistently with his new text, which also functions as the screenplay of the film being watched. As Bart演绎s this role, his battle with the text emerges as a narrative theme, intertwined with the domestic setting of the flat where he works and cares for his young daughter. The intimate atmosphere provides fertile ground for illusions crafted through spatial manipulation, shifting light, color play, and even interactions with a pair of cats. The seemingly straightforward confines of the room grow more complex due to the fluid dimensions of the text, displayed on a computer screen and serving as a counterbalance to the ever-changing environment. The frequent shifts in perspective complicate responses to probing questions: What defines "truth" versus "illusion"? Which world holds precedence among those depicted? Is there any stable point to anchor the narrative space?

The film is cheap-looking and unattractive, failing even to engage the children in the audience, save for a mildly amusing toilet joke. Christopher Lloyd, while past his prime, feels particularly tiresome in this role, and the weak attempts at humor from the writers do little to help. Elizabeth Hurley delivers an embarrassingly amateur performance in what was intended as a comedic role. In contrast, Jeff Daniels and Darryl Hannah manage to escape humiliation. There’s no compelling reason to watch this movie, particularly when it invites inevitable comparisons to Robin Williams' inventive and often brilliant work on *Mork & Mindy*.

This was everything this isn’t: it had energy, flair, and actors unafraid to go big. It also boasted a decent script. This version left me puzzled. If Farrah wasn’t serious about a long-term acting career, why did she even have a manager—and why would he bother? And if Kate and Barney are supposed to be artists, why would they agree to join a show as absurdly gratuitous as *The Mother of All Jiggle Shows* (like the “Brady Bunch” movie, where Robert Reed tries to do Shakespeare, only to end up on the “Brady Bunch”)? They may not have been A-listers, but they weren’t struggling, either. Plus, the timeline gets wonky—Silverman rejecting pitches for *Funniest Home Videos* and *American Idol*, and Spelling promising his daughter Tori that he’d create a show for her, clearly didn’t happen.

What frustrated me most was how Spelling’s role was misrepresented. He’s portrayed as both the creator and showrunner, despite being neither. His alleged “inspiration” for *Charlie’s Angels* is laughable!

How could Spelling and Goldberg enforce an oral contract with Farrah when everyone else signed official deals? And why didn’t Farrah or Bernstein speak up?

This film, released in 1999, actually boasts fairly solid production values. The actors are appealing and display a reasonable level of talent. There’s no chaotic scene of clowns firing wildly without ever hitting anyone, nor are there excessive car chases resulting in the destruction of expensive vehicles. 

The interior sets appear contemporary and architecturally respectable, and the equipment looks credible enough—though the high-tech computer room does feature what appear to be relics from a 1950s electronics lab. And let’s talk about the “corpse makeup,” which resembles dried pancake batter smeared over their skin, meant to suggest calcification due to the virus. How this transformation occurs is left as an intellectual exercise for the viewer.

Speaking of the virus, I wish I could assure you it’s one of the better premises for a sci-fi/horror movie, but alas, it’s not. A computer virus transmitted through a TV or computer screen that mutates into a deadly biological pathogen? Really? As if warp drives weren’t far-fetched enough...

This movie stands out for three key reasons. First, it's visually stunning. I absolutely adored its aesthetic appeal, thanks to a bold color palette, striking costumes, and beautifully designed sets. Even though the cinematography appears lavish, it likely didn't come with a hefty price tag. Second, the story revolves around a group of misfits or loners forming a makeshift family—a trope that often falls into clichés, but this film avoids that pitfall. The ensemble delivers strong performances, portraying flawed yet highly likable characters. Alan Larkin shines brightest, and his presence, combined with the van and the road movie vibe, reminded me of "Little Miss Sunshine," my favorite film from last year. I also discovered Fabrizio Bentivoglio, whose acting was intriguing, while Til Schweiger occasionally grated on me. The opening scene and moments when their magic tricks go awry are hilariously entertaining. The film balances humor and emotion seamlessly, culminating in a satisfying ending. Ultimately, the magic theme ties everything together—just like a skilled magician, the film directs your attention where it needs to go to create its own illusions.

The title alone speaks volumes. I saw this movie with my dad when it first came out, and given his service in Korea, he held great respect for the subject of the film. What’s disappointing is that it focuses solely on a brief segment of the man’s life—a life so extraordinary that his entire story could have been an unparalleled biopic, making the film’s production costs unimaginably steep.

Some reviews touch on the subject’s flaws, but these criticisms feel like unnecessary jabs. The film’s central theme—“Duty, Honor, Country”—isn’t just empty rhetoric recited by a ceremonial figure; it’s a profound testament to one man’s unwavering commitment to his nation.

Interestingly, Gregory Peck, despite being a known liberal, seemed to grasp the subject more deeply than many. He portrays the general as both fearless and deeply humane, delivering a performance that captures the complexity of the character.

This is a clever film that explores love across different eras. It follows Buster Keaton as he pursues a ladylove in the Stone Age, ancient Rome, and the present day (1920s). In each setting, Keaton plays the typical hapless character, competing with Wallace Beery for his love interest. Among the three timelines, I found the Roman segment to be my favorite, despite acknowledging that it might have been the most kitschy. I was particularly amused by the scenes involving the lion, which was clearly a man in a costume, and the bizarre chariot race set in the snow. What truly stood out to me, however, was witnessing Keaton’s incredible acrobatics. All three eras offered lighthearted fun, and although this isn’t Keaton’s finest work, it remains a remarkable and enjoyable film. Give it a watch!

Jordan, I hate to say it, but the acting was terrible. A movie is in trouble when its lead can’t deliver convincing performances. The script and plot weren’t strong enough to save it either. I also found the character of Pamela to be underwhelming—bordering on pitiful.

Despite those issues, there were a couple of decent performances, particularly from Spencer, Hollywood, and Ronnie. Unfortunately, they weren’t enough to salvage the film.

1) How Spencer’s character could possibly fall for hers. Gross. I checked the ages and while he’s only about four years older than her in real life, their chemistry in *Go Figure* felt off. Jordan is attractive, but in *GF*, she seemed...

I’ll leave it there.

I might be giving this movie more credit than it deserves, simply because it’s Halloween, I’ve just come from “Knott’s Scary Farm,” and I was in the mood for a super cheesy horror flick. Plus, it only cost me a dollar. 

Normally, I’d fast-forward through something like this to get to the “good parts,” but I resisted the urge this time—and I’m still not sure why. From the very first scenes, it was clear this wasn’t a proper movie, not even a B-movie. It felt more like a DeCoteau-style “horror” film, shot on cheap video that looks like film, made for about fifty cents. In fact, I half expected one of his beefy college guys to stumble out at any moment, rubbing himself awkwardly in his underwear or something. There were no fancy cutaways—too expensive to set up multiple cameras—and the lighting was flat, but… it’s hard to put my finger on it. There’s something refreshing about watching a director with no budget manage to make a halfway decent movie. Kudos to him for trying, and despite its flaws, this film does have its merits—the acting isn’t bad, the cinematography is actually pretty good (though way too bright to be truly scary), and there are…

Sidney Franklin's *The Good Earth* has earned its place as a classic due to its enduring narrative and exceptional performances, particularly from Luise Rainer, who won an Academy Award for her portrayal of O-Lan. Rainer's performance is so immersive that she becomes nearly unrecognizable. With minimal dialogue throughout the lengthy film, she conveys emotion through nuanced facial expressions and body language, embodying the character so convincingly that viewers unfamiliar with her work might easily mistake her for Chinese.

The film retains its relevance today by exploring the timeless rags-to-riches tale and the universal themes accompanying it. After years of famine and poverty, Lung and his wife O-Lan attain financial prosperity, only to discover that wealth brings possessions but lacks true meaning. Their fulfillment returns only when they reconnect with the land following a locust invasion, whose stunning special effects remain impressive even by modern standards. The film’s common storyline, viewed through the unique lens of a Chinese family (especially notable for 1937), cements its status as a classic. It masterfully underscores the idea that money holds no value without friendship and family.

The notion that this movie is bad is absurd. In reality, it's the finest film I've ever watched. The storyline is outstanding, and the cast delivers some of the most impressive performances. I have no criticisms for any of the actors. This movie is unparalleled and will remain so forever.

Busy Phillips delivered an outstanding performance, blending comedy and drama seamlessly. While Erika Christensen gave a solid performance, Busy truly stole the spotlight. This film served as a refreshing follow-up to "The Smokers," which, despite its shortcomings, showcased Busy's talent. If Busy isn't recognized for this role, it would be a major oversight. Skip "Mona Lisa Smile" and check out "Home Room" instead.

Well, I dislike Hollywood but enjoy cinema, so I feel compelled to watch these mediocre films in theaters. I was hoping *Vanilla Sky* would be good. I thought they might either stick closely to the original *Open Your Eyes* or put their own spin on it. Unfortunately, it ended up being a mix of both—and it fell flat.

It started well. I love Radiohead, and I wished there had been more of their music. But by the end, we were subjected to *Good Vibrations* by The Beach Boys. Talk about a massive tonal shift! They included one or two decent tracks in the club scenes and maybe a couple more, but why on earth did they have to play *Good Vibrations* during the climax? It was more annoying than confusing or heavy-handed. Especially since it had absolutely no connection to the plot. At least try to give the music some meaning. Radiohead’s *Kid A* felt far more fitting as the core soundtrack.

The club scene was decent, but that was about it. Otherwise, the film was one big exercise in self-importance. As if the audience would somehow magically "get" the movie. Those who do understand foreign films probably read subtitles, while everyone else...

When the United States joined World War I, the government compelled Hollywood to produce propaganda films. Among these, *The Little American* stands out as perhaps the finest due to its star, Mary Pickford.

In the film, Pickford portrays a young woman caught between two suitors: Jack Holt (portraying a German) and Raymond Hatton (representing a Frenchman). Her choice is postponed due to the war, as both men join the military.

After the ship Pickford is traveling on is torpedoed by the Germans (a nod to the *Lusitania*) for transporting munitions, Pickford delivers a memorable performance as she stands in a lifeboat, shouting at the German commander. Later, she encounters both Holt and Hatton while being held as a war prisoner in a château.

Director Cecil B. DeMille includes one particularly striking scene in the movie when Pickford and Holt wander through a devastated village. Passing a ruined church where only one wall remains standing, they see a massive crucifix against the wall. As they observe, the wall crumbles, yet the Jesus figure stays suspended in midair—a hauntingly surreal moment amidst an otherwise direct and unsophisticated film.

Mary Pickford shines as usual, proving her prowess...

I watched this film on DVD last night and decided to read some reviews this morning. "I, Robot" appears to have deeply divided critics on IMDb, leading to plenty of harsh comments and insults. 

This surprises me somewhat, as the movie isn’t great or even particularly good, nor is it truly awful or terrible. Instead, it’s... disheartening. It’s disheartening to see how readily U.S. moviegoers embrace shallow, cliché-ridden remakes and hail them as groundbreaking new works. From its plot—a jumbled mix of Asimov and over-the-top modern action—to Smith’s character—a wisecracking, cynical hero with unshakable resolve, and even the special effects—borrowed liberally from *The Matrix* and other films—this movie feels like a collection of tired tropes.

Sadly, "I, Robot" might just be the ideal action flick for today’s audiences: a superficial storyline, trite and snappy dialogue, and an abundance of adrenaline. Smith gives a forgettable performance, though we already knew that—he seems to be Hollywood’s latest effort to mold a black Bruce Willis. The story is riddled with plot holes, big and small, but I doubt many viewers will notice.

In Bridgeport, high school teacher Richard Fenton (Johnathon Schaech) becomes obsessed with his teenage student Donna Keppel (Brittany Snow). After witnessing him murder her family so he can stay close to her, Donna is traumatized, though Richard is arrested and sentenced to life in prison. Three years later, Donna is recovering but remains under psychological care and medication. On prom night, she goes to the Pacific Grad Hotel with her boyfriend Bobby (Scott Porter) and a few friends. However, Richard, who has escaped from prison, is also staying on the same floor, hunting Donna while killing her friends and anyone else who crosses his path.

The forgettable slasher film "Prom Night" is a regurgitation of clichés with no originality. The nonsensical plot is shallow and absurd, featuring subpar performances, especially Johnathon Schaech as the deranged villain. The predictability of the script is staggering, as viewers can easily anticipate every twist. I give it a 3 out of 10.  

*Title (in Brazil): "A Morte Convida Para Dançar" ("The Death Invites to Dance").*

This has to be one of the worst films I’ve come across in quite some time. 

Heath Ledger as a heartthrob? Hardly. He appeared deformed, at least to me. If I had known he was dating Naomi Watts in real life, I would have wondered even more about what she saw in him during these two excruciatingly long hours. 

Orlando Bloom? A heartthrob? His scruffy beard and deer-in-the-headlights expression left me unconvinced. 

Rachel Griffiths delivered her usual stellar performance, but Geoffrey Rush seemed like he was eager to wrap up filming. 

I’m supposed to sympathize with bank robbers and murderers? This movie is a world away from *Butch Cassidy*, which was actually enjoyable. This film felt clichéd, bland, and painfully dull. We stuck around hoping it would improve, but it never did. 

The final 10-15 minutes were unintentionally amusing. Heath’s character and his gang were trapped in a frontier hotel, where civilians were suffering due to their actions. That scene wasn’t meant to be funny, but it was when they emerged wearing armor—it just reminded us of the *Black Knight* scene from *Monty Python and the Holy Grail*.

This film didn't resonate with me at all. It failed to capture my interest intellectually, emotionally, or aesthetically. The dialogue felt heavy and disengaging. I struggled to form a connection with any of the characters, and I find it difficult to highlight anything positive about the movie. 

I’ve read that understanding it fully requires familiarity with certain obscure elements of Catholic theology. As an atheist, I acknowledge that I may lack insight into some of the nuances of Catholicism. However, I’ve watched numerous films addressing religious themes that moved me deeply because their messages are universally relatable and don’t depend on specialized knowledge or beliefs.

"The Bourne Ultimatum" kicks off with reckless intensity in the middle of a high-stakes chase and doesn’t let up, hurtling forward with relentless momentum. Jason Bourne (Matt Damon, delivering another outstanding performance) races against time to uncover the architects of the CIA’s clandestine operations, which transformed him into the ultimate assassin, while also seeking answers about his true identity. Adding a chilling presence to the mix is David Strathairn as the enigmatic "man behind the curtain," joining returning favorites like Joan Allen (who gives an excellent performance) and Julia Stiles (whose role feels disappointingly underutilized).

Much like its predecessor, I found myself wishing director Paul Greengrass would稳住那摇晃的手持摄影机至少在几段安静的场景中。然而，不可否认的是，这种手法完美捕捉了近距离肉搏战的紧张与压抑感，同时也为追逐戏增色不少——无论是徒步奔跑还是跨越屋顶，甚至偶尔还有壮观的大规模车祸场面。《伯恩系列》的乐趣之一就在于其不断的世界穿梭以及对科技和通讯手段的巧妙运用，这些设定仿佛超越了物理法则与现实限制，构建出一种充满科技魔幻色彩的硬核超现实世界。令人费解的是，故事中似乎总有人能恰好出现在最恰当的位置……

This cartoon was unusual, yet its story held more depth and emotion compared to many other animated films. It follows a girl at summer camp struggling with low self-esteem and having few friends, except for a brother and sister who are equally downtrodden. She hits rock bottom, and when an opportunity presents itself, she essentially makes a deal with a demon-like entity. I found the film refreshingly realistic. Just when things seem bleakest, the girl realizes her mistake, feels genuine regret, transforms, and even helps this mysterious, dark creature understand the human concept of love. The twins also grow, aiding little bears and gaining self-worth in the process. Despite some odd elements, it’s a surprisingly uplifting message for kids, and overall, an enjoyable movie. Stephen Bishop’s music, known for songs like those from *Tootsie*, added extra charm to the film.

This is the kind of movie you'd enjoy sipping a glass of wine to, with the fire lit and your feet up. It’s not taxing on the brain, making it perfect after a long day. While it's highly unrealistic, it’s also quite humorous. The idea of a businessman willingly living in a slum just to experience something different, and then actually enjoying it, is absurdly funny. If you’re looking for light entertainment, I’d definitely recommend this film.

There’s no doubt that Ealing comedies are exceptional, but for me, this film shines as one of the finest. 

The story revolves around a small section of Pimlico in London discovering it belongs to Burgundy, not the UK. As the residents navigate their newfound status, they face challenges like guarding treasures uncovered after a bomb explosion while fending off opportunistic black marketeers who exploit the area’s exemption from UK laws, including rationing. When the government decides to封锁 the border, confining them to their own street, they push back against authority.

Forced to ration water and food during their fight for justice, they find themselves worse off than before. This moment underscores the moral lesson: when they lose all their supplies and consider surrendering, the entire city of London rallies to their aid, delivering an overwhelming amount of food. This helps them persist in their cause.

The film strikes just the right tone throughout, with outstanding performances from the cast.

I recall being five years old and thinking I was watching just a regular cartoon movie—until the bras and bullets started flying. This film has the potential to upset literally anyone and everyone due to its divisive nature, but it’s undeniably hilarious while also tackling deeper themes. I recommend it for fans of cult classics. Check out *Fritz the Cat* and *The Nine Lives of Fritz the Cat* as well; if I’m not mistaken, Ralph Bakshi directed those too. It’s about a cat navigating life’s challenges, from family issues to street life and jobs. Once I was older, I rented all these films. *Coonskin*, which had an offensive title back then, was also known as *Street Fighter*. Bakshi also directed *Cool World*, featuring a young Brad Pitt. Another notable work is *Heavy Traffic*, a cartoon that explores the gritty realities of urban life for a young man.

The soundtrack features drones, ethnic drumming, poorly played synthesizers, children's singing—everything you'd expect from the most condescending "world music" imaginable. This is clearly a tourist film, and not a very good one at that. Its biggest flaw lies in its jarring, disjointed sequences. One moment we're in India, then Egypt, followed by South America and Africa, with no transitions or visual explanations for these abrupt jumps across continents. There’s no coherent narrative conveyed through imagery, just random footage of people from the Global South, as another reviewer noted, portrayed as caricatures with "baskets on their heads," walking endlessly as though it carried some profound significance. If the filmmakers had intended to create a Third World music video, they could have simply headed south of where the better parts of *Koya* were filmed and captured scenes in Mexico instead. That would have provided a far more authentic setting for "life in transformation." 

But no. Instead, they chose a haphazard travel itinerary spanning half the globe, complete with tiresome, overused filter effects. The only faint praise this film deserves is that it doesn't fall as flat as *Naqoyqatsi*.

Allow me to begin by saying that I generally appreciate Renny Harlin’s directorial style, and the cinematographer deserves credit for some of the film’s visuals. Unlike his work on “A Nightmare on Elm Street 4” and “Die Hard 2,” which I thoroughly enjoyed, something feels off in this movie. Unfortunately, that "something" is entirely absent—and it's a script. The dialogue in films like this is often subpar, but this one takes the prize for sheer idiocy. There are countless cringe-worthy lines, and I’d rather not even recall any of them. On top of that, the delivery is woefully poor, bordering on laughable, as if it were written for a low-budget adult film rather than an action-adventure flick. It’s almost as though Harlin believed slowing down the dialogue would somehow elevate the writing. Alas, no dice.

What’s truly disheartening is the presence of talented actors stuck in poorly written roles. While Sylvester Stallone has never been my personal favorite, it’s concerning that he outshines Lithgow, Turner, and particularly Rooker in terms of performance. Lithgow delivered one of cinema’s greatest villains in “Ricochet,” yet...

Lessons from "The List":  

A talented cinematographer, a attractive actress, and Malcom McDowell couldn’t save this film from being terrible.  

Blockbuster won’t refund your money.  

Even after reading the script and groaning, “Ugh! Really?!", Malcom McDowell still gives it his all.  

Chuck Carrington clearly needs acting lessons.  

Hire a proper screenwriter.  

Jesus apparently holds a grudge and punished me by forcing me to spend $5.50 to watch this movie.  

When creating a movie, skip the ending. Leave everything unexplained, unresolved, and dull enough for the audience to doze off before the finale. Masterful.  

Apparently, any random landlord can resurrect the dead with a simple cross drawn on a window—so befriend them.  

Your housekeeper might have hidden vocal talents capable of reviving you.  

Chuck Carrington *still* needs acting lessons.  

Your roommate will despise you and mock you if you bring home this movie.  

Apologies won’t cut it.

Cheesy '70s horror films… you just can’t help but love them. Unlike today’s monotonous slasher movies, these low-budget gems actually manage to be genuinely frightening instead of relying on stale formulas. 

This is a B-movie about the making of another B-movie—one that takes a dark turn for the worse. Faith Domergue (known from *This Island Earth*) stars as a fading B-movie actress playing the lead role in a film based on a series of grisly murders that occurred within a family home. Her self-absorbed director boyfriend, who resembles a surlier version of Gordon Jump, is shooting on-location with an unyielding deadline. The handsome co-star stumbles upon a book of Tibetan chants and incorporates them into the script to lend authenticity—though this “authenticity” proves to be anything but welcome.

Meanwhile, John Carradine, no longer searching for the mythical 17th gland (*The Unearthly*), plays the caretaker of the estate where they’re filming. He goes about his routine tasks but keeps running afoul of the demanding director.

The tension mounts gradually: a dead cat here, Carradine investigating a crypt there, ultimately culminating in a shocking total of seven murders. (At least the filmmakers delivered on their promise.) What’s unfortunate is that the supernatural forces unleashed seem unaware—or indifferent—to how predictable and clichéd the human drama has become.

Does anyone know what type of pickup truck John T. drove in the movie? It appears to be a mid-to-late 1970s Ford. This film is one of my favorites, as well as my wife’s. It was the first memorable movie we watched as a married couple. The pickup truck is particularly interesting because it resembles the first truck I ever drove, and I recently found another similar one. I’d like to restore the pickup I own to look like the one in the movie. Additionally, the music was fantastic, and the acting was superb. Whatever happened to the actress who played John’s aunt? And did John have a stunt double for the scene where he almost fell from the tower? Also, what year Mustang did Debra W. drive in the series? It seemed like a 1960s model. Thanks!

This Three Stooges film is equally delightful as my all-time favorite, "Disorder in the Court." It's a hilarious treat for any fan of the Stooges.

The trio works as janitors at a recording studio where they discover Christine McIntyre delivering an impressive rendition of "Voices of Spring." Fearing her father’s disapproval, Christine hesitates to pursue her singing career seriously. After she leaves, the Stooges decide to play a prank by dressing Curly up as Christine and playing her record. Mistaken for Christine, Curly is invited to perform at a prestigious event. However, their antics disrupt a rival performer's act, leading to retaliation.

This classic Stooges comedy is a must-watch!  

Rating: 10/10

In *The College Girl Murders*, a deranged scientist develops an almost imperceptible poison gas. Just before he can capitalize on his invention, he’s murdered by a mysterious, whip-wielding monk in a hood. Following a student’s death at a church due to the gas, Scotland Yard steps in to investigate, yet the murders persist. Can anyone halt this elusive killer who seems to move freely in and out of the college?

**What Works:**  

- **The Killer:** Who wouldn’t enjoy a murderer lurking around in a striking red outfit reminiscent of the KKK, complete with matching gloves? The stark contrast of the white whip against the vibrant red robe makes for a memorable look. Even though the concept of a pointed-hooded figure creeping through a girls’ school is somewhat implausible, it’s one of the most unsettling costumes I’ve encountered.  

- **Groovy 60s Music:** I’m determined to find the theme song for *The College Girl Murders*. Its jazzy, cool, 1960s vibe was utterly captivating.  

- **Bizarre Touches:** Beyond the killer’s...

Initially, I was deeply drawn to the central premise of identifying the "intruders" within the delicate self, explored across multiple levels—primarily subconscious, yet occasionally more allegorically. In truth, these intruders are omnipresent throughout the film: they appear at the Swiss-French border where the protagonist lives a solitary life, resurface in his recurring daydreams and nightmares, and even manifest within his ailing body following a heart transplant. By the latter half of the movie, he transforms into an intruder himself, revisiting an old French colony in an effort to make amends for his past.

The overall tone leans toward bitterness rather than pathos, suffused with regret and guilt, dominated by a pervasive sense of failure. This paints a starkly bleak portrait of old age—externally self-reliant but inwardly hollow and isolated. The director crafts the visuals primarily to evoke fleeting sensations of anxiety and desire, rather than conveying explicit meanings. Some scenes are captivating, albeit imbued with a touch of humor, resembling an absurdist play only a sleepwalker could imagine.

(BIG SPOILERS) I’ve seen one other Takashi Miike film, "Audition," which was a deeply disturbing and brutal exploration of Japanese ideals of femininity. In "Visitor Q," which I believe translates to "Visitor Question," Miike delves into the concept of the family unit in an equally unsettling and grotesque manner. While his surreal take on a dysfunctional family aspires to echo David Lynch’s trademark confusion and cinematic complexity, it falls short in terms of style and intrigue. From the opening scene, where the father (played by Kenichi Endo, who delivers a compelling performance) pays for sex with his estranged daughter (Fujiko), we are thrust into a series of bizarre scenarios. After being struck on the head with a rock by the enigmatic Visitor (Kazushi Watanabe), the two somehow end up back at the family home. Here, the mother (Shungiku Uchida) is abused by her son (Jun Muto), who in turn is tormented by his schoolmates. Once the Visitor becomes part of the household, he assumes a vaguely threatening presence within the family dynamic. Gradually, under the Visitor’s influence, the family begins to mend their relationships—though not without engaging in unsettling acts such as breast-milking, murder, and strange rituals.

I am continually astonished and appalled by the evil that has been perpetrated throughout history in the name of religion. It seems that the manipulations of the Catholic Church in twentieth-century Ireland stand out as particularly egregious—despite the lessons of history and the insights of modernity, which should have fostered greater caution.  

_A Love Divided_ tells the story of a real family torn apart by ignorant intolerance and prejudice, all in the name of an illogical Church doctrine. At the start of the film, we see a picturesque life in a small Irish village where Sheila and Sean Cloney are blissfully married, raising two young children. Sean is Catholic, while Sheila is Protestant, yet she has no issue with their children being raised Catholic. There appears to be no tension or hostility between Catholics and Protestants in the village. However, this peace is shattered when Sheila expresses her wish for their older child to attend the Protestant school. The local priest intervenes, deeming this a “sin,” and quickly turns Sheila’s husband and the entire Catholic community against her.

This is a common example of technically proficient directors from the music video or commercial world attempting their first full-length feature film. While the visual elements—such as imagery, cinematography, lighting, CGI, and even sound—are highly refined and exude an undeniably "high-end" aesthetic, the lack of substance in the story becomes glaringly apparent. Even the performances showcase some promise, but no amount of talent can salvage a weak narrative.

In this instance, however, it’s not just a poor plot; there’s scarcely a plot to begin with. Half of the dialogue revolves around variations of “What the hell was that?” and “What was that?”—and in none of these instances does either the characters or the audience receive even the smallest hint of an explanation. Much of the remaining dialogue feels improvised, as if the actors were left to fill in gaps in a storyline they never fully understood themselves.

The sole redeeming aspect might be Skye Bennett's performance, which shines because her character—an autistic girl—was spared the opportunity to deliver the painfully contrived lines delivered by the rest of the cast.

If you enjoy solving mysteries and complex narratives, this film is perfect for you. Directed by Francis Leclerc, son of the legendary French-Canadian singer Félix Leclerc, it's a brilliant and intelligent movie. Known for its flashy visuals and clever editing, the film is brought to life by Roy Dupuis' dynamic performance in the lead role.

The story revolves around Alexandre Tourneur, a veterinarian in his 40s, who awakens from a coma after being mysteriously unplugged. Having been attacked while euthanizing a deer on the road, Tourneur struggles to recall his attacker. As he searches for answers, his behavior becomes increasingly erratic, suggesting something—or someone—has taken control of him.

Though not overtly spooky, the film is filled with mystery and delivers strong performances. I have my own theory about the ending (I believe the Native American character was involved in the accident), but the conclusion leaves room for multiple interpretations. 

Highly recommended, with a rating of 9.5/10.

This film is a small ray of sunshine during a gloomy season. It embraces a simple yet profound virtue—plain old friendliness. Morgan Freeman portrays a character reminiscent of himself—a successful actor nearing 70. Arriving at a small, somewhat dingy grocery store to research a role as a store manager, he quickly wins over both employees and customers. Among them is Paz Vega’s character, a charming but grumpy young woman who oversees the "10 items or less" checkout line.

*10 Items Or Less* isn’t out to make a grand statement; it simply follows Freeman and Vega as they form an unlikely friendship. In exchange for a ride home, Freeman’s character offers advice to Vega’s, after a movie-company assistant fails to show up and he forgets his phone number. On a melancholy Sunday afternoon in New York City, this light-hearted film lifted my spirits when I needed it most.

Ladies and gentlemen, please do not be deceived by the "Stanley Kubrick" label on this film. It is an exceptionally poor movie, unfortunately celebrated as one of the scariest horror films ever made. True horror films should evoke such terror that people tremble at the thought of them in the dead of night. *The Shining* fails to deliver any genuine scares; instead, it offers a simplistic and amateurish effort to induce chills. Everyone can recognize when an attempt falls short of reality. The only redeeming aspect of the film is the breathtaking view of the icy valley. The hotel where many of the actors stayed also appears impressive. Regarding the performances, Jack Nicholson comes across as a disoriented, lethargic figure, unsure of his role throughout. There is little to praise about the bald, Black actor, who spends most of his time indulging a child co-star. The tragic outcome cannot be blamed on the weather—it was inevitable given the film's execution, and sadly, Kubrick is no longer here to make adjustments.

I can hardly believe this movie was released as late as 1984. The performances are cringeworthy, and the plot might just be one of the most ridiculous ones ever put on screen. Who in their right mind would task the portly Texas sheriff Joe Don Baker with escorting an Italian he illegally detained in Mexico all the way back to Italy? To top it off, the film’s title is incredibly vague, offering no real insight into its story—it’s practically the most generic title imaginable for a B-grade action/cop flick.

Thankfully, I only watched this movie during an episode of *Mystery Science Theater 3000* (MST3K), with Mike and the bots providing much-needed comic relief. They couldn’t resist poking fun at the female lead’s resemblance to Elaine from *Seinfeld* ("None of them are spongeworthy"), and they mercilessly roasted Baker's size throughout. While this movie may not reach the depths of awfulness as *"Mitchell"*, Baker's reputation precedes him. When his name appears onscreen at the start, Tom quips, "I wish I was illiterate so I wouldn’t have to read that."

The movie boasts a solid genre-based storyline, complete with all the familiar Columbo elements: the way Lieutenant Columbo connects with his suspects, the unfolding of the mystery for him, his trusty dog, the engaging cat-and-mouse dynamic—this one excels particularly in that aspect—and thankfully, some well-timed comedic relief, mostly centered around the Columbo character. Despite lacking a wholly original premise—the plot involves a detective/mystery novelist being pursued by Columbo, a scenario already seen in previous Columbo films—the story remains engaging.

Directed by James Frawley, who would helm five additional Columbo movies in the '70s and '80s, the film showcases exceptional craftsmanship. Frawley infuses the movie with style and several standout, unforgettable moments.

Although it’s one of the more leisurely-paced Columbo films, its deliberate tempo works effectively here, likely due to the strong performances from the cast. Most Columbo movies featured either a major star or a veteran from classic cinema.

I must confess, I consider Al Pacino a guilty pleasure. He was an excellent actor until *Scent of a Woman*, where he seemingly overplayed his hand beyond repair. Hoping for a hidden gem, I anticipated a forward-thinking, intelligent, and engaging urban political thriller. This film, about which I knew very little during my upbringing, turned out to be far from that.

*City Hall* is a movie that obfuscates its plot with countless characters, names, and overly "realistic" municipal issues, initially leading you to believe it has a sprawling, mind-blowing scope. In reality, though, these subplots amount to tired, conventional tropes like the Corruption of Power, Two-Faced Politicians, and Mafia ties to law enforcement. Theoretically, this setup should create edge-of-your-seat tension, leaving you unsure whether any character is truly safe. But alas, it fails to deliver.

Regrettably, the only events that unfold are entirely predictable, culminating in several "confession" monologues intended to weave a modern fable and illustrate the moral ambiguity of real-world politics.

Let’s start with the theme song performed by Christopher Cross. The track, titled *"If You Get Caught Between the Moon and New York City"*, remains an iconic anthem even after all these years. It’s a timeless classic, especially when it comes to capturing the essence of New York City. Moving on, the brilliant Dudley Moore CBE takes the lead role as a pampered, alcoholic millionaire who’s engaged to Jill Eikenberry’s character. Later, Jill gained fame for her role on *LA Law*. In the film, Moore’s character is attended to by his loyal British butler, none other than the incomparable Sir John Gielgud OM, who won an Academy Award for his outstanding supporting performance. Meanwhile, Arthur, played by Moore, falls head over heels for Liza Minnelli’s character, who delivers an exceptional performance, though she doesn’t get to sing here. Instead, she plays a hardworking diner waitress. I also adored Geraldine Fitzgerald as the matriarch of the Bach family, whose decisions shape the family’s fate. She was phenomenal and deserved an Academy Award nomination for Best Supporting Actress. Rounding out the cast, Barney Martin, best known as Jerry’s father on *Seinfeld*, plays Liza’s dad—and he nails the role. The movie itself was superbly written, acted, and executed.

This features what is quite possibly Robert Duvall’s weakest performance, as his portrayal throughout the film resembles an exaggerated version of William Buckley. His overly dramatic acting overshadows any potential dramatic tension. It’s unclear whether this was intentional scene-stealing or simply inadvertent, but it’s the sole aspect of this thoroughly forgettable movie that remains memorable. This film should be used in every amateur acting class as a cautionary example of what not to do. Thankfully, Duvall moved on to greater roles and abandoned his attempt at a cultivated accent. While he is a capable character actor, that’s where his talent lies. Klaus, on the other hand, delivers a far superior performance—subtle yet impactful.

This film is a captivating movie inspired by the life of a man named Grey Owl during the 1930s in Canada. I found it just as gripping and emotionally resonant as *Rudy* and *Awakenings*. The story focuses on Grey Owl’s later years, chronicling his most tumultuous and impactful period.

The film revolves around a Canadian Indigenous trapper who begins advocating for the plight of the over-hunted beaver. He also raises awareness about the decline of natural habitats and the unsustainable use of Earth’s resources—a radical idea in the 1930s that surprisingly garners significant attention. As he gains recognition, he becomes a prominent speaker, and people are eager to hear his message.

Pierce Brosnan’s casting might seem unusual at first, but it works effectively, and viewers should watch the film to fully grasp its success. Brosnan delivers an excellent performance, as does Annie Galipeau. Galipeau is a compelling actress whose chemistry with Brosnan feels refreshingly organic compared to the mismatched pairings in recent Bond films.

I highly recommend this movie to those who enjoy powerful dramas, stunning landscapes, or environmental themes. It’s also suitable for families, though children under 10 (depending on their maturity level) may struggle to follow the narrative.

I don't recall who recommended this film, but they mentioned it was among their top favorites. It’s definitely an oddity—like rubbernecking at a car accident on the highway. 

As someone once said, truth is often stranger than fiction, and in this case, the reality is quite extraordinary. I find it baffling that a fictionalized adaptation of this documentary is set to premiere this year. How does one enhance such a story? The film revolves around Jackie Kennedy’s aunt and cousin, who withdraw from New York high society and retreat to the Hamptons, where they gradually become reclusive and, ultimately, what can only be described as "crazy cat ladies." Their seclusion might have continued indefinitely if not for the city’s plans to condemn the property due to its squalid condition, which prompted Jackie to step in and rescue them. Filmed after this intervention, the documentary leaves viewers pondering just how dire things must have been prior to the rescue. It offers a chilling yet captivating glimpse into the darker side of upper-class life, and it’s completely enthralling.

I was eagerly anticipating the release of this film during its production. However, it ended up being a major disappointment—a far cry from the imaginative world of Dr. Seuss. It was crude and distasteful, and I doubt Dr. Seuss himself would have approved. "How the Grinch Stole Christmas" was much better, with only a few subtle adult jokes that my kids didn’t pick up on. On the other hand, "The Cat in the Hat" was blatantly vulgar, and my children noticed far more than I would have liked. As someone who grew up with Dr. Seuss, it was disheartening to see such a timeless classic treated so poorly on the big screen. Let’s hope the adaptation of "Horton Hears a Who" does justice to his legacy.

Oh my goodness! This movie seriously undermines everyone's intelligence. Come on, who believes that three kids could take on 30 to 40 ninjas and emerge victorious? And let's not even get started on the mindless humor. This film is absolutely terrible. It's a complete disaster—only good for passing the time or providing unintentional laughs.

When a peculiar killer dubbed "The Fiend" begins targeting the cast of a stage production, fear grips everyone involved. As two reporters and their bumbling photographer attempt to uncover the truth behind "The Fiend," they soon become targets themselves. Just when it seems like the trio of protagonists is closing in on solving the case, a shocking twist emerges, leaving audiences questioning the identity of the real murderer, according to the DVD sleeve summary.

Taking inspiration from Victor Hugo’s "The Hunchback of Notre Dame," this film, produced by Sam Katzman, benefits visually from its avoidance of studio settings, lending an intriguing aesthetic, particularly in scenes featuring 1930s traffic. However, the direction leaves room for improvement, notably in the poorly executed camera angles during the fight scene. With a modest budget, the cast—many transitioning from silent films to talkies—delivers commendable performances under the circumstances.

****  
*A Face in the Fog* (2/1/36)  
Directed by Robert F. Hill  
Starring Lloyd Hughes, June Collyer, Al St. John

..."For Paris is a moveable feast," said Ernest Hemingway. It's impossible to tally the countless great talents who have immortalized Paris in paintings, novels, songs, poems, brief yet unforgettable quotes, and, indeed, movies. The renowned film director Max Ophüls once remarked about Paris, 

"It offers glistening, rain-slicked boulevards under streetlights, cognac accompanying breakfast in Montmartre, coffee and tepid brioche, and gigolos and prostitutes by night. Everyone in the world has two fatherlands: their own and Paris."

Paris is forever linked with love and romance, and *Paris, Je T'Aime*, subtitled "Petite romances," is a compilation of short films—often sketches—by 18 acclaimed directors hailing from across the globe. Each segment introduces us to one of the City of Light’s 20 arrondissements and its diverse inhabitants—men and women of all ages, races, and backgrounds—all navigating love in its myriad forms and phases. Some of these "petite romances" capture serendipitous encounters between strangers that spark immediate attraction, intimacy, and perhaps even relationships: such as the chance meeting of Podalydès and Florence Muller on a Montmartre street in the opening film or Cyril’s story.

I’ve wanted to watch this film for the longest time, and I consider James Merendino a talented director. *SLC Punk* is one of my favorite movies, and within the first ten minutes, I thought this felt like a worthy sequel. However, it starts to lose momentum afterward. The acting and direction were superb—everything flowed seamlessly except for the script. At times, the only thing holding my interest was the presence of Claire Forlani, who is, without a doubt, the most beautiful woman in the world. While the movie was decent, I had higher expectations. 

P.S. Keep an eye out for fantastic cameo appearances by Chi McBride and Chris McDonald.

No movie has ever made me laugh harder. From the opening scene where four troublemakers are shipped off to Wienberg Military Academy by their dads, the absurd tone is established and never wavers for a moment. 

Describing *Up the Academy* isn’t easy—its humor is so perfectly executed that at first glance, it just seems like another dumb 80s teen comedy. But it’s so much deeper than that! Straight out of the minds at *MAD Magazine*, this film delivers a unique blend of silliness and satire that Hollywood hasn’t managed to replicate in decades. Filled with juvenile jokes and over-the-top antics, it feels like it was written by a pair of 14-year-olds having way too much fun. If you’re ready to embrace your inner child, this is a must-watch. A true classic. ★★★★★

I have to admit—I only purchased this movie because I’m a huge fan of both Gackt and Hyde. Initially, I anticipated an entertaining film filled with visually appealing scenes, though I expected the plot to be somewhat clichéd. The storyline seemed a bit far-fetched, but now that I’ve finished watching it, I can’t help but rave about its brilliance! Hyde and Gackt delivered incredibly moving performances, and my eyes are puffy from shedding tears throughout the final half of the movie. The narrative draws you in, and by the end, you genuinely empathize with the characters. The vampire theme, which I adore, was skillfully woven into the story so that it felt natural to the setting rather than intrusive or gratuitous. I initially rated it 9 out of 10, but after pondering why I hesitated to give it full marks, I couldn’t pinpoint any specific flaw.

This movie is simply fantastic. If you ever get the chance to watch it, you should rush to see it. Although it shares little connection with its 1932 predecessor, Al Pacino delivers an outstanding performance as Tony Montana. 

Pacino possesses a unique ability to deliver any line in any manner and make it sound incredible. If you were impressed by the profanity in *Pulp Fiction*, you’ll appreciate *Scarface* for showcasing another perspective on how an actor can wield such language—almost poetically. 

Despite the film’s fast-paced plot, numerous action sequences, and deviations from real-time storytelling, it remains engaging and easy to follow, provided you stay focused throughout. Personally, I’ve discovered that watching this movie feels like a swift journey, as three hours pass effortlessly. It truly stands out as a remarkable piece.

This is one of those films where the acting and direction are so exceptional that it's easy to overlook the fact that it was made in...

I accidentally came across *Act I* entirely by chance, many years ago. Interestingly, the content wasn’t even close to what the tape’s cover described. It left me astounded, yet also somewhat intimidated and surprised. After a while, I forgot all about it, only to rediscover it nearly a decade later. Upon revisiting it, I immediately purchased both *Act I* and *Act II*. They exceeded my initial impressions, proving even better than before.

My sole issue lies with the Tank Police. Despite their constant boasts about being locked in a "war" against crime, which supposedly justifies their use of tanks and heavy weaponry, they seem remarkably ineffectual when it comes to actually catching criminals. Whether this incompetence is deliberately downplayed or simply ignored is unclear, but their laid-back demeanor suggests otherwise. If their war rhetoric was meant to be propaganda, it hasn’t been portrayed as such in the series.

As for the adaptation, I believe the Americanized version surpasses the original Japanese one. However, while the storytelling holds up well, certain nuances may have been lost in translation, which is understandable given cultural differences.

Chris Rock leads the cast in this reimagining of Warren Beatty's *Heaven Can Wait*, which itself was a remake of the 1941 classic *Here Comes Mr. Jordan*. The film is a comedic tale about a man who prematurely meets his demise before achieving his dreams, only to embark on unexpected adventures in a new—and temporary—body. While Beatty’s version featured a backup quarterback for the Los Angeles Rams as its protagonist, Rock gives the story a modern twist by centering it around a struggling young standup comedian who lacks talent but has big aspirations.

Watching the razor-sharp Rock portray a terrible comedian is hilariously entertaining, akin to seeing Tom Hanks play an incompetent actor. Lance Barton, our protagonist, dreams of performing at the legendary Apollo Theater outside of amateur nights. Yet, every time he attempts his material, he's mercilessly heckled offstage, earning him the unflattering nickname "Booie." His jokes are cringe-worthy, and his delivery is painful. To put it simply, Lance embodies everything that the real Chris Rock is not.

In addition to being a struggling comic, Lance works as a bike messenger. One day, as he races through the streets en route to another audition, tragedy strikes: BAM! He gets hit by a truck. Perhaps his abrupt departure from his body was meant to happen sooner rather than later—or maybe fate had other plans.

For Christmas, I received the first *Bill and Ted* movie, and as soon as I spotted the sequel in a store, I knew I had to get it. This one was just as hilarious as the first but had an even stranger storyline. I found it amusing how they ended up in their own personal hells and had to play the role of Death. What made it funnier was that they treated him like a game, playing silly activities such as Clue. The only thing I’d tweak is having Station and Death be part of the band, but apart from that, it was fantastic.

Clearly, someone was having a laugh when they created this film. 

To start with, there’s no way this movie was made in 1993. The fashion and music scream "seriously '80s." My bet is that it gathered dust on a shelf for years until some eccentric distributor decided to release it into an unsuspecting world.  

Now, there is a plot—sort of. A strange loner meets a random bearded man who claims that if the loner meditates while singing his favorite song, he’ll be able to transform into anyone he wants. Here’s the kicker: his favorite song is “London Bridge Is Falling Down.” Yes, you read that right. And why does he love it? Because he’s apparently an idiot. By the first minute, this film has already achieved a jaw-dropping level of absurdity. Spoiler alert: it only gets worse from here.  

Oh, and let’s not forget that this guy is apparently the world champion of nostril picking. Two separate scenes confirm this delightful habit, which finally explains the title. Deciding to transform into a woman so he can get closer... well, you can imagine where this is going.

A captivating film by Powell and Pressburger, whose work I am now eager to delve deeper into. The movie explores the blurred lines between what we consider reality and what is truly real, highlighting the challenges of discerning between the two. It boasts stunning cinematography and出色的 performances, though David Niven's age seems inconsistent with his character's claim of being 27. It’s intriguing to spot a remarkably young Richard Attenborough. This film stimulated my thoughts both during and after viewing.

If you're looking to understand the fundamentals of quantum mechanics, spend your $9 on a used textbook rather than this movie. I’m somewhat concerned that the money I spent might be funding shipments of Kool-Aid to Guyana. It seems the filmmakers didn’t manage to convey a clear message, but it appears they were attempting to touch on several ideas: 1) Science can explain all human actions, implying our lives are predetermined; 2) Science has its limits and cannot explain everything, suggesting we possess free will; 3) Science is awesome, man; 4) We are God; 5) The world is merely a construct of our minds; 6) Playing Sarah Norman is a daunting challenge; and 7) Here, place this small paper square on your tongue, and you’ll experience something truly mind-blowing.

This is the type of film that scares me the most—arrogant and irresponsible. It offers such a trite and foolish depiction of the Colombian conflict that it feels like an insult to the entire Colombian population. The performances are atrocious, from Grisales (her nude scene is embarrassingly bad) to Bejarano, to Fanny Mickey (who looks like she stepped out of a Tim Burton nightmare), to Díaz, who tries valiantly to breathe life into a character so one-dimensional, clichéd, and poorly written that all he’s left with is a mustache. And then there’s the gratuitous ending—a gory mess so cheesy it would make Ed Wood wince. It fails in every aspect: cinematography, art direction, costumes, makeup, editing, and, above all, directing. Jorge Alí Triana has never been a great filmmaker, but even his earlier works had some semblance of dignity. I can’t find anything positive to say about this waste of resources, except that I hope Colombian filmmakers take this ill-intentioned disaster as a lesson in honesty, integrity, and responsibility.

I need to begin by sharing how I discovered this movie. It was wintertime in Alaska, around 1990. A friend from Australia was visiting me and my girlfriend at our tiny apartment, which felt more like a shoebox. Alaskan winters can be harsh, so most people tend to stay indoors, drink heavily, and watch whatever plays on TV. One day, I found this film outside a thrift store, half-buried in a snowbank, and instantly knew it was a hidden treasure. It might just be the best bad movie ever made. For the next two weeks, my friend and I couldn’t stop watching it, drinking endlessly like fish. We even watched it so frequently that we’d sometimes turn the TV sideways or upside down for an enhanced experience—it’s that kind of gem. The laughter never stops, and the memories last a lifetime. If you spot this movie for rent in a video store, take it—steal it if you must. You won’t regret it!

I initially expected *The Sentinel* to be an average film. However, after watching it, I was pleasantly surprised. While it may not be groundbreaking, it's highly entertaining, and its action sequences are particularly well-executed. The movie evoked comparisons to TV series such as *24* or *Alias*, and it also brought to mind Wolfgang Petersen’s *In the Line of Fire*. If you approach it expecting one of the most innovative and iconic thrillers in cinematic history, you might be let down. But with modest expectations, you'll find enjoyment in *The Sentinel*.  

Rating: 7

You wanted to see "THE Gamers" by Dead Gentlemen Productions, but this isn't it. This film isn't amusing; it's a complete waste of time. 

Most of the positive reviews here appear to be thinly veiled self-promotions by those involved. The filmmakers seem desperate to create artificial buzz around their project.

This movie doesn’t measure up as a well-executed mockumentary. Comparing it to "Spinal Tap" or Christopher Guest works would be an insult.

The film is so cruel-hearted that no one familiar with the subject matter could possibly find it entertaining. Having a sense of humor about oneself is crucial, but if you're the target of such mockery, you'd need to lack self-respect to enjoy it.

It’s not offensive due to bold satire of taboo subjects but rather because of its relentless mediocrity.

This ranks as one of my all-time favorite movies. The dialogue, filled with constant puns, is sharp and well-crafted, the cast delivers outstanding performances, and the plot is refreshingly original. 

Take my recommendation to heart – watch this movie and experience its brilliance for yourself.

The star power in *The House of Spirits* is so immense it could potentially birth another galaxy, yet the final outcome is somewhat questionable. The film and its themes are undoubtedly noble, and I suspect many would concur with its messages—liberal democracy is good, fascism is bad; open-mindedness is commendable, while racism is condemnable, and so on. However, these ideas are hammered home incessantly, leaving little room for subtlety. 

In the end, we’re left observing idealized characters devoid of imperfections clashing with villains who lack any redeeming qualities. The tension feels as predictable as a poorly choreographed professional wrestling match.

Jeremy Irons delivers a compelling performance as the enigmatic patriarch, while Meryl Streep shines as his gifted spouse and Glenn Close brings depth to her sister-in-law. When the focus remains on these actors, the film flows smoothly and proves engaging. But alas, *The House of Spirits* gets bogged down by an overwhelming number of subplots and fleeting character introductions. These peripheral figures materialize and vanish like targets at a shooting gallery. As such, we fail to connect with them or feel invested in their stories, leading to an experience marked by disinterest and ennui. 

Directed and co-adapted by Bille August from Isabel Allende’s原著...

This was the first regularly filmed Columbo movie episode, though it aired as the second, following Steven Spielberg's "Columbo: Murder by the Book." It’s also considered one of the stronger entries in the series!  

Bernard L. Kowalski was a highly talented and creative director, which explains why he was later tasked with directing three additional Columbo films. The movie features some truly inventive and innovative camera work, and the overall production is crafted with style, passion, and meticulous attention to detail. Each shot feels purposeful, contributing to the film’s superior quality compared to typical made-for-TV movies. It stands out as one of the best-directed Columbo films.  

This particular episode is quite unique for several reasons. The murder occurs more or less by accident and is an impulsive act rather than a premeditated one. Consequently, the killer has no time to plan a “perfect murder” and must hurriedly cover their tracks and dispose of the body. In this case, the killer isn’t portrayed merely as someone who committed the crime but also as someone who inadvertently becomes entangled in its consequences, adding layers of complexity to the story.

Sandra Bernhard is quite a personality, and undeniably one of the funniest women around. She started her career as a stand-up comedian in the 1970s, but her breakthrough came in 1983 when she starred alongside Jerry Lewis and Robert De Niro in Martin Scorsese’s often overlooked gem, "The King of Comedy." While her film career didn’t fully take off, she did appear in a few quirky yet engaging movies like "Dallas Doll" (1994) and "Dinner Rush" (2000). However, her most remarkable performances were those she crafted for herself.

"Without You I'm Nothing" is unquestionably her finest work. A film adaptation of her groundbreaking off-Broadway show, it propelled her to superstardom and solidified her friendship with Madonna for nearly four years. In ten meticulously choreographed and staged segments, Sandra transforms into icons like Nina Simone and Diana Ross, shares stories from her childhood, discusses her experiences with Andy Warhol and San Francisco, and performs beloved songs by Burt Bacharach, Prince, and Sylvester. Director John Boskovich captured a 90-minute tour de force performance from Sandra that is both sensuous and hilariously unique. For any Sandra Bernhard enthusiast, this movie is a must-watch—it’s a celebration of her (eccentric) charm and her extraordinarily unconventional talent.

I picked this up for 50 cents at the flea market and was pretty excited. 

At first, I found it fascinating for about 15 minutes, but then it became repetitive and dull. 

It’s interesting to see Mick and the gang in their prime, but I wish there wasn’t so much overdubbing of dialogue so I could hear what they were saying and playing. 

The sketches are politically dated, naively simplistic, and kind of like poorly written Monty Python on acid. I spent more time admiring the '60s English backdrops than paying attention to the silly sketches. 

This movie serves as a good reminder that times change, and what seemed important quickly becomes silly. The songs are good, but this DVD has played them to death.

I recently bought the restored version of a film that holds fond memories from my childhood, and it provided an intriguing way to spend the afternoon. "Bedknobs" undoubtedly makes more sense in its complete form; the deleted scenes, particularly those featuring McDowall, tie events together seamlessly. What's somewhat jarring is how the remastered scenes were handled. Evidently, the original soundtrack for these clips was lost or damaged, so someone at Disney decided to re-record the dialogue. While this could have worked well, half the cast wasn’t available—some understandably so—and the result feels rather amateurish. Some of the lip-syncing is off, and David Tomlinson’s voice was replaced by someone who sounds nothing like him (I detect a faint German accent, oddly enough). Still, it's great to hear the full versions of all the songs, even if "Step in the Right Direction" remains missing. The film’s magical moments still shine brightly, and you’ll struggle not to laugh when young Paul stares adoringly at Angela Lansbury and murmurs.

I clearly don’t belong to the target audience for this film. At almost 50 years old, I’ve only recently discovered the world of independent cinema, purely by chance. It all began one night when I stumbled upon *Clerks* on TV. Two things struck me immediately: 1) its amateurish production quality and 2) its exceptional writing. Intrigued, I read an interview with the director in a local paper where he mentioned *Clerks* as one of his inspirations. That piqued my interest further. Then, when he revealed that *The Station Agent*—a film I’d watched just days earlier—was his primary influence, I knew I had to see what he’d created. The end result mirrors *Clerks* in some ways, though the content is entirely different. Both films suffer from technical flaws but excel through their remarkable storytelling. While *Clerks* follows a man with no direction in life and a fear of confronting tough truths, *Less Like Me* centers on a man who keeps himself perpetually occupied, seemingly avoiding deeper introspection.

I entered the theater knowing it was a drama centered around a man with a supernatural ability, turned into a monster by society. To say I was unprepared for what unfolded would be an understatement—but it turned out to be a delightful surprise. Both my friend and I found the film incredibly romantic (let’s be honest, the attractiveness of the male lead didn’t hurt). There was just the right balance of plot progression, action, and even some humor—like the moment when the characters finally learn each other's names in Part Three, prompting laughter throughout the theater. All in all, it wasn’t what I anticipated, but it was an excellent twist. I’ll definitely purchase this movie once it’s released on DVD.

For years, it was rumored to be on the back burner, but when this television reunion of two of the most cherished sitcom icons finally came to fruition, it got off to a rocky start—and never recovered. Mary Richards (Mary Tyler Moore) and her best friend Rhoda Morgenstern (Valerie Harper) reunite in New York after a lengthy separation to reconnect over their lives. What a fresh idea! Yet, regrettably, neither character has experienced anything remotely noteworthy in the years since the original series ended. Consequently, the screenplay resorts to rehashing tired tropes (many involving older women in professional settings), entirely overlooking the unique wit and sophistication that made the original show so successful. The supporting actors are forgettable, the humor lacks substance, and the chemistry between Moore and Harper, which once shone brightly, is now absent. Reports suggest Moore delayed the project for years, holding out for the perfect script. If this was the one she deemed acceptable, what must the rejected drafts have been like? It wasn’t the advanced age of the characters that doomed this effort—after all, time passes for everyone—but something far more fundamental went awry.

I believe this might be the funniest movie I’ve ever come across. Robert Harling’s script is nearly flawless—seriously, take a look at the “quotes” section. Actually, scratch that—just go ahead and rent the DVD, because it’s the delivery that truly brings the lines to life. 

Sally Field delivers a comedic, over-the-top performance unlike anything else I’ve seen from her, while Kevin Kline shines with effortless humor. Robert Downey Jr. is as brilliant as always, and Kathy Najimy steals every scene she’s in with her riotous portrayal of the harried costume designer in her small yet memorable role. Though I wasn’t particularly fond of Elisabeth Shue in the past, she’s fantastic here as the sole “real” person amidst a cast of larger-than-life caricatures on the set of “The Sun Also Sets.” It feels like Ernest Hemingway is either spinning in his grave—or roaring with laughter. 

Five stars. Hilarious, hilarious, hilarious.

Following their work on *The Baron*, Monty Berman and Dennis Spooner created this fantasy series centered around three superhuman spies, a concept that foreshadowed *The Six Million Dollar Man*. As a child, this show was a favorite of mine, and I still enjoy revisiting it today. Stuart Damon and William Gaunt shared an undeniable on-screen rapport as Craig Stirling and Richard Barrett, while Alexandra Bastedo brought charm and allure to her portrayal of Sharron Macready. The late Anthony Nicholls delivered a formidable performance as the stern Tremayne. The standout episodes were penned by Tony Williamson, Terry Nation, and Brian Clemens, and Spooner’s *The Interrogation* stood out as comparable to *The Prisoner*. It’s unfortunate that a second series was never produced, as the premise held immense potential. Could Craig and Richard have vied for Sharron’s affection? What would have happened if Tremayne discovered the Champions’ true capabilities? Did they possess other hidden talents beyond what we witnessed? Alas, these questions remain unanswered.

This film is undoubtedly an unusual love story. While it may not be particularly remarkable, Nicole Kidman single-handedly carries the movie, while the rest of the cast could easily be overlooked, although Ben Chaplin does manage to provide a solid portrayal of life in Hertfordshire, with scenes featuring St Albans and Hemel Hempstead's town center capturing the true spirit of the area. What initially seems like a typical episode of the popular British TV show "Heartbeat" quickly transforms into an intense gangster getaway thriller. Nothing especially memorable occurs in this straightforward, small-scale film, making it ultimately enjoyable weekend fare. It’s worth watching, and if you can relate to the lonely, thirty-something protagonist, you might find aspects of his character that resonate with you.

I suppose everyone has to make a comeback at some point, and that’s precisely what Jack Dundee (Robin Williams), an embarrassed resident of Taft, aims to do in "The Best of Times." This time around, the same guy who went wild with the radio in "Good Morning, Vietnam" is now playing football. His goal? To replay a game that cost his high school a coveted championship. However, his former teammate Reno Hightower (Kurt Russell) isn’t about to let him have it easy. 

While it may not be the best film for either actor, Williams and Russell make a surprisingly solid comedy duo. And let’s not forget the chuckle-worthy supporting cast—some of these names are sure to amuse (to put it mildly). Give it a watch!

Steer clear of this movie at all costs. It's undoubtedly the worst film I've ever watched. Most movies usually have at least one positive aspect, but this one has absolutely none. It's completely terrible!

This summer saw its fair share of disappointments, including films like *Snakes on a Plane* and *The Da Vinci Code*, so calling *Superman Returns* a bold choice is quite something. However, I firmly stand by my opinion. Much like *King Kong* six months prior, *Superman Returns* feels overly long, excessively indulgent, and drowning in CGI. Honestly, all these effects are giving me a headache.

Richard Donner’s two *Superman* films focused on keeping things grounded and realistic—a philosophy I respect. His approach to special and optical effects seemed far more fitting. On the other hand, Brian Singer saturates the screen with CGI, which pulls you right out of the narrative and constantly reminds you that you're watching a movie trying too hard to be a blockbuster. It blows $250 million—ridiculously irresponsible spending—on flashy visuals that fail to deliver. We’ve already experienced everything CGI has to offer; there’s no real atmosphere or emotional engagement here. Given that 95% of the film relies on this nonsense… well, you get the point.

I’ve read countless reviews from die-hard fans praising the movie’s "soul," but

I was only thirteen when I first watched this series, and now, more than three decades later, I'm revisiting it on DVD. The images from the opening credits have stayed with me all these years. It has profoundly shaped my perspective on the world and its people. Fortunately, my parents were around long enough to watch it with me, and we always talked about the episodes afterward. It kindled my passion for history and earned me the best grades in our school’s public exams!

Sir Laurence Olivier’s voice and delivery remain timeless and flawless. Those who experienced the events firsthand might see this as their definitive portrayal of World War II history. I doubt I'll ever tire of watching it. Perhaps a similar series about the Cold War could be considered, though finding someone to match Sir Laurence’s brilliance seems nearly impossible.

Get your hands on it—you won’t regret it!

Mario Lewis from the Competitive Enterprise Institute has penned a comprehensive 120-page refutation of this misleading film, which should arguably be named *A CONVENIENT LIE*. His debunking report, titled *"A SKEPTIC'S GUIDE TO AN INCONVENIENT TRUTH"*, can be accessed at [www.cei.org](http://www.cei.org). A condensed 10-page version is available at: [www.cei.org/pdf/5539.pdf](http://www.cei.org/pdf/5539.pdf). After reading these critiques, it becomes clear that所谓的 "global warming" is no more genuine or alarming than the Y2K scare of 1999, which Gore also supported, just as he did with the pseudoscientific film *THE DAY AFTER TOMORROW*, based on a book written by alleged UFO abductee Whitley Strieber. In the same way that James "The Amazing" Randi exposes psychics, Philip Klass tackles UFO claims, and Gerald Posner debunks JFK conspiracy theories, Mario Lewis dismantles Al Gore’s movie and the entire "global warming" hoax.

Scott Henderson, portrayed by Alan Curtis, is wrongfully accused of murdering his adulterous wife. The night she was killed, he was seen out with a mysterious woman who declined to reveal her identity. Following his arrest, the police investigate the locations he visited with her, but witnesses recall only seeing him alone. Convicted and sentenced to death, his secretary, played by Ella Raines, takes it upon herself to uncover the true killer, driven by her love for him. 

Though produced as a low-budget B-movie by Universal, featuring a supporting cast of character actors and a declining star in Franchot Tone, the film stands out as one of the finest examples of noir cinema from the 1940s. Skillfully directed by Curt Siodmak and adapted from the gripping novel *The Bride Wore Black* (written under the pseudonym William Irish by Cornell Woolrich), the movie moves swiftly and boasts a stunning visual style. A standout scene features an electrifying jazz session between Raines and Elisha Cook Jr., exuding raw sexual tension—remarkable given the era’s censorship standards.

Despite its strengths, the film isn’t flawless. Tone delivers a lackluster performance that detracts from the otherwise compelling narrative.

Anyone who praised this film should watch more movies. It follows a clueless protagonist who films his dysfunctional family. Filled with moronic characters and cringe-worthy scenes like "teabagging," it offers little redeeming value. Save yourself the time—this movie won't improve as it progresses. Avoid it entirely.

I was thrilled to watch this film, thinking that Australia had finally produced a great movie. Unfortunately, I couldn't have been more mistaken.

This was hands down the weakest attempt at a slasher film I've ever seen. I felt sorry for Molly Ringwald for having to come to Australia only to star in such a poor-quality production.

The acting was subpar, particularly the Australian actor's effort to speak with an American accent, and the storyline was equally lackluster.

Initially, when I heard about the film, I thought its title was cringeworthy, reminiscent of the cheesy "Stab" from *Scream 2*. Still, I was hopeful that the movie itself might redeem it. 

**WARNING: HEAVY SPOILERS AHEAD!**

The worst aspect of the film was undoubtedly its ending. I anticipated a shocking twist revealing the identity of the killer, but instead, the murderer turned out to be something inhuman. This transformation ruined the film's otherwise realistic tone, turning it into a laughable horror flick.

Avoid this movie—it’s bound to leave you disappointed!

Of the three remakes of this plot, I enjoy them all. I own all three versions on VHS and also have a DVD copy of this particular version. The variations in the scripts keep each rendition entertaining and re-watchable. Has any other film been remade three times with such an impressive all-star cast in each iteration? While the main stars in this version are outstanding, the supporting actors are equally exceptional. I especially admire William Tracy as Pepi; his talent for stealing scenes is remarkable, leading me to seek out other films he appeared in. Unfortunately, many of those are unavailable. Like others who have commented, I highly recommend purchasing this version.

If this film had a $20 million budget, I’d love to know exactly where all that money went.
