A monkey could’ve created better CGI effects than what was squandered over the course of its painful three-hour runtime. While I will admit, the machines and Martians might have looked impressive in a retro PlayStation 1 game or an early '90s PC title—if such a project had ever come to fruition—they don’t belong in this mess. The real mystery here is where the funds disappeared to. Pendragon Films could’ve crafted something worthwhile using practical models, computer-controlled cameras (ala George Lucas from 1975–1983), and actors who seemed even remotely invested—realistically, for the same price. This has to be one of the absolute worst films ever made. I’d endure a full 24-hour loop of *Ishtar* before sitting through this again. I loathed every second. To clarify, I stand by my claim that this is THE WORST FILM EVER MADE because, unlike classics like *Plan 9 from Outer Space*, *Attack of the Killer Tomatoes*, or *Santa Claus Conquers the Martians*, those at least occupy a niche as hilariously bad cult favorites.

Rated NR (would be Rated R for pervasive strong language and crude sexual humor). Quebec Rating: 16+ (should be 13+) | Canadian Home Video Rating: 18A  

_Eddie Murphy Delirious_ is Eddie's first stand-up comedy special, released in 1983. At the time, he was starring in movies like *48 Hrs.* and *Trading Places*, and appeared regularly on *Saturday Night Live*. Eddie produced two stand-up comedy films: *Delirious* and *Raw*. While I personally preferred *Raw* due to its more humorous subject matter, *Delirious* is also incredibly funny. In this special, Eddie shares stories from his childhood and pokes fun at celebrities like Mr. T and musicians such as Michael Jackson. Any fan of stand-up comedy should check out *Eddie Murphy Delirious*.

I sat down to watch a documentary about Puerto Rico, but I ended up watching one about Nuyoricans instead. When I visit Puerto Rico, I don’t notice the 50% living in poverty. The struggling individuals I encounter are often recent arrivals like Haitians, Dominicans, or Cubans. Spanglish doesn’t exist—either you speak Spanish, or you don’t. And based on what I’ve heard, you don’t. Pedro Albizo Campos is not the MLK of Puerto Rico to me. MLK was an incredible figure, while Campos is only seen as a great leader by the 1% advocating for independence. To everyone else, he’s as delusional as Osama Bin Laden. Those who support Puerto Rican independence are misguided. If you’re dreaming of an independent Puerto Rico, look at Cuba, Haiti, the Dominican Republic, the Bahamas, all of South and Central America, and Mexico—they’ve reaped the benefits. This documentary isn’t about Puerto Rico; it’s about the Nuyoricans and their challenges.

To the person who complained there wasn’t enough Africa featured—it was supposed to be about Puerto Rico, not Africa. Denzel will make a movie about it soon.

I adore watching early color films—seriously, those 40s styles weren’t all gray, were they?

Margaret Rutherford absolutely owns this movie. Her "eccentric" outfits are surprisingly stylish, and yes, her hourglass figure is impressive. However, I think she overplayed her part a bit too much. She likely developed this characterization over numerous performances, and no one seemed to tell her, "If it gets a laugh, dial it back." She goes overboard with exaggerated antics when she’s meant to come across as unexpectedly grounded. The humor around Madame Arcati lies in the fact that mediums were often depicted as ethereal women in flowing attire. Here, Arcati acts more like a former headmistress ("Let's really throw ourselves into it!"). The contrast between her casual demeanor and her quirky beliefs doesn’t quite shine through.

Just because the cast is predominantly English (with the exception of Cummings), American viewers can’t resist saying "Brit," "stiff," "lip," and "upper." Please, enough already! All three main characters frequently lose their temper and toss out risqué comments ("Did he make love to you?" "Yes, but very discretely—he was in the cavalry!").

A remarkable show and an underappreciated classic, *The League of Gentlemen* stands as one of the greatest modern comedies of recent times. 

With its dark and surreal brand of humor towering above the tired, formulaic approach of its inferior yet far more recognized successor, *Little Britain*, *The League of Gentlemen* was truly extraordinary during a relatively quiet era in British comedy. 

Before its arrival, there had never been anything quite like it.表面上看似简单的素描剧，很快展开为一个生动、阴暗却又令人捧腹的奇妙宇宙，充满了各种令人叫绝的喜剧角色。与竞争对手不同的是，这部剧讲述故事的方式独树一帜。它没有重复使用千篇一律的笑料，而是让每个角色或群体经历各自的旅程和故事线。每次造访都带来新鲜感，充满惊喜。 

渐渐地，在三季和一个圣诞特别集里，虚构的罗伊斯顿·维塞镇变得拥挤不堪，居住着一群既怪诞又搞笑的居民。

Several reviewers have pointed out that the movie falters during its final half-hour. Prior to that, however, it suffers from predictability and a shockingly vacuous performance from Kate Capshaw, who seems to have missed her character entirely, detracting significantly from each scene she participates in. While Sean Connery and Margaret Yeakey deliver competent performances, the overall tone feels manipulated for dramatic impact rather than authenticity, lending the narrative an air of artificiality. The conclusion is also perplexing. It appears the filmmakers recognized the disjointed nature of the story they had assembled, akin to preparing only sweet potatoes and pumpkin pie for Thanksgiving, so they amplified the soundtrack with overly dramatic music. Each minor event is underscored by swelling orchestration, eventually becoming comical. For those interested in witnessing a prime example of poor filmmaking, this is worth viewing; otherwise, it’s best to avoid it.

Ettore Scola is one of Italy's most significant filmmakers, yet he remains somewhat underrated. My parents and I once watched "C'eravamo tanto amati" on a summer evening. We found it enjoyable, but it didn’t resonate with us as much as "A Special Day." I think Scola is often overlooked, perhaps because his later works failed to impress. Regardless, last night, my mom and I revisited this gem. The film’s writing, direction, cinematography, score, and production design were understated yet meticulous. What struck me most, though, was the incredible chemistry between Sophia Loren and Marcello Mastroianni. Both are exceptional actors, portraying Antonietta and Gabriele, respectively. Antonietta is a housewife married to a fervent Fascist who wishes to have another child to win a prize for large families. Gabriele, on the other hand, is an Anti-Fascist. Together, they share a pivotal day in 1938, during Hitler’s visit to Rome to meet Mussolini. I won’t reveal more of the story—seek out this film yourself!

"One of the movie aficionados remarked after watching *LOVE AT THE TOP*, the mistranslated title version of stylish director Michel Deville’s *LE MOUTON ENRAGE*: 'It felt like the first brush of pleasure and guilt, akin to an impulsive youthful flirtation of wonder and dread, a peak of conflicting emotions.'"

"Vincent Canby of *The New York Times* noted shortly after the 1974 premiere of the film: '*LOVE AT THE TOP*, which debuted yesterday at the 68th Street Playhouse, is a 1973 French comedy loosely reminiscent of several 1950s British comedies featuring the meteoric ascent of cynical young men driven—and consumed—by ambition.' The key distinction he highlighted was that *LOVE AT THE TOP* did not delve into the English class system... (January 27, 1975)."

"Allowing individual opinions to stand while the passage of time renders its verdict, it is undeniable three decades later that finding films as enchantingly provocative as *LE MOUTON ENRAGE* is rare. In these works, decadence feels disarmingly pure, relationships exude youthful ardor, and emotions seem ingeniously orchestrated."

"For fans of Romy Schneider, emphasizing the significance of this film goes without saying."

A fairly mundane TV movie that debuted on the TBS cable network, it follows Antonio and Janine as they chase a deadly computer virus. For those interested in trivia, it's worth noting that this film premiered during the same weekend the actual "Melissa" virus began spreading through email worldwide.

Certain films are so poorly made that they become enjoyable in their own strange way. This movie, however, is certainly not one of those. Loosely based on a true story, its accuracy was about as reliable as Pinocchio's chance of becoming a real boy. The acting was atrocious, the direction lackluster, and the pacing rushed to the point of absurdity. It felt as though the director simply wanted to wrap things up and leave the set as quickly as possible.

Melissa Joan Hart, while not necessarily untalented, has never impressed me, and this film is no exception. Similar to her other projects, which were mostly low-budget, she undermines her characters by overacting and speaking too rapidly, as if accelerating her dialogue will enhance the drama. Instead, she comes across as if she’s aware of the camera and crew rather than fully immersing herself in her role. This undermines the entire film, leaving it without any redeemable qualities.

The only remotely positive aspect of the movie is the somewhat satisfying conclusion, but even that failed to deliver genuine satisfaction. Overall, this film is forgettable at best.

This is utter and total garbage—a perfect illustration of how a BAD movie should not be made. No one, not even fans of B-movies, could find this remotely appealing. Trust me; do NOT squander any valuable moments of your life on this abysmal film. The acting is atrocious, the direction nonexistent, and the screenplay borderline unwatchable. It’s as if the creators had no concept of what constitutes entertainment in any capacity. I purchased the DVD for just three dollars, and I’d have been willing to pay someone to take it off my hands. Simply burning it wouldn’t足夠彌補這部電影給我帶來的損失。我喜歡B級片，像是殺人玩具或怪異的沼澤怪物電影，但這部完全無法與之相提並論。你是否知道有些電影糟糕到居然帶點喜感？這部甚至連那都達不到。它只是單純、毫無遮掩地可悲。

I stumbled upon this movie around 1990 on video accidentally, having no idea what to expect. Many horror enthusiasts might have overlooked it, assuming it was just a standard prison film, while those who did watch it were disappointed because it wasn’t what they anticipated. These factors likely contribute to its low ratings, but if you’re a fan of the genre, don’t let that deter you—give it a try. 

The film shines in every aspect, from its script and atmosphere to its performances and the prison setting itself. It’s an absolute gem, one I’ve kept on VHS to this day. Give it a watch.

"52 Pick Up" never received the recognition it truly deserved. The film excels on multiple levels, boasting a complex yet engaging storyline that remains accessible to viewers. The performances delivered by its cast are exceptional, with standout portrayals from Ann-Margret, Roy Scheider, and John Glover, who embody their characters with depth and authenticity. Particularly noteworthy is Vanity, whose talent hints at an untapped potential for a successful acting career, and Kelly Preston, whose character leaves a lasting impression. For those who appreciate action intertwined with a gritty, intricate narrative, this film is sure to captivate.

Initially, I wasn't certain whether I was viewing a documentary, a propaganda film, or a dramatic presentation. Given its production timeframe, it seemed to blend elements of all three.

While the dramatic plot was somewhat predictable, there were moments that promised intriguing scenes as the film progressed. We observed what appeared to be authentic training routines and equipment.

For me, the movie truly came into its own toward the end. The scenes exhibited a realism (as I perceived it) that I hadn’t often seen before. It allowed viewers to immerse themselves in the action and envision the thoughts of the young combatants. However, this was coupled with the typical challenge of depicting believable Japanese soldiers at a time when finding actual Japanese actors might have been difficult.

This film is an excellent reflection of the American mindset in 1943 amid the ongoing war with Japan. Additionally, it included a critique of the Japanese regarding the assistance the U.S. had provided to Japan in earlier years.

I don't typically criticize films, as I prefer to highlight their positive aspects rather than dwell on the negatives. However, in this instance, there are scarcely any redeeming qualities. If the goal is to create something so poorly executed, one must wonder why it was made at all. A significant portion of the movie features close-ups of Anne's face as she takes deep breaths, accompanied by violin music in the background. The remainder is filled with subpar, stiff performances. Rupert Penry-Jones appears completely devoid of emotion, while Jennifer Higham portrays Anne's younger sister with distinctly modern mannerisms. Anne is depicted as timid and self-effacing, which works initially but remains unchanged throughout the film, offering no explanation for Captain Wentworth’s attraction to her. The production lacks any authentic sense of period, riddled with historical inaccuracies like characters rushing out of concerts, kissing in the street, or walking around without hats on (why include a scene that undermines one of the novel’s most romantic moments?). To put it simply, this is a dreadful film—highly disappointing.

Pacino's delivery of the speech over the dead child's coffin deserves full marks; Shakespeare's Mark Antony would be left in awe!

Should Paul Schrader or Ken Lipper be commended for the remarkable dialogue? The lines are rich, intelligent, and well worth your time if you appreciate films with strong scripts. I found the narrative development to be solid right up until the voice-over epilogue.

There is not much else to discuss regarding this movie; even John Cusack has delivered better performances than this role. Interestingly, the film is highly male-centric—the female characters serve only as afterthoughts.

If you're a kid, it's rated 7; if you claim to be an adult, it's rated 6. This semi-sequel to "The Lion King" focuses on fan-favorite side characters Timon and Pumbaa, retelling the original story through their perspective, including the tale of how they met. Following Disney’s tradition, inferior sequels are often created, along with TV series featuring the adventures of secondary characters from their most successful films. While you may approach this film skeptically, younger audiences and dedicated fans will likely enjoy it, as it boasts plenty of jokes, songs, and engaging moments, making it one of the better sequels in the franchise. Its success stems from the charm of its beloved central characters, a fast-paced narrative, in-jokes referencing the first film, and even some clever humor for older viewers. The animation quality remains strong, though slightly less extravagant than the original, but the movie's essence lies in its laid-back philosophy: "Hakuna Matata." 

Timon and Pumbaa decide to watch the events of the first film, often pausing to make humorous comments about certain scenes, just like a real audience would. Viewers see how Timon feels like an outcast, struggling...

The summer was brimming with blockbusters and much-anticipated film comebacks, though unfortunately, some of those returns fell short of expectations. As a result, I found it increasingly difficult to discover a movie I could truly relax and enjoy. 

For those who prefer a quick summary without spoilers, here it is: This film is more mature than *Ella Enchanted*, featuring some potentially unsettling violence, several scenes of death, and a few moments with minor bloodshed—definitely not suitable for young children. However, it avoids being overly cheesy or overreaching in its storytelling. Think of it as a darker, more magical version of *The Princess Bride*, and you’ll have a good idea of what to expect.

-------------------------------------------------------------------

Perhaps I’m not as frequent a moviegoer as others—I might catch one or two films a month if I’m feeling particularly inspired. My preference leans heavily toward sci-fi and fantasy. I lose interest in recycled storylines and movies that prioritize flashy visuals over substance far quicker than most. This film stood out like a rare gem amidst the chaos.

By late August, I was weary of the underwhelming performances of the big-budget releases, so I decided against watching *Bourne*.

Michael Stearns portrays Mike, a man grappling with sexual frustration who holds a peculiar moral perspective on sexuality. While he feels no qualms about gazing at naked dancers, his tolerance ends when women engage in sexual acts with men. To him, such behavior strips them of their "innocence" and "beauty." Consequently, Mike wanders the Hollywood Hills, covertly tracking intimate couples from afar, eventually dispatching the men with a high-powered rifle equipped with a scope.

The film’s main purpose appears to be showcasing sexual encounters repeatedly. The narrative feels like an afterthought, which might please many heterosexual viewers, offering extended scenes of nudity—where the female performers appear particularly appealing unclothed—and sex, providing ample titillation. Viewing these moments through the scope amplifies the unsettling voyeuristic element, as Mike spends minutes observing couples before acting. Accompanying this are intrusive yet somewhat evocative background scores, adding further tension to the unsettling atmosphere.

In summary, this film lacks a coherent plot and is essentially 80 minutes of erratic characters either consuming alcohol or delivering poor jokes. The soundtrack is dreadful, the humor falls flat, and the female characters are either portrayed as promiscuous fools or socially awkward nerds. To me, it feels as though the script was penned by a 14-year-old boy who idolizes drinking, views women as objects to please men, and dismisses anyone who disagrees with these notions as "geeks." Furthermore, this movie bears little resemblance to the original *American Pie* series, save for a few character names and the minor presence of Mr. Levenstein. The sole redeeming quality here is the appealing appearance of the actresses. Avoid this movie at all costs; its 5.4 rating is misleadingly high and unjustifiably generous—it scarcely deserves more than a 2.

Movie trailers for this film might suggest scenes of violence or unconventional sexuality, but these are merely isolated fragments, selected to captivate viewers. In reality, they only hint at the core message of the movie:

It explores individuals who endure relentless mistreatment in their careers and personal lives, only to wield power—perhaps acquired elsewhere—to viciously dominate others. At the bottom of this power dynamic often lie women.

A film as unflinching as *Hundstage* is difficult to confront, yet enduring such existences is far harder.

In terms of structure, it mirrors *Short Cuts*, comprising episodic segments in a documentary style, portraying ordinary folks like neighbors, performing naturally without embellishment. Most unsettlingly, there's no glimmer of hope. The documentary approach amplifies the distress, as viewers come to understand that such people exist—and in significant numbers—despite society’s focus on polished exteriors. Somewhere, the adult entertainment industry thrives; somewhere, domestic abuse goes unnoticed; somewhere, dreams crumble. I’ve encountered such individuals firsthand.

If you're seeking a film devoid of...

Bogmeister and others have largely captured the essence of this episode. "Shore Leave" marks Star Trek: The Original Series' first foray into lighthearted sci-fi, a style they would later refine with the beloved classic "The Trouble with Tribbles." It provided both the crew of the Enterprise and its viewers with a welcome break from the high-stakes, universe-threatening stakes of episodes like "The Corbomite Maneuver."

Seeking a chance to unwind, the Enterprise discovers a seemingly idyllic M-class planet and dispatches an exploration team to investigate. Before long, various absurd situations arise—some appearing dangerous—but it all plays out as a chaotic mix of human emotions wrapped in a surreal blend of mysterious fantasy (McCoy finds himself in a Wonderland-like scenario), psychological thriller (Kirk is pursued by a relentless figure from his past), and romantic comedy (let’s just say Kirk gets more than he bargained for).

Unlike subsequent series in the Trek franchise, TOS was the least serialized, making it easy to overlook how many first-season episodes centered on intense, potentially catastrophic drama. Unlike later writers, the TOS production team wasn’t afraid to boldly venture into uncharted narrative territory.

Did HeidiJean actually watch this movie? A great Christmas film? Hardly. It was dull, uninspired, and entirely devoid of creativity or charm. Throughout the movie, I kept wondering which genius decided Carly Pope was right for the lead role. She lacks any discernible personality and delivers a thoroughly mediocre performance. Baranski, as always, was excellent and provided the only remotely engaging moments in the entire film. Her participation likely got the project approved in the first place. Perhaps I’m asking too much for a Lifetime movie so close to Christmas, but I couldn’t help thinking that with a different director and a more sympathetic actress in the lead role, this could have been a sweet little holiday flick.

The film opens with a voiceover explaining the setting and introducing the characters, a choice that immediately made me disapprove. Given the countless creative tools available to filmmakers, relying on a voiceover to spell out everything feels lazy and unoriginal to me. In my view, voiceovers undermine the essence of cinema by bypassing the visual storytelling potential.

I cringe when a narrator spells out our location, the date, or—worse yet—details about the characters' emotions and thoughts. A skilled director should convey these through visuals, allowing the audience to interpret the story organically. 

Despite this uninspired beginning, the movie quickly shifts gears and becomes unexpectedly compelling, maintaining its engaging pace for a significant duration. The film portrays the everyday lives of a middle-class family and its individual members with remarkable realism. The director demonstrates a clear talent for capturing authentic, relatable scenarios. For instance, a father resorting to making private calls in the bathroom may initially seem odd, but such moments reflect how reality often surprises us.

I had no idea a movie this terrible could actually get released. The premise seemed so appealing, but you'd think with a cast of 20, at least one of them would have some acting ability. My wife left halfway through the first act and went to bed. It was hands down the right call.

The film is highly accomplished in its execution, maintaining constant engagement through flashbacks of childhood and成长 alongside a peculiar father, while weaving in tales of serial murder. There's no denying its entertainment value. The storyline, at its core, offers ample opportunity for creative exploration, and director Bill Paxton seized this chance with great success.

From start to finish, the narrative keeps you on edge, eagerly anticipating each twist and turn. The ingenuity behind the plot is top-notch, leaving you feeling that the film was meticulously crafted from beginning to end. It stands as one of those rare gems devoid of any dull moments, with scenes transitioning smoothly, swiftly, and seamlessly. 

It highlights just how far individuals can go—committing atrocious acts against their loved ones and committing evil deeds in the name of "God," especially when driven by delusions, as seen in this case. It also...

I grasp the jokes just fine—they simply aren’t good. The show itself is awful. I can follow it, which is actually another reason it’s so terrible. The only remotely interesting character in the entire series was that one homeless guy in a single episode, but after watching the other episodes, including that one, the show remains unwatchable. It’s not funny—nowhere close. I don’t want anyone to claim, “Only smart people get it,” because if they’re so intelligent, why do they judge people they don’t know and dismiss them as unintelligent or uninformed? It’s like saying, “The sky is red,” without even checking outside. Anyway, this is hands down the worst show I’ve ever encountered. The humor is dreadful; you might understand the jokes, but that doesn’t make them any better. Her controversies feel forced and immature, and her fart jokes and bodily fluid humor are painfully unfunny, often accompanied by poor acting. I’m not sure what so-called “smart” viewers see in this series, but criticizing others based on assumptions isn’t particularly wise.

While there are numerous new styles of the sitcom, the format that has proven most successful is the classic setup featuring a live audience and an indoor set. *That '70s Show* is a prime example. When the show first aired, few people were familiar with Kurtwood Smith or Debra Jo Rupp, let alone the talented young actors like Topher Grace and Ashton Kutcher (both of whom are departing this year to explore new opportunities). I hope Topher stays, as the series began with his character, Eric, and his tight-knit group of friends at its core. Ashton, meanwhile, has become the John Travolta of our generation—imagine him paired with Demi Moore, similar to how John was once romantically linked to Diana Hyland in *Eight Is Enough*. It’s fortunate that none of the cast members were celebrities beforehand, as having a star加盟 could have ruined the show. I miss Mo Gaffney, who played Don’s girlfriend Joanne, and Lisa Robin Kelly, who originated the role of Laurie. Her replacement simply couldn’t measure up, which is disappointing. I appreciated the choice to cast Tommy Chong as the laid-back yet beloved father figure to Steven Hyde. And while watching Tanya Roberts, I fondly recall her work beyond *Charlie’s Angels*.

I would rate it a 2 out of 10.  

I was extremely disappointed. The storyline lacked depth; the incidents felt rushed and underdeveloped, making the moral unclear. While Brenda Song delivered a commendable performance, Shin Koyamada appeared to struggle with his role. Although incorporating Western elements into the show was necessary, certain aspects, like the villain’s design, missed an opportunity to embrace Chinese culture. For instance, the antagonist looked more robotic than inspired by traditional Chinese motifs. The most significant issue, however, was the presence of inaccurate and distorted facts throughout the series.  

Some might argue that this is a "kid's show" and thus doesn't require such high standards. Still, other Disney productions like *Mulan* have excelled in storytelling and cultural representation.  

In summary, I believe Disney productions should prioritize thorough research and meticulous planning. A compelling show cannot rely solely on martial arts sequences.

Anyone who finds this film dull is undoubtedly a narrow-minded simpleton who would be better off watching car chases and romantic comedies. This movie is utterly captivating and never once bores its audience. Why? Because it features highly intelligent conversations among realistic characters in moments of crisis, portraying their attempts to overcome that crisis. Let me reiterate—intelligent dialogue! This is what defines most of Rohmer’s films, which is precisely why some people dislike them. They prefer action. Fine. Let them spend the rest of their lives indulging in action-packed films while those of us with refined tastes will keep seeking out masterpieces like this one.

Rohmer has often been criticized for being "too talkative," but to me, that’s a compliment, not a fault. After all, Shakespeare was talky as well. Is there any play more dialogue-heavy than "Hamlet"? When the essence of a work of art revolves around ideas and conflicts over values, there must inevitably be discussions of those concepts. And that is largely what this film is about. It explores themes such as aristocracy versus egalitarianism and tests the loyalty of old friendships when that friendship is pushed to its limits by...

While I don’t want to be a spoilsport, Brad Sykes is behind at least two of the dullest, most clichéd films I’ve ever encountered — this one and *Camp Blood* being prime examples. 

The performances are dreadful, the print quality is poor, and every aspect of this movie shouts, "Seriously, you could do better yourself." Perhaps this is a dare to all of us to flood YouTube with our own zombie-themed nonsense? 

I picked this up for £1, but let’s face it, you can’t put a price on 71 minutes of your life. It’s best to steer clear of this turkey, even if it’s dirt cheap.

Have you ever heard the saying, "Live every moment as if it's your last"? Regardless of whether it's your final day or not, I implore you not to waste any part of it on this! Nichole Hiltz offers a few visually appealing moments (though unfortunately remains fully clothed), while David DeLuise demonstrates that he might be better suited for the small screen or advertising dog food. With a superficial, unrealistic plot and atrocious dialogue, this film lacks any semblance of "Art" in "The Art of Revenge."

I attended a special advance screening of this film today. To be honest, I’m not a big fan of either Dane Cook or Steve Carell, so I didn’t have high expectations going in. Surprisingly, I really enjoyed it.

"Dan in Real Life" follows a widower with three daughters who spends a weekend with his family. During a trip to a bookstore, he meets the woman of his dreams, only to discover she’s also his brother’s girlfriend.

The movie is well-crafted—its soundtrack, cinematography, and performances, particularly Steve Carell’s, are excellent. My main issue was the lack of depth in character development, especially regarding Dane Cook’s role. The relationship between his and Steve Carell’s characters wasn’t explored thoroughly, which left me wanting more insight into Dan’s internal struggle over falling for his brother’s girlfriend. Still, aside from this, "Dan in Real Life" is a heartfelt and engaging film—a refreshing change from the horror and action movies we’ve seen this year.

One redeeming aspect of this film is Lola Glaudini's physique. While it may seem blunt, it’s the honest truth. It’s disappointing she didn’t appear nude; that might have made the experience more bearable. There’s another instance of female nudity, but it pales in comparison to Lola’s presence. Armand Assante looks significantly aged and his performance doesn’t help matters. "Consequence" delivers the standard B-movie fare one would anticipate. The premise had promise, but it feels as though the creators had good ideas without the ability to execute them properly. The cinematography is subpar—downright ugly—and the direction lacks inspiration. The final product is a bland thriller filled with lackluster twists and underwhelming performances from veteran actors. Lola Glaudini excels as the seductive character in a provocative manner, yet even her contribution can't elevate "Consequence" above its status as forgettable trash—certainly not the amusing kind, just plain, uninteresting junk.

I read the comment by Chris_m_grant from the United States.  

He wrote: "A fantastic documentary from 1924. This early 20th-century geography of today's Iraq was powerful."  

I would like to thank Chris and those who are interested in the Bakhtiari Nomads of Iran, the Zagros Mountains, and their landscapes for watching the film *Grass: A Nation’s Battle for Life*. These traditions, which you saw in the movie, have endured for centuries and will continue as long as life does. I am from this region of Iran myself—I am Bakhtiari.  

Chris, I apologize for bothering you, but the Bakhtiari region of Zardkuh is in Iran, not Iraq as you mentioned in your comment. Iran and Iraq are two separate and distinct countries. Mistaking an Iranian for an Iraqi is almost like confusing an American with a Mexican. Thank you,  

Ziba

Could someone remind Shaq to stick to what he excels at—basketball? This movie wasn't even enjoyable on a trivial level. In it, Shaq plays a genie living inside a boom box, which is hardly an original concept—a genie in a boom box instead of a lamp! His job is to assist a little boy, portrayed by the equally grating Franck Capra. The storyline is the flimsiest I've seen since *Waterworld*, the acting is dreadful, and I suspect anyone who claims to enjoy this film might feel embarrassed to admit it.

May and her husband travel to visit their children and grandchildren. The reunion feels strained because the grandchildren and their parents don’t connect as closely as one would hope. There’s an emptiness where warmth should be. After dinner, May’s husband claims he isn’t feeling well, jokingly attributing it to his daughter-in-law’s cooking. With irritation, he declares he wants to return home immediately. That night, he passes away.

Now widowed, May feels adrift. While her marriage wasn’t particularly passionate or exciting, it gave her purpose. She had someone dependent on her, and despite years of neglecting her own needs, she had structure in her life. 

Devastated and listless, May moves in with her daughter, Paula. Not long after May arrives, Paula expresses frustration, accusing her mother of never truly investing in their relationship. She lashes out, angrily voicing how her mother failed to nurture her adequately. Taken aback but seemingly without the strength to defend herself, May softly replies, “I’m your mother, and I love you.” But what *does* that really mean?

I wasn’t particularly fond of the first *Cube* movie. While it had a solid concept, the irritating performances and characters prevented me from fully enjoying it. I didn’t feel the urge to watch its sequel, but when I learned they were making a third film that served as more of a prequel, I became curious. I hoped they might address the original’s flaws and give us compelling, memorable characters. Unfortunately, my expectations were misplaced.

*Cube Zero* begins effectively, introducing us to the two characters responsible for monitoring and maintaining the endless labyrinth of deadly traps within the Cube. The filmmakers do an adequate job creating a sense of mystery through the depiction of these men’s daily routines. This setup raises several unanswered questions about why people are sent into the Cube and the true nature of those running the operation, leaving everything open to interpretation. Overall, the first half of the film progresses fairly smoothly, despite some underwhelming acting.

As the story advances, one of the “watchers” starts to...

I missed the start of this film, which might explain why I didn’t enjoy it as much. On the other hand, I’ve spent years studying the fall of the Roman Republic, so I’m familiar with the story. Ironically, that familiarity might also be why I found the film disappointing.

The movie is riddled with historical inaccuracies—more than extras, in fact. It’s so inaccurate that it feels like they didn’t even try to get it right, which could be somewhat excusable. But what’s odd is that at times they go out of their way to be historically precise, only for it to become confusing. For instance, they mention Antonius’ marriage to Octavia but drop it just two scenes later without any meaningful resolution. Why include it if it doesn’t serve the plot and Octavia herself isn’t even shown? Similarly, they alternate between calling Antonius by his real name, Marcus Antonius, and his Anglicized version, Mark Antony, within the same scenes.

Even ignoring these historical flaws, the film could have been entertaining were it not for its leading actress. She lacks any sense of dignity; she’s overly emotional, overly dramatic, and completely out of control.

Hello. I’m Paul Raddick, aka Panic Attack from WTAF, Channel 29 in Philadelphia. Let me share my thoughts on this dreadful movie that helped launch Adam Sandler’s career but was quickly forgotten.

*Going Overboard* follows an aspiring comedian, played by Sandler, who takes a job on a cruise ship—and apparently doesn’t do well. Or at least that’s what I gathered. Along the way, Sandler meets women who are into *History of the World Part 1* and *Rebound*. These ladies were supposedly committed to someone else, but it turns out they’re captured and killed by Sawtooth, the cruelest cannibal in existence. Sandler didn’t exactly shine in *Going Overboard*, but he did better in *Big Daddy*, *Billy Madison*, and—Jen Leone’s favorite—*50 First Dates*. Drew Barrymore was definitely a knockout back then. *Spanglish* was pretty good, but *Going Overboard*? Not even close. End of transmission.

This movie follows one family’s extraordinary journey and allows you to experience every moment of their odyssey. With outstanding performances and stunning visuals, it captures the bittersweet authenticity of their story. Its final line, filled with poignant hope, remains one of the most memorable in cinema.

Please, people, don't waste your time on this movie! It's terrible. A complete waste of time with no redeeming qualities. The plot is ridiculous, and the acting is subpar. I'd rather endure being hit than watch this film again.

This was always my all-time favorite film growing up. The special effects were groundbreaking for their time and even earned awards. I can still recall the dialogue as though I heard it yesterday. It’s an undeniably fantastic and enduring adventure. The score is by Miklós Rózsa, widely regarded as one of cinema's greatest composers. Sabu plays the Thief, while Conrad Veidt embodies the menacing villain. I keep a copy nearby, ready for the next journey down memory lane. Hold on tight—Rex Ingram is eager to break free from his genie lamp!

**Elvira, Mistress of the Dark (1988)**  
Directed by: James Signorelli  
Starring: Cassandra Peterson, W. Morgan Sheppard, Daniel Greene, and Edie McClurg  

**Plot:** Elvira (Cassandra Peterson) leaves her gig as a horror hostess to claim her late aunt’s inheritance in the conservative town of Fallwell, Massachusetts. Hoping to strike it rich and launch a Las Vegas show, she ends up with a spooky old house, a poodle, and a magical cookbook instead. As she navigates Fallwell, Elvira works to earn money, revitalize the local teens, woo a charming hunk (Daniel Greene), evade being burned at the stake, and protect the cookbook from her sinister uncle (W. Morgan Sheppard), who seeks to unleash its apocalyptic powers.  

**My Thoughts:** I adore both Cassandra Peterson and her iconic persona, Elvira. Peterson is witty, striking, and full of charm, while Elvira embodies all that plus a delightful mix of morbid humor and hilariously innocent naivety. Her ample assets? Well, they’re just icing on the cake. This film puts her charisma front and center.  

I really enjoyed the "fish out of water" vibe. Picture this: Elvira saunters into Fallwell in her figure-hugging black gown, clearly out of place but unbothered—her confidence is infectious.

This poorly executed sequel to Joe Dante's 1981 classic, "The Howling," is marred by subpar cinematography, clumsy scripting, and amateurish pacing. Despite being one of the few truly noteworthy werewolf films ever made, "The Howling" was unfortunately followed by a string of irritating and unbearable sequels, including this one. At least this installment, titled "Stirba," is loosely tied to the original only in name; there's no continuity with the characters or events established in Dante's film. Here, the story centers on a bloodthirsty cult of Transylvanian werewolves, mostly female, led by Stirba, portrayed by Sybil Danning. She morphs from a curvy older woman into a blond vixen with a prominent figure at the drop of a hat and grows fur whenever sexually stimulated. Her adversary is played by an apparently weary Christopher Lee, whose character, Stefan Crosscoe, is an occult investigator journeying to Stirba's domain alongside an American couple whose friend fell victim to the werewolf cult. If your primary interest lies in excessive gore and gratuitous nudity, this movie will satisfy you. Every minor killing is depicted in excruciating detail, and we're subjected to scenes like exploding eyes and the revolting image of a dwarf being impaled.

Evaluating this or any other film from the early sound era using typical film criticism terminology proves challenging. During this period, many silent-era actors, likely anxious about being left behind as the industry embraced sound (as ultimately occurred with some), struggled to adapt. Rin-Tin-Tin, however, came across as entirely natural. Amid the hodgepodge of disconnected scenes, certain moments stood out, such as John Barrymore’s soliloquy from *Richard II*, a scene undoubtedly worth preserving. Generally speaking, only those with prior stage experience appeared self-assured. Despite its unevenness, the film remains reasonably engaging and is essential viewing for "film buffs," particularly those fascinated by the transition from silent to sound cinema.

I originally planned to watch this movie in theaters, but it was sold out. Instead, I ended up seeing *Solaris*, which turned out to be the worst film released in 2002.

Victor Rosa (played by John Leguizamo), a street-smart "pharmacist," has a panic attack after witnessing a shooting and resolves to go straight, investing all his money with Jack (Peter Sarsgaard). At first, things seem to be going smoothly, but then Jack absconds with Victor’s money and his girlfriend Trish (Denise Richards). This happens relatively late in the movie, so if the trailer hadn’t already spoiled it, it might have been a decent plot twist. But since they revealed it beforehand, it feels predictable and unoriginal.

In reality, there isn’t a single interesting moment in this film; the trailer gives away every detail. If you’ve seen even one preview, you’ve essentially watched the entire movie. You might as well save your time and just piece together the remaining parts in your head. Visit the website, download the trailer, and skip spending $3.99 on the DVD. The only mystery here is how bad the soundtrack is.

I can only hope the person responsible for the music was distracted or underqualified, because nothing else explains why it’s so terrible.

"The Cobweb" is just one example among many films that showcase strong, and occasionally memorable, performances, yet it suffers from a convoluted plot and a lack of engaging elements that leave the audience disinterested. Richard Widmark plays a doctor at a mental institution whose personal life spirals out of control due to family issues and a contrived, overly complicated conflict that feels entirely trivial.

The story is absurd. The hospital plans to replace the library curtains, but an elderly woman insists on keeping her original ones while some of the patients insist on creating their own. Somehow, this ridiculous and unintentionally comical dispute escalates to the point of endangering lives and tearing families apart. It reads more like something that might unfold among preschoolers than adults.

The implausibility of the plot is so glaring that one can't help but question how anyone could take it seriously. The acting, however, is not to blame; the supporting cast features talented performers alongside Widmark.

The movie *Kazaam* starring Shaquille O'Neal as the genie is a complete trainwreck. His rhymes are cringe-worthy, the acting is atrocious, and the special effects are laughable. The plot is confusing, and the entire film feels like a bad joke. It’s the kind of movie that falls into the “so bad it’s funny” category. Watch it with your friends for a few laughs, but don’t expect anything remotely impressive.

The Dentist begins on the morning of Dr. Alan Feinstone (Corbin Bernsen) and his wife Brooke's (Linda Hoffman) wedding anniversary.表面上，艾伦和布鲁克夫妇似乎过着幸福的生活——他们在洛杉矶拥有一栋美丽的房子，他事业有成且备受尊敬。然而，表面之下却危机四伏。艾伦发现布鲁克正与泳池清洁工马特（Michael Stadvec）有婚外情，更让他颜面尽失的是，马特还与他们的隔壁邻居、一名叫宝拉·罗伯茨（Lise Simms）的女子发生了关系。此外，艾伦还背负着巨额债务，令美国国税局（IRS）步步紧逼。这一切让艾伦濒临崩溃，他开始认为周围的一切都如同病人腐烂的牙齿一样腐败不堪，而他必须亲自“修复”这些烂牙。当天在诊所工作时，他将内心的愤怒和挫败感发泄到病人身上。他先是伤害了一名叫做乔迪（Brian McLaughlin）的男孩，接着在幻觉中将一名名叫阿普尔·莱恩（Christa Sauls）的患者误认为是妻子并实施性侵犯，随后又对另一名病人进行毫无必要的痛苦治疗。艾伦的精神状态逐渐恶化，行为愈发失控。

"How The Grinch Stole Christmas" captured my heart and became my favorite movie almost immediately upon my first viewing. Even after eight re-watches, it continues to resonate with me just as powerfully as it did the first time.

Jeffery Price and Peter S. Seaman, known for their work on "Who Framed Roger Rabbit," deliver an exceptional adaptation of Dr. Seuss's classic tale. Ron Howard’s direction brings the story vividly to life, while Jim Carrey’s high-energy portrayal of The Grinch dominates every scene.

Critics who claim the film strays from the essence of the original story may disagree, but having read the book, I find their arguments unfounded. The movie conveys the same message about the true meaning of Christmas as the original, and it deepens the narrative by exploring the motivations behind The Grinch's transformation. 

*(Mild spoilers ahead—these probably won’t spoil the movie, but if you’re someone who prefers knowing nothing about a story beforehand, proceed with caution.)*

I would like to commend the series as a significant achievement. Despite needing some refinements, the storyline was quite compelling, particularly in Season 1. However, Season 2 took a turn towards becoming more of a spectacle, losing some of the show's original charm. Season 1's narrative was more engaging, balancing a lighthearted look at life at Jam Pony with a focused, serious plot involving Manticore's pursuit of the X-series. I eagerly anticipated new seasons, and I continue to do so. I hope the Fox team and the Dark Angel production crew recognize that many fans are still waiting for the show to make a comeback. Even two years after its cancellation, Dark Angel has the potential to succeed if handled appropriately, and I believe someone with a reputation like James Cameron should take on this challenge.

Collusion Course is far worse than your average "evil white male corporate capitalist" film. It's less enjoyable than a toothache. Jay Leno can act, and he was commendable in his underrated debut film, The Silverbears, where he delivered a performance fitting for his character. However, this movie is so poorly made that even Leno's sanctimonious buffoon comes across as less irritating than Morita's sanctimonious fool.

In this charming Ealing Studios comedy, a chemist invents a fabric that never soils or deteriorates, yet it is viewed as a threat to multiple industries. Guinness delivers a brilliant performance as the unassuming yet determined scientist. Greenwood, with her alluring voice, portrays the love interest, while Parker embodies her frazzled father. Thesiger provides comic relief as the head of the textile sector. As the narrative unfolds, the film explores thought-provoking themes related to science, economics, and politics. Expertly helmed by Mackendrick, who later directed "The Ladykillers" and the acclaimed "Sweet Smell of Success" in the 1950s, this movie masterfully balances entertainment with deeper inquiry.

To what depths might someone stoop while chasing past glories? *ST:HF* is eager to demonstrate.

If you’re accustomed to the qualities that made classic *Star Trek* great, avoid this at all costs.

The writing is disjointed, the performances lackluster, and the design work is abysmal. Here, commanding officers appear feeble, the proud spirit of the Federation is mocked, and even ensigns sport outrageous hairstyles like spiked hair—a far cry from any disciplined setting.

Within two minutes of the first episode, a junior officer with spikey hair is already attempting to arrange casual rendezvous with an engineer. It only spirals downward from there. Uniforms are mismatched, some too tight or too loose, with varying styles from different series thrown together haphazardly. The once-disciplined traditions of Starfleet are entirely absent, right down to the details. 

The sole redeeming quality is the graphics, which improve slightly as the seasons progress. Actually, scratch that—I’ll amend: who...

If Todd Sheets were to admit that this movie was meant to parody the zombie genre, I’d bump my rating up to an eight. Imagine a film where every scene, every line, and even every acting choice was crafted as a deliberate satire. I could probably spill alphabet soup, rearrange the leftover bits, and still end up with a better script. Two scenes in particular stand out when I think about this movie. SPOILER ALERT! One involves Mike’s dad and the other dad navigating a crowded staircase filled with zombies. Despite brushing against the flailing undead, they remain unscathed. At the bottom, the ex-Marine quips, “God you’re a horny bastard,” before shooting just one zombie. Another scene takes place in the military complex, where a girl stabs a zombie with a machete and is suddenly encircled. For nearly 40 seconds, the camera circles her as she stands surrounded by zombies mere inches away. She then calmly escapes the mob and rejoins the group. SPOILER ALERT OVER! These scenes deserve...

Robert Wuhl is instructing a class of film students at New York University in Manhattan, New York. He delves into historical fallacies and lesser-known truths, and I wish there were more episodes of this series. It’s incredibly engaging. Mr. Wuhl employs examples and "show and tell" techniques to convey his ideas effectively. For instance, he revealed that the individual who actually undertook the Midnight Ride of Paul Revere wasn’t Paul Revere himself! Longfellow chose Revere’s name because it had a better ring to it.

I’ve been watching Robert Wuhl for years, from his early days as a stand-up comedian to his role in "Arli$$" on HBO. While he’s a talented actor and comedian, he shines as an exceptional teacher. I strongly encourage you to watch one of his episodes—it’s thoroughly worthwhile.

A disappointing film.

The story introduces us to Chrissy, a young and somewhat sulky character who appears aimless, accomplishing little. Since she contributes minimally to the plot progression, it’s unsurprising that attention shifts to her relatives. It’s unfortunate, as Chrissy seemed like an intriguing character.

The narrative is predictable and at times feels overly formulaic. The question arises: When will filmmakers like the Campions, Jacksons, and Tamahoris deliver captivating, visually compelling stories that inspire rather than merely entertain for two hours?

Technically, the film is poorly executed.

Someone—or perhaps something—is leaving puncture marks on the jugular vein and draining victims of their blood until they are dead. Police detective Karl Brettschneider (Melvyn Douglas, before moving on from B-movie horror to greater acclaim) is baffled by these chilling crimes. The village is consumed by fear and hysteria, and Karl relies on his trusted medical expert, Dr. Otto von Niemann (Lionel Atwill, once again excelling in a quintessential mad scientist role), for insight into what could be causing the deaths of innocent people. Karl also worries for the safety of his beloved Ruth (the captivating Fay Wray, who co-stars with Atwill for the third time after "Doctor X" and "The Mystery of the Wax Museum"), as she serves as von Niemann’s assistant.

Dwight Frye delivers a standout performance as a peculiar and unstable village idiot who collects bats and exudes a demented aura wherever he goes. It’s no surprise that he becomes a prime suspect as paranoia runs rampant in the town. Maude Eburne brings levity to the film as a gullible patient of von Niemann’s, easily influenced and prone to imagining ailments she reads about in books near the laboratory where he works. Von Niemann humorously indulges her frequent claims of fictional illnesses.

I haven't seen the first movie, and based on this one, I don't have much interest in watching it. 

Just a few hours after viewing it, I'm already struggling to recall any details. 

From what I can remember, the main plot revolves around a group of extremely irritating individuals staying at a house with the creepy old lady from "Friday the 13th." They're pursued by some guy wielding a piece of wood as a weapon. 

Some characters die, the movie ends, and I’m considering filing a lawsuit against whoever sold me this film for wasting my time. 

I’d pay you £1 to take this off my hands... oh wait, I’ve already given it away to a "friend."

Even then, even they can manage to live without witnessing it. Honestly, this so-called film is of genuine interest only to those with an extreme fascination with bondage. Bettie Page enthusiasts won’t discover anything new here—absolutely nothing—and they certainly won’t find comfort in reliving anything familiar, beloved, or cherished.

Forget about the atrocious screenplay, the stiff, sub-community-theater-level performances, the complete lack of direction, the poor lighting, or any of the other bargain-basement production elements. This is textbook "Hey, kids, let’s make a movie" filmmaking at its absolute worst. One might almost be grateful they figured out how to operate the camera. But no, I regret to say that none of that explains why this mess is so fundamentally *flawed*.

It’s flawed because the actress portraying Bettie Page—a young woman who shares little more than dark hair and the iconic bangs with the legendary Queen of Curves—fails entirely to breathe life into the role beyond her willingness to be bound and gagged. While this seems to have been advantageous for her career both before and after this dreadful project, it does nothing to salvage this debacle.

I recently watched this movie when I rented it the other day, expecting it to be yet another story about a girl trying to prove a point. However, I was pleasantly surprised to discover that Diane decided to join boxing because she genuinely wanted to. I found the movie enjoyable and gave it an 8/10 rating. It’s that good. And let’s not forget, any film featuring Michelle Rodriguez tends to be great, even if she has only appeared in six so far.

This is a prime illustration of a growing issue in films. Why is the background noise and soundtrack consistently much louder than the dialogue? What’s the logic behind this? This film isn’t unique; most movies seem to follow this trend these days. For two years, I thought it might be a problem with my TV, but after getting a new one, the issue persisted. The overwhelming background noise, which sounds like it's happening a block away from the actors, drowns out their dialogue.

In this particular film, it was even more distracting, especially in the English version, where the female lead constantly mumbles. I kept imagining Jean Reno’s character saying, “Excuse me, would you speak up or get the marbles out of your mouth?” If you watch it on DVD and understand basic French, I suggest switching to the French version with subtitles—it’s far better.

I rate it a 4 because Reno was exceptional in *Léon*. Some people praise the scenery, but I watched it on a TV, and having lived in the Rockies, I wasn’t particularly impressed.

The movie begins slowly, focusing on the mundane life of Wallace Napalm, an employee at a photo drop-off station. His wife wears an ankle bracelet due to a previous conviction for arson. Wallace is deeply involved in the local volunteer fire department and takes his duties seriously.

As Wallace's monotonous routine unfolds, a sudden change occurs when a traveling carnival arrives in town. Among its performers is Wilder Napalm, Wallace’s brother, who works as a clown. Unlike his reserved sibling, Wilder possesses a unique ability.

Both brothers share this extraordinary skill—they are pyrokinetics, individuals who can ignite fires with their minds. While Wallace hides his powers, Wilder openly demonstrates his abilities to those around him.

Spoiler alert: Their differing attitudes stem from a tragic event in their childhood when they unintentionally caused the death of a homeless man. Wallace chooses to suppress his powers, while Wilder seeks recognition by revealing his talents on national television.

Adding tension to their rivalry, Wilder harbors romantic feelings for Wallace’s wife, creating further conflict between them. This animosity escalates until the brothers engage in an explosive showdown.

Though engaging, the film falls short of greatness.

Let me start by saying I’m not from the South, but I am American. While I don’t particularly adore Country music, I can tolerate it. I wouldn’t be caught dead in a cowboy hat, though I do wear hats occasionally. I don’t live in a trailer, but I enjoy tuna salad and own a home. So what does all this have to do with the comment? Quite a bit, actually, especially if you’re someone who insists this movie is only for “Country” folks. This film is loosely centered around the “love and loss” theme. James Bridges crafts an authentic American love story that feels painfully real. In an era dominated by shows like *Jerry Springer* and a culture that revels in oversharing, this movie remains truer than ever.  

Bud is “coming of age,” moving to the big city with the help of his aunt and uncle. There, he becomes immersed in the local honky-tonk scene as a form of cheap escapism. Before long, he meets Sissy, who shares a similar upbringing, and they dive headfirst into a passionate yet tumultuous romance filled with highs and lows.

"Satan's Little Helper" stands out as one of the more compelling B-movies in the horror genre, particularly because its storyline feels refreshingly original compared to many clichéd entries in the genre. However, despite its clever premise, the film raises several absurd questions that linger throughout your viewing experience. 

I stumbled upon this movie while browsing the Horror section at HMV, weary of over-hyped Hollywood blockbusters and craving something unique. The cover art instantly drew me in; it’s chilling and intriguing. Knowing it was a direct-to-DVD release, I decided to take a gamble—especially after surviving the underwhelming "Boogeyman" the previous night. Though not perfect, the movie left me somewhat satisfied. The plot was genuinely unsettling, especially how the killer managed to pose as the little boy's friend, ultimately believing they'd form an unholy partnership. It’s twisted logic at its finest.

Branagh is among the rare few who grasp the distinction between a film and a play. "Hamlet" stands as one of the most忠实 adaptations of Shakespeare to cinema while remaining an incredibly dynamic film, bordering on an action thriller. The scene where Hamlet encounters his father's ghost is unforgettable.

Xizao is a rare gem of a film. Simple yet unpretentious, it delivers immense emotional depth and joy. The straightforward narrative introduces the clash between old and new masterfully in its opening scenes, making this theme central to the movie. However, the brilliance of the characters and the exceptional performances bring this concept to life, preventing it from falling flat.

Master Liu, the aging patriarch, represents China’s past before its expansion. Running a bathhouse in an old neighborhood, every scene set there evokes envy in even the most stressed and dissatisfied viewers. Even the most cynical hearts cannot find fault with this enchanting backdrop.

Er Ming, Master Liu's mentally disabled son, stands as the second compelling figure alongside his contemporary brother. Their interactions, along with those of the bathhouse visitors, are richly detailed and emotionally resonant, featuring moments that surpass the emotional depth of many cinematic experiences.

Despite its poignant critique of societal systems, the film faced censorship and received disproportionately limited attention. While this could be coincidental...

This is the worst film I’ve ever watched, but honestly, it’s somewhat entertaining and surprisingly funny. The filmmakers clearly didn’t aim for a Hollywood blockbuster caliber production. It’s just a ridiculous story about a serial killer who gets covered in toxic waste, triggering a bizarre reaction with the snow (since it’s winter). He then transforms into a killer snowman, which is hilariously absurd on its own. The film is undeniably silly, yet it has its comedic moments. Even the killings are oddly amusing. I wouldn’t recommend buying it (like I did—boy, was the cover misleading!), but if it happens to be on TV one night and you’re in the mood for a laugh, go ahead and give it a try.

LOL! Not a bad way to kick things off. I thought this was an original idea, but it turns out it’s just a knockoff of the 1976 remake of *King Kong*. I didn’t watch the original *King Kong* until I was 15, but I caught this movie when I was 9. The film’s funky disco music will definitely stick in your head! And let’s not forget the theme song by the Yetians. Honestly, this has the worst creature effects I’ve ever seen. Despite that, it remains a cult classic among B-movies. Some memorable quotes include: “Take a tranquilizer and go to bed.” “Put the Yeti in your tank and you have Yeti power.” I remember watching this on *Elvira’s Movie Macabre*. There’s a scene where it feels like *King Kong* in reverse—except instead of grabbing the girl and climbing up a building, here he climbs down while grabbing the girl (who was falling)! Around the same time, there was another *King Kong* clone, *Mighty Peking Man* (1977), from Hong Kong. This film features tons of traveling matte scenes and motorized body parts. Ultimately, it’ll leave you laughing. As I said, it’s just another…

First, let me clarify that the average user’s lack of appreciation for imagination is disheartening. What sets this show apart is its ability to create a hyper-realistic world that captivates viewers. You don’t need to understand why Ned can bring people back to life or why it’s limited to just a minute. Where has the sense of wonder from childhood fairytales gone, much like *A Wrinkle in Time*?

I find it refreshingly original because it stands in stark contrast to the over-explanatory, unimaginative TV shows that leave no room for creativity or curiosity.

Adding a touch of escapism to the television experience is a welcome change.

The hyper-realism is my favorite aspect of the show. The 1950s-inspired setting, the endearing and uncommon characters, and the scenery that isn’t meant to be taken literally make it unique.

While other shows delve into the darker aspects of death, this one softens them, making it all the more engaging. It surpasses other entertainment options, restoring a sense of curiosity, imagination, and wonder to television.

*Pushing Daisies* quickly climbed to the top of my list.

I saw this movie many years ago and was quite impressed... at least, that's how I felt at the time because I was only 12 years old. Recently, I revisited it, and I wish I could have those hours back. The film is really terrible. Although I enjoy actors like Lee Majors, Chris Makepeace (check out *My Bodyguard* from 1980 for a GOOD performance from him, or *Meatballs*, which also stars Bill Murray, if you're looking for some entertainment), and Burgess Meredith, this particular role did little to advance their careers.

In the movie, Lee Majors plays Franklyn Hart, an ex-race car driver planning to drive his stored race car across the country to California. The problem? Private transportation has been banned by the government. While the concept wasn't the worst idea I've come across, the way it was executed was disastrous.

This movie serves as a perfect illustration of how even amusing jokes can fall flat. I had high hopes for it after watching the hilarious trailer, but the film failed to deliver half as much entertainment. 

What's strange is that the humor itself—like the parodies of the smoking ban and Jo Bole...—is genuinely good. Yet, I'm unsure who to hold responsible for its failure. Potential culprits include: 1) the underwhelming actors and actresses, 2) the director, or 3) the person responsible for casting both. If you're extremely bored, give it a watch, though I'd recommend instead grabbing the movie's ads or teasers for a far more enjoyable laugh.

On a positive note, the only亮点s in this film are Mahesh Manjrekar and the amusing Chappu Bhai.

A thoroughly unpleasant film, it boasts impressively stomach-churning special effects by Rick Baker but offers no other redeeming qualities. Similar to many 1970s films, it leaves viewers feeling contaminated, as though they need a long shower to wash away the slime. The characters are uniformly unlikable, and the plot is nonsensical.

In "The Omen IV," the malevolent legacy of Damien Thorn resurfaces in the form of Delia York, born Asia Vieila, who seeks to terrorize those around her — including her adoptive parents, schoolmates, neighbors, and ultimately, the entire world. Plucked from the St. Francis orphanage by the devout but misguided Yorks, Karen and Gene (played by Fay Grant and Michael Woods), Delia quickly reveals her dark nature.

From the moment she arrives, Delia makes her presence known. At a house party, she scratches her mother, setting the tone for the chaos to come. A near-fatal encounter with a runaway truck is thwarted when a mysterious "Devil Dog" named Ryder saves her. In school, Delia exacts swift revenge on a local bully by publicly humiliating him, causing him to wet himself in front of his peers. When her adoptive father’s legal threats against the Yorks escalate, Delia orchestrates a fatal car accident, slicing off his head.

Elsewhere, Delia’s adoptive father, Gene, enjoys rising prominence in his community after being elected to Congress as an advocate for clean air and green spaces. Unbeknownst to him, his meteoric rise may be tied to his unwitting role in fostering Delia's sinister ambitions.

This story lacked any original ideas, borrowing themes from numerous sources, including "The Ninth Gate," "In the Mouth of Madness" (another Carpenter film), and "The Ring." It even reused the infamous glowing circle from "The Ring" as its central motif. The soundtrack by Cody Carpenter felt like a direct rip-off of "Suspiria." Let’s not kid ourselves with the term "homage"—seeing "Deep Red" playing in the theater doesn’t justify such blatant copying. This was rock-bottom material. Simply throwing gore and unsettling visuals into the mix does not make for a good horror film. Carpenter used to understand this, so he should either retire or find a time machine.

I saw this film at a screening during the Sundance Film Festival and was utterly awestruck by its undeniable impact. It delves into the psychological consequences faced by courageous soldiers who enlist with the hope of serving their country with dignity, expecting proper care from the government in return. The movie intricately captures the transformation soldiers undergo in boot camp, where they are molded into "killers for their country," sent off to war, and explores the lingering effects upon their return home. It also sheds light on how taking a life affects the human mind. Unlike other films, this one honors soldiers without casting judgment on them, instead critiquing a system that fails to address the full range of physical and psychological needs of returning veterans.

This film is powerful, poignant, and emotionally stirring, leaving viewers deep in thought. It serves as a rallying cry to genuinely support our troops—not just through symbolic gestures like stickers or parades—but by actively listening to them and advocating for improved care and well-being.

Director Vincenzo Natali brought a stylish flair to this film, employing intriguing camera angles and impactful close-ups. It was particularly refreshing to see Jeremy Northam and Lucy Liu take on leading roles, showcasing their versatility as actors. The movie also featured one of the most inventive "escape" scenes in recent cinema history. The collaboration between the director and the talented cast resulted in a compelling thriller.

Despite a convoluted plot, the storyline unfolded clearly as it exposed layers of corporate greed and deceit. 

In 1949, George Orwell's seminal novel "1984" envisioned a future dominated by a totalitarian state controlling both minds and personal freedoms. It was thought-provoking that, in this engaging futuristic film, the corporate world—not the state—was portrayed as the entity manipulating and devaluing human workers.

In truth, the scene where the puppies watched *Lady and the Tramp* while Chloe and Kevin enjoyed dinner was better than I anticipated. I also enjoyed the parrot pretending to be a dog, and it was impressive how well the dogs had been trained for their roles.

To begin with, the well-known actors likely needed the money. The surgical scenes were comical at best. It’s hard to believe that anyone with even basic medical knowledge wouldn’t find these portrayals completely unrealistic. Anesthesiologists never leave the operating room during a heart transplant, and such surgeries certainly aren’t performed in cramped spaces lacking essential equipment, heart-lung machines, or proper sterile techniques. This film is more of a farce than anything else, making it nearly impossible to focus on the storyline due to the ridiculousness of the surgical sequences. Halloween tells the story of a boy who grew up misunderstood. As an adult, he channels his frustrations onto his older sister, whom he kills early in the film. This marks the beginning of the terror unleashed by Michael Myers. 

Donald Pleasance portrays a doctor who has spent years studying Myers. He senses something uniquely sinister about him, an evil that cannot be contained or stopped. 

After escaping from an institution, Myers sets out to find his younger sister, believing that killing her might finally put an end to his torment. However, his efforts are repeatedly thwarted as he encounters others who get in his way. Despite these obstacles, he continues his relentless pursuit of the one person he seeks. 

Countless horror films have since featured masked or grotesque killers hacking apart teenagers. Yet, this movie essentially paved the way for many of them. Think about it—most of the classic horror films we remember involve characters like Freddy Krueger or Jason stalking nearly naked victims. If it weren’t for...

For those who have experienced and fallen in love with the stage musical *A Chorus Line*, the movie feels like a poor substitute. Not only are several songs omitted, but unnecessary plot twists are introduced, new dance sequences are choreographed, and let’s be honest—Richard Attenborough simply doesn’t know how to capture the essence of dancers on film.

Onstage, *A Chorus Line* was pure Michael Bennett: his vision, his choreography, his direction, and his monumental gift to Broadway and beyond. It was two intense hours of raw, unflinching realism that truly made you empathize with the “boys” and “girls” on stage. In contrast, the film version lacks emotional depth and authenticity: the actors appear to be auditioning *for* *A Chorus Line* rather than embodying the experience itself. Every movement and line of dialogue feels overly calculated and staged. Michael Douglas, in particular, portrays Zach as far too controlled to make him believable as the volatile choreographer. Even during his tantrums, it’s hard to suspend disbelief because every gesture, inflection, and subtle detail appears painstakingly rehearsed. And as for his lack of dancing prowess, Kevin Kline originally auditioned for the role on Broadway. While Michael Bennett admired Kline’s performance, his inability to dance ultimately led to his exclusion from the role.

He portrays the character with originality, boldness, and profound humanity. I deeply regret that sequels were never produced.

This independent film stood out as one of the best I've seen at the Tall Grass Film Festival. I absolutely loved it; there were countless aspects that made it incredible. Adding to its brilliance, the cast and crew I had the chance to meet were exceptional. Avi delivered an impressive performance, and Ricky Ullman truly embodied his character. As a Disney actor, he impressed me with his ability to transition seamlessly from lighthearted teen comedies to a more mature role. The talent showcased in the film was remarkable, and the cinematography was outstanding. If you're looking for a must-see indie film, this is definitely it. I believe Mr. Gruver would have been proud to have such a submission at his festival, and his parents enjoyed it so much that they watched it twice after it won the Audience Favorite award. This film was dark, humorous, poignant, and deeply emotional—truly fantastic. I’m genuinely thrilled by it and can’t stop thinking about how incredible it was.

Great fun for both adults and kids, this film excels on multiple levels, featuring everything from high-octane car crashes to playful pie-in-the-face moments, while also sneaking in clever, adult-oriented humor that’s both witty and understated. Glenn Close delivers a masterclass in villainy as Cruella ("call me Ella") De Ville, showcasing her remarkable ability to embody sublime evil. Having spent three years in Dr. Pavlov's Behavior Modification Clinic, she overcomes her obsession with fur—even the controversial puppy-skin variety—and donates all her fur coats to the dungeon of her extraordinary castle. However, no *Dalmatian* movie would be complete without Cruella’s conniving schemes, and it doesn’t take long for her to devise a new plan involving one final puppy (hence *102 Dalmatians*) to execute her latest sinister plot.

Ioan Gruffudd shines as the charming protagonist who runs the "Second Chance" dog shelter. Although I recognized him from his role in *Titanic* (as Fifth Officer Lowe), I didn’t connect him to his portrayal in last year’s TV adaptation of *Great Expectations* (as Pip). Gerard Depardieu also makes an appearance.

At a time when Hollywood profits by showcasing our vulnerabilities, despair, crime, drugs, and warfare, this film emerges as a beacon of hope, reminding us of the "Indomitable Spirit." If you're feeling weighed down, this movie will liberate your mind and inspire you to rise above. Life can be challenging, but we occasionally need to be reminded that perseverance and bravery will see us through. This is precisely what the film did for me, and I hope it does the same for you.

I still have grainy, late-night VHS copies of this show from way back, complete with no cable, cheap dubs, and late-night commercials. I’d stay up until whenever they aired the show, just so I could record it.

The series wasn’t really about Freddy Krueger—only the first few episodes featured him as more than a Rod Serling-esque narrator. Each episode was its own distinct nightmare, exploring traditional horror themes like horrific childhoods, dating, cannibalism, money, death, and... well, mostly dating. 

There was an episode where a teenage boy accidentally confesses “I will love you forever” to the wrong girl, and gets stuck with her—literally, as they start growing together. Another had a young flight attendant going home with a mysterious man, only to discover his trophy room filled with the preserved bodies of other flight attendants. There was even one I can’t fully recall, where blind dates were compared to hockey (with all its injuries and penalties). Dating was hands-down the scariest part of the series. 

In one episode, Jeffrey Combs (of *Re-Animator* fame) played a driven pizza delivery guy who…

A deliriously romantic comedy filled with intertwining subplots that come together seamlessly, "Moonstruck" boasts actors with impeccable comic timing, creating a performance that is a joy to watch. When Cher’s spineless fiancé asks her to help reconcile with his estranged, brooding younger brother, no one could anticipate the chain of events that unfolds. From operatic symbolism and Catholic confessions to love bites and falling snow, the film is both timeless and effortless. While the pacing lags slightly in the first 15 minutes—particularly during a scene with the grandfather and his dogs at the cemetery and another with Cosmo and an elderly man at the gate—the plot ultimately weaves its threads with graceful precision. The movie’s quirky charm and unpredictable tone prove contagious. ***1/2 out of ****.

John Boorman's "Deliverance" tells the story of four suburban Atlantans embarking on a journey down the rapid waters of the Cahulawassee River. Soon to be submerged due to the construction of a dam, the river flows through the last uncharted stretches of wild terrain.

Each of the four friends embodies distinct personalities: a rugged sports enthusiast who eschews insurance because he sees no significant risks in life (Burt Reynolds); a devoted family man and talented guitarist (Ronny Cox); an overweight bachelor working as an insurance salesman (Ned Beatty); and a reserved, contemplative family man who enjoys smoking his pipe (Jon Voight).

What ensues is a harrowing descent into the unforgiving brutality of nature, as well as a profound exploration of how civilized individuals confront the primal forces of the wilderness. 

Brilliantly filmed, this gripping adult thriller features several genuinely suspenseful moments.

Certainly! Here's the rewritten version:

"A quick addition to the previous comment: *Fear of a Black Hat* doesn’t feature the criminal whose image was stolen by the band, that’s in *CB4*. The two movies are easily mixed up since they’re quite similar, but *Fear of a Black Hat* is undoubtedly the better film. Yeah."

How can you take seriously the tale of a hard-living, glamorously violent bounty hunter with *that* accent? It's laughable. On top of that, the director's visual style feels nauseatingly gimmicky, the plot is a shallow, uninspired rehash of a generic gangster movie, and the performances lack credibility. The film introduces new characters continuously and employs fragmented flashbacks—mostly out of sequence—for no apparent reason other than to confuse viewers. It even shows scenes that appear to happen but later claims they didn’t, like the supposed murder of the fake "first ladies." If those initial events were false, why were they shown at all? 

The poor casting choices, convoluted narrative, and headache-inducing direction make this a frustrating watch. 1/5.

I first watched this movie many years ago on a black-and-white TV in a tiny Samoan village, and at the time, I found it absolutely hilarious. However, having revisited it now after such a long gap, I no longer find it amusing. In fact, I rarely laugh at anything these days. That said, this is still a clever and lighthearted comedy that flows smoothly without faltering, and I truly enjoyed it.

Set in 1945, the story follows Fred MacMurray, a 4F who desperately wants to join one of the armed forces. While working in a scrapyard, he rubs an old lamp and a genie emerges, ready to grant his wishes. (Sure, it might sound cliché, but even though the setup isn’t exceptional, the subsequent fantasies are quite lively.) MacMurray requests to be part of the army, and instantly, he’s marching alongside Washington’s troops.
