They arrive at a particularly cozy USO, where June Haver and Joan Leslie are adorned with what looks like lace doilies and lavender wigs. Washington tasks MacMurray with spying on the enemy—red-coated, German-speaking Hessians, not the British. The Hessians are packed into a Bierstube, singing an amusing drinking song celebrating the glories of the Vaterland, “where the...”

This movie is great—provided you’re a fan of B-movies. It’s a quintessential 1980s college slasher flick, featuring the same song playing repeatedly throughout the soundtrack. Terrible, yes, but it’s definitely worth renting for a good laugh or to enjoy watching awkward moments like old men jumping out of closets with knives. Pretty amusing, if you ask me.

This movie is uplifting for anyone who has ever faced a difficult situation, whether financial or emotional. It’s sure to make you laugh, which is the best remedy! :) After her husband passes away, leaving her in a tough financial spot, Grace must find a new way to earn money, and while it’s not entirely lawful, this adds to the humor. Even my boyfriend enjoyed it, so don’t dismiss it as just a “chick flick.”

Two houses, one street, a phone booth, a car, a girl next door, a boy next door, and a zombie—these elements form the perfect recipe for a horror movie. Add some blue lighting, eerie background music, and you're set. At least, that’s how it works for most filmmakers. But not for Dutch director van Rouveroy!  

Every now and then, I host "bad movie nights," where friends and I enjoy the worst cinema has to offer while sipping on drinks. And this movie is one of the crown jewels for such occasions. Guaranteed laughter!  

What’s strange is that van Rouveroy seems proud of this mess. To experience her defense firsthand, you’ll have to listen to the DVD commentary. Once again: disbelief and laughter guaranteed!

I generally avoid TV movies since you can tell it’s one within the first five seconds of watching. However, this particular film caught my attention due to its intriguing title and the somber, expertly crafted atmosphere that was immediately established. Although the constant rain reinforced my suspicion that the setting might be off (despite being set in California, much of the movie was filmed in stormy Vancouver, B.C.), the dreary outdoor environment perfectly enhanced Olmos' exceptional performance.

Caution: May contain spoilers...  

I’ve watched this movie three times, and I’ve enjoyed it each time. Every viewing reminds me just how great it is. As an HBO TV movie—typically of high quality—it deserved Oscar nominations for its performances if it hadn’t been made for television but rather released for general audiences.  

As anyone familiar with reviews likely knows, this film tells the true story of the Soviet Union’s infamous serial killer, Andrei Chikatilo, who murdered 56 people over eight years in the former USSR. Despite the efforts to locate all his victims, three bodies were never found, leaving him officially charged with 52 out of 53 confirmed killings. While the narrative centers on Chikatilo, it primarily follows forensic analyst Victor Burakov, portrayed masterfully by Stephen Rea. Burakov becomes deeply fixated on catching the killer, even as bureaucratic interference from party officials complicates his work. His role in the story is pivotal. One particularly poignant moment near the end highlights how, in the U.S., investigators are often reassigned or taken off serial murder cases after 18 months, regardless of their personal desires, due to the immense emotional toll.

I had high hopes for this film, especially with James Spader, one of my favorite actors, in the lead role. Unfortunately, it fell flat. By the end of the first half-hour, I was ready to fast-forward through the rest, clutching the remote control. The plot was clichéd and predictable, with scenes and dialogue so formulaic that you can practically recite them word for word. It's one of those films that leaves you wondering how it ever got made. On a slightly positive note, there are a few mildly engaging special effects. Overall, though, if you've seen five sci-fi movies or are older than nine, save yourself the time and skip this one entirely.

Alan Alda portrays real-life "Sports Illustrated" writer George Plimpton, who was famously invited to join the Detroit Lions football team as an honorary member. This rather uninspired and lackluster drama oddly mixes elements of fantasy. Director Alex March takes an intriguing approach to the material, filming it in a quasi-documentary style with bold, macho narration, while also infusing it with a touch of Capra-esque whimsy. However, by emphasizing cinematic flair in this setup, the central storyline becomes convoluted. Alda’s smug and uncharismatic performance poses another challenge, though the supporting cast includes actual professional athletes and a standout turn by Lauren Hutton as Alda’s girlfriend—a touch of fantasy indeed. **1/2 out of ****.

A brief synopsis  

The film begins with soldiers leaving their all-male environment. One follows another with a peculiar plan that the latter consistently rejects. Later, both find themselves trapped in an office building, attempting to crack a safe during the Christmas holiday. What starts as hostility evolves into playful banter and ultimately becomes a life-or-death struggle (as they joke around, all drinkable liquids are lost, making the situation dire). Shirtless and muscular, they break through a wall and manage to escape—only to discover they’ve been double-crossed by women. One is captured while the other remains free, shielded by his partner’s silence. In their final meeting, they share one last cigarette before parting ways with a poignant farewell.  

I couldn’t help but perceive hints of closeted homosexuality in the relationship between the two leads, portrayed by macho icons Alain Delon and Charles Bronson. Their attraction to each other is undeniable, and their interactions with women are consistently dismissive and contemptuous. The narrative carries a symbolic undercurrent, reminiscent of *Deliverance*, with layers of subtext that make it particularly compelling.

I caught this a few nights ago, not having high expectations—and predictably, it failed to deliver anything particularly thrilling. The premise—a team of vampire hunters (V-San, for "vampire sanitation") traveling through space in their ship, routinely exterminating space vampires and saving people—is actually pretty solid. With better execution, the film could have been surprisingly enjoyable. Unfortunately, after a reasonably strong start, the quality begins to wane significantly, leaving behind something that’s mildly entertaining but hilariously awful. I don’t expect miracles from movies on the Sci Fi Channel, and at least this one avoided the usual pitfall of featuring an embarrassing CGI monster trudging around like a disaster—but it was still pretty糟糕, largely due to the writing and acting. The music, however, deserves special mention for its spectacular contribution to the overall cheesiness. While the soundtrack’s occasional sci-fi-inspired odd noises worked adequately, the overuse of hilariously bad soft rock completely derailed scenes, pushing them into absurdity. I might have forgiven the general cheesiness of the acting and writing if only the music hadn’t been so...

I’ve rarely watched online movies throughout my life, but if I had to choose one, it would be *Spatula Madness*. This clever parody of films like *Star Wars* (and others) showcases Jason Steele’s talent. Using a camera and a sharp wit, he transforms ordinary images into paintings, then animates them frame by frame to create a world populated by spatulas. The story starts in the middle, how’s that for a director's twist? Then the middle becomes the beginning, and so on. When I first saw it, I anticipated a grainy, pixelated aesthetic, but Jason, like me, is obsessed with visuals, so he pushed every detail to perfection. While I wouldn’t recommend it for children, and I’m not sure anyone else would enjoy it as much as I do, I urge you to search it up online (it’s a short film by Film Cow). Its style reminds me of *South Park*, but with less violence. It earns a 10 for visuals, 6 for humor, and 6 for the storyline, making it a solid 10/10 overall. Great work!  

Jason Steele, I’m eager to see what you create next.

Hello! This movie is... well... okay. Just kidding! IT’S AWESOME! It’s not a blockbuster smash hit, and it’s not supposed to be. But it’s a huge hit in my world—and my sister’s too. We’re total Ramones fans. GO RAMONES!! This is a great movie... for me!

At first glance, this film might seem unsettling, especially for those like me who have a fear of dentists. It's creepy and uncomfortable enough to make viewers squirm, which is part of its charm. However, its slow pace costs it some points. I deduct 3 stars for that reason alone. 

*Warning: Spoilers Ahead*  

The story centers on Dr. Alan Feinstone, whose life spirals into chaos after discovering his wife’s infidelity. Haunted by hallucinations, he descends into madness, torturing his patients, eliminating colleagues, and brutally murdering both his unfaithful spouse and her lover.

*End Spoiler*

This movie is undeniably graphic and violent. If you're a fan of gore, it will likely appeal to you.  

All things considered, I rate this film 7 out of 10 stars. Dr. Alan Feinstone certainly isn’t your average dentist!

An independent film can now be viewed as both a work of cinematic art and a video résumé. Step into *Broken*, a boldly promoted, twenty-minute short film brimming with style and enthusiasm. But the question remains: is it compelling as a movie, or does it function solely as a demonstration piece? That, indeed, is the challenge.

*Broken* tells the story of Bonnie Clayton, who is kidnapped by a "sadistic stranger and his colorful entourage" (as stated on the video cover) after waking from a recurring nightmare one night. Held captive, Bonnie discovers unsettling truths about herself that even she was unaware of. As her captors interrogate her, a black-clad soldier bursts into their hideout in a rescue attempt, leading to chaos and confusion.

Thankfully, director Alex Ferrari appears to have a clear vision, or perhaps he’s adept at creating the illusion of one. *Broken* shines with undeniable visual flair, a feat particularly impressive given its limited budget and the inexperience of those involved. However, it stumbles when it comes to its writing, which feels weak and somewhat derivative. Picture *Long Kiss Goodnight* meeting *The Matrix*, crafted hurriedly after a quick read of *Fight Club*.

"Deliverance" is a gripping thriller, every bit as exhilarating as a great thriller should be, yet it's also intensely and viscerally frightening. Although it’s not a horror film, it evokes the same dread as classic horror cinema. The idea of being an average, red-blooded man enjoying an adventurous weekend far from civilization, only to be overpowered and brutalized by a pair of violent backwoodsmen, is undoubtedly the worst fear of nearly 99.9% of the global population. It would have been simple for "Deliverance" to descend into exploitative territory, but director John Boorman skillfully avoids this pitfall, crafting a film that delves into, questions, and challenges the very essence of masculinity. In so many movies, you walk away longing to inhabit the hero’s shoes, relishing their bravery and triumphs—but with "Deliverance," you leave thankful to never face the harrowing experiences endured by these four protagonists.

Four urbanites—a diverse group including Ed (Jon Voight), Lewis (Burt Reynolds), Drew (Ronny Cox), and Bobby (Ned Beatty)—set off into the wilderness for a few days of respite and adventure.

It surprises me that critics enjoyed this film, as its plot is convoluted, and its characters feel lifeless. Michael Bowen spends much of the movie spying on others, yet consistently misreading them. None of the characters possess likable traits or engaging qualities. This isn’t an edgy or imaginative piece; it lacks irony or wit. Instead, it’s a dreary, confusing effort. Its failure to secure a theatrical release isn’t surprising. That “This Network” airs it only cheapens their programming. I strongly suggest watching a rerun of *GardenSMART* on PBS or something equally informative if you come across this mess late at night. If it appears during the day, go for a walk instead—even in smog, you’ll feel better avoiding this trainwreck. Life is short, and this movie is far too long.

I genuinely enjoyed this movie—it was delightful. However, if you didn’t like it, that’s on you. Emma Roberts delivered a solid performance as Nancy Drew, though she differs from the book character. The vintage outfits seemed odd in a modern context, but she pulled them off well. Personally, I thought the wealthy characters’ outfits lacked sophistication; it felt like they picked them out blindfolded at a garage sale. Most of the clothing choices were questionable, especially the penny loafers paired with casual outfits. I don’t mean to knock the film—it’s great! So head to the theater and give it a watch. Trust me, you’ll have a good time!

"People I Know" is a disappointing film with little to root for and no characters to truly care about, despite the valiant efforts of a skilled cast. 

Al Pacino gives his signature powerhouse performance as Eli Wurman, a once-prominent publicist whose morality has eroded over time. However, unlike Michael Corleone, it’s difficult to form any emotional connection to this character, his predicament, or his future. 

The story follows Eli as he prepares for a political fundraiser, juggling this responsibility with a client’s (Ryan O’Neal, solid in an underwritten role) latest scandal — involving a TV actress embroiled with unsavory types. Tea Leoni brings her typical charisma to her supporting part, though the script offers her limited material to work with. Meanwhile, Kim Basinger elicits sympathy as Eli’s sister-in-law, even amid contrived plot devices. 

This movie will appeal primarily to fans of Pacino and the other lead actors. Regrettably, both the writing and direction feel amateurish, which explains its brief theatrical run and quick transition to DVD. Proceed at your own discretion.

I understand why this film was nominated for an Oscar for Best Live Action Short—it was crafted with exceptional skill. Even if you're not a fan of the Blues (though to me, it sounded more like jazz), you can still appreciate its quality. The film is undeniably well-made. However, I can't comprehend why director Gjon Mili only helmed this one movie. While the film received recognition, it didn’t seem to launch his career. Similarly, the Black performers in the film likely didn’t experience a significant boost in their careers, as much of white society remains indifferent—or worse—to either them or their music.

If you watch this film and find yourself less engaged at first, skip ahead to around the 5:50 mark; the pace improves significantly. Once the singer paused and the musicians started improvising, the energy and flow of the film became much more engaging.

This film holds great appeal for a fairly specific audience, one that doesn’t include me. I attended a preview without much expectation and left feeling disappointed. The story of a deeply troubled (and often outright "distorted") Hungarian Jewish family simply isn't my kind of narrative. An epic tale like this should deliver greater depth or insight to its viewers. At its core, such films explore the human condition, yet this one sheds little new light on any of its more significant themes.

I have no interest in rap or ghetto culture; as a white person who prefers classic rock, this comedy still managed to win me over. It’s essentially a sequel to *This Is Spinal Tap*, but instead of rock, it focuses on rap. Despite its similarities, it’s incredibly hilarious. While there are plenty of laugh-out-loud moments, some jokes don’t quite land. The characters are funny and feel genuine. I tuned in simply because it made me laugh at 3 a.m., which is enough reason for any film to earn at least a test screening. What made this movie particularly amusing was how it pokes fun at rap from an outsider’s perspective. Today’s rap often prioritizes flash over substance, relying on studio polish and minimal talent. This film hails from an era when rappers were more deserving of respect. Overall, it’s a humorous movie filled with jokes about racism, sex, and music culture, among other comedic themes. Fans of *This Is Spinal Tap* will love this—it’s essentially the same concept, just set in a different world, and the humor works equally well in both.

I’m not entirely convinced that Rob Schmidt qualifies as a "Master" within the horror genre, given that his only previous foray into the field was directing the somewhat forgettable "Wrong Turn," which barely surpassed mediocrity. However, it’s undeniable that he delivered one of the most chilling and captivating episodes of the second season of the "Masters of Horror" series with "Right to Die." Interestingly, there was a similar tale of unexpected brilliance in the first season when William Malone crafted an exceptional episode titled "The Fair Haired Child," despite his full-length features, "Fear Dot Com" and "House on Haunted Hill," being largely disappointing.

"Right to Die" skillfully taps into the highly relevant contemporary debate surrounding euthanasia while seamlessly weaving in classic horror elements such as ghostly retribution, sinister conspiracies, dark humor, and exaggerated, comic-book-style violence. As Cliff and Abby Addison drive home late one night, engaged in a heated discussion about Cliff’s repeated infidelity, they find themselves caught up in a devastating car crash. Cliff escapes unscathed, but Abby suffers severe burns and requires life support. Meanwhile, Cliff and his slimy lawyer (Corbin Bernsen of "The Dentist") begin plotting...

I’ll acknowledge that I didn’t give this movie much of a chance. Early on, I decided it wasn’t really my type of film. 

For the most part, it shines in its cinematography. The scenes capturing early 1970s Manhattan look fantastic, and the lead actress stands out. The stark black-and-white gives the movie a timeless, almost fresh appearance. However, certain techniques used by the filmmakers completely undermine that impression. The disjointed editing is heavily reminiscent of late-1960s styles, veering into both surrealism and new wave aesthetics. Similarly, the story feels rooted in a particular era—caught between free-love idealism and artistic experimentation. 

The plot revolves around a young woman navigating the city in search of a man she only interacted with via anonymous phone sex. Along the way, she encounters eccentric characters, each revealing their unique quirks. Intended as an offbeat, irreverent comedy with an avant-garde twist, the film might appeal strongly to fans of Andy Warhol’s work. If you’re a fan of his style, *The Telephone Book* may feel like a hidden gem. 

That said, there were a few issues I encountered. For one, near...

While reactions to "The Aristocrats" were polarized, with some adoring it and others walking out mid-show, Eddie Izzard's performances are unlikely to provoke such extremes. Those who can accept a cross-dressing comedian (who insists he likes women) with a penchant for colorful language — enough to make his act resemble one long expletive on network TV — will find plenty to enjoy. His dedicated fans tend to view his work as flawless, but I found this particular show to be uneven at times, occasionally as flat as Izzard's chest, though consistently humorous and occasionally side-splittingly funny. Izzard doesn’t rely on storytelling, punchlines, or manic energy like Robin Williams. Instead, he experiments with ideas, some of which land brilliantly while others, like a routine involving San Francisco's cable cars and Alcatraz, fall completely flat. Despite these missteps, he adeptly moves past the weaker bits and amplifies the stronger connections between his routines. Overall, I rated this performance a 7, and while it wasn’t perfect, it kept me entertained more often than not.

The film received 11 Oscar nominations but didn't win a single award. I still don’t fully grasp why—none of the actors went on to do anything particularly extraordinary afterward that would justify awarding them for minor roles, unlike what happened with Halle Berry and Denzel Washington. Whoopi Goldberg, Oprah Winfrey, Margaret Avery, and Danny Glover all delivered incredible performances, and I’m dying to read the transcripts of the Oscar deliberations that year. It definitely falls into the "Shoulda-woulda-coulda" category for the judges.

The book is fantastic, but Alice Walker’s writing style often makes it seem like she’s overemphasizing her characters, which is why I’m relieved the filmmakers toned some things down for the screen adaptation.

The cinematography was stunning, but the African scenes left much to be desired. In the book, the African setting is meant to be in Liberia, located in West Africa. However, Steven Spielberg seemed to think the world couldn’t picture Africa beyond safaris, so naturally, there had to be a zebra-and-wildlife scene, even though everyone knows that’s not accurate.

I've read the book several times, and this movie doesn’t adhere to it as closely as it should. While I might overlook that to some extent—after all, it is a movie—I have significant problems with how the setting is portrayed. No one seems to mention that both the book and the movie are based on actual events that took place in Nebraska. I live here; I grew up in the town this movie claims to depict. First off, the “small” town mentioned in the story is actually the third-largest city in the state, with a population of around 50,000. Grand Island is the biggest city between Lincoln and Denver. Secondly, the scenery in the movie is inaccurate. Grand Island sits in the Platte River Valley, which is extremely flat with very few trees. Trying to watch this movie made me angry to see my hometown misrepresented so poorly. This was a real event, and large parts of the city were destroyed. In the book, they describe biking from Mormon Island to Fonner Park. You could do that, I suppose, but only if you’re okay cycling about 15 miles.

This is an incredibly compelling film. During my first attempt to watch it, the thick Scottish accents proved challenging, making comprehension difficult and detracting from the overall experience. Eventually, I set it aside but later decided to give it another chance after acquiring the DVD. Using English subtitles helped immensely, and I soon found myself thoroughly engrossed, realizing what a remarkable film it truly is. It’s exceptional.

The widescreen format enhances certain scenes, showcasing breathtaking, rugged landscapes. The storyline bears a resemblance to *Braveheart*, offering an engaging narrative of good against evil. In this case, it’s Liam Neeson representing the forces of good, while Tim Roth embodies the epitome of evil. Both deliver impressive performances.

Few actors can embody despicability quite like Tim Roth. His character is so detestable that viewers may find themselves wanting to punch him square in his smug, obnoxious face. (Ironically, his villainous portrayal is so despised—yet oddly beloved—that it has become the standout performance among critics.) Meanwhile, Liam Neeson embodies a quintessential masculine hero, reminiscent of Mel Gibson’s role in *Braveheart*. Jessica Lange also delivers a commanding performance as the leading lady. The film captivates its audience entirely, ensuring an emotionally charged viewing experience.

Why does every film about Cleopatra, the last pharaoh, bring out the worst in filmmaking? The allure that drew the greatest Roman leaders, Julius Caesar and Mark Antony, seems reduced to nothing more than the exaggerated hormonal escapades of over-sexed high school students on screen. Even with extravagant sets and costumes, this movie is as poor as any 1950s Italian "sandals and toga" spectacle. Admittedly, this type of grandiose production works best on the big screen, which is why "Gladiator" succeeded, but unlike that film, this one leans heavily into romance-novel levels of sexualized drama.

Despite lacking Elizabeth Taylor's charisma, Miss Varela possesses no more acting ability. In contrast, Timothy Dalton showcases abundant talent, yet it’s unfortunate that none of it rubbed off on the rest of the cast.

Whenever people ask me to name the scariest movie I've ever seen, I immediately say "Black Noon," and to this day, no one has ever heard of it.  

I watched it alone about 30 years ago, when I was just 13, while my parents were out for the evening. As far as I know, it was only aired once in the UK and remains unavailable on DVD or VHS.  

If anyone can find a copy, please let me know.  

If I were to watch it again now, it would likely be underwhelming, but it has always stayed with me as an especially unsettling little film!

I was eagerly anticipating this movie due to its previews and the attention it garnered from the press. However, after watching it, I was extremely disappointed. "Slums" is a completely humorless film combined with a disturbing family reality reminiscent of Todd Solondz's work, but without his signature wit. The plot drags on, and each scene is more unbearable than the last. Perhaps I misunderstood the intention, but if this is meant to represent every girl's coming-of-age experience, I'm grateful to be male.

Many thoughts come to mind when considering the concept of captivity, including uninteresting, uninspiring, predictable, mundane, incomprehensible, and dull. 

I once loathed the slasher films of the mid-to-late '90s, which were essentially rip-offs of "Scream." However, the recent wave of "Saw" imitations is making those earlier films seem almost nostalgic by comparison. These new movies target the same demographic that made the original slashers so popular, but they've added an extra layer of depravity that makes their young female audience feel edgy and trendy. 

This film is pure drivel! What on earth has become of Larry Cohen? The last time he was associated with something worthwhile was back in 1993! Still, I wasn’t prepared for just how terrible this project would turn out to be. Were any viewers genuinely shocked when the supposed love interest revealed himself as a psychopath? Anyone who hasn’t seen countless other movies would have been the only ones caught off guard.

This episode is one of the most lighthearted, with the plot feeling more like an opportunity for pure entertainment. However, I enjoyed this carefree approach, making it one of the best episodes purely for its fun factor. Consider this: the crew interacts with characters like the White Rabbit and Alice from Wonderland, a Bengal tiger, a samurai warrior, a knight on horseback who fatally wounds McCoy, and numerous other odd occurrences that only come together meaningfully by the conclusion. Even amidst the peril, it’s impossible to treat everything too seriously—it’s just too enjoyable, and the entire episode has a dreamlike quality. Thus, on a purely non-serious level, it’s fantastic.

Usually, I’m not the type to be scared by horror movies, but this one is an exception. Somehow, this film has stuck in my mind! It’s a very simple movie, yet incredibly effective. The atmosphere it creates is fantastic, leading to some truly shocking moments. The scene where the girl’s father comes down the hill is particularly memorable. Another standout moment was the family photo; I wasn’t prepared for it and literally jumped out of my seat! I highly recommend everyone watch this movie—it will haunt you for a long time if you watch it with the lights off!

The premise might appear silly, but because Murphy's character approaches it lightheartedly, it effectively eases the audience into a blend of mysticism and contemporary hard-boiled child abduction. The outstanding cast, especially Charles Dance and Charlotte Lewis, shines, while Murphy delivers one of his best performances from the peak of his 1980s comedy/action career. The film also features impressive special effects, a highly surreal dream sequence, and an unusually fresh storyline. Frequently overshadowed among Murphy’s movies, this one is definitely worth checking out.

**Warning:** I urge anyone who hasn’t seen the film yet to avoid reading this comment.

Even though I haven’t watched every movie out there, *The Hamiltons* definitely served up a lackluster piece of entertainment—it didn’t entertain me one bit! I found the subpar acting, ridiculous plot, and especially the poorly executed twist at the end utterly cringeworthy. This movie was awful! Oh, apparently these characters consume human flesh. Wait—do they qualify as cannibals, or are they just inbred? Or maybe they’re something else entirely? Are they even human? Ugh, the film never clarified! 

Was it supposed to be mysterious or intentionally vague? Either way, it fell flat. If they’re meant to be “things” studying human taste, then why bother pretending to act like regular folks? And if they’re lifelong cannibals, where’s the payoff? This movie was downright terrible—HORRIBLE, in fact! So, to those who enjoyed *The Hamiltons*, I’d love to know why, because to me, it was just plain bad. Boo to *The Hamiltons*! Instead, check out *The Gravedancers*, *Tooth & Nail*, or *Borderland* for better horror experiences!

"Return of the Jedi" is often criticized for its flaws rather than celebrated for its achievements, which is unfortunate because it stands as a remarkable culmination of the Star Wars saga. This final chapter expertly ties together all the storylines from the earlier films, delivering a satisfying and convincing conclusion.

While the film features Ewoks—adorable creatures introduced to expand the franchise’s audience—and slows down somewhat midway through, the final act is undeniably one of the strongest in the series. It culminates in a breathtaking showdown between Luke and Darth Vader, cinema's most iconic villain.

"Return of the Jedi" gets so much right that audiences often miss its brilliance: it provides a definitive and compelling resolution to the Darth Vader arc, builds excitement with the opening sequence at Jabba’s Palace, showcases Ian McDiarmid’s commanding portrayal of the Emperor, marks Luke’s full emergence as a Jedi, resolves Han and Leia’s romantic tension, and delivers emotionally resonant final moments on the Endor moon.

The portrayal of the UK police in this film seems absurd, with officers depicted as heavily armed and CID officers magically changing into uniform when they leave work to head to the pub. This depiction is one of the least realistic representations of British policing ever shown to the public. It’s hard to understand why accomplished actors like Wesley Snipes and Charles Dance were involved, especially when Snipes may have been motivated by financial troubles but Dance’s inclusion remains baffling.

This movie is even worse than the lowest-budget "B" films from the 1950s. Spending an hour and a half watching it feels like wasted time I’ll never recover. Avoid it at all costs—it’s truly dreadful.

I rarely take the time to write comments, but for this film, I felt compelled to warn others who might expect a comedy. It doesn’t even come close. The concept itself—though poorly executed and already done better countless times—is bad enough, but the transformation of two Black actors into two white women ranks among the least believable in cinematic history. To make matters worse, the script demands that the Wayans brothers not only appear as white women but impersonate two specific individuals. Spoiler alert: they utterly fail. I’ve seen drag queens with minimal makeup look more convincing than these two, despite Hollywood’s top special effects and makeup teams. It’s abysmal. Throw in an NBA player with a physique like a skyscraper, atrocious dialogue, and enough plot holes to host a golf tournament, and this movie sets a new personal low for me—and I enjoy cheesy films! Stay far away from this one—it’s toxic.

Too many sources tend to indiscriminately group this thought-provoking period drama—partly rooted in historical fact—together with the superficially similar "nunsploitation" genre, which dominated '70s Eurotrash cinema, ignoring the righteous anger that propels the entire narrative. Coincidentally or not, it was also director Gianfranco Mingozzi's sole foray into narrative filmmaking outside his acclaimed body of documentary work.

Set securely within a historical framework, *Flavia* follows the burgeoning rebellion of an early 15th-century Italian nun (a career-defining performance by Florinda Bolkan, even eclipsing her stellar work in Lucio Fulci’s *Don’t Torture a Duckling*). Locked away in a convent by her less-than-noble father, who seeks to suppress her emerging sensuality, Flavia questions why women are confined to secondary roles in both life and holy texts. Confronted by the ways male dominance fractures female existence, she is inspired to rebel, driven by the fiery rhetoric of the semi-mad Sister Agatha (memorably played by veteran actress Maria Casarès, known for her role in Marcel Carné’s *Les Enfants du Paradis*) and, more constructively, by a Muslim invasion. Embracing the oppressors and perhaps subtly manipulating them to serve her purposes, Flavia fully embodies the outcast she has long felt herself to be.

Although the title, *The Sword Bearer*, and the DVD cover (which features action-heroic poses of The Sword Bearer) suggest otherwise, this is not a typical superhero film.  

(Minor spoilers ahead) The story follows Sasha, known as The Sword Bearer, who is cursed with a retractable sword in his forearm. While that might sound cool, this is set in the real world. Imagine having such power as a child—how would you handle it if faced with danger, like a deranged person, or if forced to intervene when your mother’s boyfriend is abusing her? If you can’t control it, how do you deal with being responsible for two accidental killings by the age of 12? This is where Sasha finds himself when we first encounter him, wandering aimlessly after another incident, much like in *A Bout de Soufflé*. He meets Katya, and they quickly fall in love, giving Sasha a genuine reason to seek redemption and change his life. However, his troubled past continues to haunt him in the form of two relentless police officers.  

That’s essentially the plot, and while the premise is intriguing, there’s barely any action shown onscreen, even as much of it is implied.  

I genuinely enjoyed this movie. Unlike many Hollywood "superhero" films, we receive very little exposition about Sasha’s backstory. Instead, the focus remains on his emotional journey and the moral complexities of his situation.

Oddly enough, this film never premiered in Danish cinemas, so I had to wait for its video release. My expectations were high, yet they remained thoroughly fulfilled. As usual with Ang Lee, the movie features outstanding performances, an intelligent and gripping storyline that keeps you guessing until the very end, and exceptional cinematography. Alongside "Unforgiven," this is undoubtedly one of the top two westerns of the 1990s.

Those expecting something similar to Mel Gibson's "The Patriot" (corny) or "Braveheart" (acceptable) will be sorely let down. However, viewers who value the aforementioned qualities will thoroughly enjoy the film. 9 out of 10.

Before I continue, I must admit that I’m a massive Bon Jovi fan. In fact, that’s what initially drew me to the DVD case. I likely would have purchased it regardless, given my love for horror movies and my enjoyment of the first *Vampires* film. 

However, this sequel doesn’t come close. Not even Jon Bon Jovi could salvage it for me. My primary issue is that it simply isn’t scary. Aside from Jon’s character, Derek Bliss, none of the other characters leave much of an impression, and you don’t really care whether they live or die—especially the irritating vampire/drug addict character. The female vampire isn’t remotely scary or seductive; instead, she looks like an anorexic 14-year-old, which explains why she’s so desperate for blood. Another significant flaw is that everything feels overly bright. There’s no atmosphere or sense of dread. While the first *Vampires*, set in New Mexico, wasn’t particularly creepy, it still managed to feel dark and ominous when necessary. This movie lacks any tension like that. 

The plot is essentially...

In *"The Kennel Murder Case,"* William Powell makes his final appearance as the suave sleuth Philo Vance. The story begins with the mysterious murder of a champion show dog, which sets off a chain of events leading to two more murders and one attempted killing of a human nature. Unraveling the connections between these crimes is key to uncovering the "who" and "why."

S.S. Van Dine’s Philo Vance mysteries were immensely popular during their time, and Van Dine ingeniously sold his books to different studios, ensuring a wide range of adaptations. This explains why there are so many Philo Vance films across multiple studios. Had Powell not achieved even greater acclaim as Nick Charles in the *Thin Man* series for MGM, he might well have been remembered as the definitive Philo Vance.

The plot thickens when it’s revealed that Powell’s own little terrier, Captain, competed in the same contest as the murdered dog. A rival owner becomes the first victim, and as expected, Powell outshines Eugene Palette’s Sergeant Heath, whose main contribution involves using his physical presence to break down a locked door concealing the first murder victim.

This series takes place a year after the mission to Abydos depicted in the movie *Stargate*. It fills in many details left unexplained in the film, such as how the Stargate functioned without a human operator, the origins of the Goa'uld (Ra's race), and their numbers. 

In the first episode, retired Colonel Jack O'Neill (spelled with two Ls) is recalled to active duty by General George Hammond following an attack on Earth by the reactivated Stargate, orchestrated by Apophis, a powerful Goa'uld who killed four men and abducted one woman. Viewers meet Dr. Samantha Carter, a highly intelligent scientist who insists she should have accompanied the first expedition through the Stargate and is now determined to join the mission. It’s revealed that Daniel Jackson married on Abydos, and there are countless Stargate addresses they can explore. Tragically, Daniel’s wife is captured by Apophis and becomes his new queen.

The second episode sees General Hammond announce the creation of the Stargate Command (SGC), which includes nine teams, with Jack’s team named SG-1, comprising Jack, Samantha, and Daniel. Their first mission is to infiltrate Chulak, a Goa’uld homeworld, to rescue Daniel’s wife.

There are countless negative reviews of *Stay Away, Joe* here, and I simply couldn’t remain silent any longer while this injustice continued. Let me share a perspective you might not have encountered yet.

Elvis Presley’s films are my guilty pleasure, and the reason is straightforward: they’re ideal for pure relaxation because I don’t need to think while watching them. There’s no complex plot to follow since these movies rarely have one to begin with. All I have to do is kick off my shoes, grab a beer, lean back, turn off my brain, and savor the overall zaniness along with those unforgettable, easygoing rock ‘n’ roll tunes from the grooviest era of all time.

In my opinion, *Stay Away, Joe* firmly belongs in the “so bad it’s good” category. If you’re like me and value “trash value,” this is the quintessential 1960s camp experience. It’s so poorly made that it borders on being surreal to watch, and just when you think it couldn’t possibly get worse, it somehow manages to surprise you in the most unexpected ways. By the end, you’re so taken aback by its sheer stupidity that you’re left wondering whether to laugh or...

This film boasts a strong cast, but for a thriller, it needs more than just recognizable names and dialogue. The first third of the movie consisted almost entirely of talking—endless conversations, most of which involved women complaining to one another about everything under the sun. 

With the first five actors listed being women, it’s clear this is essentially a "chick flick" and little else. It likely airs on networks like Lifetime. 

There was a brief murder scene early on, followed by more talking. By the midpoint, I was already checked out. 

Oh, and Sally Field looked remarkably youthful, appearing closer to 15 years old rather than her actual age.

I had assumed the French couldn’t make a bad movie, but I was evidently mistaken. As noted previously, this film uses its titular subject primarily as a starting point; its depiction of her life and persona bears little to no resemblance to the actual Artemisia Gentileschi. 

The screenplay is dreadful—pretentious, stilted, and vacuous—and its manipulation of historical facts is particularly egregious, even for a genre that frequently thrives on distortion rather than accuracy. While the production boasts commendable set design, Valentina Cervi’s attractiveness is the film’s main draw. From the outset, it’s clear the creators were conscious of this, as they hastily devise numerous “erotic” scenes designed more for arousal than narrative progression or character depth. Regrettably, the allure of watching an attractive young woman simulate sexual excitement fails to carry the film. The performances are forgettable, and the score, though occasionally intriguing, remains largely uninspired. The cinematography is adequate, featuring vibrant colors, yet also includes some questionable artistic choices.

*Things to Come* is a rarity, a film centered on ideas. While many movies depict visions of the future, few explore how those futures come into being. The initial segment, where war devastates Everytown, is brief yet impactful. (Ironically, when the film premiered, audiences dismissed reports of enemy planes attacking England as absurd, as appeasement was at its peak. Wells' prophecy would tragically prove accurate far sooner than anticipated.) The subsequent montage of unending warfare, despite subpar special effects, remains highly effective. The explanatory intertitles echo the stark, angular aesthetic of German Expressionist graphic design. Art director William Cameron Menzies crafted the ruins of Everytown with remarkable skill, showcasing some of his finest work. Margaretta Scott delivers a captivating performance as the Chief’s mistress. The futuristic Everytown design for the 21st century is equally striking. However, the acting in the later storyline lacks depth—perhaps an unsuccessful effort to contrast the rationality of this era with the barbarism of 1970. Regrettably, the model work depicting angry crowds on elevated walkways is hilariously poor and could have been executed far better, even with 1930s technology. This oversight is particularly disappointing.

This film, much like Fred Astaire's *Royal Wedding* (which aired after it on the Turner Classic Network last night), is renowned for a single memorable musical sequence that cemented Gene Kelly's legacy. In a scene reminiscent of Astaire's iconic dance with a clothing rack and later his gravity-defying dance around a room's walls and ceiling, Kelly is seen dancing in a cartoon sequence alongside Jerry Mouse. The sequence is beautifully executed. However, what often goes unnoticed is the context Kelly provides. He narrates the story behind the cartoon to Dean Stockwell and his fellow child classmates at school during a break, setting the stage by encouraging the children to visualize a pastoral backdrop. Kelly even transforms his navy uniform into an exaggerated white "Pomeranian" version with blue stripes for the fantasy. 

Jerry Mouse doesn't just dance with Kelly; he also speaks—a rarity for him that wouldn’t occur again for many years. Additionally, he gives Tom Cat his comeuppance, briefly appearing as King Jerry’s butler, attempting to cheer him up with a tray of cheeses.

Though the cartoon sequence with Kelly is striking, it’s worth remembering the narrative foundation Kelly lays beforehand, bringing the audience into the imaginative world he creates.

I didn't watch this movie until I purchased the tape last year, but it captivated and delighted me instantly. It contains every element I adore in a sci-fi story, whether in a book or on screen—social commentary, speculation, and a compelling narrative. 

It’s both unsettling and amusing to observe a 1936 portrayal of the "far-off future" in the 1960s and '70s. 

In my opinion, it’s a must-see film, not just for sci-fi enthusiasts, but for everyone.

"Flame in, flame out." That pretty much sums up Gammera, the prehistoric beast capable of dishing out and enduring destruction with equal fervor. Not usually a fan of Japanese monster movies, I found myself watching every film in Mill Creek/Treeline Films' fifty-film sci-fi DVD collection, which is a steal at around $25—essentially 50 cents per movie. Of course, the real cost is the time invested to enjoy some of these quirky offerings.

Awoken from his centuries-long slumber by a nuclear explosion, Gammera isn’t exactly pleased. Similar to Godzilla, he unleashes chaos on Tokyo, prompting the United Nations to scramble for a solution. Enter "Plan Z," humanity's last hope. A nice touch occurs when a large shed labeled the "Z Plan" building appears in a scene. 

Even by the mid-1960s, this country hadn’t fully embraced political correctness. In one American military segment set at the Alaskan Air Defense Sector, General Arnold asks a female sergeant to make coffee.

Sure! Here's the rewritten version:

You know, I went to see "The Hills Have Eyes 2" hoping to enjoy it. I genuinely loved the original, and while the remake was entertaining enough, they clearly had a bigger budget for special effects this time around compared to Wes Craven’s efforts. Although I still favor the first film, the sequel was well-made and served as a guilty pleasure for me—bloody, intense, and boasting impressive special effects. In short, it’s a solid popcorn movie for any horror enthusiast.

Now, let’s talk about "The Hills Have Eyes 2." Where do I begin? The plot—or rather, the lack thereof—is painfully thin. This feels like uncharted territory only in the most clichéd sense. The military decides to monitor the area, and suddenly everyone starts disappearing. What’s the next move? Naturally, they send in the National Guard to investigate. Of course, in classic Hollywood style, these soldiers are portrayed as the dumbest and worst fighters imaginable. Wow, never seen that before, right? To cut to the chase, the mutants proceed to gruesomely eliminate the dim-witted soldiers one by one. Once again, the special effects by Nicotero are fantastic, but...

I purchased the DVD of *Before Sunset* and watched it for the first time just a week ago. After seeing it twice, I found myself irresistibly drawn to *Before Sunrise*. It wasn’t that the sequel lacked quality—it was fantastic—but rather that these two films complemented each other in a way no other sequel has. Each time I finished one, I felt an overwhelming urge to watch the other immediately. As a result, over the past few weeks, I’ve been cycling through both movies repeatedly. I’ll admit I lost count of how many times I’ve seen them—they’re starting to blur together in my memory! 

What stands out most about *Before Sunrise* is how seamlessly it captures the evolution of the characters’ feelings for one another. At first glance, it seems simple—the gradual buildup of chemistry—but I believe most romantic films fail to truly convey this progression authentically. Even though I’m not a fan of Nora Ephron’s work, *Before Sunrise* remains the first film that made me feel this connection on a visceral level. The first time I watched it, eight years ago when I was 20, I enjoyed it enough to consider it decent. However, at the time, I wouldn’t have called it a "great film." To me, it still felt like just another...

With its status as the prototype of the classic Errol Flynn adventure film, a compelling storyline, and two remarkable co-stars in the stunning Maureen O'Hara and the charismatic Anthony Quinn, this movie is sure to delight anyone with even a modest interest in romance and adventure. Hollywood at its finest!

I first watched this movie around 1990, and it had me laughing nonstop throughout. It quickly became a beloved cult classic among my group of friends, and we would quote lines from it constantly ("I'm going home in a bag!"). To this day, the humor remains just as sharp, even 15 years later. During Halloween, it's become a tradition for me to introduce this film to new friends (thankfully, it's still available on eBay). There's something about watching this movie that makes Halloween candy taste better when viewed with a touch of playful skepticism—and this film delivers it all: pathos, suspense, unrequited love, nobility, and more. Royal Dano gives an incredible, heartfelt performance as Old Man Wrenchmuller. I vividly recall seeing him in *The 7 Faces of Dr. Lao* as a villainous figure with a grim fate. In this film, however, you genuinely empathize with him from the start. 

Be warned, though—some of the movie’s humor is subtle and layered. The filmmakers cleverly incorporate offhand remarks, sly costume references to other sci-fi films, and even a nod to a classic *Wile E. Coyote* gag. You might miss these nuances if you're not paying close attention.

Before leaving my own review, I wanted to read the other comments, and the consensus is clear: this movie is terrible! From the subpar acting to the unrealistic animation and numerous errors, it’s hard to find anything redeeming. Honestly, I was expecting the characters to use their imagination to extend the flaps (which isn’t possible without engines), and the landing gear situation made no sense either—it can’t be lowered without electricity. That small fan they showed clearly wasn’t enough to do the job. One scene stood out as particularly baffling: when they landed, the rear wheels touched down first, but then the nose wheel snapped off, leaving the plane suspended on its back tires in mid-air. If the wheels aren’t touching the ground, how could the pilot even apply brakes? And where were the spoilers? A word to the director: Research everything you can about airplanes before making a “plane” movie. Sorry for the technical rant, but this film deserves only 1 out of 10.

This documentary recreates the final years of Betty Page's (played by Paige Richards) career. As the iconic "Tennessee tease," Page was the most recognizable pin-up queen in history. Her most memorable work took place in the 1950s, featuring fetish photography, bondage, and catfight "girly flicks." Under the guidance of Irving Klaw (portrayed as Dukey Flyswatter), who ran Movie Star News, Betty learned how to pose for the camera. Despite the absence of nudity in her famous photos and "stag films," Klaw faced charges for distributing obscene material and was ordered to destroy them to avoid prosecution. It’s no wonder Betty amassed a cult following during her peak. The alluring, blue-eyed brunette with curves to spare, whether clad in fetish attire or not, captivated audiences for decades. In fact, some say she was photographed more than Marilyn Monroe and only surpassed by the most photographed person ever—Elvis Presley. After retiring, Betty devoted herself to religion. While this film doesn’t reach its full potential, it remains engaging enough. 

Paige Richards shines, and let’s be honest—her outfit of bra, panties, garter belt, and stockings certainly helps.

I must say, Uma Thurman is the sexiest woman on Earth. This movie was incredibly charming—seriously, uber cute. It contained all the typical "sex" elements found in most Ivan Reitman comedies, but it had an added touch: chemistry. Uma and Luke shared an awkward yet believable chemistry that shone through in every scene. They crafted an unusual, twisted, and intriguing relationship filled with intense "sexual" tension, making you laugh so hard you'll forget how your face feels. Anna Faris and the supporting cast played off each other flawlessly, and even Wanda Sykes’ relatively small role kept me entertained. While这类喜剧并不适合所有人，但我和一位通常不喜欢这种电影的朋友一起观看时，他笑得前仰后合。这部电影显然不是为每个人准备的，尤其是年幼的孩子，因为有些场景涉及成人内容，可能不太适合他们。总体而言，我对这部电影感到十分惊喜，只是结尾部分相较于整部影片略显薄弱。（3 ½ * out of 5*）

This movie is terrible—there’s no sugarcoating it. Buried within this mess are a couple of decent scenes, but they’re not enough to salvage the weak plot. Colin Farrell resembles Brad Pitt from *12 Monkeys* and adopts a similar acting style. Usually, I dislike him due to his flamboyant persona, but he’s passable here. The film follows two primary storylines: one involving a kid throwing rocks at moving cars’ windshields and another centered around a woman with a mustache. Let’s be honest—it’s clear this movie has no clue what message it wants to convey or where it’s headed. While the character arcs intersect somewhat, these plot threads don’t justify their inclusion in the script. The entire film feels flimsy and pointless, with only occasional tolerable moments. Overall, skip it unless you’re obsessed with Irish accents; even then, it’s only saved from total failure by the actors' charming delivery, which has propped up plenty of subpar films.
A乏味的儿童奇幻片，让乔安·普洛赖特享有领衔主演的头衔，却赋予她极少的戏份。感情化的孩子们追逐自己的梦想。弗兰基想成为芭蕾舞者和棒球选手（令人反感），而她的最佳好友海泽竞选市长——她才13岁！整部影片在各方面都毫无亮点，再加上女孩们以及棒球男孩们过于甜腻的表演，更是雪上加霜。对Showtime来说，这无疑是较为平庸的一部作品——难道真的没有底线吗？

Bill Boyd, Robert Armstrong, and James Gleason star as carnival workers on Coney Island competing for the affections of Ginger Rogers, a vendor selling saltwater taffy. When World War I begins, the trio enlists in the military and continues their pursuit of Ginger from a distance. The first portion of this RKO Pathe film is challenging to watch, as the三位主演以夸张的表情和过度使用俏皮话让剧情显得冗长乏味。影片后半部分则转向动作戏，聚焦美国海军追击德国商船和U型潜艇的场景，这些片段充满活力且拍摄精良。然而，总体而言，这部电影是一部情节拖沓、令人失望的喜剧与剧情片结合之作，结局也平淡无奇，仅适合喜爱这些演员的观众观看。

I typically enjoy comedy films and find them enjoyable, but "Envy" just doesn't resonate with me. The plot feels lackluster, and it isn't particularly humorous either. 

Even though the performances are decent, they aren't strong enough to make the movie engaging. Both Ben Stiller and Jack Black seem to hold back in this film, failing to showcase their usual comedic prowess. 

If you're considering renting a comedy, I'd advise steering clear of this one unless you're in the mood for something uninteresting. Clearly, I’m not alone in this view, as Jack Black himself acknowledged its shortcomings, as noted in the trivia section.

For over a quarter-century (and frequently banned), it seems its mystery was its greatest strength. After all, it’s often preferable to be talked about rather than seen if you can’t deliver on the hype. Recently, the film has screened in Los Angeles a few times and is now available on home video, gradually pulling back the curtain on its enigma. Though it still contains plenty to shock people, it’s more likely to bore them than ignite genuine passion. Aside from a gratuitous and drawn-out XXX sex scene featuring two horses ("Nature Documentary," anyone?), the rest plays out as a tedious arranged marriage drama spanning nearly an hour. Once the sexual content kicks in, it’s a relentless sequence involving masturbation, a lengthy flashback to a supposed “beauty and the beast” encounter, and a naked woman wandering the mansion (no one—not even her supposedly protective aunt—bothers to clothe her). On video, you could fast-forward through the tedium, but it’s not particularly worthwhile. The nudity doesn’t surpass what’s found in something far more substantial like Bertolucci’s *The Dreamers*.

I attended a screening of this movie at a cast and crew event because a friend, who produced the film, invited me. Ignore everything you've seen in the commercials and heard elsewhere—go see this film for yourself. I was thoroughly astonished by it. Amidst movies like *The Grinch*, *Charlie's Angels*, *The 6th Day*, and *Unbreakable*, this is one that’s truly worth your money. Breathtaking visuals, stunning cinematography, and a cast so compelling you’ll feel like embracing them with your heart. I consider this one of the standout powerhouses of the year, and rightly so. Robert De Niro delivers a performance deserving of an Oscar nomination. If Oscars were awarded to entire teams rather than individuals, this would be the perfect film for it.

I appreciate the charm of low-quality filmmaking, and this one definitely delivers in that regard. The CGI looks either otherworldly or like it belongs in a completely different era. Watching a six-foot man in a rat costume chase people around is hilariously bad. While parts of it were entertaining, the acting is atrocious, and even the obligatory nude scene lacks anything remotely noteworthy. It's an utter waste of time—there's no doubt about that. I’m not sure whether I wasted more time watching it or the cast wasted theirs hoping this would kickstart their careers. Spoiler alert: it won’t. On a slightly positive note, I did manage to connect this film to Kevin Bacon through six degrees of separation, which makes the 91-minute runtime feel somewhat justified. Almost.

One word sums up this movie: WOW! I watched "Darius Goes West" at the Tribeca Film Festival, and the audience was deeply moved, many sobbing openly. The film highlights the challenges faced by Darius, who has Muscular Dystrophy. It is exceptionally well-made and immerses viewers completely. I was incredibly emotionally affected because it reminded us how fortunate we are to be healthy while showing the struggles others face. It also inspired me to think about lending a hand to those in need. I’d award this film ten stars. The creators didn’t do it for money—they helped Darius out of friendship. Darius went west, and the world should know his story.

If your idea of a thriller revolves around car chases, explosions, and scenes of mass violence, then "House of Games" might not be the film for you. However, if you enjoy psychological drama and suspense, it’s definitely worth watching.

"House of Games" follows Dr. Margaret Ford (played by Lindsay Crouse), an accomplished psychologist and author, as she attempts to assist a patient and becomes entangled in the dangerous world of con artists, led by the charming yet enigmatic Mike (Joe Mantegna). Revealing any further details about the plot would spoil the suspense. Honestly, I find it hard to believe anyone who claims they saw the twists coming. Like a skilled con artist, this movie draws you in and gradually lowers your guard.

The story is tight and meticulously constructed, the dialogue sharp and concise, and the performances are consistently strong (Mantegna shines with his charisma). Some critics have argued that Dr. Ford isn’t particularly likable, and questioned why David Mamet made Lindsay Crouse appear less attractive. However, Dr. Ford is meant to be distant and unapproachable; her lack of conventional beauty is, in fact, crucial to the storyline (at one point, I think...).

I find it hard to believe this film isn’t on IMDb’s worst 250 list—it’s that bad. The first time I watched it, I recall discussing it in a college class, and a couple of other students had also seen it. We all warned our classmates against watching it, emphasizing just how terrible it was. By the end of our ranting, some classmates actually expressed interest in seeing it, simply because they couldn’t imagine something being as awful as we described. Don’t fall into that trap—just skip it. I’m sure everyone who worked on this movie would also prefer you never watch it.

Along with its partner, this is the greatest piece of animation ever created. The images and styles are remarkable, perfectly complementing the story, which is a brilliantly realistic reinterpretation of our world, exploring where it has been and where it might be headed. At times affecting and even painful to watch, it stands as a masterpiece of visual art.

I had heard of Eddie Izzard before, but I had never actually seen him perform. I knew he was a transvestite, and when I noticed he was appearing on HBO one summer evening, I decided to watch, unsure of how my husband would respond. To our surprise, he completely blew us away. Eddie Izzard surpasses even Robin Williams in terms of talent. He has an incredible ability to command the audience’s attention; during his "Englebert is dead—no, he's not" routine, the crowd is left utterly bewildered by the end. His portrayal of God as James Mason is a brilliant touch, and his reinterpretation of the Python Spanish Inquisition, carried out by the Church of England with the famous line "Cake or Death?" is absolutely hilarious. By the time the show ended, my cheeks hurt from laughing so much. After that unforgettable performance, we spent months searching through TV listings just to catch him again, and we were fortunate enough to record him the next time he appeared. If you ever have the opportunity to see this show, make sure to clear your schedule and record it—you won’t regret it.

This heartwarming, humorous film stars Morgan Freeman, who plays a version of himself, as he encounters a spirited Spanish woman named Scarlet (played by Paz Vega) at a small store while scouting locations for an indie film project. Initially skeptical about the movie, my interest surged once Freeman entered the store, and I found myself thoroughly enjoying the story. The film beautifully illustrates how maintaining a positive outlook can transform circumstances. While lacking intricate plotlines, it’s straightforward to follow yet manages to uplift even the most despondent spirits, leaving viewers smiling throughout without relying on tired romantic tropes. Several laugh-out-loud moments pepper the narrative, making it a truly exceptional gem.

My Observations: A touch of postwar exuberance. Tom Drake and the grandfather from *Meet Me in St. Louis* two years later (the year I was born). Donna Reed is delightful and radiant. Margaret Hamilton delivers her usual stellar performance, though in a smaller role compared to *The Wizard of Oz*. Spring Byington is equally lovely and possesses the quintessential petite, perky nose absent in Hamilton. The tent scene at the end with the former boy-next-door was laugh-out-loud funny. As someone who spent two years in Army tents, his youthful inexperience seemed palpable when I met his gaze.

I once worked in a department store, just as refined as this one. Regrettably, it has vanished and faded into oblivion. Our claim to fame were the stunning display windows designed to entice passersby inside, encouraging them to purchase all that enticing merchandise.

10/10

Man has explored the farthest corners of Earth and now ventures into uncharted worlds. Yet, with these new realms come ancient evils—space vampires, not just individuals, but entire tribes. In this film, originally titled "Bloodsuckers" and also known as "Vampire Wars," we witness the clash between imperialist humans and imperialist vampires.

I’ll keep this review brief, as the film doesn’t merit much praise. Its only saving grace is an intriguing cast of B-list and rising actors. Natassia Malthe plays Quintana, looking far better here than in "Bloodrayne 2." Michael Ironside portrays Muco, a fan-favorite due to his reputation as the "poor man's Jack Nicholson." Even Carrie-Ann Fleming appears as "Damian’s wife," recognizable to horror enthusiasts as the iconic Jenifer from Dario Argento’s "Jenifer." While the film may be lackluster, it does boast notable names—though the same could be said for Uwe Boll’s work.

The premise of military forces hunting and eliminating space vampires isn’t inherently bad, but it quickly succumbs to...

I believe that, hidden in the murkiest corner of everyone’s heart, there’s a secret fondness for Jerry Springer. Despite its offensiveness and sheer absurdity, his show offers a stark reminder that, compared to some, our lives aren’t so bad. Watching the trailer-park dwellers, whiskey-swigging, dysfunction-heavy characters on his program makes even the toughest days feel manageable. Jerry is doing society a favor, and we ought to be thankful. He gave up a political career to bring this to us.

However, there’s absolutely no reason to thank anyone involved with the abysmal movie "Ringmaster." This film tries to depict the lives of people who appear on his show—or at least that’s what they want us to believe. The plot follows the classic Springer template: love triangles abound. In one, we have Connie, her daughter Angel, and her husband Rusty; in the other, Starletta, Vonda, and Demond. When these mismatched groups cross paths in Los Angeles, their chaotic lives collide, leading to a dramatic finale on the Springer stage. It’s as if someone took "Short...

A thoroughly mundane cinematic experience, "Las Vegas Lady" stars Stella Stevens, following orders from an unidentified figure (whose identity I deduced early on). Set in an old Nevada town near Vegas, the film revolves around a heist planned at the Circus Circus Hotel. Stevens heads a trio of female accomplices, who soon realize they need to act faster than expected. While the film offers picturesque views of 1970s Las Vegas and features decent, believable performances from the cast, it ultimately fails to deliver excitement. The storyline holds promise but falls flat, moving sluggishly and never gaining momentum. Disappointed by this flick, I had hoped for a campy 70s exploitation-style film, but this isn’t even close. No fatalities occur, and the action sequences are lackluster—particularly a limp shootout between Stuart Whitman and George DiCenzo, whose later portrayal of Bugliosa in "Helter Skelter" would prove far more compelling. This shootout lacks tension, feeling more like watching water cascade down a fall.

What words could possibly do justice to the sheer brilliance and beauty of *A Matter of Life and Death*? Powell and Pressburger’s visual ingenuity knows no limits—every frame brims with audaciously bold compositions. The seamless transition between the vivid hues of the "real world" and the stark monochrome of heaven is nothing short of ingenious, conveying visually the vibrancy of life itself. The climactic courtroom scene is equally masterful, as the judge and jury descend from heaven to preside over Peter's (David Niven) fate.

Each performance is pitch-perfect, with Roger Livesey delivering a standout portrayal. The film's romantic essence is exquisite; there has arguably never been a more romantic movie. *A Matter of Life and Death* celebrates the transformative power of love and the inestimable value of life. Jack Cardiff's cinematography alone makes the film worth watching—the way he illuminates Kim Hunter's face elevates her beauty to new heights. He possesses an extraordinary talent, turning even mundane moments, like a game of table tennis, into thrilling spectacles. The film’s sound design further enhances its magic.

A busload of passengers becomes stranded during a snowstorm when the police shut down the bridge, deeming it too dangerous to cross. With no choice but to wait out the weather in a small café, the group grows increasingly bored. That is, until they begin to suspect that one of their fellow travelers wasn’t actually on the bus when it departed. Could this mysterious person *really* be an alien? What follows is a conclusion that’s both ironic and hilariously absurd in its simplicity.

While not your typical episode of *The Twilight Zone*, this installment eschews deep philosophical themes or shocking twists in favor of pure entertainment. It’s light-hearted, amusing, and entirely enjoyable—so why overthink it? You’ll just have to watch to discover the specifics!

And speaking of enjoyment, this episode features none other than John Hoyt, a familiar face from countless classic TV shows and films. Hoyt had an uncanny ability to play irascible characters with such gusto that you couldn’t help but laugh at his grouchy antics. His performance here is no exception—perfectly embodying the type of curmudgeon we all love to see on screen.

I recently stumbled upon a copy for just $5 at a video store and grabbed it enthusiastically. Although the music and (naturally) the graphics don’t quite match the high standards of my favorite from the series, *Beyond the Mind's Eye*, I’m still completely captivated by one particular segment:  

*Stanley and Stella in "Breaking the Ice."* The music is exceptional, and the emotions portrayed feel genuine. Unfortunately, the clip on Odyssey’s website lacks both the storyline and the music.

As I watched this movie, I struggled to understand why it was made. Despite the potential of its central plot, the film is cluttered with unrelated and unnecessary subplots. It seems the marketing team at Hollywood intervened, insisting on multiple villains, constant betrayals, and a romantic entanglement between a man and a woman. It’s strange that we see more of their intimate moments than those involving the President and his mistress. The numerous storylines dilute the focus, and none of the characters are adequately developed—apart from their collective corruption, I felt I knew nothing about any of them. The conclusion is frustratingly unresolved, leaving viewers not just craving what could have been, but also what should have been clarified. Ultimately, no character motivations are truly explained, serving only as excuses for further betrayal and corruption. I’m baffled that so many talented, established actors signed on for such a shallow production. This feels like a film crafted by fledgling college filmmakers working on their early projects. 

Save yourself the time.

This movie boasts a strong cast and attractive location shooting, yet it falls short. Director Richard Brooks appears to have been somewhat fatigued by this point in his career; his earlier film, *The Professionals*, was far superior. The pacing felt sluggish, as both the horses and action scenes seemed to drag, even when they weren’t in slow motion. The film would have benefited from being slightly faster-paced. The fake-looking horse sweat and obvious tire tracks in the desert scenes were glaringly unconvincing—clearly lazy and sloppy work. A real shame. The actors gave decent performances, but I’ve seen them excel more in other roles. Ben Johnson was delightful as always. I first watched this film nearly 30 years ago and was let down at the time; rewatching it three decades later, my disappointment remained unchanged.

A thoroughly abysmal film that left me feeling污秽不堪after enduring around forty minutes of it. The blame doesn’t lie with the actors, but the writer, director, producers, financiers, and others involved should be severely reprimanded. Perhaps the filmmakers thought they were being profound, but they utterly failed. Unlike *A Clockwork Orange*, this gratuitous violence and rape offer no insight or contribution to our understanding of humanity. And it falls far short of *Straw Dogs*, which some have foolishly compared it to. In truth, it feels like something Pete Walker might have created, and even that comparison is likely giving him too much credit.

Revenge is a potent human emotion, and *The Bedroom Window* could have explored that theme along with male emasculation, but this pathetic effort fails to do so effectively.

I wouldn’t label it overtly misogynistic, but it revels too gleefully in certain scenes—like the blood running down GA’s leg after the rape. It’s neither challenging nor confrontational, despite the filmmakers’ self-perception of boldness; it’s simply deeply unsettling.

Is this really the best we can aspire to? Was this what drove the people behind it to make movies?

I watched *The Perfect Son* at the 2002 Gay and Lesbian Mardi Gras Film Festival in Sydney, Australia. 

Following their father's death, two estranged brothers reunite at the funeral and embark on a touching journey of reconciliation when one discovers he is dying from AIDS. The lead actors deliver an outstanding performance, skillfully portraying the evolving warmth and respect that grows between them throughout the film. My only criticism is that while the character with AIDS is convincingly portrayed as sick, he doesn’t appear visibly unwell. Someone with zero T4 cells would likely look much more frail or ill than the actor does, and there’s no makeup to enhance this effect. It’s a minor issue, yet it detracts slightly from the realism. Regardless of this small flaw, *The Perfect Son* is a beautiful film, and if you get the opportunity to see it, don’t miss out. I’m hopeful for a DVD release soon!

What on earth was this? It feels like someone took Stephen King and Jean-Paul Sartre courses in the same semester and mashed them together—existential dread mixed with bargain-bin horror. Some moments were unsettling, but every single one was undermined by terrible music, laughable CGI, or cringe-worthy performances. 

The issue with trippy stories like this one is that they often come across as lazy. Even David Lynch’s work can feel that way sometimes, and just like his quirky yet engaging films and series, this drags on far longer than necessary. To be fair, it clocks in at only 98 minutes, which makes its sluggishness even more frustrating.

The actors were decent-looking, but that’s about the only positive thing here. I guess it tries to explore adolescent emotions and our universal fear of loneliness, but it fails to make the characters likable or compelling enough for us to actually care about what happens to them. And the ending? Ambiguous to the point of frustration.

Sure! Here's the rewritten version:

I recently had the opportunity to rent and watch *Santa Claus Conquers the Martians*. While the children in *SCCTM* were quite sadistic, I have to say that *Santa Claus* was an even worse film. For a Spanish 5 assignment, we were all required to watch it. Usually, when we watch movies, everyone just chats and snacks, but this one was different. Everyone sat silently, jaws agape, wondering what evil Mr. Pitch would do next. Would Merlin save Santa Claus?! Or would his robot reindeer rescue the day? I recommend renting it because it’s the biggest piece of nonsense I’ve ever seen, and I absolutely love it for that. :D

This is one of the best movies for all ages. Once you've seen it, you'll never watch *The Lion King* the same way again, as it adds an intriguing layer of backstory. Although nearly 40 years old, I recently watched it with my wife and two sons after work, and it’s been a long time since I’ve laughed and enjoyed a movie so much.

Set aside some time to watch it with the kids. It’ll bring back memories of how Disney used to be when you were younger.

I’m a huge fan of Fred MacMurray and Carole Lombard, and Charles Butterworth, a delightful supporting actor, also appears in this film... so why didn’t I enjoy it? Well, even with such a talented cast, this ranks among the worst-written and most predictable “A pictures” I’ve ever seen. Considering the resources and budget poured into its production, it’s astonishing how lazy the writing feels. I lost interest early on because I could predict every single plot twist—down to the exact words—with eerie accuracy. It wasn’t because I possess some supernatural knack for movies; it was simply due to the complete lack of creativity or effort. The script reads like an endless parade of overused tropes strung together without thought. 

To make matters worse, Fred’s character treats Carole poorly throughout the film, yet she still forgives him in the end—a tired trope that makes my skin crawl. Honestly, there’s more drama in a Lassie episode (“Will Timmy get rescued before the rope snaps?”). 

Even though the performances might have been decent, the poor writing ruins everything.

I had high hopes for this movie,期待能找到一个精彩有趣的故事，但它的剧情非常糟糕。演员的表现也毫无亮点。当然，Shahrukh Khan参演了，但这并没有让这部电影变得“可信”或引人入胜。我了解到这部电影是根据福楼拜的《包法利夫人》改编的，但对我来说，它完全不符合印度人的思维模式。一般来说，我们看电影是为了梦想和享受快乐时光，而不是浪费时间让自己心情变得更糟。我真的不明白它怎么能获得平均6.8/10这样的“高分”。所以，这是一部你应该避而远之的电影，因为它没有任何值得欣赏的地方！除非你喜欢“黑暗”且“荒诞无意义”的电影，否则观看它只会浪费你的时间。

I didn't expect much when I decided to watch this movie. However, after having a great time mocking *Jason X* with some friends, I was hoping for a similar experience here.

Unfortunately, the film took itself far too seriously. Do I care about Jason's issues? No, I don’t. There are countless Friday the 13th movies that already explore that territory. And let’s be honest, he’s an undead serial killer—I’m just not going to feel sympathy for him.

Freddy, on the other hand, was the most intriguing part of the movie, especially with the hallucination elements. But they were sparse, and by the end, it had devolved into a poor imitation of a *Celebrity Deathmatch* episode—only without the humor.

On the night of his bachelor party, Paul Coleman (Jason Lee) encounters the captivating dancer Becky (Julia Stiles) at a bar. They share numerous drinks and wake up together the following morning. When Paul's future mother-in-law calls to inform him that his fiancée, Karen (Selma Blair), might arrive at his apartment, he urgently asks Becky to leave. Soon after, Paul discovers he has contracted crabs, and later, during preparations for his wedding dinner, he learns that Becky is Karen’s cousin. This sets the stage for a hilariously comedic journey. The film's standout feature is its central trio of actors and actresses—Julia Stiles and Selma Blair, both talented and stunning, and Jason Lee, whose comedic talent is exceptional. Their performances are strong, and I found myself laughing frequently throughout the narrative. Some moments are particularly side-splitting, such as when Paul finds Becky in his bed, spots her belongings, engages in humorous imaginings, navigates awkward scenarios in a pharmacy while purchasing medication for crabs, and experiences several outrageous interactions with his neighbor.

When I first encountered a brief clip of it in some promotional materials, I assumed the show would be enjoyable to watch. The little robot character does appear quite cute. The animation style also reminded me of some classic series. Before the show premiered, I looked into it through various sources. That’s when I started to feel somewhat disappointed. While the three children—Tommy, Gus, and Lola—are voiced fittingly, Robotboy stands out as an exception. It would have been much better if he had been portrayed by a younger actor. A great example is Robot Jones from “Whatever Happened to Robot Jones?” Although the show itself isn’t terrible, the inappropriate portrayal of Robotboy is my sole critique. As a result, I don’t watch it very often.

S.I.C.K. actually means "So Incredibly Crappy i Killed myself." There wasn't even a hint of decent acting. The only redeeming quality of the entire film was the artwork on the cover of the DVD box. The budgeting was practically nonexistent, and the filming quality was worse than Sesame Street. It looked like something filmed by amateurs for underworld activities.
