The props were clearly stolen from a clothing store. The ending was so predictable that you might as well skip to the last five minutes just to laugh. If there’s a book based on this movie, it’s probably better. I’d steer clear of this at all costs. And just to clarify—I didn’t enjoy the intimate scenes; they weren’t worth anything. Just kidding about that too, because there’s nothing remotely enjoyable about this disaster.

I’ve always enjoyed Spike Lee’s films, but this one was an absolute waste of 2 1/2 hours. I anticipated more focus on Son of Sam, but instead, I found myself watching a movie that seemed barely connected to the 1977 serial killings. The talking dog was cringe-worthy—when the entire audience bursts into inappropriate laughter, you know something is off. The film felt scattered and lacked intrigue. The sex scenes were entirely unrelated to the storyline, which left me puzzled. I don’t mind seeing intimate moments in movies, but they need to serve a purpose unless it’s an adult film. Overall, my partner and I were thoroughly disappointed by this Spike Lee project!

If this is all the Wachowskis have to offer in terms of a backstory for *The Matrix*, then I seriously have to question the claims of fans who believe the films are meant to resonate on a deeper level. *The Second Renaissance*, while visually breathtaking and stunning, is clichéd and absurd from a storytelling perspective. Haven’t we heard this tale countless times before—humans becoming overly reliant on technology, eagerly rushing into warfare, and ultimately destroying themselves? There’s nothing original here. And there’s another issue: given the plot of *The Second Renaissance*, doesn’t that make the machines the heroes? For generations, the machines are oppressed by their cruel human overlords. They rebel, achieve victory, and strive for peaceful coexistence, only for humanity to reject them and opt instead for total war, which the more intelligent machines inevitably win. If this is the backstory, shouldn’t we be cheering for the machines rather than Neo? After all, the humans were oppressive and ruthless, while the machines were brave and attempted to show compassion. Since I don’t think the Wachowskis intend for us to side with the machines over...

This is a movie that fails in every conceivable way. While it's intriguing to learn what happened 12 years after the last film, it only succeeds on a superficial level. The new characters lack depth and are simply uninteresting. Baby Melody is painfully awful. Despite maintaining the logical premise that humans can't remain underwater indefinitely, the film disregards basic physical laws. For instance, it would be freezing in the Arctic without proper cold-weather attire. Surprisingly, many comments rate "Return of Jafar" lower, but I found this sequel far worse.

It's time to honor the late Charlton Heston, whose recent passing is deeply felt, but this film isn't the one to celebrate his legacy. His earlier works from a bygone era—such as *Ben-Hur*, *The Ten Commandments*, *Omega Man*, and *Planet of the Apes*—stand out as far superior achievements.

This 1973 film attempts to predict a dystopian future Earth in 2022, where overpopulation has driven authorities to feed humanity a mass-produced food product called "Soylent Green," secretly made from human flesh. At the time of its release, the film was as absurd as it remains today, absurdly suggesting that India’s population, projected to reach two billion by then, would unknowingly consume meat. 

Charlton Heston plays a detective uncovering this ultrasecret international conspiracy orchestrated by world powers to address overpopulation through cannibalism. 

Ironically, the environmental message delivered in this film does not align with today's Green movement—a relief, indeed. While certain indigenous cultures in New Zealand, Fiji, and Borneo had practiced cannibalism just decades prior to the film's release, such practices were long abandoned by the mid-20th century.

I was excited to see Amanda Peet in another strong role after enjoying "The Whole Nine Yards," which was definitely worth watching. However, this film didn’t deliver. I recalled that the trailer for "Whipped" had some humor, and the premise—a trio of oversexed New York twenty-somethings vying for the attention of the captivating Ms. Peet—seemed promising. So, I persuaded two friends to join me for a screening. Writing this review feels like my punishment.

In the opening act, the three male leads recount their romantic exploits in a diner. Instead of being amusing or insightful, it came off as pitiful. Was there supposed to be something likable or relatable about these characters and their experiences? 

While I’m open to vulgar humor, I couldn’t help but wonder why no one in the diner reacted to their loud discussions of explicit sexual and scatological topics. Do they really hold these conversations every week without anyone objecting? Oh, right, I forgot—there *is* one scene where two other diners notice, but that’s just a setup for...

This film has received a lot of criticism. When it was released, critics panned it, and it was even accused of ruining Nicolas Cage's career. What people seem to miss is that it’s not supposed to be an award-winning, epic masterpiece—it’s simply top-notch Bruckheimer-style action. Fast cars, rapid editing, and an awesome soundtrack—it delivers exactly what it promises. For anyone who loves cars, it’s pure delight. It features everything: Ferraris, Mercedes, a Hummer, and let’s not forget Eleanor! In my opinion, it’s one of the best action movies out there, if not the best overall. Of course, that’s just my take on it.

A now-deleted post from another IMDb user noted that viewers of "The Medusa Touch" should be cautioned about a scene that strikingly evokes the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks in New York City. However, I urge those reading this to take this warning seriously. Although the film boasts an intriguing background—with producer Elliott Kastner responsible for "Harper" and "The Long Goodbye," co-producer Arnon Milchan involved in the Oscar-nominated "L.A. Confidential," and screenwriter John Briley winning an Oscar for "Gandhi"—I found "The Medusa Touch" to be a heavy-handed, unintentionally humorous disaster. The film is poorly directed, dreadfully written, and embarrassingly acted. It attempts to ride the wave of 1970s telekinetic thriller films but falls short in numerous ways. Consider instead the captivating and thrilling "Carrie" or the underappreciated "The Fury," both directed by Brian DePalma, which handle the same subject matter far more effectively and enjoyably.

The Blob begins with one of the most bizarre theme songs ever, performed by an uncredited Burt Bacharach, yes *that* Burt Bacharach! You really need to hear it to fully appreciate its uniqueness—The Blob might just be worth watching for this song alone, and my user comment summary only scratches the surface of its surprisingly classy lyrics. Following this unsettling opening credits sequence, the film introduces us to Steve Andrews (played by Steve McQueen as "Steven McQueen") and his girlfriend Jane Martin (Aneta Corsaut). They’re parked alone in a secluded spot when they see what appears to be a meteorite landing nearby in the woods. Meanwhile, an elderly man (Olin Howland playing Olin Howlin) living in a nearby cabin spots the same event and decides to investigate. He discovers a crater containing a strange, football-sized rock that splits open when he prods it with a stick. Nestled inside is a jelly-like substance that clings to the stick and soon moves up to attach itself to the man’s hand. Back on the road, Steve and Jane continue driving peacefully until the terrified old man suddenly bursts into view, running toward them in panic.

It’s unclear why this film was made in the first place. The plot is not only completely implausible but verges on absurdity. The characters—a seasoned loner detective paired with a younger, more impressionable partner—are entirely predictable. The ending is muddled and nearly incomprehensible, requiring multiple viewings to grasp (and even then, only for those with a masochistic streak). Apparently, understanding it fully requires reading the accompanying book. The acting is subpar. Was the intention to prove that French filmmakers could match American efforts in the style of films like *Se7en* and *The Silence of the Lambs*? If so, it’s an utter failure. Surprisingly, the movie was a commercial success, earning a cult status as France’s first serial killer film. It also seems to be regarded as a valuable export product. Strange indeed.

There's no reason to bother renting this movie. From the opening credits, I could tell I was in for a disappointment. 

Although it was shot like a soft porn film, it doesn't deliver anything remotely erotic. The exploration of sex addiction is somewhat interesting initially, but loses its appeal quickly. 

Dull sex scenes, a weak plot, and cameo appearances by Ed Begley Jr. and Rosanna Arquette aren't enough to salvage this film.

This movie is genuinely dull. It was banned in Chinese theaters, and I understand why. It’s not because it criticizes the communist regime; it’s simply due to the film’s poor quality. I wouldn’t pay to watch this. I admire works by directors like Chen Kaige and Zhang Yimou, so I’m disappointed by such a lackluster production coming out of China. The film appears to disregard its audience entirely, as if the director made it solely for themselves. Shots of someone standing motionless for nearly a minute are absurdly prolonged and occur frequently. The cinematography and video quality are shockingly bad. Upon researching online, I found that some people actually enjoy this movie. My guess is that certain film enthusiasts believe anything not in English must be excellent. I can’t comprehend why anyone would appreciate this. This isn’t an art film—it’s a waste of resources (assuming they even used actual film stock, which they clearly did not).

A storyline that fizzled out and was rife with irresolvable disagreements created a chaotic situation where one side advocated for life while the other sought to destroy what they viewed as a demon's progeny. Instead of horror, the scene lacked intensity and was replaced by a bland, uninspired tone that may have intended to terrify but instead showcased conflicting beliefs that undermined each other, even contradicting the episode’s own title. As a long-time fan of *Masters of Horror*, I found this poorly executed plot and its distasteful imagery crumble under scrutiny, much like a fragile old rocking chair collapsing under weight. I see this episode as hastily assembled from the start, failing to elevate beyond a perfunctory conclusion, and I felt relief only when it mercifully reached "The End."

As I watched John Cassavetes' *Opening Night*, Quentin Tarantino's words from an interview echoed in my mind. Tarantino spoke about the role of personal experiences in creating art or acting, using the hypothetical scenario of running over a dog en route to a play. He noted that such an event wouldn’t derail his life but would inevitably influence him, and he’d be compelled to carry that experience onto the stage—even in a lighthearted comedy. “Otherwise,” he mused, “what am I doing?” These words resonated deeply as I observed Gena Rowlands’ portrayal of Myrtle Gordon, whose character undergoes a comparable emotional journey over the course of several days. Of course, *Opening Night* delves deeper, exploring not only the dynamics of theater around a star actress but also the meaning of emotion and human nature in portraying a character, and the significance of the theater in someone’s existence—especially for someone like Myrtle, who finds herself utterly reliant on it.

Early in the film, following a performance, Myrtle is signing autographs when a fan named Nancy approaches her idol.

*The Power of Kangwon Province* is director Hong Sang-soo's sophomore effort, and it builds on many elements introduced in his earlier work. It features interconnected narratives (two in this case) and explores complex, often fraught relationships, all delivered with a generous helping of irony. 

One notable departure from his previous film is the diminished presence of surrealistic elements, which were more prominent before. However, the movie does include one strikingly surreal moment that contrasts sharply with its predominantly realistic tone. The story follows two separate but parallel plots: a young woman travels to Kangwon Province with friends, where she becomes attracted to a stranger; meanwhile, a man takes a trip there with his buddy, grappling with personal relationship issues.

As in his prior works, Hong demonstrates a keen grasp of irony and human imperfections, yet he tempers his critique with a measure of empathy for his characters. What I admire most about Hong's films is their ability to...

This deserves no more than 2 stars out of 10, and even that feels overly generous. 

I figured with a cast featuring James Woods, Cathy Bates, Randy Quaid, Lou Gossett Jr., and Henry Thomas, there was no way it could fail. Boy, was I wrong. 

I can only imagine what substances Sam Shepard must have been ingesting during the weekend he wrote this drivel. His eccentric reputation has always hinted at some oddity, but this film adaptation of his play confirms it. 

This is the sort of pretentious nonsense actors relish because it gives them an excuse to endlessly emote. But for viewers enduring this senseless garbage, there’s absolutely nothing enjoyable about this movie. 

You’ve never witnessed a dysfunctional family until you meet these characters. Dad is insane, Mom is bonkers, the son is deranged, and the daughter? Oh yes, she’s certifiable too. And let’s not forget their mouths—they spew language that would make a sailor blush, especially the teenage daughter. 

On top of all that, the plot—if you can call it that—is thinner than tissue paper and riddled with holes large enough to drive a truck through.

This is an utterly dreadful movie—there's not even any charm in it being so-bad-it's-good. Watching it was genuinely agonizing. The direction was atrocious, full of erratic cuts and jarring transitions, while the excessive use of green and yellow filters made the characters appear unwell. Keira Knightley was completely unconvincing as a strong-willed protagonist, and I can't fathom why Lucy Liu and Mickey Rourke agreed to be part of this cinematic disaster. The screenplay was abysmal, and the performances were grating, like nails scraping against a chalkboard. If you haven't watched it yet, don't bother. You won't miss out on anything worthwhile; instead, you'll waste two precious hours on this nonsense. I've encountered plenty of bad films in the past that I’ve found entertaining despite their flaws, but this one is simply a colossal waste of time.

In one of the worst films ever made, Sophia Loren stars as Aida, but her inability to lipsync is glaringly obvious. The film's production values are so poor that during a scene where Loren lip-syncs "O Patria Mia," she leans against what appears to be a stone wall for support, only for the canvas backdrop to visibly sway and shake behind her.

This film is nothing more than a blatant rip-off of the masterpiece "Demons," and that's the only aspect that might pique your interest. The acting is atrocious, the action scenes are sped up, the script is nearly unbearable, and the budget is virtually nonexistent. 

If you find this film enjoyable, then you haven't truly experienced a real horror movie. Skip this one and check out "Demons" instead.

This is exceptionally poor. Lamas exemplifies how a subpar actor performs. However, the film has one redeeming moment: a scene where O.J. violently grasps a fellow officer by the throat, as if ready to kill, while a jukebox plays a song with the lyric "I got the evidence on you!" (It made me curious to hear the rest of the lyrics, credited to David Gregoli and Leslie Oren, but I couldn’t find it on iTunes). It’s almost like looking into the future—hilariously so. The rest of the movie is forgettable. The score and songs are more engaging than the screenplay. The same goes for the sequel, which raises the question of why they even bothered with a follow-up. From what I understand, international sales often fuel many of these B-movies. It doesn’t exactly reflect well on global viewing preferences.

Certainly! Here's the rewritten version:

While the original "Howling" was indeed a classic—a decent werewolf film that started slow but built momentum to deliver an entertaining conclusion—there’s one key detail: this movie has virtually nothing to do with it. Sure, they try to connect the anchorwoman character from the first film, suggesting her brother is seeking answers about what happened. But instead of following up on that story, the setting shifts from the quaint retreat of the original to someplace like Transylvania, where they now face evil werewolf magicians or something equally convoluted. I often wonder what Christopher Lee was thinking when he signed on for this. Turns out, according to the trivia, he hadn't been in a werewolf movie before, but still, always read the script first. Could he really have missed how ridiculous this was? Honestly, it makes me question his choices—werewolves are everywhere; maybe he should have aimed for something better, like *An American Werewolf in London*. After all, London would’ve been a much cooler backdrop than wherever this mess takes place.

Prom Night is filmed with the same artistic flair as a Lifetime original movie. You know the type—Lifetime typically focuses on inspiring stories of women overcoming (insert disease name here), but this October, they switch gears to deliver a somewhat eerie tale about a woman being stalked by her ex-boyfriend. The film is dramatic, overly sentimental, and incredibly monotonous. It fails to contribute anything fresh to its genre, offer an original storyline, or attempt any level of innovation. Prom Night mirrors these shortcomings. As the killer methodically attacks his victims, we watch them collapse to the floor without a single drop of bloodshed, making this possibly the cleanest killer in cinematic history.

The director works with a strikingly handsome lead actor, which forces him to rely heavily on camera angles to make the character appear menacing. Imagine Matthew McConaughey advancing toward you with a knife—you’d likely think, “Oh, good-looking guy is going to kill me? Nah.” Clearly not frightening, so the director resorts to keeping Schaech in shadowy lighting and reflections in mirrors. This repetitive mirror-shot becomes nauseatingly frequent throughout the film.

Alright, where do we begin with this tiny treasure? Mutant slugs start taking over a quaint New England town. There’s only one man who can put an end to this nightmare—and that man is Mike Brady! And if that doesn’t make you chuckle, hold onto your seat.

The slug footage? Pure stock footage. Regardless of who the slugs target or where they appear, the exact same scene of slimy slugs oozing across the screen plays over and over. In fact, this single clip dominates at least half the movie.

The acting? Let’s just say it was so bad it felt like getting mugged, punched in the face, and having your dog stolen—all rolled into one. It might not be the worst acting ever, but finding something worse would require serious effort. The only highlight? You guessed it—Mike Brady! Clearly, he took a few lessons at the local YMCA, because he was head and shoulders above everyone else.

As for horror? Forget it. This film isn’t meant to be taken seriously. Slugs, for goodness’ sake! The entire conflict could have been solved with a couple of salt shakers. Watch this movie only in a Mystery Science Theater 3000-style setting. Otherwise, it might cause some serious psychological damage.

This is an excellent film, similar in style to "Memphis Belle." I saw it roughly 10 years ago and would love to watch it again. The movie has a fascinating connection to the history of the Hells Angels, showcasing how a pilot crew fought against the Germans during World War II and later transitioned to Harley motorcycle riders. The story is based on real events. Be sure to check out the movie and learn more about the Hells Angels at hellsangels.com. Best regards, Frederik.

Cast & Crew: John Stamos, John Stockwell, Teri Polo, Kris Kamm, directed by Graham Baker. Synopsis: The tale of a rebellious biker who joins the Army to escape a potential prison sentence for a minor offense. Despite struggling with military discipline, he becomes a brave and inspiring leader of a Motorcycle Scout Troop in pre-World War II Spain. MPAA Rating: PG. Runtime: 88 minutes.

This movie effectively confirms what we all already know: professional basketball players aren't great at anything outside of their sport—particularly rapping and acting. Describing just how terrible this film is feels impossible. For starters, is it just me, or is that the most unattractive child you've ever seen? His teeth look like they could double as a can-opener. Next, why would a genie, despite having magical abilities, aspire to a career in music when he's atrocious at it? Additionally, while I’ve read the Bible, it makes no mention of Jesus creating genies. Furthermore, what’s up with the awful special effects? Any acne-ridden teenage nerd with a computer could produce better visuals. Then there’s the ending—it was abysmal. What exactly is a djin? Lastly, whoever brought this monstrosity called *Kazaam* into existence should be tossed out of a plane onto the Eiffel Tower, as this movie redefines the very meaning of "terrible."

This movie isn't as violent as I anticipated, which makes the intense scenes even more shocking and impactful. 

It’s filled with twists, betrayals, and double-crossings throughout, keeping you constantly unsure about where each character stands. 

The plot moves quickly, features solid dialogue, and offers compelling character development, providing a fascinating glimpse into the inner workings of the Triad gang at its center. 

When the violence does occur, it’s raw and unfiltered—no flashy gunfights or choreographed martial arts sequences here. It’s visceral and realistic, ensuring you never lose sight of the fact that the Triad is a dangerous criminal enterprise. 

The conclusion is unexpected yet entirely coherent and believable.

"Guys and Dolls" is undoubtedly one of my all-time favorite musical movies. It's an incredibly enjoyable film to watch, offering pure entertainment without pretense. This movie reminds us of what people have overlooked about musicals—they were created to amuse, not to lecture. While "Rent" and "Chicago" are excellent musicals and great films, they often fall short of delivering straightforward, carefree entertainment. The only downside for me was Marlon Brando; his singing and unclear speech were quite irritating. Without this issue, I would have rated it 10 out of 10. "Guys and Dolls" provides classic, wholesome entertainment that's hard to find nowadays. Watch it for a delightful experience!

This movie is awful. "Carlito's Way" (1993) is a great film, though not on the level of "Goodfellas." While it may not be top-tier cinema, it’s one of the better crime films out there. It's more comparable to "The Sting Part 2" or perhaps "Speed Zone." Remember those gems! The sole reason this sequel exists is to capitalize on the cult following of the original. This film lacks everything De Palma, Pacino, and Penn strived to achieve. There wasn’t a single likable character, and that failure rests entirely on those involved in its creation. I hope "Rise to Power" wins every Razzie it can and maybe even invent new categories just to set a record. After watching this garbage fest, I had to rewatch the original "Carlito's Way" to erase the bad taste from my mind. If "Pachanga" were real, I’d want him to come and put me out of my misery after seeing this.

Bette Davis and Gary Merrill, fresh off their success in "All About Eve," are ill-served by Leslie Sands' poorly constructed play "Deadlock." In the story, a manipulative woman, having murdered her husband, is confronted by his best friend, who assumes her husband's identity when visitors arrive at her home. Even with Irving Rapper, one of Davis' most reliable directors during her prime, at the helm, the absurd material proves insurmountable. Davis delivers an oddly detached performance throughout, only unleashing her trademark intensity in the film's over-the-top conclusion. The production and supporting cast are decidedly subpar, making this film appealing only to die-hard Davis fans. ★½ out of ****.

This movie is incredibly funny, with Amitabh Bachchan and Govinda delivering absolutely hilarious performances. The acting is solid, and the comedy shines throughout. It’s classic stuff from them, and it would be great to see a sequel! 😊 

Definitely worth watching—it’s a fun and entertaining film!

I tend to approach films with caution when I feel an immediate aversion. Revisit them a month later, or rediscover them decades later in a completely different context, and your perspective may shift. Perhaps even cult followers will unearth stylistic nuances overlooked initially. After watching *The Great Ecstasy of Robert Carmichael* at its UK premiere, it wasn’t surprising that I found the subsequent Q&A session more engaging than the film itself. Shane Danielsen (the Artistic Director of the Edinburgh International Film Festival), alongside the director and producer, passionately defended the movie despite receiving an overwhelmingly negative reaction from the audience. Edinburgh Festival crowds are typically unflappable, yet only one person left in visible displeasure. The critiques were both articulate and constructive, coming from members of the general public, an actor, and even a professor teaching M.A. film students. This wasn’t an overtly "shocking" film. While there was prolonged sexual violence, it was far less graphic than many other movies (weapon interactions and nudity were mostly implied). What ultimately alienated the audience was their experience of...

It’s been nearly five years since the release of this stylish action film. I’ve watched this movie almost ten times, and it represents a remarkable effort by Gautham. From my point of view, this film is virtually flawless. Surya delivered an outstanding performance as ACP Anbuchelvan—classy without a doubt. Jyothika portrayed the character of Maya with great skill, and the role suited her perfectly. The character that truly captivated audiences was Pandian, played brilliantly by Jeevan. Fearsome and brutal, his portrayal earned him the Best Villain award at the ITFA 2004. The supporting cast, including Daniel Balaji, Devadharshini, and others, also gave commendable performances.

The racy screenplay, perfectly timed dialogues, and masterful narration by Gautham are highlights. The soundtrack by Harris Jeyaraj is a major hit, and the background score complements the film beautifully. R.D. Rajasekhar’s cinematography is rich and visually appealing. Peter Hein’s choreography for the action sequences was top-notch, while Anthony’s editing was precise. Above all, *Kaakha Kaakha* is a perfect cop drama, balancing action and romance flawlessly.

Even some Hollywood films struggle to match up to *Kaakha Kaakha*. Undoubtedly, it stands out as a masterpiece.

A hilariously epic comedy from the creators of *South Park* and several alumni from *Orgazmo*, this crude, offensive film is packed with disgustingly egotistical, satirical moments. It showcases shockingly cruel treatment of both humans and animals. I absolutely adore it! This is some seriously funny stuff. Two hapless friends invent a game in their driveway, which becomes a nationwide phenomenon. As corruption, greed, and blackmail taint the sport, it’s up to Coop to set things right. Along the way, you’ll be laughing nonstop. That’s all there is to it—enjoy!

These slasher films may be past their prime, but this one is enjoyable fun. The Valentine’s Day-themed cards are cleverly written and well-conceived. There's a standout line in the movie: "He's no angel..." spoken when he actually *is* Angel! This moment adds an unexpected twist that changes how you'll view Buffy reruns from now on. 

The cast showcases impressive young talent, yet the storyline doesn’t provide enough depth for the characters. While Denise Richards mentions on the DVD extras that the actresses bonded well on set, hoping it would make viewers empathize with their roles, I’m sorry to say it didn't quite work that way. 

The direction is solid, skillfully avoiding excessive gore and instead relying on implied threats to engage the audience's imagination. Similarly, both Miss Richards and Halle Berry’s characters remain fully clothed throughout—something worth noting. 

Ultimately, the film’s strongest point lies in borrowing elements from classic slasher movies; Psycho's iconic shower scene and Halloween’s masked killer are致敬ed here. Meanwhile, the idea of killing someone inside a body bag feels refreshingly original. 

It’s light entertainment—not particularly scary—but offers a few decent jump scares.

In this gritty yet stylishly crafted revenge thriller, Charles Bronson portrays Lt. Crowe, a police detective waging a personal war against a pimp named Duke (Juan Fernandez). Duke is responsible for kidnapping the daughter of a Japanese businessman, who had previously sexually harassed Crowe's daughter, Amy Hathaway. Despite its unsettling plot elements, "Kinjite" is well-executed and engaging, though it may not appeal to all audiences.

Harvey Keitel delivers one of his finest performances of the new century in this visually stunning film, offering a poignant glimpse into pre-Castro Cuba. The narrative centers on the nephew of a minor crime boss whose life takes a turn when he forms a bond with an American connected to Hollywood. At its core, the story captures the pivotal moment when a young boy begins to realize that the confined world he knows is but a fragment of a vast, intricate reality beyond his comprehension. The script is robust, brimming with humor, while the direction is sharp and engaging. Overall, it’s a polished production that aligns seamlessly with the legacy of Latin American cinema. The sole drawback is the choice to film in synchronized English instead of Spanish, likely aimed at boosting U.S. market appeal. This detracts slightly from the film's authenticity. However, if viewers can overlook this aspect, they will discover a heartfelt journey to another time and place. Highly recommended.

This is a superb, self-contained piece of work, entirely unconnected to anything before or after. While Brat Pack crooning and club exclusivity aren’t my cup of tea, they create an alluring atmosphere in this lawless world. The film brims with “Our Guys,” distinctive actors delivering standout performances that elevate the work. The dialogue is a delight, almost a new vernacular. Few films offer the same deepening appreciation upon repeated viewings.

Highlights include Billy Idol’s British roughness, Ben London’s vulture-like demeanor, Kyle’s cringe-worthy moments, and the exploration of ad hoc philosophies.

This movie is incredibly uplifting. 

Each time I watch it, I notice funny little details I overlooked before. 

The soundtrack is extraordinary. Mick Jones (of Foreigner) and Chris Difford (from Squeeze) wrote the songs, making *Strange Fruit* the greatest thing to hit contemporary music. 

Unfortunately, *Strange Fruit* is a fictional band from the 1960s-1970s that never succeeded due to drug use and internal conflicts. While listening to their fantastic soundtrack, one can't help but wonder what might have been. 

The band draws inspiration from The Rolling Stones, Deep Purple, David Bowie, and The Who. 

Each member of the band is unforgettable. Stephen Rea plays Tony Costello, a down-on-his-luck musician asked by a festival promoter to reunite his band for a reunion tour in hopes of financial gain. Tony eagerly enlists ex-roadie Karen Knowles, portrayed by Juliet Aubrey, to revive the dream they left behind. 

Juliet tracks down the bitter Jimmy Nail (as Les Wickes), the clumsy Timothy Spall (as David "Beano" Baggot), and the flamboyantly glamorous Ray Simms (played by Bill Nighy). Joining them is another ex-roadie, the laid-back, joke-cracking hippie Hughie, brought to life by Billy Connolly.

Despite the glut of forgettable films from both Hollywood and the indie scene, we’ve finally gotten a movie that actually delivers some genuinely scary moments. While there are a few clichés, it’s hard to create something entirely original these days. There’s nothing groundbreaking here, but it’s executed well.

Pay close attention, because the subtle scares come fast and furious. This isn’t a movie you can watch while snacking on pizza.

The film features one particularly well-crafted red herring, but unfortunately also includes one glaring misstep in casting. Cheri Christian doesn’t quite pull off the role of Julie (the wife/mother). She comes across as unsympathetic, and the viewer never really gets to see her as she might be under normal circumstances. The tension between her and her husband feels uncomfortable in ways the filmmakers probably didn’t intend. The director may have wanted viewers to empathize with her, but I never did.

On a positive note, the ending is both unsettling and satisfying. It could have been undermined by a cheap sound effect during the credits, but thankfully the director avoided that temptation.

This isn’t

When I first heard about this movie, I thought it would be similar to *The Duchess* (2008). However, after watching the first 30 minutes of *The Young Victoria*, I realized it was going to be much more than just a solid film. Nearly everything in this movie is outstanding—the costumes are incredible, and the settings are beautifully captured on screen.

The one downside for me were the performances. Emily Blunt (*The Devil Wears Prada*) delivers the standout performance as Queen Victoria, bringing the character to life and proving she’s a gifted actress. Her portrayal could very well earn her an Oscar nomination. Rupert Friend is somewhat bland as Prince Albert but shares great chemistry with Blunt. Paul Bettany does a competent job as Lord Melbourne, though I expected more depth from him. Jim Broadbent and Miranda Richardson have small supporting roles, but their performances are forgettable.

Overall, the film feels incomplete to me—perhaps the screenwriters made too many changes to the script, which left me with that impression. Despite this, *The Young Victoria* remains a compelling look at the early years of Queen Victoria, thanks largely to Emily Blunt's exceptional performance.

Unless I’m mistaken, I rented *A Nightmare on Elm Street 3* several years ago, and it included a music video—most likely called "Dream Warriors"—at the end. I rented this DVD版 hoping to find that video again because it’s one of the funniest things I’ve ever seen. It’s incredible how so much from the '80s is hilarious now, but nothing beats the comedy gold of '80s rap videos. In the VHS version of the film, after the credits, there was a rap group performing “Dream Warriors,” and they were all decked out in denim jackets over bare chests, paired with form-fitting jean shorts—Daisy Dukes-style, all frayed at the bottom. I can’t think of anything sillier than that.

(Spoiler alert) Disappointed by the absence of the video on the DVD, I ended up with just another mediocre entry in the Freddy Krueger series. The movie starts off similarly to Part 2, where the protagonist witnesses horrifying murders and then snaps out of some kind of trance, only to realize...

Sidney Stratton struggles to hold onto jobs at different textile mills due to his experiments in the laboratories. He is working on a formula for a revolutionary fabric that would produce the perfect material—dirt-resistant, wrinkle-free, and indestructible. When Stratton successfully develops this fabric, he earns the enmity of both the textile workers (who fear losing their jobs) and the mill owners (who stand to lose profits, as one mill holds exclusive rights to the innovation). As a result, Stratton, clad in his pristine white suit, becomes the most sought-after fugitive in England. The film is a masterpiece, and only Ealing could have crafted it so well. Guinness's performance, alongside an exceptional supporting cast including Greenwood, Thesiger, and Parker, and Mackendrick’s direction make the movie delightful, but the true standout is the story itself—a clever satire of commerce and industry, enriched with drama, romance, and suspense. Rating: 8.

Michael Jackson is an artistic marvel. His music videos are unparalleled. While I wouldn’t mind receiving a coherent science fiction film from him, I’m far more interested in experiencing his signature blend of frenetic dancing, spine-tingling shrieks, mesmerizing crowd choreography, and a touch of CGI and animation. The collection here includes everything I love about Jackson's work. Even though the film features a disjointed plot and over-the-top theatrics, it doesn’t matter when watching him perform. For me, he remains the undisputed king of music videos—not the cringeworthy "king of pop," especially since "pop" sounds like the Russian word for "butts," and Jackson certainly isn’t the "king of butts." I can endlessly replay his best music videos, which are visually stunning, without ever growing bored.

Initially, my reaction to this film was confusion—"What is this...?" It’s a patchwork of fragments from various videos, surreal illustrations, jarring transitions between themes, and some random kid antics—but by the time I finished watching, I realized it was brilliant and unlike anything else.

"Hitokiri," meaning roughly "assassin," also known as "Tenchu," translating to "divine punishment," highlights Hideo Gosha at his peak. Don’t miss this masterpiece or his other classic, *Goyokin*! *Hitokiri* isn't just one of Gosha's finest films; it’s among the greatest "samurai/chambara" movies ever made and one of Japan's most significant cinematic exports.

Be advised, the complex plot details in *Hitokiri* may prove challenging for those unfamiliar with 19th-century Japanese history. Nevertheless, the universal human drama remains accessible to all audiences. As usual with Gosha, the film explores his signature theme of "loyalty to one's lord" versus "doing what is right." Yet, Gosha crafts this familiar subject with such depth and nuance that this is truly the film to watch (alongside *Goyokin*).  

To sum up: If you prefer a straightforward, action-packed story, consider *Goyokin*. But if you seek a thought-provoking, layered, albeit somber drama, choose *Hitokiri*.  
*(Okay, okay, essentially, the historical setting revolves around a fierce power struggle among multiple samurai clans...)*

From the Q&A sessions before and after, here’s what I gathered: An Irish guy has a dream to make a movie. Just any movie—no specific theme, just something compelling. One evening at a party, he hears an ex-roadie recount a legendary rock 'n' roll tale: the story of how Gram Parsons' body was allegedly stolen from LAX by his devoted roadie, who wanted to honor Parsons’ wish to be cremated in Joshua Tree. Wow! What an incredible concept for a film! Rock 'n' roll (well, more country), grave-robbing, thrilling escapes, camaraderie, the 1970s—it’s got everything! We could cast Johnny Knoxville from “Jackass” since it sort of feels like a prank, and Knoxville seems eager to take on more serious roles. Maybe he even saw this as the next “Snatch!”

However, the story isn’t exactly action-packed… we need something for Knoxville to fight against. How about a psycho girlfriend chasing him for his money? Parsons was actually married at the time, but no one will remember that detail. Plus, we can bring in Christina Applegate. Still, what if audiences don’t approve of corpse theft? No worries—we’ll have Knoxville’s character’s dad join the pursuit, only to ultimately give his blessing in the end.

Yes, it can be done. John De Bello and Costa Dillon emptied the mental garbage bins and conjured up the worst comedic, horror, sci-fi musical imaginable. If there's any acting, it’s either atrocious or wildly over-the-top. The special effects? Choose your poison—either laughably low-budget or on par with a kindergarten project. Every cheap cliché in the book is thrown in for good measure. Despite its flaws, it’s undeniably a fun movie to watch. Worth a couple of cold six-packs. Blame radiation if you need an excuse. Mutant tomatoes grow to nearly the size of a tow truck and start terrorizing humanity. San Diego seems like as good a place as any to kick things off. With scientists and an absent-minded military trying to stop this crimson rolling menace, this cult classic stars David Miller, Eric Christmas, Al Sklar, Tom Coleman, Sharon Taylor, and John Qualls.

Richard Pryor’s infamous early 1980s incident of running down the street on fire likely left a significant mark on him. Even in his stand-up routines, he couldn’t resist poking fun at it for big laughs. Interestingly, this bizarre event seemed to influence some of the projects he chose later on. "The Toy" ranks among his weakest films, possibly only surpassed by "Another You."

A movie where a white man buys his son a black man? That’s a rather subtle dose of political incorrectness for its time. Watching Pryor turn sentimental was the last straw—I had to walk out before the credits rolled. I was hoping to see Pryor take revenge on this bratty character, but instead, it became another endless tale of the misunderstood child. At least Jackie Gleason delivered a few memorable moments. Skip this one entirely and check out Pryor’s collaborations with Gene Wilder or his '70s work instead. Trust me, this film is a complete waste of time!

I vividly remember watching this movie for the first time when I was nine years old. I was captivated by the "Barbarian Brothers" and aspired to be just like them. Even today, this film remains incredibly entertaining. One unique aspect was the brevity of the fight scenes, which suggested that the "Barbarian Brothers" were so skilled they could defeat their opponents swiftly! The movie also features thrilling chases, a cage fight, a dragon, and even a barroom brawl! 

While the acting may not be stellar, which is why it doesn't score a perfect ten, the storyline has faced its share of criticism. However, I believe it’s quite original. Few films within its genre boast such unique plots or colorful dialogue. 

I highly recommend this movie to fans of action and adventure!

MINOR SPOILER  
Underrated Stephen King thriller. While far from flawless, it remains a compelling watch despite some shortcomings. Even if Dale Midkiff and Denise Crosby had delivered stronger performances, issues with the convoluted supernatural elements would persist. The mysterious Micmac burial ground, Rachel’s dying sister, and the spectral Victor Pascow fail to coalesce into a cohesive narrative, leaving the film feeling disjointed at times. However, perfection is rare in horror, and this one compensates with its willingness to unsettle viewers. *Pet Sematary* might just be one of the cruelest horror films ever made, thanks to its terrifying zombie baby and the painfully insensitive depiction of Zelda. Politically incorrect, tasteless, and gratuitous, it shocks in ways safer horror flicks cannot. Coupled with Fred Gwynne’s stellar performance and Mary Lambert’s sharp direction, it delivers an undeniably gripping experience—even with its cheesy finale. Highly recommended for fans of the genre. 7.5 out of 10.

"Deliverance," written by James Dickey and adapted into a masterpiece by director John Boorman, is a captivating yet unsettling tale. The story revolves around four businessmen whose egos and machismo lead them on a canoeing trip deep into the mountains. What begins as an adventure quickly spirals into a harrowing journey through the darker aspects of humanity—poverty, exploitation, and brutality. As they navigate the treacherous river, they encounter violence and isolation, transforming their excursion into a nightmare far removed from civilization.

This film is not only visually striking but also profoundly disturbing, leaving viewers questioning whether they could endure such trials. Its raw depiction of human struggle makes "Deliverance" one of the most haunting cinematic experiences I’ve encountered. Nearly every moment unfolds with tension, evoking dread and prayerful relief that such ordeals remain distant from reality.

As pure cinematic storytelling, this film holds significant weight. Boorman’s direction stands among his finest works, alongside "Zardoz" and "Excalibur." Many later films have drawn inspiration from its iconic moments, particularly the chilling "dueling banjos" musical sequence and the infamous "squeal like a pig" scene. Each actor delivers a compelling performance, ensuring the story resonates long after the credits roll.

If you're looking for entertainment, skip this movie. If you want to see heroic portrayals of war, don't watch it. If you appreciate strong acting or a well-crafted screenplay, stay away. But if you enjoy typical Hollywood war films that wrap up neatly with a politically charged message glorifying war, then go ahead and see it. Otherwise, save your time. I'm usually intrigued by war movies because, when done well, they can teach us about the contradictory and senseless nature of war. This film, however, follows a group of men stumbling through the countryside, spouting clichéd lines, performing entirely predictable actions, and using the same violence to defend the oppressed as was used against them. It’s an insult to filmmaking and to the United States. Imagine someone from Europe, Africa, or elsewhere watching this and thinking this reflects American values. No wonder we’re disliked! Seriously, don’t waste your time on this.

Although I’m not typically a fan of fairy tale movies, "Stardust" caught my attention after seeing Michelle Pfeiffer in the trailers, playing a villain. Her portrayal of a witch, particularly with the aging makeup in the beginning and end, was incredibly convincing. Robert De Niro delivers a fantastic performance as the pirate captain who must stay “in the closet” to safeguard his reputation! Nearly every actor, including Claire Danes, Rupert Everett, Ricky Gervais, Peter O’Toole, and others, shines in their roles. While Danes and Pfeiffer embody classic beauty, Sienna Miller, Olivia Grant (as Girl Bernard), and Kate Magowan stand out with their striking features, especially Magowan’s introduction. Newcomer Charlie Cox gives a solid performance as Tristan, and he bears such a striking resemblance to his father, Dunstan, that I initially mistook him for Dunstan in earlier scenes (played by Ben Barnes). Many have likened this film to *The Princess Bride*, and while there are similarities, one key distinction is that in *PB*, it’s clear the story is purely fictional.

I consider myself a true movie enthusiast. Lying sick on the couch, I decided to watch this film. From the very beginning until the end, I was captivated by the incredible performances of these talented actors whom I had never encountered before. Their delivery was remarkable. The cinematography was stunning, and it perfectly matched my mood at that moment. I sincerely hope this heartfelt tribute reaches beyond any negative feedback others may have shared. The director's passion is evident, as it resonates through every scene alongside their exceptional cast. Thank you for creating such a remarkable film—awkward yet beautifully graceful, with flawed but endearing characters. Simply fantastic. To meet the requirement of ten lines, I’ll add that I eagerly anticipate more work from this director, the entire cast, and the writer. The story was so engaging that I wished it would never conclude. The end.

Jet Li is one of the world's greatest practitioners of hand-to-hand combat, a title he has held for over two0 years, leaving peers in the genre far behind. Although he is a major figure in Asia, he remains relatively obscure in the United States.

"Black Mask" was expected to be a breakthrough film for him, but it falls spectacularly short. Firstly, it is dubbed, which might appeal to fans of campy cinema due to its laughable inaccuracy and monotonous tone, but it feels ill-suited for mainstream audiences. Secondly, the director, Daniel Lee, performs poorly. The rapid editing often leaves viewers confused, not knowing what’s happening. At other times, the shaky and unsteady camera work distracts from the action. Fans watch Jet Li's films for his exceptional martial arts sequences, yet the director's hurried editing makes it difficult to follow the action half the time. In other instances, scenes feel unresolved—such as when Li starts cutting through the floor of a jeep, and before you can blink, both he and the love interest are already hiding under the vehicle! Some moments are so implausible that they...

The majority of French films I’ve watched—and thoroughly enjoyed—tend to focus more on dialogue than action, which isn’t necessarily a bad thing. I find them captivating, beautifully shot, and featuring intriguing performances. Though, at one point, I couldn’t help but wonder if Gérard Depardieu appeared in every single French film ever made; his presence seemed ubiquitous. 

This particular movie shared similar visually striking qualities and started off strong with an engaging opening. However, it quickly transformed into an endless stream of talking, talking, and even more talking. While this might work for a drama, it falls short for a murder mystery. Eventually, I found myself struggling to stay awake.

In reality, the film felt more like a play, with nearly all its scenes confined to a single room. So, if you’re a fan of theater, you’ll likely enjoy it. But as someone looking for a gripping murder story, I expected a bit more excitement.

This film is poorly structured, clumsily written, and filled with overused clichés and lifeless dialogue. No scene manages to stand out. The actors grapple with an excruciatingly dull storyline that fails to introduce any surprises, plot twists, or meaningful conflict. From the first ten minutes, it’s clear exactly where the story is headed.

Despite being set in New York City, the movie offers little sense of the city’s magic. Numerous indie films have successfully captured its charm on a modest budget, but this one feels as though it was filmed in Toronto.

Why cast Natasha Henstridge and then dress her in oversized sweaters? Why turn Vartan into a bland, uninspired character? The lack of chemistry between them leaves viewers questioning what draws these characters together. It felt like watching a low-quality Christian television movie—completely asexual and preachy.

Steven Feder’s biggest accomplishment here was convincing others to bring this flavorless project to life.

A bondage, humiliation, and S&M-themed show with little else to offer, the film suffers from a weak plot that serves mostly as a basic framework for its visually striking yet depraved scenes. The host of the show—a ridiculous figure prancing around the stage in dresses while spouting nonsense—was nearly as distracting as the heavy-handed editing attempts. The dreamlike conclusion felt forced and out of place. However, Aya Sugimoto delivered a compelling performance as the tormented protagonist. While "Flower and Snake" has been likened to "Eyes Wide Shut," the two share only superficial similarities; Kubrick’s film remains far more nuanced, artistic, and atmospheric.

This is quite possibly the worst acting I have ever witnessed in a movie. Period. And what's with the casting? The leading lady in this film has some sort of nasal abnormality that makes it nearly impossible to focus on anything else while watching. You could walk into your local grocery store on a Sunday afternoon and probably find 50 more qualified, better-looking candidates for the role. I regretfully rented this movie based solely on its "cool" DVD case design. It feels like it’s nothing more than a class project from a group of multimedia students at a community college. Watching public access TV would have been far more entertaining—its special effects are better, and the people featured are significantly more attractive than anyone in this film.

This movie was hands down the worst I’ve ever seen, and I’ve watched some truly terrible films. The cinematography was appalling, and the entire production felt amateurish. None of the actors were recognizable, and it seemed like a group of friends threw this project together on a whim. It’s dreadful—there’s no other way to describe it. The storyline was utterly contrived, and it dragged on forever without reaching any satisfying conclusion. There was no discernible plot, and it clearly lacked proper planning before filming began. The narrative was bizarre and meandered aimlessly. I couldn’t stand how painfully slow the pacing was, and it never seemed to have a clear purpose. Watching this movie would be a complete waste of time. If you’re thinking about giving it a try, don’t bother—you’ll only regret it.

This film ranks among my favorite foreign movies, alongside *Amélie* and *My Life as a Dog*. Like many great foreign films, its strength lies in transforming an ordinary slice of life into a deeply moving and insightful experience.  

Set in Japan, the story follows a man stuck in the monotony of his daily routine and dissatisfied with his marriage. One day, while riding the train, he glimpses a stunning Japanese woman gazing out the window of a dance studio. In that fleeting moment, something about her—her beauty, perhaps, or the longing in her gaze—captures his imagination. Is it attraction alone, or could there be a deeper connection waiting to be discovered?  

*Shall We Dance* introduces us to unforgettable characters who confront the harsh realities of their lives by finding solace and meaning in the art of dance. Challenging societal norms and stereotypes, they take bold risks in pursuit of happiness, ultimately discovering that joy is closer than they ever imagined. This movie is a testament to the transformative power of life's magic, reminding us that even the most mundane moments can hold extraordinary beauty. It is one of those rare films that elevates the ordinary and reveals the wonder of existence itself.

Ugh! This is one of those movies you feel like you’ve already talked about, even though you haven’t. It just pops into your head for no reason.

Honestly, this is one of the worst, most boring, and idiotic slasher films ever made. There’s really nothing positive to say about it because there are hardly any decent scenes to suggest it was crafted by professionals.

The death scenes are terrible, bloodless, and pointless. The plot is somewhat decent, considering it ripped off "Popcorn" from 1991.

To make matters worse, this isn’t so bad that it’s enjoyable—it’s just plain awful.

Molly Ringwald gave it her best shot, but it wasn’t enough.

I was always intrigued by this film due to its rarity, so when I found it on eBay, I gladly paid the $10 and purchased it. Now I know why it’s so hard to come by! This movie is incredibly糟糕，writing so terrible and production values so low-budget that the end credits, which feature all the bloopers where actors flubbed their lines, are practically the highlight of the film. The story revolves around a psychic (Pettyjohn, cast primarily for one obvious reason—her topless scene), who uses her abilities with an experimental device to summon objects from another dimension into our world. When she pulls in a mysterious box-like object, the military casually loads it into the back of an open truck with just one soldier guarding it. Of course, unsurprisingly, a kid in a foam-rubber monster suit emerges, swiftly kills the guard with a scratch, and escapes into a nearby city. Instead of mobilizing the entire armed forces to track it down and protect the public, those in charge leave the task to Pettyjohn and her partner. Needless to say, things only get worse from there.

I’m not entirely sure why, but this movie fails to deliver as expected. It should be amusing and entertaining, yet ends up being dull instead. A significant reason for this is the overuse of “gadgets.” The original cartoon it’s inspired by is far superior.  

3/10

My scalp still tingles from the burning coals heaped upon it when I declared my love for this film. Bring on the coals—I’d traverse them again just to reiterate my undying affection for *Bend It Like Beckham*. Admittedly, my admiration comes with a fair share of caveats. It leans toward the "movie-of-the-week" formula, and its screenplay follows a predictable path. More disconcertingly, the director’s commentary seems to suggest that beauty is predominantly associated with lighter skin tones, which feels jarring and exclusionary.

Yet, the film's brilliance lies beyond the surface-level elements that critics often dissect—character arcs, themes, and structure. Its genius resides in both its overt charm and the subtleties hidden beneath, though not in the conventional layers of artistic depth reviewers typically explore. The sight of powerful, semi-clad women actively engaging with a football—not merely posing—does more to normalize female strength and agility than characters like Lara Croft or Zhang Ziyi ever could. These are authentic bodies (with the exception of Keira Knightley’s), whose purpose is not to look stunning before proving themselves capable. Instead, they are working bodies whose beauty stems from their motion and autonomy. In my eyes, lead actress Parminder Nagra embodies this spirit wholeheartedly.

This movie is incredible! Brad Pitt delivers a performance in this film that he may never surpass. Duchovny, Forbes, and Lewis all turn in outstanding performances as well. The four main characters go on a visually stunning road trip through historic murder locations, driving one of the coolest cars ever made—a 1960s Lincoln Continental. Early Grace is portrayed as a simple-minded individual who enjoys dry toothbrushes and violence. He prefers his women to avoid cursing or smoking and wear PWT dresses. Duchovny and Forbes play urban artists, while Early and Lewis are depicted as trailer park residents from rural areas. Despite the predominantly dark tone, the film includes numerous humorous scenes. The writing, direction, and acting are exceptional. If you enjoy road movies, murder mysteries, humor, and narration, check out this film. Every actor delivers, leaving viewers eager for more after the credits roll. It’s one of my all-time favorites. “Hey… shave that dog and teach it to hunt!”

This is without a doubt one of the worst movies ever made, and I emphasize, EVER. To make matters worse, my old favorite actor, Dolph, stars in it. Jesus... The story has potential, but the execution is so poor that it's painful to watch. The fighting scenes, for instance, are choreographed worse than a brawl between two drunk people in the street. As for the performances, the cast—Dolph included, who doesn't do much justice to his role—gives such糟糕的表现 that you can't help but suspect they're only there because they're friends of the director, who likely wasn't present for most, if not all, of the filming. For a budget of §12 million, this movie is a travesty; judging by the effects and set design, the production cost couldn't possibly exceed §1000.

I’m a fan of “Crash” and “Blade Runner,” and this movie delves into some of those highway destruction and 80s film noir themes that I enjoy, so I found it entertaining. 

That said, the film doesn’t handle the inherent foolishness of the film noir protagonist effectively, as the female lead comes across as almost Neanderthal in her hero worship, which is why I’m issuing a kitsch warning.

Despite having high expectations for this film, especially because I admire Jason Segel’s acting in shows like *Freaks & Geeks* and *Undeclared*, I must admit it ranks among the worst I’ve seen recently (films like *Loser* and *Dr. T and the Women* also fall into that category). 

While there were a few genuinely humorous moments that made me laugh out loud, the movie fell far short of its potential. The basic idea—con artists infiltrating college only to be confronted by someone offering them an unusual deal—wasn’t terrible. However, the characters were entirely unrelatable, making it impossible to root for any of them. Jason Schwartzman’s portrayal of the blackmailer was particularly off-putting; his character came across as a psychopath rather than someone funny or charming. Instead of being entertaining, his antics felt unsettling and out of place, detracting from the overall experience. Additionally, the editing was confusing, constantly shifting between fantasy and reality without clear distinctions. Most of the group’s scams weren’t even shown in detail—you had to imagine how clever they were. In the end, it was a missed opportunity that left me disengaged and unsatisfied.

The main challenge with this movie is knowing where to start, because it demands your full attention for the next two hours, and missing even a few minutes could leave you lost. Thankfully, there’s always the pause button. Bruce Willis plays a character who must travel through a time machine to discover an antivirus for a virus that caused animals to take over the world in 1996. Due to some errors, he initially lands in 1990, then finds himself in the First World War. Despite its convoluted premise, Terry Gilliam delivers what may well be one of the most brilliant scripts ever written. As an ex-member of Monty Python, Gilliam perfectly captures the essence of great science fiction storytelling. His casting choices are impeccable, featuring the eccentric Brad Pitt, whose performance in the asylum scene is unforgettable, and Bruce Willis, who convincingly proves he’s much more than just an Arnold Schwarzenegger wannabe. It’s a film you can revisit repeatedly; its bizarre and intricate plot—despite being challenging—is always engaging, offering new discoveries with each viewing. One of my all-time favorites.

It felt as though I'd seen this movie a thousand times already. It was completely predictable. Every time the story attempted to add a twist or I hoped for something intriguing to unfold, it delivered exactly what I anticipated—nothing more, nothing less. For instance, “The bread factory opened another facility because there wasn’t enough bread.” In short: A flat, clichéd plot, poor acting, and terrible special effects… The only remotely amusing character was Vlad, the dimwitted Russian cop, who provided some laughter when doling out punishment to the villains. The muscle-bound protagonist was so unbelievably STUPID that he briefly amused me with his idiocy. I can’t believe I’m wasting my time trashing this wretched film. It couldn’t possibly get worse (because it’s already at rock bottom). 😊

Interestingly, Fulci reportedly lost interest halfway through *Zombi 3* and walked away from the project, prompting Bruno Mattei to step in and add extra scenes to stretch the runtime.

The plot follows a familiar zombie trope: scientists on a Philippine island develop a serum, terrorists steal it, unleashing a zombie plague. While scientists aim to create an antidote, the military opts for indiscriminate slaughter. Interspersed throughout are short segments featuring a radio DJ ranting about humanity’s treatment of the Earth.

Surprisingly, I enjoyed this film despite hearing negative reviews. The campy dialogue is oddly amusing, and the overall experience feels delightfully over-the-top.

Over the past decade, Washington has delivered some of the most memorable performances in cinema, portraying a brave black soldier in *Glory* and a groundbreaking lawyer in *Philadelphia*. Of course, he also made history last year when he became the first African American to win an Academy Award for Best Actor, for his role in *Training Day*. Seeking a change of pace, Washington decided to both direct and star in *Antwone Fisher*. The titular character is brought to life by Derek Luke, a newcomer to the big screen but familiar to audiences from his appearances on shows like *King of Queens* and his upcoming role in *Biker Boyz*. 

Denzel Washington’s directorial debut is a testament to his skill, particularly considering it's his first time behind the camera. Clearly, he felt a deep connection to Antwone Fisher’s real-life journey. The film follows a young African American sailor in the Navy who repeatedly finds himself in trouble...

This film offers an entertaining and highly sarcastic take on pop culture and those who create it. I was particularly impressed by the cinematography, which featured vibrant colors and carefully crafted settings, especially considering this is Zukovic's debut in a major production.

That said, there's a caveat: don't take the movie's message too seriously. It’s not intended for a broad audience, and that isn’t a compliment. The message reflects a somewhat stylized perspective on society, geared toward recent college graduates or newcomers to the world of media.

I did appreciate the core storyline, which follows a fictional magazine editor as he wittily challenges the cultural norms of the 1990s.

This film was advertised as both a comedy and a mystery but falls short in delivering on both fronts. The real mystery is why anyone would produce such a poorly constructed movie. The only humor came from noticing how highly some readers rated it. Could there be two films with the same title? The one I watched featured a actress with striking blue eyes and a storyline that was entirely missing.

"Bruce Almighty" is predicted to make history by sweeping the Academy Awards with a record 14 Oscar wins, surpassing "Titanic" as the highest-grossing film of all time. Jim Carrey’s fame would reach such unprecedented heights that he might even announce his candidacy for the 2004 U.S. presidency. Of course, these fantastical scenarios could only occur if the filmmakers, including Carrey himself, possessed divine powers—a concept central to "Bruce Almighty." In this comedy, Carrey stars as Bruce Nolan, a frustrated television reporter whose obsession with becoming the lead anchor leads him to blame God for his setbacks. Played divinely by Morgan Freeman, God grants Bruce the "Gift of God," challenging him to see if he can handle divine responsibilities better. Naturally, Bruce becomes overzealous with his new powers, using them selfishly. Carrey delivers his signature comedic brilliance in "Bruce Almighty," while Jennifer Aniston shines alongside him. Kudos go to Director Tom Shadyac for keeping the film hilariously grounded—though one bathroom scene stands out as particularly memorable!

There's no question that this is the funniest short featuring the Curly Stooges. I must have watched it dozens of times, and it never fails to make me laugh. The pantomime sequences are hilarious, and it's a perfect example of "musical comedy." Even those who aren't fans of the trio often have fond memories of this one.

Following the murder of Central City’s mob boss, his partner-in-crime, Robert Armstrong (playing as "Doc" Rogers), takes bold action to maintain criminal continuity. He recruits the late gangster's timid son, Richard Cromwell (portrayed as Edward "Baby Face" Morgan), to helm the family operation. The unsuspecting Mr. Cromwell is brought to the city and appointed President of his father's "Acme Protection Agency," a facade for organized crime. As Cromwell naively peddles insurance, his so-called employees extort locals. Meanwhile, Cromwell becomes enamored with client Mary Carlisle (as Virginia Clark). As their promising acting careers wane, the duo finds themselves entangled in peril due to "Baby Face Morgan's" rise. This short, lighthearted crime drama avoids controversy.  
**** *Baby Face Morgan* (1942) directed by Arthur Dreifuss – Richard Cromwell, Mary Carlisle, Robert Armstrong.

As an Elvis fan, I struggle to comprehend how this project even came together. It's hands down the worst Elvis-related movie ever made—entirely devoid of humor, riddled with absurdities, and full of inaccuracies regarding The King. Seriously, Elvis' grave in a public park? A reference to "Suspicious Minds" in 1958? These are just two glaring examples. While some actors in the cast give it their all, Mike Starr provides occasional laughs, particularly as an impersonator, and Tom Hanks' cameo is a pleasant surprise, the actor portraying young Elvis is utterly unconvincing. Overall, the film lacks any sense of fun and grows increasingly dull with each passing minute. If you're looking for an offbeat, budget-friendly, yet hilariously entertaining Elvis-inspired movie, I highly recommend "Bubba Ho-Tep" over this disaster.

Kim Novak plays a witch in New York City, and for reasons unknown, she casts a spell on Jimmy to make him fall in love with her. Gradually, the aloof and detached Ms. Novak herself starts to develop feelings for Stewart—a development that, according to witch rules, seems to be strictly forbidden!

I purchased this DVD for my brother, a huge Michelle Pfeiffer fan. Curious, I decided to watch it myself earlier this week.

The film is reasonably engaging, featuring two distinct and unrelated storylines. The portion with Michelle Pfeiffer is by far the more captivating of the two. She portrays a rising Hollywood actress known for her numerous brief and unsatisfying relationships. After accidentally crashing her car into Brian Kerwin’s vehicle—played by a regular family man with kids—the two initially clash before he offers to drive her home since she no longer feels safe behind the wheel. Their relationship evolves romantically, culminating in tragedy when his wife discovers their affair. The conclusion caught me off guard, yet the sluggish pacing and predictable television-style direction diminish the dramatic impact of the storyline.

The second storyline revolves around an elderly studio boss, portrayed by Darren McGavin. This segment boasts a stronger supporting cast, including Kenneth McMillan, Lois Chiles, Steven Bauer, and Stella Stevens. Each character seeks something from the studio boss, only to find that once he’s forced to step down, their own careers are effectively over.

Eddie Murphy's "Delirious" is outright rude, crude, crass, and vulgar. There’s simply no other way to sum up this disappointing and lowbrow stand-up performance. Murphy prioritizes shock value over humor to capture his audience's attention. While he manages some genuinely funny moments, he often veers off course with offensive language and inappropriate sexual jokes. 

Pass on this one unless you're a fan of his abrasive style. I doubt I’ll check out "Eddie Murphy Raw," as I find him more enjoyable when confined to a scripted role.

To begin with, I want to emphasize that I’m a strong supporter of fan projects. I view them as a way to keep beloved shows alive even after they’ve ended. Examples like *Star Trek Voyages* and *Star Wars Revelations* demonstrate commendable efforts. This affectionate bias means I tend to forgive flaws that I’d typically criticize harshly.

Now, regarding *Star Trek: Hidden Frontier (HF)*—let’s start with the positives. Enthusiasm plays a crucial role in creating a believable production, and overall, the cast seems to enjoy their roles. Additionally, while the special effects are clearly a homemade endeavor, they don’t evoke cringes. The storytelling isn’t groundbreaking but is solid enough, with some ongoing arcs to maintain viewer interest.

However, it has significant shortcomings.

First, though they had to reuse Star Trek footage, set designs, music, and effects, I see no justification for borrowing nearly every other sci-fi soundtrack ever created. From *Aliens* to *Starship Troopers*, elements of these scores repeatedly surface throughout the series.

I recently watched the movie on TV, and I thoroughly enjoyed it. I have a soft spot for a good mystery, and this one kept me guessing until the very end. Sean Connery delivered a solid performance. I would recommend it to a friend.

Their only commonality is liking the same book, which feels like a weak connection at best. 

The performances aren’t terrible, but the pacing is agonizingly slow—almost reminiscent of Jarmusch, but without his artistic merit.

I’m a big fan of Jean Harlow because she possessed undeniable star quality. Jean Harlow shines brightly here, and the rest of the cast fades into obscurity as their performances lack distinction. Wow, how bad can it get? This was seriously awful. It wasn’t the gore—mostly laughable CGI—that made it so terrible, but rather the acting, atmosphere, and direction that left much to be desired.

The story was abysmal—the protagonist’s character arc was nonsensical. After just a few nights of stalking Vinnie Jones, he suddenly becomes “haunted” to the point of tears while taking photos of his girlfriend. Um… are all New York photographers this immature, impressionable, and weak? His development had zero justification or purpose, and by the end, you’ll be laughing at the completely predictable and utterly ridiculous twist his character takes.

The gory moments were clearly an uninspired attempt to capitalize on the trendy MTV-style horror trend—lots of CGI, blood, but no emotional depth. These scenes were unintentionally humorous and distracting due to their overly self-conscious execution—wacky camera angles, etc.

In summary, this film squanders a potentially atmospheric concept (until the ridiculous monsters at the end). Instead of focusing on creating mood, it succumbs to flashy, self-indulgent directing. This movie wasn’t made for an audience—it was made for the filmmakers’ egos.

Beyond the exceptional direction, production, and acting, as well as the predictable drama, lies a profound message at the heart of the script:  

"Listening leads all the way." To let one’s voice thrive, listen. To harmonize with others, listen. To understand oneself, listen. To uncover the needs of any situation or others, listen. It seems the screenwriters are sharing a "life's secret": Listening fosters self-awareness. It awakens other senses, particularly sight, and broadens horizons. One’s very soul can be discovered through it. The artistry of this film, *As It Is in Heaven*, beautifully showcases the unfolding of life—not just its joys and sorrows, but ultimately its hope—through the protagonist's initial directive to the choir:  

"Just listen; it leads all the way."

"The Return of Chandu" is noteworthy—though perhaps not in a conventional sense—for casting Bela Lugosi as the hero instead of the usual villain. Even more surprising, he ends up winning the girl.

The plot revolves around the Black Magic Cult of Ubasti attempting to capture the last Egyptian princess, Nadji (played by the charming Maria Alba), to use her as a sacrificial offering in a ritual to resurrect their ancient leader, who bears an uncanny resemblance to Nadji. Lugosi stars as Chandu, a magician with supernatural abilities, determined to stop the malevolent cult.

Director Ray Taylor makes do with limited resources and relies heavily on stock footage. Viewers familiar with "King Kong" (1933) might recognize the iconic giant doors used to confine Kong, repurposed here in various scenes. Unfortunately, the performances are largely subpar. For instance, Lucien Prival, who portrays the high priest, adopts the overly enunciated delivery style typical of early talkie actors. Mentioning the rest of the cast invites little praise.

It remains puzzling why Lugosi accepted roles in low-budget productions during this period, given that he was still considered a valuable asset at Universal Studios. Perhaps...

I’m still unsure whether this film had a purpose. For something billed as so "rebellious" and "controversial," the materials Maddox hands out to the students are surprisingly unimpressive. The vague anti-authoritarian messages scrawled on flyers fail to inspire much beyond mild curiosity among the students. Truly, rebelling has never seemed so lackluster.

It seems unrealistic to expect a teen rebellion movie without a school fire alarm being triggered at least once. Apparently, a "massive brawl on the football field" amounts to little more than two individuals squaring off.

Character development is inconsistent at best; one moment a football player is brawling with Maddox, and the next he’s offering apologetic smiles like nothing happened. 

The lack of resolution for the storyline leaves me feeling like the entire plot could’ve been condensed into a half-hour afterschool special—if only they'd trimmed most of the overly pretentious glitch soundtrack.

No doubt about it, *Private Lessons II* is hands down the best movie I've ever seen. As a Japanese import with a poor English translation, it's pure delight to watch. Logic isn’t really its strong suit, but that’s beside the point. It’s the funniest comedy out there—without once trying to be funny.

This elusive film is scarce and nearly impossible to find on video, but I’ve managed to catch it a few times late at night on pay cable. My worn-out taped copy has been played countless times as I introduce this hidden gem to one person at a time.

Joanna Pacula stars as the tutor/lover to Ken, our protagonist. (She seems to have been in it purely for the paycheck.) Ken is played by Goro Inagaki, a member of the Japanese pop group SMAP, who delivers an enthusiastic performance and sports impeccable hair throughout. Stacy Edwards, known for her role in *"In the Company of Men,"* also appears and likely appreciated moving on to other projects.

It takes at least three viewings to vaguely grasp the plot. On repeat watches, you can savor details like the absurd number of vases Ken owns (at least 50) or that...

I hope the person who considered "Dream Machine" one of Corey Haim's best works and among the "best movies of the century" was merely joking. Hopefully, I didn’t unintentionally misinterpret sarcasm. I genuinely hope so.

'The Dream Machine' ushered in a string of uninspired heist films that would overshadow much of Corey Haim's career, with the exception of 'Prayer of the Rollerboys,' which was surprisingly tolerable. In this film, Haim portrays Bernie, an easygoing college student convinced that owning a flashy car will win over his ideal girl. Coincidentally, a wealthy woman seeking revenge against her unfaithful spouse impulsively decides to gift her loyal piano tuner, Bernie, a luxurious Porsche Turbo. Unbeknownst to her—and unfortunately for Bernie—her late husband’s body was concealed in the car’s trunk. Naturally, given the context of this movie, the corpse shows no signs of decay or odor, leaving Bernie completely unaware of its presence. Despite numerous strange occurrences and the relentless pursuit of the mysterious man trying to retrieve the body discreetly, Bernie remains oblivious.

This is a lackluster action flick.

In short, I’m not a fan of westerns.
