Since I’d never managed to watch one from start to finish, I decided to give “My Darling Clementine” a try and see it through, regardless of how challenging it might be. Initially, it was as excruciating as anticipated. The acting struck me as comical, the setting (the usual desert landscapes, horses, and cowboys) felt monotonous, and the music and its timing bordered on discomforting. Yet, after mustering the mental fortitude to push forward, around the 20-minute mark, it became significantly easier to bear. Shifting my focus to John Ford’s cinematography, which transformed even the dullest moments into visually striking scenes, made the experience far more engaging. 

In the end, I wouldn’t say I thoroughly enjoyed the film, but it was crafted well enough for me to watch it through to the conclusion, which is no small feat for someone who isn’t a fan of the genre.

Eva Longoria and Paul Rudd star in a film about a deceased girlfriend haunting her replacement. It’s Gabrielle from *Desperate Housewives* paired with the actor who played “sex Panther” cologne guy from *Anchorman*. If you’re hoping for a Golden Globe-nominated movie, this might not be your pick. But if you’re open to losing yourself in a lighthearted comedy for 90 minutes, you’re in for a treat. The characters are hilarious, and they play off each other beautifully. The standout pairing is Paul Rudd and Lake Bell—Rudd is just as witty as he was on *Friends*, while Bell is both funny and easy on the eyes. My wife and I watched it together, and we both had a great time.

Famous Studios was renowned for their unique approach to cartoons, characterized by intense tension and dramatic releases. In these stories, the semi-main character often finds themselves in dire situations, only to be saved by the hero at the last moment. The Casper cartoon I recall stands out because it's the only one where death plays a direct role. Yet, even in this somber scenario, the story concludes on a positive note.

A consistent theme in Famous Studios' cartoons is that "virtue always prevails." Whether it's Popeye reaching for his spinach just in time, Baby Huey outsmarting the fox, or Little Audrey learning her lesson, the studio maintained this optimistic outcome throughout their productions. Interestingly, some of their cartoons delve into darker, more melancholic narratives.

It’s worth acknowledging their excellence; while I adore Looney Tunes and "Tom and Jerry," Paramount consistently delivered top-tier cartoon quality during that era. From vibrant color palettes to exceptional animation, the iconic scores by Winston Sharples, precise editing, and memorable voice performances, they set a high standard for the medium. Their consistency made them a shining exemplar of the art form’s finest achievements.

In today's era of digital fabrication, no computer can replace the talent of an actor or writer. Unfortunately, this kind of "character-driven" film has become increasingly rare. Both Robert Duvall's and James Earl Jones' performances remain true to the high standards audiences expect. I can't help but wonder if this movie was originally intended for television; its narrative carries an intimate, "close-up" feel. It would be an understatement to describe their performances as anything less than outstanding. The only factor preventing it from achieving masterpiece status is the absence of a top-tier cinematographer—though visually stunning imagery isn't the sole measure of greatness. How do actors like Jones and Duvall continue to deliver such remarkable performances in an age dominated by actors posing for digitization?

A stunning film, particularly for those who appreciate horses, WWII movies, and the stark beauty of the Hungarian Plateau. It tells a timeless tale of courage, compassion, and loyalty that resonates across generations. The horsemanship showcased in the movie is remarkable, and the main character's journey with his horse during training is equally impressive.

I plan to purchase this movie so I can watch it again. It’s a wonderful family film, and I highly recommend it. It’s perfect for a "Family Night." While there are some intense scenes due to the Nazi occupation of Hungary, the portrayal of the local people standing firm, even in the face of imminent danger from a Nazi officer with personal motives, adds depth to the story. This is a beautifully haunting film.

In days gone by, everything seemed better—including children’s television. And "Fraggle Rock" perfectly illustrates this. Although I’m just fourteen years old as I write this, I can’t help but fall for the charm of this show. For those of you who’ve been, well, hiding under a rock (pun intended!), "Fraggle Rock" revolves around a group of playful, quirky creatures called Fraggles who surprisingly call a rock home. However, they’re not alone; the rock is also inhabited by other fascinating beings, such as the industrious Doozers and sentient plants. On one side of the rock lives inventor-scientist Doc and his dog Sprocket (who eventually bonds with Gobo Fraggle), while on the other side resides a family of Gorgs, self-proclaimed rulers of the universe. The show’s five main Fraggles—Gobo (the fearless leader), Mokey (artistic and serene), Wembley (indecisive yet loyal to Gobo), Boober (a pessimistic domestic genius), and Red (sporty and full of spunk)—find themselves in odd predicaments every episode, all while singing and dancing their worries away. 

"Fraggle Rock" is undoubtedly a family-friendly show; its storylines might include nuanced details that younger viewers could miss, but its catchy songs and lively dances make it universally enjoyable.

I simply can’t comprehend the negative feedback surrounding this movie. While it’s undeniably a classic boy-meets-girl romance, it’s executed with such flair and refinement that the runtime feels exhilarating. Henstridge (seriously, she must have won the gene pool lottery!) remains as captivating and enchanting as ever (somebody tell those who claim the golden age of cinema is over!), and Vartan matches her effortlessly. 

The undeniable chemistry between the two leads makes every shared moment crackle; the film truly comes alive whenever they’re on screen together. Their performances are so compelling that you’ll find yourself rooting for their characters to end up together... 

Disregard the unfavorable reviews—watch this film if you're feeling down, and it’ll lift your spirits. If you're already in a good mood, it'll leave you feeling euphoric. 

(PPS: I’m 33, male, from the UK, and still a hopeless romantic, searching for my very own princess.)

The stunning seventeen-minute dance sequence from George Gershwin's 1928 orchestral work, *"An American in Paris,"* stands as an undeniable masterpiece. Expertly choreographed by Gene Kelly with meticulous precision and extraordinary flair, the vibrant interplay of color, music, and dance remains breathtakingly impactful. As the sequence unfolds, it breaks into scenes inspired by renowned master artists: Dufy in the opening Place de la Concorde segment, Manet at the flower market, Utrillo for a Parisian street, Rousseau at the fair, Vincent Van Gogh in the dazzling Place de l'Opera scene, and Toulouse-Lautrec for the Moulin Rouge, where Kelly dons his iconic white bodysuit. While the preceding 97 minutes may lack the same level of excitement, there is charm to be found in the entirety of the 1951 Oscar-winning musical.

Directed by Vincente Minnelli and written by Alan Jay Lerner, the film presents a surprisingly sophisticated yet somewhat lightweight romantic tale centered around Jerry Mulligan, a former G.I. who stays in post-WWII Paris, striving to establish himself as a painter. Despite Gene Kelly’s brash demeanor and athletic dancing style, which can sometimes make him both endearing and exasperating on-screen, he delivers a performance that feels well-suited to the material.

"Cat Soup" is a short yet captivating experience that feels like an intense journey. While browsing through my on-demand list, I stumbled upon it in the anime section and decided to give it a try. Throughout the film, I found myself utterly mesmerized, mouth agape, with thoughts either racing wildly or screaming at me to turn it off. However, I persisted, and I’m glad I did.

The animation is visually stunning—odd, dark, and incredibly artistic. Personally, I adored the stunning visuals, but the enigmatic story behind them was equally intriguing. 

In the beginning, a young boy (who is also a cat) sets out to retrieve his sister's soul. She lies ill in bed when a Grim Reaper-like figure arrives and splits her soul into two halves; the boy manages to recover one half, but the other remains missing.

Afterward, the narrative becomes somewhat unclear to me. Perhaps they return home, and their world starts unraveling? Maybe her incomplete soul holds the key to this mystery, as the remainder of the film delves deeper into this unsettling reality.

Good lord, this movie was terrible. I only watched it as a lighthearted laugh, but it wasn’t even so bad that it became amusing in an ironic way. This film felt specifically crafted to infuriate me, and it succeeded brilliantly. It’s as though the creators took everything obnoxious from the movie *Priest*, threw in a bunch of unappealing characters, stripped away anything engaging, funny, or remotely appealing or clever, and then added a generous helping of rancid cheese. That’s all this is—cheese. There’s not a single soul this movie could resonate with, nor does it belong in any conceivable universe. Why couldn’t this already silly premise just focus on celebrating life and spreading joy? Why did they take such a nonsensical idea and push it further into absurdity? Couldn’t they have at least attempted to make it a passable film, or even a decent B-movie? On second thought, what exactly were they aiming for with this mess? I went in expecting a campy romance but instead got...

When I first encountered this film in the 1980s, I was a teenager, and while I was somewhat hesitant to watch it—thinking I'd outgrown the "Sesame Street/Muppets" phase—I can’t recall whether I enjoyed it at the time or not. However, sometime during college, I revisited the movie, and it quickly became a staple in my personal "Best Films Ever" collection.

This film is packed with humor that far surpasses what you’d typically expect from the Muppets. Of course, the Muppets have always appealed to both kids and adults due to their layered humor, but scenes like Janice accidentally being overheard saying, "I don’t take my clothes off for anyone, even if it IS artistic," or a father jokingly telling his son, "If you’re in love with Kermit the Frog, I don’t want to hear about it," left me laughing. Then there’s Gonzo saving a chicken with mouth-to-mouth resuscitation and afterward declaring, "I think we’re engaged now"—moments like these had me in stitches. Combine that with clever dialogue, sharp New York/Broadway-style wit, and the Muppets' signature charm, and it’s no wonder this film resonated so deeply.

This is a dreadful film, devoid of even a single scene that conveys an ounce of genuine emotion. The characters are one-dimensional, predictable, and shallow, while the plot is a clichéd example of Hollywood's overused wish-fulfillment tropes.

William Holden, sadly, seems ill-suited for his role here; at 55, he plays someone in their early 40s but looks much older. Meanwhile, Kay Lenz, just 20 at the time, was expected to find him irresistibly attractive. To be honest, the stray dog they found by the roadside seemed sexier and more alive than their supposed chemistry.

Holden’s character, coincidentally the same age as Clint Eastwood when he directed this film, is surrounded by all the trappings of '60s pre-hippie cool: the bachelor pad, the swinging hi-fi, and fancy lunches at Yamashiro. Yet, the movie feels laughably outdated—nothing more than a jarring mess of aging adults clinging to outdated notions of coolness, longing for the freedom and allure of youth they witnessed along Sunset Boulevard or in Laurel Canyon. 

Yuck. Youth culture wasn’t that gullible, and it pains me to think that William Holden would stoop so low for such an embarrassing role.

This four-hour remake of the Rider Haggard story includes the typical additions, such as a prominent female role and an unnecessary subplot involving Russian soldiers searching for a "Stone of Power" buried alongside King Solomon's treasure. Despite its length, it is beautifully filmed, capturing the vast African landscapes vividly, and features strong performances. Patrick Swayze delivers an outstanding portrayal of Alan Quatermain, while Allison Doody is appealing as Elizabeth Maitland, the woman who hires Quatermain to rescue her father. Sidede Onyulo shines as Umbopa, Gavin Hood excels as McNabb, and the unnamed leader of the Russian soldiers also leaves a mark. While Hollywood often feels compelled to alter a good story during adaptation, this version is engagingly told, though its excessive runtime is a drawback. I generally enjoyed it. 6/10.

This film had an IMDb rating of 8.1, leading me to expect great things. Initially, it was humorous and charming, exuding a spontaneous energy. However, by the time it reached the halfway point, it started to drag, and every plot twist became painfully predictable. The office characters were delightful in the first third of the movie, but as the story progressed, they became overly familiar, transforming into caricatures rather than authentic individuals. This narrative felt like one I’ve encountered countless times, merely repackaged with minor variations. If only the dialogue weren’t so stale, I might have tolerated yet another clichéd romance! 

Worse still, the characters exhibited inconsistent and implausible motivations—a flaw that plagued "Dead Letter Office." Here’s hoping this film meets its demise soon, finding itself in the figurative "Dead Movie Office."

The film stays mired in ambiguity for far too long, with minimal explanations as it unfolds. This results in numerous bizarre sequences that appear to hold deeper significance but, due to the disjointed storytelling, end up feeling merely strange rather than compelling or comprehensible. It almost compels viewers to rewatch the movie, but there’s no way I’d subject myself to that. Watching this in the morning, I’m certain that if I'd seen it in the evening, I likely would’ve fallen asleep. To me, the movie felt like a cheap imitation of "Blade Runner."

The film raises countless unanswered questions and improbable scenarios, leaving behind an impression that feels meaningless and fleeting. Additionally, its peculiar visual style doesn’t help matters. Half CGI and half live-action, it lacks the polish, impact, or imagination of later films like "Sin City" or "300." Even stranger, they created several characters entirely via CGI, which seemed unnecessary and oddly out of place, especially since the character animations weren’t particularly convincing.

Of all the movies I’ve watched, this one ranks near the bottom (films like *Haunted Mansion*, *Nothing but Trouble*, and a couple of others prevent it from being the absolute worst). It feels rushed, its storyline is weak, and the actions of the characters are poorly executed. Some of the blame can be attributed to the book’s author. The novel on which the movie is based is overly convoluted and illogical. Oprah delivers a passable performance as “Bigger’s” mother but doesn’t come close to showcasing her full potential. Other notable actors also appear to be underperforming. The plot revolves around an African American man who takes a job as a chauffeur. While driving the family’s daughter to a communist gathering, he meets her. Things escalate, and the girl ends up drunk. Although the family employing him isn’t racist, Bigger believes they are. When he finds himself alone with the unconscious girl, her cries attract the attention of his blind mother, leading Bigger to panic. In trying to quiet her, he accidentally smothers her. Fearing severe consequences for killing a white girl, Bigger makes a decision that defies logic—he places her body...

This was an absolutely dreadful movie. Watching it was painful. Nearly every action lacked motivation within the film's context, the performances were subpar (even P. Diddy gave the strongest performance, which speaks volumes about the movie), and the plot was largely predictable. While some references to "Carlito's Way," like Carlito's dream of moving to the Caribbean, were decent, most felt forced and weak. The romantic subplot, in my opinion, was entirely misplaced, but that's open to interpretation. Honestly, my expectations were low going into this, and they still weren’t met. Poor Jay Hernandez deserves better—he’s talented, as shown in “Friday Night Lights.” Thankfully, I doubt many people will watch this film. I usually give movies a fair rating if they capture my attention, but I’ll give this one two stars. Here’s hoping the creators fare better next time. Also, I genuinely loved "Carlito's Way."

I’m a devoted fan of Neil Young’s music, so when the film *Greendale* received rave reviews from alternative and indie press outlets, I eagerly sought out the first available screening. Unfortunately, my enthusiasm didn’t last long. The sluggish plot and lackluster lyrical pacing left most viewers either dozing off or thoroughly let down.

Neil Young explained that the film began as a soundtrack, with the characters developing to such an extent that they decided to turn it into a movie. However, using this approach isn’t the strongest way to build a compelling narrative. None of the characters undergo meaningful arcs, and even when supposedly significant moments occur, viewers simply don’t care. By that point, the overused film techniques become so irritating that any emotional connection is lost. The entire film revolves around songs, and throughout, the actors lip-sync the lyrics while singing—while this might work briefly, it quickly becomes tiresome and intrusive.

The performances are subpar, with actors stuck in单一情感状态. Additionally, some scenes suffer from poor lighting. The only亮点 I can offer is the use of newscast-style shots in a few scenes, though this technique has become overly common in modern cinema.

I thought the first episode of the first series was excellent. It was incredibly enjoyable, and I found the acting to be superb. I believe it's unfair for anyone to claim it was poor, as it was tailored for its intended time slot. I find it irritating when people criticize its historical accuracy, as it’s meant to be a fun, Saturday night entertainment show, not a dry history documentary. Therefore, I think the costumes and settings were perfect. It was an outstanding beginning, and I’m excited to see what comes next! I’ve spoken to several classmates at my school, and they all love the show too. We agree that it provides fantastic entertainment with engaging storylines.

I rented this movie over the weekend, turned on the surround sound system, and enjoyed impressive audio from the special effects. It's a fantastic movie rental—while the special effects were scary enough to spook my fiancé, I did notice some appeared surprisingly computer-generated. I didn’t catch this film in theaters, but it’s perfect for a late-night stay-at-home scare session. I’d definitely recommend it!

This is a highly enjoyable film. The performances of all the actors were exceptional, bringing their characters to life brilliantly. The storyline is engaging, focusing on Raj, who falls in love with Priya. They marry, and Priya becomes pregnant, but soon faces complications, ultimately losing the baby. Later, Raj encounters Madhu, and after bribing her, she unexpectedly gets pregnant but remains unmarried. The movie is splendid, with fantastic dialogues, melodious songs, and impressive visuals. The wedding song stands out for its vibrant colors, while the cinematography is top-notch, capturing breathtaking scenes in Switzerland. Salman, Rani, and Preity delivered outstanding performances, and the entire cast contributed to making this a must-watch. It’s a worthwhile investment of both time and money. Rating: 8/10.

Inspired by a real mining disaster, this pioneering German talkie (with English subtitles) remains one of the most impactful docu-dramas ever made. With many non-professional actors, *Kameradschaft* offers a haunting portrayal of the bonds of friendship that unite miners, transcending the national divisions between France and Germany. When tragedy strikes, personal loyalties override official commands. A distressed miner receives unwavering support from his colleagues, even at the risk of great sacrifice—including their own lives.

This film echoes the selfless heroism displayed by the NYFD following the 9/11 attacks. Disregarding formal protocols, these first responders were driven solely by the imperative to save lives and locate their fallen comrades. Decades later, *Kameradschaft* continues to deliver a powerful and enduring message: A true friend proves their worth in times of need.

I’ve watched this film multiple times at various short film festivals, and it always gives me the feeling that I’m watching a movie trailer! 

Despite being a student film, it’s quite well-produced and directed. However, the story… well, it required something more to elevate it into a bigger and more engaging film. The character Tim Watcher particularly needed a deeper exploration. This is a common issue in some Portuguese short films—the scripts tend to be somewhat superficial.

That said, I still enjoyed the movie…  

Parabéns! (Congratulations!)

People often argue that "Antz" is superior, and while it’s a solid film, I personally found more enjoyment in "A Bug's Life." I can’t recall another Pixar animation—aside from the two "Toy Story" films—that had me laughing so uncontrollably. The animation is crisp, the story is fresh and doesn’t lecture, and the voice performances are exceptional. Dave Foley delivers an endearing yet hapless ant, Kevin Spacey brings depth and menace to Hopper, and Hayden Panettiere shines as Dot. The supporting cast includes standout performances from Denis Leary, David Hyde Pierce, and Madeline Kahn, among others. The script is brilliant, filled with humor and occasional poignancy. Though it lacks the social commentary of "Antz," this film offers top-notch entertainment. 9/10. Bethany Cox

Jason Lee's pecs are back! If that’s what you’re searching for, you’ve come to the right place. If not, it might be best to move on...  

Now, about the movie itself. It’s packed with clichés, features some poorly executed but somewhat exotic fight scenes (employing Jeet Kune Do), and is marred by terrible acting and cheesy special effects. Poor Jason Lee seems to be in visible discomfort throughout, and it’s not hard to see why. This isn’t exactly the triumphant return anyone hoped for.  

The film doesn’t even qualify as a decent B-movie. Sure, there was a German wannabe Rutger Hauer villain with bleached-blond hair, but not a single gratuitous sex scene or even a hint of nudity. Zero. Zilch. Nada. For comparison, *Starship Troopers 2* at least had the decency to include those obligatory nudie scenes (and trust us, our review of that gem will blow your mind). I got the distinct impression the writer was settling a score with someone while making this flick, so I’ll spare you the details of the plot or most of its related elements. All I’ll say is that it had some vague non-heteronormative undertones. That’s enough said.  

On the bright side, this movie has one redeeming quality—no Jean-Claude.

To begin with, jot down the script on a napkin. Why bother with anything more elaborate? We’re not making a Hollywood blockbuster, after all. Next, recruit amateur actors. They’ll generate buzz at the festival. Who needs seasoned professionals when you can have newcomers instead? Then, hire a cinematographer who struggles with lighting. If it’s well-lit, it might not feel “authentic,” and festival attendees might dismiss it. Who cares about achieving professional-level photography? Follow that by enlisting a ten-year-old with no camera experience as your operator. This will lend your film an overtly amateurish quality that festival reviewers may confuse for “realism.” Even if you drive away actual audiences, critics and a tiny fraction of the audience who overthink things will proclaim it “genius” because they’ll assume this chaos couldn’t possibly be unintentional.

After completing these steps, purchase your pass to the Festival of Bad Movies—aka Sundance.

What a tragic waste.

Michael Rooker is a capable actor, but he isn't suited for a leading role unless it's in a low-budget film. He lacks charisma, which is unfortunate because Ryo Ishibashi, who has far greater screen presence, doesn't get the focus he deserves. Most of the attention is on Rooker's stoic performance instead. 

Danielle Harris, known from *Halloween 4* and *5*, portrays Rooker's daughter. She’s charming and engaging, though her character is written as somewhat dim-witted, and one of her mistakes leads to the death of a key character. Comedians Fred Willard, Bobcat Goldthwait, and Stephen Furst deliver intriguing performances, making their scenes unforgettable.

Vincent Schiavelli plays the consigliere to a local mafia boss, and it's unclear if his role is meant to be comedic. Tim Thomerson, often seen in low-budget direct-to-video action films, also appears here. His presence, combined with other comedians and comedic actors, gives the movie a spoof-like feel. It's difficult to determine if this is a parody of a Yakuza film.

It was hard to believe that this film would flop, yet I was thoroughly let down. As a long-time fan of Pekinpah’s work, I picked up this discounted DVD, thinking it might be worth watching. The opening credits, familiar to any Pekinpah enthusiast, feature the signature cross-cutting between humans and animals. However, here we’re greeted with non-diegetic ambient sounds of children playing in a schoolyard while a bomb is being planted—a promising setup for suspense. Later, when Caan and Duval head to their next mission, Duval reveals that his date from the previous night had an STD, discovered by rifling through her purse during intimacy. The resulting laughter is brilliant and seems to pay homage to Brian De Palma’s *Dressed to Kill*, though it momentarily undermines Angelina Jolie’s character. The issue with *The Killer Elite* is that after those initial credits, the film loses momentum. Even *Bring Me the Head of Alfredo Garcia* feels more polished. While I use Pekinpah’s credits as teaching tools, once they end, switch off *The Killer Elite*.

Once more into the shadows. This film will inevitably invite comparisons to *The Princess Bride*, and while it falls short of that timeless classic, it remains highly entertaining and impressively crafted in its own right. The plot is somewhat unconventional, and the entire "wall" element remains unexplained, but the delivery is solid, generating plenty of suspense along the way.

Charlie Cox stars as Tristan, who pines for the unattainable Sienna Miller's character but instead embarks on a quest to retrieve a fallen star—played by the radiant Claire Danes. While there’s little mystery surrounding their romance, the tension ramps up when the wicked witch, played by Michelle Pfeiffer, and the vengeful prince, son of King Peter O'Toole, set their sights on the ruby necklace worn by the star. It’s a tale of good versus evil, with plenty of pursuit and peril.

As Tristan ventures forth, he encounters the oddest pirate imaginable—Robert De Niro, in perhaps his quirkiest role yet, as Captain Shakespeare. Beneath his rough exterior lies a man in touch with his softer side. Along the way, Ricky Gervais shines as a slick, fast-talking merchant, providing some welcome comic relief.

Overall, though it may not rival *The Princess Bride*, this film delivers enough charm, humor, and excitement to keep viewers entertained.

I had to sit through teenage, high school drama and family conflicts for nearly the entire duration of the show. Honestly, I don’t care about high school girls stressing over their relationships. I’ve already been through hell dealing with these kinds of issues, so I have no interest in watching fictional teenagers experience “light” versions of the same struggles I faced. I came here for science fiction, and that’s all I want. There were a few fleeting moments of it late in the show, which was good—but there was one problem. We finally saw a proto-Cylon, and while it was decent, its single red eye-dot locked onto objects of interest instead of scanning back and forth like a true Cylon’s eye. That constant motion gives the machine a sense of its surroundings, but this one’s eye didn’t move. I really hope the writers address this issue before the next episode.

It's pathetic when a director shows up to work merely because someone is paying them. The intentions may have been noble, with impressive locations and settings suitable for an epic film. However, the execution was abysmal. Extras in the background can be seen gawking at the camera or the actors, clearly uninformed about what to do when the director calls "Action!" The battle scenes are laughable; one wonders if the participants are serious. It's almost as though the combatants could have caused more harm by embracing each other. In slow-motion sequences, figures on the battlefield stroll casually or stand still, waving their arms aimlessly.

While there’s some semblance of activity in the foreground, it feels wasted. The storyline is riddled with logic flaws and inconsistencies, resembling a series of disconnected events arranged chronologically—or not. Dialogue is trite, and the romantic subplot is more cringeworthy than anything found in Hong Kong action flicks.

Given a budget of $40 million, one might hope to see every penny well spent on-screen, but the end product feels like little more than a shiny disc gathering dust.

About twenty minutes into the film, I found myself losing interest. The characters were rather uninspired, and while there were occasional enjoyable moments, they were often followed by prolonged lulls. Thankfully, my perseverance paid off, as the conclusion turned out to be decent. Still, it wasn’t compelling enough to make the preceding ninety minutes worthwhile. All in all, I’d describe the movie as mediocre, which is particularly disappointing given the talent in its cast.

Panic in the Streets begins with a strikingly noir-inspired scene: a camera pans along a dimly lit street, tilting upward toward a window where a sordid card game unfolds. This opening sequence, along with some evocative location shooting, foreshadows the atmospheric style that Orson Welles would later bring to cinema in Touch of Evil. As one of the players flings open the window—an apt gesture—it serves not only as an introduction to the unfolding drama but also symbolically reveals our first glimpse into the underbelly of society.

Filmed in stark black-and-white, Panic in the Streets gains considerable depth through its talented ensemble cast and excellent location work in New Orleans. From scenes set in the bustling mortuary to the cramped shipping office or amid the peeling walls of "Frank's Place," the film captures a singular, often suffocating ambiance that feels impossible to replicate on a studio set. These elements reflect the influence of Jules Dassin’s groundbreaking Naked City, released just two years prior, which helped define the gritty, near-documentary aesthetic within the noir genre. Coincidentally, Widmark’s previous role was in Dassin’s even more acclaimed Night and the City, a film where...

We bought this movie as a joke for a friend, and it might have been our worst prank ever. The film is nearly unwatchable, with dreadful acting throughout. The child actor delivers one of the worst performances ever, and David Hasselhoff gives a below-average performance. The plot is appalling, and at times, we were so bored that we found ourselves confused about what was happening. It attempts to be gruesome in some parts but ends up being laughable instead. Absolutely terrible.

Everyone might assume that Christopher Meloni and Janel Moloney are serious actors, best known for their roles in intense TV dramas like "Law & Order: SVU" and "The West Wing." But put them together in a film, and you're in for a delightful surprise—a charming romantic comedy filled with laughter. 

With remarkable talent, the两位 stars bring their characters' evolving relationship to life, making audiences root for Barry Singer (Meloni), even though he’s a bitter, sexist comedian. As Barry pursues Thea (Moloney), despite their stark differences, you’ll find yourself cheering for him, especially when he confronts his insecurities. Despite Thea’s reluctance, it’s hard not to question why she doesn’t reciprocate his feelings once Barry opens up.

"The Souler Opposite" shines with its exceptional cast and brilliant writing, proving to be a must-watch romantic comedy.

No, I’ve never watched any of the “Santa Slasher” films, like *Silent Night, Deadly Night*, the original *Black Christmas*, or this one, *Christmas Evil*. I’ve heard about their reputation, or what could be called MADS (Mothers Against Deranged Santas). I decided to rent this one because it’s come up as a reference on an episode of *Fat Guys at the Movies*. 

Mothers really *should* be against this film—not because of some over-the-top “killer” Santa, but because this movie is just plain terrible. It’s boring, dragging on for 92 minutes despite its short runtime, and ultimately, a waste of time.

In 1947, a little boy watches Santa climb down a chimney, deliver presents, enjoy some snacks, and then magically ascend back up the chimney. The boy goes to bed but later sneaks downstairs to see his mom and… well, sort of Santa… getting intimate. This, apparently, scarred him for life. Though the scene is about as risqué as when Ralphie’s dad unveils the “Leg Lamp” in *A Christmas Story*. Traumatized, the boy retreats to the attic, where he ends up cutting his own hand. 

Fast-forward to 1980. The now-grown man works at a toy factory. We’re greeted with…

If derivative and predictable rape-revenge thrillers are your genre of choice, you might consider this film a rare gem... However, it didn’t resonate with me at all, and I couldn’t pinpoint anything noteworthy about this odd narrative. It feels like something from the 1980s, a time when such films were often direct-to-video releases. Gillian Anderson and Danny Dyer deliver competent performances despite a weak script and a monotonous plot. But it’s baffling that Anderson chose to star in this project following her exceptional performance in the BBC's *Bleak House*. The director claims inspiration from witnessing a near-rape incident and his documentary work, yet even that doesn’t justify the absurd scene where a pack of country dogs attacks Dyer—a moment that likely had viewers, myself included, laughing in disbelief. What’s harder to comprehend is the participation of major backers like FilmFour and Verve Pictures. These companies have championed many出色的 independent British films, such as *Bullet Boy*, *Code 46*, and *Red Road*. *Straightheads* simply doesn’t belong in the same breath as their other projects.

That summer, I had observed several days of filming for this movie, only to see its final outcome reduced to just two scenes in the film. The setting was Sylvan Lake in the Black Hills, with scenes involving a wagon coming to a halt and similar moments. As a Dakota youth, I was eager to watch the movie and wasn’t let down. The local buffalo herd was being thinned out, making the action sequences quite authentic. (Yes, Doris, some animals did suffer during production.) I believe the ending might have inspired Jack Nicholson’s work in *The Shining*. This is a remarkable western and social commentary from the 1950s. It deserves to stand alongside *High Noon* for its genuine portrayal of western drama or serve as a social statement akin to *Blackboard Jungle* or *Rebel Without a Cause* for 1950s youth.

This film offers a decent summary, though it falls short in several areas. While it’s a noteworthy movie from the sixties, it lacks a strong sense of accomplishment. Maggie Smith delivers a respectable performance that feels authentic, though it doesn’t reach her full potential. Unfortunately, the rest of the cast delivers subpar performances, resulting in poorly executed portrayals. The humor misses its mark, failing to make the film amusing enough to fit comfortably into its intended genres. Though not entirely comedic or dramatic, it does manage to deliver a somewhat satisfying romantic element. The film fails to connect with its intended audience and conveys mixed messages, leaving viewers puzzled about its purpose and target demographic. The plot and story feel overly simplistic and aren’t executed effectively, leading to confusion among the audience. Still, Maggie Smith shines through, and there are moments when the storyline shows promise.

4/10

Certainly! Here's the rewritten version:

---

First of all, yes, I’m white, so I approach the sensitive topic of race with caution... Anyway, hating Black people is wrong, but hating White people is somehow acceptable because, apparently, we deserved it! Where do I even begin? The only redeeming aspect of this movie might be its unintentionally funny moments. There’s the infamous scene where Ice Cube and his friends beat up a group of massive, intimidating Neo-Nazis—despite the fact that these guys were literally twice their size! And then there’s the chase sequence, which is hilariously over-the-top. This film isn’t about promoting race, tolerance, or understanding; instead, it reinforces every racial stereotype imaginable. The portrayal of the white, wimpy roommate transforming into a skinhead after being roughed up by his Black roommate is just painfully stereotypical. It’s awful, and I regret watching it. Save yourself the time and avoid this poorly written, poorly acted, dull, and blatantly biased movie. If you’re interested in the topic, rent *American History X* instead—it’s a far superior film.

Allen visits a countryside location (a place he despises in reality) for a weekend getaway with his friends—typically the successful, middle-class, whiny characters seen in many of his films. 

Usually, I can find some humor in Woody Allen's comedies, but here he completely flops. Even his signature one-liners seem absent. There’s barely any plot (just fragments of pseudo-Shakespearean dialogue), and Allen tries to create a semi-mystical atmosphere, which only makes the movie feel even more aimless and poorly executed. 

The film fails on every level and is just excruciatingly dull. The only redeeming aspect (besides the end credits rolling) seems to be that the negative reviews might have made him realize that slapping together a hasty script and casting his friends doesn’t automatically result in enjoyable entertainment.

Knowing a film's age should prepare viewers for certain expectations, and keeping those in mind might make the movie more bearable. That was my experience watching *Revolt of the Zombies*. The heavy use of tiresome dialogue and cheesy acting should come as no surprise, along with the rudimentary (or nonexistent) special effects typical of its era. It demands a lot from the audience's imagination—perhaps too much in this instance. The plot is also challenging to follow: some Southeast Asian soldiers during WWI inexplicably perform exceptionally well. Though their success raises questions, the reason behind it must remain hidden, prompting a team to investigate archaeologically. One member uncovers the secret to long-distance hypnosis, using it to eliminate competition for the affections of his love interest. To prove his devotion, he releases everyone from his influence, only to regret it later when they seek to harm him upon regaining their senses. Even with prior warnings, it remains below average. Recommended only for the extremely devoted fans of early cinema.

This movie is supposed to be a mysterious, serious thriller centered around a man searching for a missing girl. However, just 30 minutes in, it transforms into an absurd, unrealistic tale filled with irritating characters and bizarre, random scenes. It’s hard to believe anyone could take it seriously, especially when Nicolas Cage randomly karate-kicks a blonde woman or "bear" punches an elderly lady. From the start, the dialogue, character development, and performances are all subpar. While I’ve always appreciated Nicolas Cage as an actor, he’s had a string of disappointing films this year, and this one is by far his worst (so far…).

I wouldn’t recommend this movie to anyone seeking an engaging, suspenseful thriller. If you're determined to watch it, approach it as a comedy instead—laugh at the over-the-top lines and ridiculous ending rather than trying to take it seriously. That’s the only way you’ll find any enjoyment in this film.

What were they thinking? Over the years, the *Columbo* series has experimented with fresh ideas, stepping away from its tried-and-true formula. However, this movie takes it too far. Unlike any other *Columbo* film, this one strays significantly, and unfortunately, not for the better.

The most glaring difference is that no murder occurs in this movie. Its premise is entirely unique, placing Columbo in an unfamiliar setting and scenario as he assists his nephew following the sudden disappearance of his bride on their wedding day. The overall tone is distinctly more "modern," though not in a way that enhances the story.

Alan J. Levi, who previously directed several *Columbo* films adhering closely to the classic formula, seems like an unusual choice to helm this project. 

Even the titular character feels altered—possibly due to the shift in environment and situation. The lack of familiar Columbo humor further distances this installment from its predecessors.

Richard Dix chose to retire, and Michael Duane stepped into his role as Ted Nichols, who encounters a young French woman named Alice Dupres Barkley (played by Lenore Aubert). Despite knowing each other for just two days, the couple decides to marry by the justice of the peace (a judge). When they arrive at the judge’s home during a heavy downpour, they discover he isn’t there and won’t return until the following day. While inside the house, someone lifts the car hood and removes an essential part from the engine. This unsettling incident foreshadows a series of unexpected and mysterious events tied to Alice Barkley, leaving Ted Nichols with no marriage and plenty of trouble. It’s a compelling mystery, though I couldn’t help but miss Richard Dix. Still, it’s worth watching.

When it was released in 1984, Prince was one of the biggest names in music, and people were eager to see this film, which was essentially an extended music video. The acting wasn’t great, but given that most musicians struggle with their debut performances on screen, it’s understandable. Still, it was a fun watch! Morris Day and Jerome Benton deliver timeless comedic moments, particularly their take on "The Password," reminiscent of Abbott & Costello’s "Who’s on First." 

Appolina (who later dropped her single name persona) contributed some eye-catching visuals with her appearance, providing the film’s brief nudity while also being quite attractive. Meanwhile, the accompanying soundtrack remains one of Prince’s strongest works. Although he eventually had a rift with Warner Bros. and famously changed his name, at this point in his career, he was unstoppable.

While *Purple Rain* may not be considered among the greatest films of all time, it’s undeniably entertaining.

When I was nine years old, my parents took me to see this movie. I’ve never forgotten it. Up until that point, I had never seen anyone as stunning as Elizabeth Taylor. (She was twenty-two when she filmed *Elephant Walk*.) Keep in mind, I was only nine, so my feelings weren’t romantic—they were more awe-inspired. I couldn’t take my eyes off her. I just wanted to sit at her feet, gazing up at her like a puppy. Though she’s now nearing seventy-four and showing signs of aging, I still consider her one of the most breathtaking women who has ever lived.  

Over the years, I’ve watched the movie several times, and it’s definitely a melodramatic tearjerker. What keeps it engaging is, without a doubt, Miss Taylor’s ethereal beauty, the magnificent scenery, the unforgettable elephant stampede, and its poignant commentary on human arrogance in the face of nature.  

All things considered, it’s a worthwhile couple of hours whether you’re streaming it on the movie channel or renting it on video.

This film delivers some intense and suspenseful moments for its debut. Following the tradition of the best horror movies, it keeps you on edge throughout, with your stomach tightening in anticipation. The conclusion is exceptional. The creators of "The Blair Witch Project" clearly took inspiration from this film, as its ending feels like the beginning of something far worse. It’s a fantastic movie and just one example of Japan's prowess in crafting terrifying experiences. With its perfect balance of thought-provoking themes and sheer terror, it's a must-watch.

"Rosenstraße" is a film about courageous women during the Nazi era in Germany. However, it drags on far too long, fails to evoke emotion, and at times becomes monotonous. The movie is riddled with clichés and lacks compelling performances.

The narrative structure is flawed. Similar to James Cameron's *Titanic*, an elderly woman reflects on her past, providing a perspective. Then another woman is introduced, also recounting someone else’s life events. It’s disorienting since both are recalling the lives of others! This demonstrates a lack of understanding of fundamental storytelling principles—how could Riemann possibly know details about the little girl’s mother and her interrogation?

The timeline of the scenes is poorly organized, leaving viewers confused about when events occur. For instance, when Riemann proposes to Fabian, it’s unclear when this happened. The setting appears to be from the 1920s...

Riemann’s character is predictably gifted as a pianist and is even a baroness—impressive. Her brother returns from the Eastern Front proudly displaying his "Knight's Cross," marking him as a war hero.

Kimi wa Petto is a heartwarming tale about a girl who discovers a wounded boy inside a box near her apartment one day. Deciding to help him, she brings him in and tends to his injuries. Before heading to work, she leaves him a note instructing him to eat the meal she prepared and then head home. However, when she returns, she finds him still there. The boy explains that he wants to stay with her, like a brother or cousin. Hoping to persuade him to leave, she jokingly suggests that if he becomes her pet, he can remain. She clarifies that being a pet means having no rights and following her instructions—not in any inappropriate sense! Surprisingly, he agrees, and from that moment on, he is known as Momo, her loyal pet.

This is to the *Zatoichi* movies what the *Star Trek* films were to *Star Trek*—except that in this case, each of the original entries was more engaging and captivating than this flashy remake, and better crafted, especially if substance matters more than style. If I hadn’t seen the originals, I might have found this visually appealing yet hollow. Since I had, I felt its tone was ill-suited and its depth lacking. The idea of rebooting the character in a more polished, high-budget production probably seemed appealing, but there was little purpose to it beyond financial gain; it’s merely spectacle that largely misses the essence of Zatoichi’s world and entirely fails to push the character into new territory (not to mention the lead actor wasn’t at his strongest). I had hoped for a story that would explore Zatoichi’s later years, offering a graceful conclusion to his journey and drawing meaningful insights from his experiences. Instead, this retread simply recycles fragments from earlier films, spiced up with gratuitous sex and over-the-top action. It’s not the same experience at all.

What an underrated '80s soundtrack! I picture John Travolta performing some of the songs, though the movie itself feels like a quintessential representation of '80s kitsch. It’s clear that films featuring mechanical bulls, bartenders, and immature relationships were all the rage back then. The highlight? His hilariously terrible Texas accent. For a deeper dive into the "dumbing down" of cinema, check out *Cocktail* and *Stir Crazy*. And don’t forget *Made in America*, starring Ted Danson and Whoopi Goldberg—a delightfully bad gem. Another quirky entry in this category is *Cadillac Man* with Robin Williams. Remember, even big stars like Tom Cruise, Richard Pryor, Robin Williams, and John Travolta took part in these cheesy classics.

This Chinese film resonated with me on many levels, highlighting numerous similarities to a culture I neither belong to nor fully understand. With an almost Buddhist sensibility, the movie encourages viewers to connect deeply with each character and appreciate the joy found in simple, everyday routines.

Every actor delivers a remarkable performance, and Xu Hzu portrays a nuanced blend of kindness, wisdom, vulnerability, and even a touch of harshness. Er Min, the intellectually challenged brother, reminds us that intelligence and wisdom are not synonymous, and that profound insight can emerge from the most unexpected individuals. This portrayal offers a distinct vision of China, one that departs from traditional Chinese realism but brims with a unique form of humanity and emotional authenticity.

Don’t miss it—trust me, you won’t regret it.

This movie may not be great, but here's an intriguing tidbit about it: It was shot in 1976 at Northern Arizona University in Flagstaff and Oak Creek Canyon near Sedona. Many of the extras were drama students from NAU at the time. I was a freshman there that year, minoring in theater, though I didn’t participate in the production. However, I knew several people who did, and they shared this unusual fact: 

In one scene, two main characters are shown running naked into the woods as part of a hazing ritual. While viewers see them from behind, those aren’t actually the actors—it’s two guys from the theater department that I knew. Their identities will remain undisclosed here, unless they choose to, ahem, “come forward”!

I am a huge fan of Anthony Hopkins as an actor, so I was eager to see how he would handle the roles of writer and director. Unfortunately, this film left me thoroughly disheartened. The story felt disjointed, and the cinematography was overly elaborate, to the point where I nearly turned off the screen. While the performances from the cast were solid, it was incredibly disappointing to see such talent wasted on a project that missed the mark so dramatically. Clearly, not every actor excels in writing or directing, and Mr. Hopkins appears to fall into that group. Among the countless films I’ve watched over my 50 years, this ranks as the absolute worst. Please, Mr. Hopkins, stick to what you do best—acting—and leave the writing and directing to those with a flair for those crafts. If I could rate this movie below one star, I would毫不犹豫地这么做。

I believe Michael Ironside's acting career must be coming to an end if he's starring in this kind of low-budget nonsense. He surely deserves better than to waste his talent on such drivel.

This film could have been decent with a proper budget, but it's painfully obvious throughout. There’s a scene set at an outpost that looks like the front of a railway station, and I wouldn’t be surprised if that’s exactly where it was filmed.

The only moment that redeemed this movie enough for me to give it a 3 was the scene of the spacecraft landing and taking off over a lake surrounded by forests. That part was well-executed, but unfortunately, the rest of the film is forgettable at best.

Another scene supposedly takes place in a space outpost, but it looks more like an engineering plant, which I’m guessing is exactly what it was. 

Overall, this movie is absurd, suffers from a woefully low budget, makes little to no sense, and I can only hope Michael Ironside didn’t take this role seriously.

I watched this film last night on cable, and it’s remarkable. What I admire most is its subtlety and restraint, yet it conveys profound emotion. Henry Thomas, known for playing the child in *E.T.*, delivers an impressively quiet and nuanced performance, perfectly embodying a man of few words. David Strathairn shines as the wonderfully over-the-top villain. Even more impressively, given its Hollywood origins, a baby plays a central role without speaking or acting—simply existing, and doing so beautifully. It’s intriguing how Thomas’ mysterious connection with E.T. defined the earlier film, whereas his bond with the baby forms the heart of *A Good Baby*. 

The music deserves special mention—Gillian Welch’s songs are exquisite, and the soundtrack captures the essence of evocative hill country music. 

This film is wonderfully immersive and atmospheric. I highly recommend it.

This film appears to promote or favor Muslim identity.  

Why do I say that? The protagonist has a Muslim father and a Christian mother and spends the first 20 years of his life in a Christian village. By the film's conclusion, he seemingly identifies as Muslim due to his headwear, the retention of his amulet, and his overall attire. He also has a six-year-old child who wears similar headwear, suggesting the child may be raised as Muslim, even though the mother is Christian. This implies the protagonist chooses to embrace Islam, and his child follows suit. None of the other primary male characters, all of whom are Christian, appear to have children. As a result, the Muslim population in the film's world seems to increase by the end, reinforcing a narrative that leans toward Muslim identity.

Legendary film producer Walt Disney adapted three of the world's most beloved fairy tales for the big screen, and they remain some of the most cherished animated movies in history. His groundbreaking classic, "Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs," premiered in 1937 as the first. Later came "Sleeping Beauty," an underrated gem released in 1959. Between these two, Disney crafted perhaps his most satisfying rendition of a timeless tale: "Cinderella" (1950). Among the three films, "Cinderella" remains the most loyal to its source material. Interestingly, while "Snow White" became the definitive version for many, "Cinderella" did not follow suit. Despite its success and its role in reviving the struggling Disney studio, it never received the widespread acclaim it truly merited. This time, Disney excelled by choosing not to overhaul the classic but enhancing it with exquisite detail and depth. The outcome was captivating. 

The film's charm lies in its stunning Technicolor animation and the impeccable casting of voice actors, which breathed life into the story with a brilliance that has stood the test of time.

Television certainly shapes society—just consider the spike in cappuccino shop visits after this superficial show hit the airwaves. Plus, real individuals as attractive as the characters on this program wouldn’t have the issues depicted. 

Moreover, does anyone genuinely think these folks could afford a chic Manhattan loft given their careers? NBC consistently underestimates viewers' intelligence, even aiming no higher than Forrest Gump-level naivety. A friend of mine earns six figures as a web designer yet resides in a cramped one-bedroom apartment in Manhattan paying $2,200 monthly in rent.

I’d much rather watch *Phriends*, a show featuring six unattractive nobodies stuck in dead-end jobs, living in a seedy neighborhood where sirens blare constantly and muggings happen weekly, while the landlord hikes the rent. That’s a series I’d tune into.

For the first 20 minutes or so (I was watching it on a PS2, so I have no idea how long it actually took), *Alienator* presents an intriguing premise. I don’t think I’ve ever seen a slasher film where the villain is an alien from another planet. However, interest quickly gives way to stunned disbelief when you realize the "alien" is actually a massive bodybuilder in a steel bikini. Yes, *Alienator* is undeniably absurd.  

But I don’t fault it for that. In the realm of schlock-horror, being patently ridiculous is often a good thing. Still, the movie’s blatant stupidity is all it really has going for it. While *Alienator* is hilariously entertaining, it’s also an absolute mess. Actors fumble their attempts at seriousness, painfully cheesy dialogue is delivered with cringe-worthy incompetence, and the direction fails to deliver even a single decent scene. By the end, the original concept is almost completely buried under a mountain of utter nonsense.  

Adding to this, the "Alien" simply vaporizes its victims instead of offering any real combat, which makes things even more laughable.

I was looking forward to in-depth background information on the Apollo 11 mission, but instead, I received decent interviews with Buzz Aldrin, Gene Krantz, and others connected to the mission. These were interspersed with an overly dramatic, catastrophe-predicting narration that followed the worst traditions of television production. 

If the voice-over had been removed and the focus shifted to a positive narrative highlighting how people can overcome challenges to accomplish extraordinary goals, this could have been excellent. Instead, I feel like I’ve lost around 45 minutes of my time during this 60-minute program, and I wish I could have those moments back.

I must be the only person in America who didn’t enjoy this film. It seems this just wasn’t my style—I simply can’t understand its appeal. This movie was barely entertaining, let alone one of the greatest achievements in cinematic history. 

It’s essentially the story of a man who starts with nothing and becomes a drug lord. That’s a pretty straightforward summary of the entire plot, and unfortunately, that sums up my feelings about the movie as well. Many people seem to think that simply setting a story in the world of organized crime makes it great, but they’re forgetting the importance of good storytelling.

I've watched numerous excellent Korean films, including intense thrillers and those with a darker tone, but this particular movie is terrible. The director appears to be a sadist who somehow managed to find funding for this trash. The film offers no entertainment value whatsoever and doesn’t even qualify as a proper thriller. It’s astonishing that anyone could produce something like this. While the acting is passable, the storyline and the overall experience it delivers are dreadful.

I’m certain I won’t be watching any more films from this director. There’s no sense of craftsmanship, and the attempt to create thrilling moments is utterly lacking. This movie consists mostly of scenes featuring a psychopath, filled with poorly executed shots, excessive blood, and gratuitous violence—all in the mistaken belief that this would make it exciting. It's a deeply disappointing film, and I highly recommend avoiding movies of this kind entirely.

One of my favorite "Amitabh comeback" films, this movie marked a strong period for Govinda under David Dhawan. The songs were fantastic and full of the classic "masti" vibe. A timeless entertainer featuring the versatile Anupam Kher, it boasts a storyline filled with the trademark hilarious twists seen in Dhawan’s films. With a surprise appearance by Mrs. Madhuri "Nene" Dixit, the film turned into a complete laugh riot toward the end. It was wonderful to see Amitabh deliver such energetic and humorous performances after a long hiatus. While some might label it a typical "Bollywood Masala" film, I’d watch it anytime. I’m giving it an easy 8/10 simply for its authentic Bollywood charm.

Good lord! (and that’s saying something coming from an atheist), this “movie” is terrible! 

Much has already been said by previous reviewers (the ones who gave it a rating of 3 or lower) with which I wholeheartedly agree, but I’d like to add a few thoughts of my own: 

Among the trio subjected to eating their own waste, getting hacked up with an axe, and enduring bizarre torture involving a broomstick—arguably the ex-boyfriend experiences the cruelest fate as he’s forced to endure the girl’s ceaseless, meaningless chatter at the kitchen table (just like us, though at least we can hit the mute button). 

If the director had trimmed out the pointless and endless graveyard and reversed scenes, our torment would’ve ended within the first half hour. 

The only thing that made this film even remotely tolerable was Emily Haack’s appearance (which earns it one point). 

Forget about it. Don’t buy it. Don’t waste your time—or your sanity. My mind is so fried from watching this that I feel the desperate urge to dive into another painful experience like “Scrapbook.”

Like countless dedicated Trekkers (or Trekkies—I don’t mind!), I endured all seven seasons of *Star Trek: Voyager*, longing for something better to take its place after *Deep Space Nine* ended in 1999. My prayers were answered. *Enterprise* is incredible. A fresh perspective, radically different characters, stunning new visuals, and even a catchy pop song for the intro—shocking, right? I can’t think of a single thing I didn’t love about it. Count me in for 10 more seasons of this show. *Star Trek* is back, and *Voyager*—no one misses you. Keep on Trekkin’!

The outstanding performances from an exceptionally talented ensemble cast, combined with an intelligently crafted (and highly quotable) screenplay, exquisite cinematography, and a stunning original score by Carter Burwell, make *Rob Roy* a cinematic experience nearly impossible to fault in any aspect. 

Though it has drawn comparisons to *Braveheart*, released the same year, *Rob Roy* surpasses its predecessor in terms of engagement. While Mel Gibson’s film feels overly self-conscious and preachy, *Rob Roy* immerses viewers effortlessly through its tightly woven narrative. Every scene serves a purpose.

Balancing drama, action, and subtle humor, *Rob Roy* presents fully realized characters who authentically reflect their historical context through language and behavior. These figures are far from simplistic portrayals of good versus evil; instead, they feel grounded and multidimensional. For instance, though we root for the heroic Rob Roy, we also understand that his challenges arise naturally from his circumstances, adding depth to both his triumphs and setbacks.

Many of the critiques on this thread appear to focus on comparing this film to either *"The Mortal Storm"* or *"Casablanca."* While individuals are free to make whichever comparisons they wish, the parallels between *"The Mortal Storm"* and *"Watch On The Rhine"* primarily revolve around the theme of refugees facing persecution from the advancing Nazi regime. In contrast, the discussion regarding *"Casablanca"* seems to center on what some perceive as an unfair slight toward Humphrey Bogart by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, who awarded the Best Actor Oscar to Paul Lukas instead. I don’t find this decision entirely unjust. Lukas enjoyed a successful career in cinema, both in Hollywood and the UK (*he notably played the villain in *"The Lady Vanishes"*), and this role marked his finest performance. Meanwhile, Bogart delivered numerous exceptional performances beyond *"Rick Blaine,"* such as his roles in *"The Maltese Falcon"* and *"High Sierra,"* which went unrecognized at the time. Despite this, he would later deliver even more iconic performances, like *"Fred C. Dobbs"* in *"The Treasure of the Sierra Madre,"* the conflicted writer in *"In a Lonely Place,"* and *"Captain Philip Francis Queeg"* in *"...And the Sea Will Tell."*

Certainly! Here's the rewritten version:

While some aspects of this film are undoubtedly dated—such as its all-white male crew—it shares common traits with most pre-"Star Wars" science fiction, often spending excessive time indulging in self-admiration. 

Nevertheless, no other movie has managed to encapsulate the essence of Golden Age Science Fiction quite like this one, right down to its use of "electronic tonalities" for the musical score. Robbie the Robot became the quintessential depiction of Asimov's robots and served as the blueprint for countless successors, including C-3PO and Data. 

The storyline is a direct adaptation of Shakespeare's "The Tempest," with Morbius embodying Prospero, an exiled sorcerer whose domain is encroached upon by intruders. This film was groundbreaking in its treatment of science fiction as a mature genre, potentially the first of its kind.

Aldolpho, played by Steve Buscemi, is an aspiring filmmaker living in a rundown New York City apartment, relying on his mother’s financial support to pay the rent. His beautiful neighbor, Angelica, portrayed by Jennifer Beals, might or might not be married, but she’s the muse Aldolpho dreams of casting in his movie. When a mysterious man named Joe unexpectedly offers financial backing for his project, Aldolpho believes his dream is within reach. However, Joe drags him into a wild adventure to steal a Porsche as partial funding, throwing Aldolpho’s moral compass into disarray. Will the film get made before he loses his ethical bearings entirely? And will Angelica agree to star in it? In this viewer’s opinion, the movie is dreadful. The script is weak, with a meandering plot that lacks direction. Beals delivers her lines with forced intensity, while Buscemi, though charming, feels bland. The film also includes questionable content and unlikable characters. On top of that, the production quality is subpar, giving the movie a consistently low-budget appearance. Even if you’re bored and have time to spare, it’s best to avoid taking the risk.

I enjoy watching movies and will give any film a fair shot by watching it in its entirety. However, I can now say I’ve encountered a movie I couldn’t finish. The acting is dreadfully bland and monotonous, the CGI looks like it was created by an amateur in their basement with basic software, and there are endless scenes of... just walking! This movie is three hours long, and I couldn’t even last 15 minutes before fast-forwarding the DVD. The alien scenes are incredibly brief. Instead of calling this “War of the Worlds,” they should rename it “War of the Walking Long Distances.” For a film that reportedly cost $5 million to produce, I wonder what they spent the money on—was it the over-the-top opening theme? 

On a slightly brighter note, there’s one scene worth checking out: when the aliens start killing people. It’s unintentionally funny—not because of the deaths themselves, but because the skeletons continue to twitch for a full 20 seconds after being killed.  

So, if you’re into dull, uninspired, action-free films, here’s one for your DVD collection. But this review isn’t for you; it’s for everyone else who deserves a heads-up.

The story is solid, and the animation is top-notch. The influences of Frazetta and Bakshi are evident, which is definitely a positive aspect. Fans of "Conan the Barbarian" or "Dungeons & Dragons" will likely enjoy it. Despite appearances, the battle between good and evil remains clear-cut, even if the protagonist seems neutral at times. In fantasy films, elves are typically depicted with fair skin and blonde hair, while goblins and orcs are often shown with darker features—a stereotype challenged by the work of Frazetta, Bakshi, and Tolkien, who are not racist in their portrayals. This movie should appeal to any fan of fantasy cinema. However, it’s not suited for young children due to its violent content and suggestive themes. The casting is strong, and the visuals and soundtrack are top-tier. I hope this hidden gem makes it to DVD soon; I feel fortunate to own a well-preserved VHS copy.

"ALMOST GOLDEN: THE JESSICA SAVITCH STORY"

Aspect Ratio: 1.33:1

Sound Format: Stereo

A clichéd, soap-operatic retelling of the rise and fall of America's pioneering female television news anchor. With a more polished script, stronger direction, and a better ensemble, it could have been passable, but the weak storyline doesn’t justify the effort. A compelling documentary on the same subject might have been a wiser choice. Despite the usual high production standards of a TV movie, it feels as shallow as outdated fluff—hardly engaging.

The central crime at the heart of *In Cold Blood* may come across as somewhat subdued for audiences accustomed to the archetypal serial killer narratives (Gein, Bundy, Dahmer) or even the splashier cases in Hollywood lore (O.J., Manson). At its core, the case is relatively straightforward: Perry Smith and Dick Hickock (played here by Robert Blake and Scott Wilson, respectively) met through happenstance, hatched a plan to steal money from a Kansas farmer’s safe, and ultimately murdered a family of four with a shotgun and dagger, only to escape with a mere $43. Beyond their brief flight to Mexico and eventual return to the U.S., there’s not much ambiguity surrounding the resolution. They were apprehended due to an ironic twist of fate—a police officer spotted them driving a stolen vehicle while they assisted a father and son collecting bottles for change—and were eventually executed in 1965.

Yet what elevates this tale is the masterful storytelling, poignant moments of moral ambiguity, and the unforgettable performances. Brooks, along with the legendary (and late) cinematographer Conrad Hall, crafts a film that transcends its simple premise, delivering a hauntingly cinematic experience.

This film narrates the poignant story of a deranged scientist whose fiancée is tragically decapitated. Driven by obsession, he embarks on a disturbing quest to admire strippers in search of a compatible body to reunite her head with. Every character in this movie radiates an unsettling level of sleaze, especially the protagonist.

This film is a perfect choice for both true romantics and sports enthusiasts. 

Drew Barrymore delivers an outstanding performance, and as a big fan of hers, it was delightful to see her shine again after a string of underwhelming projects. Initially, I wasn’t sure about Jimmy Fallon’s acting abilities, but he exceeded expectations as Ben, portraying the comedic, sports-obsessed sweetheart flawlessly. The humor in the movie is fantastic, filled with numerous laugh-out-loud moments. 

Their first date takes an unexpected turn when Ben arrives at her apartment with flowers, only to find Lindsay feeling unwell after eating something new. Rather than leaving, he stays to help, assisting her into pajamas and tidying up before cracking a joke about her being "very lady-like... no chunks." Throughout the winter, their relationship blossoms, but once baseball season begins, things change. Lindsay starts realizing just how deeply Ben is devoted to the Red Sox and why he remains single. Despite this, she brushes it off, focusing on her busy work life and reasoning that it won’t make her feel guilty for prioritizing her career.

"Robot Jox" doesn’t suffer from a weak story or poor effects. Keep in mind, this was 1990. "RoboCop 2" still relied on stop-motion animation, as many films did throughout the '80s. If you look at major blockbusters from that era, most made do with the special effects techniques available at the time. It wasn’t until "Terminator 2: Judgment Day" debuted the following year that a technological breakthrough occurred, inspiring filmmakers to push boundaries. However, if you’re a fan of shows like "Transformers," "Gundam Wing," or even "Power Rangers," you’ll enjoy this film. The enemy robot is particularly menacing, making you rethink going into battle unprepared. There are also some standout moments, such as the revelation of a traitor hiding in plain sight. Someone you trust completely might actually be your greatest threat. Doesn’t that idea give you pause?

While the historical accuracy may be debatable... (and given the widespread acceptance of inaccuracies in works like *The Lord of the Rings*, such issues are easier to overlook now), I appreciated the artistic flair of the film. Although it doesn’t quite qualify as an art house production, it occasionally delivers emotionally charged moments.  

My two main criticisms are: 1. The runtime feels too brief, and 2. The whispered voice that occasionally appears remains unexplained.  

Rating: 8/10  
Quality: 10/10  
Entertainment: 7/10  
Replayable: 5/10

Even if you know nothing about Ireland, it's hard not to be captivated by "My Left Foot," particularly by Daniel Day-Lewis's incredible performance. He portrays Christy Brown, who suffers from cerebral palsy, leaving him largely isolated throughout his life. Despite his efforts to warn others, people often dismiss him with laughter. His one source of solace is his ability to control his left foot, which he uses to paint and write poetry, ultimately earning him recognition and fame.

Daniel Day-Lewis and director Jim Sheridan delivered a stellar collaboration with "My Left Foot," and their subsequent work on "In the Name of the Father" was equally commendable, though "The Boxer" fell short. "My Left Foot" evokes a range of emotions—sadness, hope, and more—but without a doubt, Day-Lewis delivered a career-defining performance. It’s a remarkable film in every way.

When American author Edgar Allan Poe travels to London, he encounters British journalist Alan Foster, who becomes the subject of an unusual wager. Disbelieving Poe's claim that his eerie tales stem entirely from personal experiences, Foster accepts a challenge from Poe and his acquaintance Sir Thomas Blackwood: to spend an entire night in the allegedly haunted Blackwood Castle. Once inside the abandoned fortress, Foster learns he is not alone, as he is approached by several enigmatic figures—beautiful women, handsome men, and even a metaphysician—who reveal themselves to be trapped spirits doomed to relive the circumstances of their deaths on the anniversaries of their demise.

The first time I viewed this superb piece of classic horror, I was captivated throughout. The film struck me as both genuinely chilling and deeply sorrowful. Babs Steele is undeniably stunning. The haunting musical score amplifies the terror of the atmosphere. The unexpected topless scene caught me off guard, adding an unexpected twist. It seems Synapse performed an excellent job enhancing the visuals, as this movie looks fantastic for its era, and it’s the uncut international version.

Hearing such praise for this play, I decided to watch it when I came across it on cable. I fail to see how it "elevates" women and their "struggles" by concentrating on the subject matter. If you're interested in stories centered around women's private lives and how they impact their existence, this might be up your alley. Otherwise, it’s quite dull and unengaging. In fact, I found it somewhat demeaning.

When I discussed it with a female friend who also watched it, she agreed that it was terrible. So, it’s not just a case of a man “not getting it.”

This film had potential: my favorite actor starring in a historical drama set against the backdrop of the Independence War. It evoked memories of *Dances with Wolves* with its expansive prairies, Native Americans, and military battles, while also drawing comparisons to *Barry Lyndon* through its portrayal of the British and candlelit atmospheres.

However, the screenplay is dreadful. The narrative lacks coherence, with abrupt jumps like “five months later” and “three years later,” and the romance is so contrived that it’s nearly impossible to invest in it. In a country as vast as America, it’s absurd how the characters keep crossing paths. And then there’s the ending—a textbook example of how to ruin a story (imagine if *Titanic* had ended like this).

Occasionally, a weak script can be salvaged by a skilled director, but unfortunately, that’s not the case here. Hudson, who previously stumbled with *Greystoke*, exhibits the same shortcomings: static scenes, uninspired editing, and a lifeless score. The film is tedious, slow, and monotonous.

I already knew this movie marked a low point in Pacino’s career, and after watching it, I fully grasped why. As my final review for 2006, this film encapsulates the struggles of the year for me: painful and forgettable.

It’s probably for the best that I didn’t watch this while I was pregnant. I likely would have been in tears or felt nauseous. The film was somewhat graphic and mostly unsettling. Personally, I found the baby oddly endearing in its own bizarre way. However, as a mother, I winced during the scenes where Beth stabbed herself in the stomach and when Virginia performed a third-trimester abortion using rusty tools. As someone who loves animals, I nearly broke down when she violently scratched the cat until it bled. Despite the baby’s eerie and menacing nature, I found myself hoping it would survive. Even though the movie was twisted, it has left me extremely curious about the sequel.

Just by examining the set design, staging, and editing, it's clear that this project was hampered by insufficient funding. Perhaps Bela Lugosi's presence is intended to distract from such limitations. In this film, young brides collapse at the altar immediately after uttering their vows. Their bodies are then stolen by Dr. Lorenz (played by Lugosi), a renowned horticulturist, along with his eccentric accomplices, for use by his aging wife (Elizabeth Russell). She requires regular injections of glandular fluids extracted from these young virgins to preserve her youth and beauty indefinitely. Meanwhile, a curious local cub reporter (Luana Walters) notices that each missing bride had worn the same rare orchid during their weddings—a variety of flower that Dr. Lorenz would surely know well. As a typical horror-movie storm gathers, a visit to the Lorenz estate becomes increasingly eerie, particularly given the unsettling presence of a dwarf and a drooling hunchback on the premises. Additional cast members include Angelo Rossitto, Tristram Coffin, Minerva Urecal, and Frank Moran.

I won’t recap what’s already been mentioned about this movie, but I do want to add that I was eagerly anticipating its release—the star-studded cast, the picturesque locations, and the talent of director Michael Winterbottom, among others. From the start, the plot seemed to echo “Don’t Look Now,” with a grieving family seeking solace in unfamiliar Italian surroundings. My expectation was that the story would evolve, offering a fresh twist on their European journey. Yet, as the minutes passed, my anticipation faded—because absolutely nothing happened. Not even remotely. There wasn’t even enough substance to connect with the characters, who were flat and devoid of depth. The pacing initially suggested an impending revelation or transformation, but it never came. The eldest daughter’s flirtations with local Vespa-riding boys hinted at potential intrigue, while the younger sister’s visions of her deceased mother appeared meaningless and unresolved. Even the father’s flirtation with one of his female acquaintances fizzled out without consequence.
