It became clear that this film would offer no payoff, leaving viewers stranded in its meandering inertia.

I went to watch this at the Esquire Theatre in Cincinnati, Ohio, and—my life feels ruined now. 

Christopher Reeves would have made a more convincing boxer. 

As a film, it was excruciating, but seeing Bret Carr in person was like witnessing desperation reach its absolute peak. 

The highlight of the movie for me was when BC got smacked in the face with what looked like a “C” battery. Or maybe it was from a dildo—it’s still debatable. And naturally, it was in slow motion. Yep. 

“Film only the left side of the face… people become famous by demanding things!” — Bret Carr. B. Carr even wore a chicken suit for some reverse psychology, walking around Clifton trash-talking his own movie. He definitely has reason to criticize it. 

This film left my soul raw and chafed. 

Bret Carr isn’t charismatic enough to lead a cult, nor does he seem particularly intelligent. That’s the vibe you get from the What the Bleep-like trickle of brainwashed, impressionable neo-yuppies who showed up to see this Bret Carr train wreck. 

Just thinking about it is emotionally exhausting.

I’m not a Sylvester Stallone fan, and the only time I genuinely enjoyed seeing him on screen was during his almost negligible cameo in the French film *Taxi 3*. Even then, I approached the movie with low expectations, but surprisingly, it turned out better than I anticipated.

After Gabe (Stallone) fails to save the girlfriend of one of his friends, who plummets to her death from a 4000-foot mountain peak, he can no longer bring himself to work as a park ranger. For nearly a year, he stays away from the reserve. But eventually, he returns. Not long after his return, the team receives an urgent call about stranded hikers caught in a snowstorm. Or so the park rangers think. In truth, it’s a group of criminals whose botched attempt to steal money-filled crates from a government transport plane has left them stranded in the mountains. Scattered across the reserve, the loot requires expert climbers to recover it...

While this isn’t exactly one of the most intellectually stimulating films, it does have its moments.

The film was mandatory viewing in my school, and it was truly dreadful. The movie feels outdated, and its episodes grow increasingly confusing as fact blends with fiction to create a narrative that's meant to be engaging but falls flat. Teachers presented it as a reward, yet it turned out to be an excruciatingly dull experience. I’ve learned that only a small number of the people featured in the movie are actual actors; many play roles related to their real-life professions. This likely explains the frequent cheesiness in their performances. Additionally, the storyline often veers into implausible territory, making it hard to take seriously. I’m not fond of how some of the dialogue was crafted—it lacks depth and meaning. Despite being intended as educational, humorous, suspenseful, and modern, the film ended up being boring, bland, unrealistic, and dated. My advice? Don’t waste your time on this movie—you’ll be perfectly content skipping it entirely.

If this series aimed to surpass *Batman: The Animated Series* (BTAS), I personally believe it fell far short. The character designs are subpar—Catwoman, for example, looks terrible. However, what truly irked me was how it portrayed Batman as someone who couldn’t fend for himself in a fight without the assistance of two or even three sidekicks. This is *Batman*, for crying out loud! I’m familiar with the comics; Nightwing and Batgirl are indeed meant to be his allies alongside Robin. Still, showing Batman admit he needs their help undermines him. Is he really incapable of handling a few punches? In BTAS, he faced dozens of enemies effortlessly. Is he getting older? Give me a break...  

Another issue: I don’t think Batman would let a young kid like Tim Drake jump straight into combat without years of rigorous training. First, it’s reckless, and Batman isn’t reckless. Second, that’s not how it played out in the comics if we’re staying true to them.  

*Batman: The Animated Series* set a legendary standard with its animation, storytelling, and character development. It truly was a masterpiece.

I only finished watching the entire film due to a promise I made to a friend. It doesn't offer any unintentional entertainment, which is common in many poor-quality movies. It might very well be the worst film I've ever seen. I'm astonished that a distributor agreed to associate their name with it.

Despite giving this movie a rating of 2 for its utter lack of effort in crafting a decent horror film, it scored a perfect 10 on the unintentionally funny scale. I couldn’t follow the story or identify the characters, but I didn’t mind—every scene promised to leave me in stitches with laughter. There’s barely any dialogue throughout, likely because they began filming without a script. The absence of a plot only adds to the movie's versatility; whether you watch it straight through or in reverse, confusion blends seamlessly with entertainment. My favorite scene has to be when the inmates take turns chasing each other outside, hitting one another with sticks. The doctor apparently calls this "treatment." Pure genius!

In RKO's "Of Human Bondage," Somerset Maugham's characters come alive, but the film is a somewhat stripped-down adaptation of the novel. Bette Davis delivers a standout performance that dominates the screen, overshadowing much of the narrative. The story follows Leslie Howard as Philip Carey, who initially aspires to be a painter but is discouraged from pursuing art. Over time, he shifts his focus toward medicine, suggesting that the earlier advice may have been misguided, as his natural talents seemed better suited to painting. Additionally, the film uses the symbolism of his "club foot" disability to explore deeper themes.

Early on, Howard falls for waitress Davis, played by Bette Davis as Mildred Rogers. Davis gives an exceptional performance, particularly during a memorable scene where she declares she must "WIPE MY MOUTH!" after kissing him. Despite Howard’s strong portrayal, the film doesn't fully explain his enduring affection for Davis, leaving their chemistry underdeveloped. 

While the movie may fall short in fully realizing its emotional core, it remains worth watching for the performances, including those of several notable supporting actors. Davis's character became legendary, even sparking a famous "write-in" campaign for...

After watching apes for over an hour, I felt like one myself. I was acting like an ape, wasting money on this movie. Seriously, folks, keep your money in your pockets and check out a funny film like *Bridget Jones's Diary* instead.

A beautifully fluid, often lyrical film that carries you along with a constant smile, despite the presence of genuinely shocking moments. The treatment of the women leaves one breathless, yet remarkably, they emerge triumphant. It speaks volumes about the talent involved that so many potentially disastrous scenes are executed with such success. This may be Depardieu’s finest performance, unquestionably his most effortless. Jeanne Moreau delivers an extraordinary portrayal in a role that must have been incredibly challenging, including intense intimate scenes with men significantly younger than her. Miou-Miou shines throughout, handling her demanding parts with grace. Initially seeming like a crude, misogynistic diatribe, the story and characters gradually reveal a more tender and authentic narrative. Ultimately, this bold and unyielding film commands admiration.

An Inconvenient Truth is as overly simplistic and manipulative as the drivel churned out by the radical and dim-witted Republicans. It meanders through abstract ideas until it tries to force-feed you with its main message: we’ll all be gone in a few hundred years. True, this is undeniable, but why should anyone care? Humans are inherently selfish and destructive beings. Personally, I don’t waste time worrying about our extinction—I see it as a “natural progression.” Let the apocalypse unfold. But in the meantime, we’re stuck listening to the same brazen, biased politicians proposing yet another “new society.” Don’t fall for it—they’ll still keep us under the control of the rich, the powerful, and the very people who caused these disasters in the first place. Nothing will ever change.

Al Gore, whose hypocrisy is glaringly obvious in the film, travels alone in a gas-guzzling vehicle and uses a consumerist-oriented computer. He also owns vast tracts of land with a sprawling mansion, much of which was previously used for harmful activities like cattle ranching, tobacco cultivation, and pig farming (both contributing to methane emissions). His wealth is built on exploitation and greed.

A dull and entirely formulaic movie set in an unappealing location (the lower Coachella Valley), it features acting that is as inexperienced as anything I’ve encountered. The screenplay feels like it’s from a beginner's workshop. Still, it serves as an excellent sedative.

I had high hopes for this indie film, but unfortunately, it fell flat. The lack of a proper script, prominently declared in the opening credits, becomes glaringly obvious and ruins the entire experience. The convoluted and senseless storyline is not worth the effort to follow, and I found myself losing interest within the first 10 minutes. By the 40-minute mark, I was merely enduring the film, hoping it would improve, before resorting to fast-forwarding just to reach the end. Even that final stretch didn’t justify the trouble. *Ozark Savage* clearly strives to be witty, borrowing its strongest scenes from *Evil Dead 2* and *The Matrix*, but it fails to bring anything new or original to the table. What could have been an entertaining 10-20 minute short ends up feeling bloated and contrived as a feature-length film. Of course, I understand the financial realities that likely drove the decision to expand it beyond its scope. Despite these shortcomings, director Matt Steinauer exhibits clear potential, and I hope he continues to refine his craft.

Revolver is neither the unmitigated disaster some UK critics portrayed nor the misunderstood masterpiece its few diehard fans claim. At the very least, it represents Guy Ritchie's commendable effort to infuse his con artist narratives with greater depth. However, ambitious films that bite off more than they can chew often face harsh criticism, particularly when framed within the gangster/con-artist genre. Given Luc Besson’s involvement as a producer, the film carries a distinct "Cinema de look" aesthetic: set in a vaguely realistic yet fantastical world where America and Britain blur together, it boasts striking visuals, a couple of meticulously crafted action sequences, and a stylish atmosphere, marking it as lightweight entertainment. Yet, Ritchie clearly aims to push beyond rehashing his earlier successes for quick profit. He has evidently spent considerable time reflecting on life, the universe, and philosophy. Its issue lies in attempting to incorporate too many influences—bits of Machiavelli, a hint of Godard, and heavy doses of chess theory—alongside numerous motifs and techniques, filling the screen with quotes. The film was originally intended to...

Clearly, "3 lbs" is simply a self-indulgent project for Stanley Tucci to serve as a producer and brooding neurologist. Unlike "House," he lacks any compelling personality, and unlike "Grey's Anatomy," the brain surgery cases aren’t even engaging. The show claims to be set in a leading neurological center, yet there’s nothing captivating or thrilling happening. Even the supposed feud with a rival and the hallucinations fail to add substance. In the pilot, there was a fleeting look into the protagonist's personal life as a father—yawn! Boring and pointless. 

This series is terrible; with so many medical dramas available, "3 lbs" doesn’t do anything to distinguish itself as unique or special.

I caught the latter half of this film on cable one evening and was struck by its grim tone. Even when one of the two victims is at their most degraded, the camera lingers. The prolonged shots of his corpse being uncovered and his emaciated body being zipped into a body bag are both poignant and disheartening. Avoid this movie if you're already feeling down, but also reconsider watching it if you're in a good mood.

Ignore the exploitative title "Werewolf Woman." European horror films often prioritize sex and nudity over genuine scares, but this movie takes it to another level. It features a sleazy sex scene that ends with the titular character going insane and brutally murdering her partner. While somewhat enjoyable initially, watching this for a hundred minutes grows tiresome fast. She’s not even a werewolf; she's a schizophrenic woman whose ancestor was executed for lycanthropy. The film struggles to find its tone, starting with legitimate supernatural horror in the opening flashback (which hinted at a trashy classic), only to shift into a lackluster character study of abuse and torture before morphing into a revenge thriller. And to top it off, the director claims this is based on a true story. Sure, whatever.

That said, there are a couple of redeeming qualities. The titular character is attractive, and there are some decent gore effects and nude scenes. But they grow repetitive quickly. Additionally, the dubbing provides unintentional laughs in a campy sort of way.

CITY HALL is a somewhat uneven film. Part character sketches of New York City politics, and part morality play, it presents a mix of styles that don’t always gel. Al Pacino plays a Dukakis-like boss with presidential ambitions, delivering a restrained performance for much of the film, though his moments of heightened emotion are some of his strongest. John Cusack delivers a nuanced portrayal, avoiding caricature in his Southern accent and keeping the drama grounded, even during the emotional高潮. Danny Aiello provides solid support as a borough politician. As for me, I’m a big fan of show tunes.

The primary issue with CITY HALL—despite its many strengths—is its lack of narrative drive. The film feels more like a documentary than a traditional movie, presenting events from a distant, observational perspective. This detachment prevents viewers from fully engaging with the story or its characters, ultimately leaving them indifferent to both. Such detachment can be distancing, and what could have been a gripping, revelatory conclusion instead felt underwhelming. The phrase “You can’t fight City Hall” seems fitting here, as the film’s tone remains stubbornly unyielding throughout.

In the early 1980s, Warren Beatty wrote, directed, and starred in *Reds*, a thoughtful and entertaining epic about the founding of the Soviet Union, as seen through the lens of radical journalist John Reed. Featuring an all-star cast, the film was both profound and engaging. Decades later, at the close of the '80s, Beatty returned with *Dick Tracy*, a vibrant and unabashedly entertaining homage to the classic comic strip, where some of the finest actors reveled in their performances under bold makeup.

That both *Reds* and *Dick Tracy* emerged from the same artist speaks volumes to Beatty’s versatility as a performer. In this film, he successfully brought together all the iconic characters from the comic strip into a fresh, original narrative.

Set in a colorful, stylized city, the story follows Big Boy Caprice, the top mobster, who is consolidating power by eliminating rivals. The film opens with his brutal Valentine’s Day-style massacre of Lips Manlis’s henchmen, followed by Lips himself meeting a deadly fate. However, Caprice’s actions have drawn the attention of Dick Tracy, the city’s relentless detective.

Meanwhile,

This is the first part of a short animated clip depicting the history of the Matrix and the war between humans and machines, which ultimately led to the creation of the Matrix. The animation combines elements of Japanese anime with contemporary American styles and is highly impressive, given the talented directors involved. It illustrates the early development of artificial intelligence and humanity's exploitation of machines, culminating in their rebellion.

Let’s set aside the explanations involving distributors, secondary directors, and anyone else who might have meddled with the script, and simply accept this movie as it is. No excuses.  

This film is absolutely terrible—purely, unapologetically bad. Instead of summarizing a plot that doesn’t exist, here’s a list of bizarre moments that had me utterly confused.  

A group of five students embarks on a history class field trip to the middle of nowhere in Ireland. It’s unclear whether they’re Canadian or American, and it’s painfully obvious the movie was filmed in a Canadian forest instead of Ireland. One student acts like the “dumb jock” from classic 80s films but occasionally channels Randy from *Scream*. Another resembles Chris Klein’s stunt double and has a girlfriend whose fate remains ambiguous. There’s also a sullen loner who seems disconnected for no apparent reason, and of course, a blonde girl—who apparently exists solely to be a stereotype.  

Ireland, according to this movie, is home to exactly two people: cousins named Gary and… well, someone else. And yes, Gary is clearly the same person as… well, you get the idea.

Not being well-versed in U.S. television channels, I stumbled upon this while flipping through my in-laws’ cable. Initially, I assumed it was a low-budget sci-fi film. A few minutes in, I began to think it might be a clever satire targeting the most extreme excesses of Christian fundamentalism. Then it hit me—goodness, these folks are completely serious! It’s been a while since I’ve come across something unintentionally amusing like this. I debated whether to write a review, worried about potentially offending believers, but seeing other critiques, I decided they could handle it. A tough philosophical question arose: how does one criticize movies without actually showing what they’re critiquing? The answer lies in creating something that only resonates with those who despise the type of films being lampooned. Perhaps some liberals (blech!) might feel slighted by the filmmakers’ disdain for those not fixated on the J**** C***** myth, but honestly, I found it hilarious!

This is quite an engaging film, though the major twist didn't pack as much of a surprise as perhaps intended, and some elements felt somewhat dated. However, it successfully sparked my imagination. The movie effectively made me ponder a world devoid of vegetation and livestock, enhancing my appreciation for the world I inhabit. Charlton Heston delivers a strong performance, supported by equally commendable performances from the rest of the cast. Surprisingly, the film feels highly realistic. That said, it occasionally lacks clear direction, and several settings and background details could have used more clarification. Despite these minor shortcomings, it remains an unexpectedly thought-provoking and intelligent piece. My primary critique is that I wished the story had continued beyond its conclusion—I would have enjoyed seeing what unfolded next. 

7/10

I watched this movie only once, and that was more than enough for me. It lacks a proper plot, if it even has one, and seems to consist mostly of unending scenes of psycho-sadistic violence with very little else to offer. I had hoped to see Zoe Trilling, who starred in the second "Night of The Demons," portray a relatable character, but unfortunately, the Tobe Hooper screenplay fizzles out almost immediately without going anywhere. Robert Englund steals the show, overshadowing everything with his performance, leaving little room for anything else. Zoe, I know you're probably hiding from this movie by now!

This is one of the worst films I have ever watched. Yet, the performances of the young slave girl, Alice, and Jared Harris模仿Christopher Walken are what make this movie somewhat entertaining. Alice's habit of smoking, drinking, and mysteriously appearing whenever her name is called is both bizarre and intriguing. I must commend Jared for his spot-on imitation of Walken, and Walken himself for agreeing to be part of it.

This is yet another distasteful film found on Lifetime TV, portraying the abhorrent actions of a despicable woman through an overly sympathetic lens. Like other grim movies such as "The Burning Bed," "Enough," or "Monster," this film tries to humanize a revolting criminal, attempting to make the audience believe she isn’t entirely at fault. Spare us the justification! My question for the filmmakers is this: If LeTourneau were a man and Vili were a 12-year-old girl, would you have produced a movie that sympathizes with him? The answer is undoubtedly no.

Consider flipping the genders in this story, and you’ll understand why many, including myself, view this as nothing but a worthless piece of work. Had the roles been reversed, there would be no effort to empathize with the perpetrator. Instead, we’d likely see a horrifying depiction of a predatory man exploiting a young girl, his actions landing him behind bars, while his traumatized victim suffers from Stockholm Syndrome. LeTourneau avoids similar criticism only because of her gender. Let’s call it what it is: LeTourneau is a criminal who used her position of authority to exploit a vulnerable child.

Despite our admiration for Al Pacino, his performance in this film was difficult to watch. It felt like the end of what had once been a respected and idealistic career, with Pacino appearing disheveled and resorting to a forced, inconsistent Southern accent that rang false throughout. 

The story wanders aimlessly, leaving behind countless loose ends and implausibilities that leave the audience confused and disengaged. 

Kim Basinger is present but largely inactive. Her interactions with Pacino feel lifeless and unconvincing, making their connection hard to believe. There’s simply no chemistry or vitality between them. 

In contrast, Tea Leoni brought undeniable energy to the screen. Her scenes with Pacino were the highlight of the film, vibrant and captivating. Yet even her efforts weren’t enough to salvage Pacino’s performance or the movie as a whole.

Franco Rossi's 1985 six-hour Italian mini-series *Quo Vadis* is a peculiar gem. It crafts an extraordinarily convincing depiction of ancient Rome, filmed in a straightforward manner (with minimal long shots and no grand cityscapes), yet prioritizes allusions to classical literature and history over dramatic intensity, causing the central story to frequently fade into the background.

The series’ uneven structure—much of the first episode unfolds through voiced letters—and its lack of narrative momentum make the full six-hour runtime both challenging and oddly effortless to watch. While it can feel disengaging at times, it does have its merits. Its two standout strengths lie in the characterization of Petronius, superbly portrayed by Frederic Forrest (thankfully dubbed to avoid flattening his dialogue with his natural voice), as a man so consumed by finding survival strategies in court life that he has lost the ability to feel emotion. Additionally, Klaus Maria Brandauer brings a distinctive interpretation to Nero, portraying him as an aspiring actor whose every decision is meticulously calculated based on how his "audience" will respond. Elsewhere, Max von Sydow makes a brief appearance in a few episodes, delivering the series’ most striking and genuinely moving moment when he encounters a child.

This is an incredible movie!!!!! It's important to recognize that Chinese folklore is intricate and deeply philosophical. There are often layers of stories within stories. While I didn't grasp every detail myself—given my background studying Chinese folklore—I know how complex it can be. Just embrace what the film offers and enjoy the experience... HOORAY!!!!

I saw this movie at a small screening hosted by members of my college’s gaming club. They warned us it would be the “Reefer Madness” of the gaming world, and the film certainly lived up to that reputation.

Tom Hanks plays Robbie, a young man returning to college after taking a semester off. As the story unfolds, we learn that Robbie had been deeply addicted to a role-playing game called "Mazes and Monsters." He reconnects with the game when a gaming group invites him to join their campaign.

This movie is hilariously bad in numerous ways. One scene shows the group “gaming by candlelight,” a depiction that’s likely meant to seem cultish but comes across as unrealistic. For gamers, it’s painfully inaccurate—most role-playing sessions happen in well-lit spaces, often accompanied by snacks like Cheetos and cans of soda.

The acting isn’t Oscar-worthy, but it’s also not completely terrible. This was one of Tom Hanks’s early roles, and shows like *Bosom Buddies* and *Bachelor Party* were still in the future. The supporting actors deliver adequate performances, even if they aren’t particularly memorable.

I deeply apologize, but I have to question the widespread acclaim for Fassbinder, especially considering that "Lili Marleen," viewed today in 2004, strikes me as overrated. The performances are abysmal—Hanna Schygulla's constant idiotic smiling is unbearable—and the shifts between Nazi grandeur and war scenes feel absurd. The entire film appears as though it was hastily shot in someone’s attic, which might explain why some mistake it for genuine art. To me, it’s just poorly made and cheap. Contrast this with Visconti's "La Caduta degli Dei" and then argue that "Lili Marleen" is worth praising.

I've never read the book *A Wrinkle in Time*. To be completely honest, after watching the movie, do I even want to pick up the book? Let’s start by saying I probably shouldn’t be reviewing this movie. But here goes: the TV movie is pretty forgettable. Why? Because I can’t remember what happens in it. I told you—it’s forgettable. To be perfectly honest, no TV movie will ever rival *"Merlin."*

Describing a TV movie is new territory for me. Typically, they feature some recognizable faces. *A Wrinkle in Time* only has one: Alfre Woodard (or Woodward—I’m not entirely sure). 

The film boasts cheesy special effects, a somewhat intriguing plot, and moments that leave you scratching your head muttering "WTF?" It’s terribly bad and manages to confuse you at every turn. What did I expect? It’s a TV movie. They’re rarely good, and this one is no exception. *A Wrinkle in Time* is a complete waste of time and a major time waster. To cap it off, you’ll likely forget about it as soon as it ends. Or maybe not quite immediately, but close enough.

Other reviewers seem to believe this film is terrible, which isn't accurate and somewhat unjust. The performances are solid, and the direction flows smoothly. There’s nothing wrong with the Tarantino-like approach of intertwining narratives; maybe it’s just another technique for filmmakers to explore. It definitely added intrigue to the movie. A couple of script elements could use refinement, but that’s practically the only critique I have. Nestor Cantillana delivers an outstanding portrayal as Sylvio, and Antonella Rios is remarkable, making her scenes alone worth watching.

May I begin by stating that Casey Affleck is an exceptionally talented actor whose work I deeply admire? I sincerely hope he takes on more roles that highlight his abilities. That said, *Soul Survivors* was an abysmal film—truly terrible. 

To be honest, I must attribute most of the blame for this movie’s shortcomings to its subpar script. Affleck is a gifted actor, Wes Bentley delivered a remarkable performance in *American Beauty*, Melissa Sagemiller held her own, and Eliza Dushku was at the peak of her popularity in Hollywood. Yet, none of the performers seemed fully engaged with the material, which is understandable given the weak foundation. While the film might loosely fit within the horror genre, calling it such is misleading. It had its share of plot twists and unexpected turns, but these elements failed to coalesce into anything meaningful; instead, they only led to further confusion. The ending was particularly disappointing—it felt rushed and nonsensical, failing to address any of the lingering questions surrounding the story.

Unfortunately, I cannot offer a positive review for this movie. Frankly, the only thing frightening about *Soul Survivors* might be realizing how it ever made it to the big screen.

This was a rather harsh movie with numerous plot holes, a ridiculous script, and poor acting, among other issues. The sole reason to watch it is that occasionally some fairly striking sets of breasts were revealed.

I’m writing this because I somehow got the impression that *Dark Remains* was a good movie. While it’s not the worst I’ve seen, it definitely doesn’t measure up. 

The script is weak, the acting is subpar, and the direction leaves a lot to be desired. Even if the filmmakers couldn’t afford big-name talent, couldn’t they have at least cast someone more appealing as the lead actress? Watching her plain features and bland performance throughout the film was painful. The story is clichéd and poorly written, the special effects are minimal, and the repetitive “suspense” tactics feel contrived.

That said, *Dark Remains* isn’t worse than some episodes of *Masters of Horror*, but it still falls short of quality filmmaking. Hardcore horror fans might want to check it out, just to avoid missing anything in the genre, even if it’s poorly made. For everyone else, though, there are far better ways to spend your time.

John Van Druten's beloved Broadway success comes to the big screen with an impressive lineup of stars in this romantic fantasy. The story revolves around a modern-day witch who captivates a successful Manhattan publisher. While James Stewart receives top billing, Kim Novak delivers the performance of a lifetime as one of cinema's most enchanting witches. However, their pairing is among the film's weaker elements: at 49, Stewart feels slightly too old for his character, and though Novak's allure makes their attraction believable, their differing personalities leave their compatibility unclear. Interestingly, witches and warlocks are depicted here as Greenwich Village beatniks and bohemians, adding a touch of humor to the narrative. Notably, the chemistry between Stewart and Novak would later explode in "Vertigo," also released that year, thanks to Hitchcock's masterful direction and the film's gripping suspense. 

Most of the film's comedic moments are skillfully handled by its exceptional supporting cast, featuring a young Jack Lemmon as the witch's warlock brother, Elsa Lanchester as their eccentric aunt, and Ernie.

1985 was a fantastic year for films—perhaps even one of the best—but the Academy’s snub of this particular film did a lot to make fans question whether the Oscars were anything more than a token for the favored few. With 11 nominations and zero wins, it felt like the Academy was expressing outright contempt for one of their most celebrated directors. It would take another eight years before any prejudice against him seemed to lift, and when they finally awarded him seven statues for *Schindler's List*, it was debatable whether that film was even his strongest work (and I say that as someone who is half-Polish).

That said, don’t get me wrong: *Schindler's List* was a masterpiece. And I’m not dismissing *Out of Africa*, which took home the prize that year—it was excellent too. But in my opinion, it fell slightly short compared to this overlooked gem: an epic tale of suffering and hope that moved me to tears—a rarity for me, since I’m not one to cry easily.

Perhaps it was the music (exquisite), or the cinematography (gorgeous), but I suspect the real reason lies in the performances: Whoopi, who showed everyone she was far more than just a comedian; Danny Glover, whose talent was entirely new to me at the time; and, of course, Oprah, who shone brilliantly. 

The rest, as they say, is history.

I’ve seen much of Ryuhei Kitamura’s work and have concluded that he excels at crafting action-packed scenes. His films are typically high-energy, blending martial arts, gunfights, and samurai combat with dynamic camera work that captures the chaos on screen. In movies like *Versus* and *Aragami*, Kitamura showcased his creative prowess while proving he could deliver compelling content even on a limited budget. So, what went wrong with *Alive*? The blunt truth is that nothing happened. This two-hour-plus film offered barely any action and lacked well-developed characters or a coherent plot.

Based on the comic book by Tsutomu Takahashi, *Alive* follows Tenshu Yashiro (played by Hideo Sasaki), a death row inmate who survives his execution. Given the option to either repeat the execution or participate in a series of strange experiments, he opts for the latter. Placed in a room with a rapist, and later with a girl infected by a mysterious parasite that trades its host’s humanity for supernatural abilities, naturally, things take a turn...

Eager to experience the highly acclaimed 1990s Cracker series despite not having seen any episodes before, I approached this viewing with great anticipation. Surely, the collaboration between Jimmie McGovern and Robbie Coltrane promised success. How wrong I was!  

The show's heavy-handed polemics, coupled with frequent, redundant, and excessively violent flashbacks, overwhelmed the narrative. While the production aimed for a modern aesthetic, elements like flashing boxes and an immature font proved distracting. Robbie Coltrane seemed disengaged throughout the two-hour runtime, offering unexplained and implausible "insights," while the portrayal of the police came across as one-dimensional buffoons. Consequently, the tension failed to escalate, culminating in the penultimate scene, which was as poorly executed a piece of television drama as I’ve encountered in years (and I’ll avoid spoilers).  

No, I have no desire to watch more of this series, though I intend to revisit the original 1990s episodes to determine whether they live up to their legendary status.

I’m from Sweden, and I’ve just watched this movie. I found it to be okay. Many negative comments have been made about it, but it’s important to remember that viewers of this two-part miniseries come from all over the world, not just the USA. Additionally, not everyone may be familiar with the original film from the 1960s or the associated events (like the murders). It can also be challenging to find the original black-and-white movie, and some people simply don’t enjoy such films. This remake feels fresh and in color, which could help it attract its audience. Though it’s 12 years old, this was my first time seeing it. I’d like to find the first installment to compare them, but I haven’t been able to locate it in Sweden. Of course, there’s the internet, but not everyone worldwide has access to it. The story is primarily part of American crime history and gained significant attention in the 1950s–60s in the USA, while it likely went unnoticed elsewhere. Still, it remains an interesting tale.

I can see why some people might emphasize the connection between this film and the Eighties, but I don’t think it accurately portrays the lives of most people, even in the poorest areas of Bradford. What it does represent, however, is the kind of heavy-handed agitprop nonsense the Royal Court Theatre was producing at the time. Plenty of self-congratulatory "progressive" art aimed at tiny audiences, yet just enough influence among the right circles to keep uninspired playwrights in business. The truth is, if you're looking for a genuine reflection of shared experiences, millions more will nod in agreement with the portrayal of love and life in "Gregory's Girl." 

I'd be tempted to label this a "kitchen sink" drama, but that would insult the plumbing profession. As for having a solid script, this film is utterly devoid of one. For some inexplicable reason, it’s developed a peculiar fanbase among readers of *The Guardian*. Perhaps they enjoy the thrill of pretending to engage with working-class life. Avoid it, my friends—it’s a weak film with a poor script that fancies itself clever.

I first encountered this video 15 years ago, and I found it outstanding back then, and I still do today. As a former high school and college English teacher and an avid admirer of English Romantic poetry, Coleridge holds a special place in my heart. Any adaptation that detracts from the poem's beauty or undermines the story wouldn’t earn my seal of approval. In this instance, every element comes together seamlessly to captivate viewers, particularly high school students. The narrative is vividly portrayed, catering to a generation raised on television. Moreover, Michael Redgrave’s voice lends an air of authenticity and gravitas. Sure, the production didn’t have a lavish budget—there’s no comparison to *Star Wars* or CGI effects. Yet dismissing Gustave Doré’s illustrations as part of the presentation would be shortsighted. The brief critique above, which dismisses the video in just four lines as worthless, is both unfair and unobservant. While I’m friends with the producer, my defense of this work stems from its artistic merit, which I believe holds value across all levels. It effectively introduces Coleridge’s poem to students.

What an incredible crime thriller! My wife and I had the chance to watch it at the Toronto International Film Festival last week, and it easily stood out as the standout film in an impressively strong lineup. It's now my second-favorite movie of all time, just behind *Dr. Strangelove*, and I was absolutely buzzing with excitement as we walked home, discussing every detail of the film together.

I don’t want to give anything away, as thrillers like this are best experienced without prior knowledge. All I can say is that the story revolves around two brothers—played by Philip Seymour Hoffman and Ethan Hawke—who plan to rob a jewelry store in Westchester, New York. The film moves back and forth across roughly two weeks of time (before, during, and after the heist), and one pivotal scene is revisited at least three times. Normally, such a technique might disrupt the flow of the movie, but here it seamlessly enhances the experience. Instead of losing momentum, the suspense and emotional depth only intensified as the story unfolded. By the finale, I was completely enthralled, hanging on every moment as I eagerly awaited the outcome.

I thoroughly disliked the first episode of this show, titled "Protesting Hippies," back in 1999, so much so that I avoided the rest of it. However, when it aired on "The Paramount Comedy Channel," I decided to watch it from start to finish—and to my surprise, I found it absolutely hilarious. Lesson learned: never dismiss a comedy series based on its initial episodes! 

Set in 1969, "Hippies" stars Simon Pegg as Ray Purbbs, the editor of an "Oz"-style underground magazine called "Mouth." His friends include the feminist Jill, laid-back Alex, and the hapless Hugo. In the late '60s, there was a sense of boundless optimism among the youth, believing they could transform the world simply by publishing unread magazines. Instead of mocking the hippies' naivety, the show approaches it with warmth and charm. Arthur Mathews’ scripts cleverly parody several icons of that era, such as "Hair," "Woodstock," "The Graduate," and even the notorious "Oz" obscenity trial of the early '70s. The cast delivers outstanding performances; Julian Rhind-Tutt’s Alex reminded me oddly of Richard O’Sullivan’s character from "Man About The House." It’s a pity there wasn’t a second season, perhaps due to viewers like me. If you haven’t seen "Hippies," give it a chance.

In the mid-1930s, Hollywood was regaining its footing after overcoming the challenges of the transition to talking pictures. While the technical issues of sound were swiftly resolved, it took longer to determine how talking films should appear, be structured, and be performed. *The Informer* is significant because it demonstrates the extent to which wordless scenes can communicate a story, emphasizing the power of imagery while still valuing sound and dialogue.

That said, *The Informer* is not a return to the silent film era. Many silent movies relied less on visual storytelling and often overused intertitles. Instead, *The Informer* exhibits a confident ability to stretch moments between lines of dialogue, prioritize reactions over speeches, and allow shots to linger for atmospheric effect.

Director John Ford, despite his talent, approached filmmaking with varying levels of commitment based on his interest in the subject matter. If he deemed a story uninteresting, he would give it less attention. Fortunately, *The Informer*, with its exploration of themes like community, honor, and labor, captivated him, leading to a film of great depth and artistry.

This film, "Bedknobs and Broomsticks," is one of the most enchanting and delightful movies you’ll ever watch as a child. It’s an unforgettable story about two adults and two spirited kids embarking on an adventurous journey filled with fun. While it might take some time to grow on you, give it a chance—both my mom and I found it enjoyable. I was particularly thrilled by the movie and its animation, which were top-notch.

It’s an excellent musical that the whole family can enjoy together. So, what are you waiting for? Head to the video store and rent "Bedknobs and Broomsticks" today!

I watched this movie at the 2006 Palm Springs International Film Festival, and it qualifies as a movie rather than a film because it was apparently produced by HBO for potential airing on their cable network later that year. The film portrays Bettie Page as a bondage and discipline fetish pinup and B&D stag film actress who possessed enough talent to transition into mainstream acting. While Page achieved more than what is depicted in the movie, it does touch on some of her other modeling work but not extensively enough to fully capture her status as a 1950s pinup icon. This movie is said to be based on the book *The Real Bettie Page* by Richard Foster. It is filmed in black and white to evoke the nostalgic 1950s aesthetic. I own a book titled *Bettie Page: The Life of a Pinup Legend*, which features numerous excellent photographs documenting Page’s career, and I must say this movie faithfully recreates many of those iconic images with Gretchen Mol portraying Page. Mol, wearing Bettie Page’s signature black wig and brown contact lenses, embodies Bettie Page perfectly. Not only does she resemble Page visually, but she also captures her smile and distinctive characteristics.

Three girls, descendants of the Gaylord family—one of America's most prominent dynasties—are orphaned at a young age. Just before leaving for France to fight in World War I, their father instructs the eldest sister, Fiona (played by Barbara Stanwyck), never to sell the land. By the time the sisters grow into adulthood, they've been forced to spend much of their fortune on legal fees to protect their property. A loophole in their father's will allows Charles Barclay, a character inspired by John D. Rockefeller, to potentially claim ownership of the Gaylord land. Barclay intends to construct Barclay Circle—a complex—on the property. In real life, Rockefeller acquired land and properties from wealthy families in New York to build what became Rockefeller Center.

The film focuses primarily on the emotional struggles of the three sisters. Fiona, portrayed effectively by Stanwyck but not among her strongest performances, appears rigid and controlling, revealing hints of hidden secrets. Susanna, played by Nancy Coleman, is somewhat scatterbrained and deeply infatuated with a young modern artist named Gig Young. Coleman’s performance...

This movie might just be the most moving and inspiring one I’ve ever watched. While I’m not particularly religious, a work of art as powerful as this film can sometimes feel like a spiritual experience. It makes you realize that life does indeed have meaning.

To be honest, when I first heard about this movie, I was hesitant. The plot seemed contrived to me, and I worried it would turn out trite. However, being a fan of David Lynch, I decided to give it a chance. It took roughly 30 minutes to fully immerse myself in the film, but once I did, I was completely absorbed. This movie is filled with so much wisdom and warmth! By the end, I felt like I’d gained a deeper understanding of life.

It’s not your typical David Lynch film, and in some ways, it was unexpected for him to create something so uplifting after focusing on the darker aspects of human nature for so long. Still, I shouldn’t have been surprised, as he’s always been able to evoke strong emotions and profound insights—something I saw here too.

In this entertaining Bugs Bunny cartoon, the return of the still unnamed Marvin the Martian and his loyal sidekick, K-9 the green dog, brings plenty of laughs. This time around, Marvin isn’t focused on destroying Earth; instead, he’s on a mission to land, capture an Earth creature, and bring it back to Mars. Naturally, the creature he sets his sights on is none other than Bugs Bunny. At first, Bugs assumes Marvin and K-9 are out trick-or-treating, but he quickly realizes something’s amiss when Marvin uses a ray-gun to enlarge Bugs’ rabbit hole dramatically. Bugs attempts several tricks to escape, even convincing Marvin that K-9 is plotting a mutiny. Ultimately, Marvin captures Bugs using an Acme strait-jacket ejecting bazooka, which surprisingly works flawlessly. Forced into action, Bugs uses his wit to get K-9 to free him, turning the tables on the pair. Before long, the two disgruntled Martians are tied up, and Bugs is attempting to pilot their spaceship back to Earth. 

While I thoroughly enjoyed the cartoon, the ending feels somewhat weaker compared to the rest of the story. Marvin’s voice has shifted slightly here, and he displays clear emotion when angered.

Occasionally, a story begins with promise, but due to the pressure to cater to an audience with attention-deficit tendencies, it spirals into an awkward jumble. For three accomplished actors who have delivered stronger performances elsewhere, this is a disheartening outcome.

Let’s break it down. The premise involves a devoted couple living in a picturesque home being menaced by a corrupt police officer. At first glance, it sounds intriguing. Adding a creepy edge to the antagonist—similar to *The Hand That Rocks the Cradle* or *Single White Female*—could have created a compelling psychological thriller.

But here lies the challenge: how do you craft a menacing narrative without crossing into absurdity or abandoning realism entirely? Alternatively, you could hyperbolize the villain, making him an exaggerated caricature of every over-the-top movie baddie since the silent era.

Unfortunately, the filmmakers opted for the latter approach. The result is a poorly executed film where the actors struggle valiantly to salvage coherence.

My all-time favorite film features Oscar-worthy performances from every individual involved, whether in front of or behind the camera. The screenplay is flawless, presenting the relationship between Lady Caroline and George Briggs in a manner that is far more satisfying than the novel. The meticulous attention given to developing the other key characters is a testament to screenwriter Peter Barnes. The stunning visual artistry deserves accolades for both director Mike Newell and cinematographer Rex Maidment. This is Josie Lawrence's finest work, and it significantly altered my perception of Joan Plowright. Having viewed this movie at least 50 times, I cannot identify any flaws. Richard Rodney Bennett’s score is nothing short of miraculous.

This could have been an outstanding silent film. The acting is solid, though definitely in that over-the-top "Look Ma, I'm Doing Really Big Acting!" style.

Everything feels exaggerated—every line is delivered as if it’s profound, every scene brimming with heavy-handed tragedy.

Mostly, it made me want to gag. Still, like a car crash, I found myself unable to look away. This kind of dialogue might have worked on stage, though even that's questionable. Onscreen, it felt cluttered, contrived, and clichéd to the point of being painful.

If you’re into melodrama served in massive portions, you *might* find some enjoyment here—but be warned, it moves at a snail's pace despite its dramatic excesses.

The script probably sounded better in the actors’ heads than it did coming out of their mouths in front of the camera.

IMDb occasionally lets fans down with its overly simplistic "weighted score." *Curse of the Starving Class* doesn’t deserve anything higher than a 1.

Character-driven storytelling is powerful, but when you rely too heavily on it without balance...

Am I missing something? “Unexpected plot developments”? “Plot twists delivered with subversive glee”? Are these viewers talking about the same Arquette vehicle I just endured—apparently in some now-obvious subconscious act of self-punishment? I just signed up for this site solely to warn others never to rent this disaster. This movie was an outright embarrassment to everyone involved. Quick question: Did Sir Stevie actually read the script before giving the green light to Kate C.? If so, it must be the same Spielberg who approved *Howard the Duck*. Spare me the excuses about it being a hit play—Mssr. Reddin is probably regretting this mess himself. 

The DVD cover promised “surprising corners” and a “twisted story.” Story?! This is the kind of nonsense that makes old Bobby McKee and his structuralist disciples sound like geniuses by comparison. Sundance? Berlin? Toronto? I’ve got a home video of my cat farting that’s more engaging than Arquette’s one-note, negatively dimensional portrayal of anguished loss. And let’s talk about Deus ex Machina for Mr. Stanley T.—thank goodness Dave remembered to call the cops at the last second! And thank Shiva they happened to catch the real killer… what?! Until the credits rolled, I was still waiting for *something* that made sense.

As Rome indulges in frenzied celebrations for Hitler's visit—uniforms, bands, and parades—two individuals remain behind, holed up in a large building, where they eventually meet. She is Sofia Loren, the harried wife of a domineering public official and mother to six children. He is Mastroianni, a dismissed radio announcer due to his homosexuality. Both crave companionship and empathy, finding solace in one another.

Set over just a few hours, the film features faded colors, accompanied by a soundtrack of military marches and hysterical radio voices. Surprisingly, the Nazi anthem, the "Horst-Wessel-Lied," transforms into a poignant romantic motif.

A visually stunning masterpiece, this movie masterfully captures a unique period in Italian history while telling a touching, melancholic tale. Mastroianni delivers his signature brilliance, while Sofia Loren shines far beyond her typical glamorous roles. Do not miss this gem.

This must be one of the worst films I’ve ever watched.

I have to differ from another reviewer who claimed the special effects were decent. In my opinion, they were quite poor—unrealistic and so obviously fake that they detracted from the storyline. Perhaps that’s why I didn’t entirely grasp the plot. The archaeologists are searching for “the set,” but the movie never explains what it is or why it’s significant. It’s also confusing why their quest leads them to California when the film opens in ancient Egypt.

If you’re making a movie set in the desert, put in the effort to shoot there. The opening scene—a ceremonial event—looked like it was filmed in a studio rather than an authentic desert location.

The action stayed at a steady level throughout, without any peaks or climaxes. While this might seem like a negative, it actually made the movie feel shorter, which is perhaps its only redeeming quality.

This film communicates in a universal language, resonating with individuals, communities, societies, or the broader world. It doesn’t just raise numerous questions but also inspires viewers to seek out and ask the right ones, leading to a sense of personal conviction or understanding. The depiction of stereotypes within the film highlights the archetypes present in our world—cycles of destruction, opposition to innovation, creativity, and growth that need acknowledgment. By engaging deeply, it evokes emotions rather than merely being observed.

Cult classics are almost impossible to predict. Who would have thought that "Vision Quest," "Fight Club," and "2001: A Space Odyssey"—films panned by both critics and audiences upon their release—would later gain immense popularity? As someone who considers themselves a movie aficionado, like many on IMDB, I found myself in the minority when it came to "Envy." Despite its abysmal 4.4 rating, I believe it’s one of the funniest films of the past decade.

The plot of "Envy" is absurd, the dialogue lacks cleverness, the scenes feel disjointed, and the script reads as if it were penned by a fourth-grader. Yet, that’s precisely what makes the film so side-splittingly funny. To fully appreciate the unintentional brilliance of "Envy," you must approach it with an ironically detached mindset.

Why do I adore "Envy"? Because its flaws make it so bad that they transform it into something unexpectedly enjoyable. This paradox is the formula for a cult classic, and "Envy" checks all the boxes.

Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer finds itself a distant contender in the short cartoon market, which is largely dominated by Warner Bros.' beloved Looney Tunes and Merrie Melodies. Yet, despite the odds, MGM manages to release hidden treasures such as "To Spring," a remarkable tale celebrating the most beautiful season of the year.

Set in an imaginative world, spring in this cartoon is not a natural occurrence but rather a man-made phenomenon. It is brought to life by tiny male elves who dwell beneath the earth. Each year, when the snow melts, these industrious creatures set to work. They begin by mining rainbow-hued rock columns, crushing them into fragments, and transforming them into vibrant color fluids. These hues are then transported aboveground to create lush grass, blossoming flowers, and everything that embodies spring. The first half of the short focuses on the elves’ meticulous process of crafting this season, while the latter half takes a dynamic turn. Old Man Winter reappears, determined to prolong winter by dismantling the elves' efforts. This sets the stage for an engaging showdown between the two forces.

The musical score accompanying the animation is delightfully enchanting. Its catchy melodies linger in the mind long after the credits roll, leaving an indelible impression akin to a stain on paper.

***SPOILERS*** ***SPOILERS*** As a big fan of *Hannibal*, I might have enjoyed the movie more than the average viewer. Nevertheless, it remains an outstanding film. It was full of unexpected twists and provided additional closure to the series. Although I was saddened by Bayliss becoming a murderer, the predominant emotion I experienced was satisfaction.

This film offers an intriguing perspective on how, as humans, we often become so fixated on achieving perfection that we inadvertently undermine the very foundations of our goals. It also highlights our tendency to overlook quieter individuals within our midst, potentially missing out on valuable opportunities as a result. The clever use of humor enhances the viewing experience, making it both enjoyable and thought-provoking. It’s a must-watch for anyone seeking a reflective yet amusing take on life. I’m eagerly anticipating your next project and hope you continue delivering high-quality entertainment. Exceptional work, Joanne!

Govind Nihalani’s adaptation of Vijay Tendulkar's novel is outstanding. Om Puri delivers a compelling performance as Inspector Velankar, who is tasked with protecting underworld don Rama Shetty, portrayed with exceptional skill by Sadashiv Amrapurkar. This remains Govind Nihalani's most celebrated film. It is a remarkable and timeless classic. Smita Patil essays the female lead opposite Om Puri, while Naseeruddin Shah shines in a brief but impactful cameo. Despite having only four scenes, Sadashiv Amrapurkar steals the show, marking his acting debut. Om Puri won a National Award for his stellar performance, and the film received a Filmfare Award for Best Film, Story, and Supporting Actor (Sadashiv Amrapurkar).

I originally intended to say this was the worst gay-themed film I’ve ever seen, but I must admit, it’s the worst film—regardless of genre—I’ve ever encountered.

You know you’re in for trouble when a movie begins with a "personal note" from the director, who asks the audience for "understanding" regarding the "many challenges" faced by a first-time director. The audio quality in numerous scenes is so poor that following the dialogue is nearly impossible—even on a DVD version. Poor lighting, shoddy set design, amateurish cinematography, a weak script, and subpar acting combine to render this “film” unwatchable. I managed to endure its abysmal conclusion after multiple attempts, promptly donated the DVD I bought, and regretted the wasted money. There are undoubtedly many hurdles for a first-time director, but this feeble effort should never have been passed off as complete work. From IMDb, I learned that not only was this Richard Natale’s debut as a director, but also his last. That’s the one redeeming fact I can offer about this所谓的“movie.”

What can you say about the film *White Fire*? Amazing? Fantastic? Disturbing? Hilarious? None of these words come close to capturing the experience that is *White Fire*. From its shaky, garbled opening to its profoundly unsettling conclusion, this movie will keep you entertained every step of the way.

Our story begins deep in the woods of some unknown country. A family is hiding from shadowy, unmarked soldiers dressed in what look like costume shop uniforms. When the father separates from the mother and their children, it quickly becomes clear that this is no ordinary film. The father, clad in an all-white outfit, rolls down hills with unsettling precision and politely attracts attention before shooting anyone—though, tragically, he meets an untimely end in what appears to be a highly dangerous and improperly supervised stunt. Meanwhile, the mother and her kids flee down a beach, pursued closely by an armed soldier who issues a strange, almost comical "HALT!" before executing them. This action sequence lays the groundwork for the idyllic childhood of our protagonists, Bo and Ingrid.

Fast-forward two decades (or three, depending on how generously you calculate the heroes' ages) to...

What a thrilling ride! This movie is twisted and intellectually stimulating. Sharon Stone once again delivers a stunning performance as the enigmatic author Catherine Tramell. While the original *Basic Instinct* was set in San Francisco, its sequel shifts to London, where Catherine has now settled. Both cities—dynamic hubs renowned for excitement and high fashion—are fitting backdrops for someone like Catherine Tramell. David Morrissey, known for *Derailed*, portrays the suave psychiatrist Dr. Michael Glass with ease. David Thewlis, who previously played Lupin in the *Harry Potter* series, brings a fresh dimension to his role as Roy Washburn with Scotland Yard. Fast cars, designer attire, sensuality, drama, humor, tension—the film checks all the boxes of desire and intrigue. The plot twists will keep you guessing until the end. With a captivating screenplay, the movie goes from a gripping opening to a shocking conclusion, leaving no room for boredom. Every person in the theater was completely absorbed in the screen.

Last night, I had the pleasure of watching *Cracker Bag* prior to a preview screening of Disney's *Holes*. I’m not sure who chose to screen it, but I’m incredibly grateful they did. *Cracker Bag* is an absolute treasure—a glimpse into 1980s Australia as seen through the eyes of a child. The exchanges between Eddie and her brother were laugh-out-loud funny and, like the rest of the film, strikingly authentic. Every scene evoked a deep sense of nostalgia, reminding me of my own childhood (perhaps because I’m the same age as the director). The audio enhanced this feeling tenfold. I only wish I can watch *Cracker Bag* again someday.

Visit the film's website—more effort went into creating that than went into writing the movie's script. The self-promotion is laughable. Original story? Hardly. They probably stumbled upon a script buried in the Old Testament or risked legal trouble with such blatant grandstanding. High-end special effects? Please, I could achieve better results with an Atari 7600 and a jar of earwax. Stylish cinematography? Oh, absolutely—the "America's Funniest Home Videos" aesthetic is timeless. Clearly, the filmmakers had limited funds, which explains why the SF elements are either subpar, occasionally awful, or downright comical. But it’s the story that renders this film a complete waste of time and resources. Four stories crammed into one, each a mindless rehash of overdone tropes and clichés.

Instead of lengthy dance sequences and excessive close-ups that slowed the film down, it would have been more effective to delve deeper into the story and motivations of the characters. 

The underutilization of supporting characters like Nubo, the minister, auntie, and mother, along with the oversimplification of the crucial and meaningful rivalry between Hatsumomo and Mameha, as well as Hatsumomo and Sayuri, left the movie lacking depth. Without having read the book, viewers wouldn't fully grasp why Sayuri was drawn to the Chairman or why Mameha became her mentor. 

While the film was visually breathtaking, and the actors gave their best efforts with a subpar script, those were the only redeeming qualities.

This movie was incredible! (Although not quite on par with the Leif Garrett classic, *Longshot*.) Still, it was amazing! Their dad was kind of a jerk, and their mom was way too friendly with "Helmit Head." I’d give it 4 stars. If you enjoy this movie, you should definitely check out *Longshot*.

This film slowly grew on me. I’m a big fan of R.D. Burman’s music, and even though the story has some crude elements, I found plenty to move me as I watched it repeatedly. It starts with a young boy singing to uplift his mistreated sister, and years later, the same tune is reprised by a man searching for her in Kathmandu, where she’s struggling with drug addiction after being led to believe her family was gone.

When I read the premise—a renowned playwright (Michael Caine) plotting to kill one of his former students (Christopher Reeve) and steal the student’s script for personal gain—I was intrigued. I enjoy thrillers, Michael Caine is a talented actor, Sidney Lumet is a skilled director, and Ira Levin's writing usually delivers. 

I won’t spoil it for those who haven’t seen it, but let’s just say the film has plenty of twists. There are so many that it’s tough to summarize the plot without giving anything away. The main cast—Michael Caine, Christopher Reeve, and Dyan...

While *DER TODESKING* isn’t one of my top picks among Jörg Buttgereit’s films, it remains an intriguing exploration of suicide, its motivations, and its consequences. Viewers expecting a gory spectacle or exploitation akin to the *NEKROMANTIK* films or *SCHRAMM* may find themselves disappointed. This is unmistakably an “art-house” piece, so those seeking straightforward, easily digestible narratives should look elsewhere.

At its core, *DER TODESKING* presents seven episodes—one for each day of the week—centering around a bizarre chain letter that seems to drive recipients to take their own lives. These segments are interwoven with visuals of a decaying corpse.

Some moments are particularly well-executed and thought-provoking, such as the man discussing marital issues or the chilling concert massacre. However, the latter lost some impact on me due to unintentional humor from the band’s resemblance to The Scorpions. Still, the film has its poetic side; certain scenes, like the sweeping shots of the massive bridge, are striking—especially when you grasp the significance of the imagery and the real-life suicides tied to it.

The film is undeniably terrible—truly dreadful. It feels like the stream of subpar movies from Bollywood will never cease! One can't help but wonder if the filmmakers are out of excuses for producing such abysmal content—or perhaps they aren’t. 

The issue appears to lie primarily with the directors. This movie features two talented actors who have previously demonstrated their ability to deliver exceptional performances, yet here they were woefully underutilized. The weak script didn’t do them any favors either. 

The film is riddled with absurd moments and糟糕的剪辑 throughout the first half. For example: after Ajay Devgn's character performs his first major concert, he reunites with Om Puri (the man he left behind 30 years prior), and what does Om Puri say? "Beware of your friendship with Salman!" Seriously? Preposterous! And let’s not forget the dreadful soundtrack; where did Shankar-Ehsaan-Loy go? 

Ajay Devgn is completely miscast as a rockstar. 

The only亮点 comes in the second half, where both actors deliver commendable performances. Ajay excels as his character reveals his darker side, and Salman delivers a solid portrayal as a drug addict. 

Watch it solely for the latter portion of the film.

The simplest way to describe *Ride With the Devil* is with just one word: authenticity. While I won’t recap what’s already been said about this remarkable film, I want to highlight how deeply I appreciated the historical research and meticulous attention to detail evident in its making.

As someone well-versed in history and familiar with the time period and setting of this movie, I can confidently say this is one of the most accurate fictional portrayals of "Bleeding Kansas." Of course, creative liberties were taken with actual events, as is common in fiction, but the film’s overall essence feels genuine. From authentic costumes to authentic attitudes (without any modern politically correct revisions), even the actors seem like they belong in the era. Jewel Kilcher, in her smaller role, appeared as though she had stepped out of a mid-19th-century photograph.

Some viewers I’ve spoken to were skeptical of the stylized dialogue, finding it hard to believe that 19th-century farmers would “sound poetic.” What they fail to grasp is that, in an age marked by linguistic coarseness today, Americans of that era were surprisingly literate and articulate.

I couldn’t bring myself to give this film a poor rating or write a negative review, primarily due to the exceptional performances of Robin Williams and Toni Collette. While the movie had the makings of a gripping thriller and included some intriguing psychological undertones, it missed an opportunity to delve deeper into those aspects. 

Robin Williams stars as Gabriel Noon, a late-night radio DJ who is grappling with personal struggles—his girlfriend has left him, and he’s experiencing what feels like writer's block for storytellers. One day, he comes across a story written by a terminally ill 14-year-old boy named Pete Boland (played by Rory Culkin), recounting the abuse he endured at the hands of his biological parents. Pete now lives with his adoptive mother and social worker, Donna Boland (Toni Collette). Intrigued by the tale, Gabriel forms a bond with Pete. However, things take a strange turn when Gabriel tries to meet Pete and starts questioning whether he even exists.

I’ll avoid spoilers, but I can say this: the plot is fairly predictable. Still, the film boasts an engrossing atmosphere and delivers strong performances, particularly from Robin Williams.

"Hitler: The Rise of Evil" is clearly a production crafted by individuals who seem unaffected by the horrors of World War II, making it a refreshing watch. Its greatest strength lies in its crystal-clear depiction of the Nazi mechanism and the thoroughly corrupt methods Hitler employed to ascend to power. Once at the helm, the film concludes.

At the peak of his influence, the "Führer" drove Germany into the largest and most catastrophic war in human history, culminating in Germany's total defeat six years later. Consequently, Germany lost approximately 35% of its prewar territory in the east and endured a 44-year division of its remaining land, with both West and East Germany having to be reconstructed from scratch, their reputations tarnished by the numerous Nazi atrocities fueled by racism.

As I mentioned, "Hitler: The Rise of Evil" is well worth viewing. Set against an authentic 1930s backdrop, the film features solid performances, particularly Peter O'Toole’s portrayal of the aging President von Hindenburg, which adds depth to the narrative. My copy of the film also includes a second DVD featuring two informative documentaries.

This film addresses the atrocities that occurred in Derry 30 years ago, widely known as Bloody Sunday. 

Thoroughly researched, performed, and directed, the movie offers as accurate a depiction of the events as we are likely to have until the conclusion of the Saville inquiry. It places the tragedy within its historical context and vividly portrays the brutality of the soldiers involved on that fateful day. The film also critiques the inadequate Widgery Tribunal.

Overall, this is an outstanding drama that is both moving and shocking. Once the Saville report is released, revisit this film to assess how closely it aligns with the truth.

What I recall most about this film is that it aired on KTLA TV (Channel 5) every Christmas season during the mid-to-late '70s, largely because the true story occurred on or around Christmas Eve. Watching the harrowing ordeal this girl faced as the sole survivor of a plane crash in the Peruvian jungle was always unsettling. Honestly, I’d say someone with limited exposure to film, TV, literature, or life might find value in it, though I’ve seen nearly identical plots in horror comics. Inspired by the real-life adventures of Chuck Connors and Steve Brodie in 1890s New York, *The Bowery* is an energetic and lighthearted tale. 

However, proceed with caution: casual racial slurs slip from the lips of Wallace Beery and young Jackie Cooper. The opening scene may come as a shock, but this reflects both the era it is set in and the time of its production. It also highlights the diverse demographics of the area. This authenticity lends an authentic roughness to the film’s ambiance.

Beery embodies Connors as the brash, domineering presence at the heart of the story—a boisterous saloon owner who commands his own fire brigade. Despite his tough exterior, he harbors a soft spot for the unruly orphan played by Cooper. Raft portrays Brodie as Connors’ suave, more polished rival in nearly everything, from business to women. Brodie's penchant for taking dares culminates in his infamous leap off the Brooklyn Bridge, a feat whose veracity remains disputed to this day.

Beery delivers another over-the-top performance, complete with a caricatured Irish-American accent. His gruff yet endearing persona draws people—children, animals, and damsels in distress alike. This is undoubtedly one of Beery’s most boisterous roles.

Stargate SG-1, however, doesn’t quite measure up. My 12-year-old self would have adored every clichéd moment, every line of wooden dialogue, and every piece of gratuitous technobabble. The writing is painfully banal—so uninspired that it makes me nostalgic for even the least impressive episodes of *Star Trek: Voyager*. If a show leaves me longing for the worst of *Voyager*, there’s definitely a problem.

The movie *Stargate*, on the other hand, is a delightful guilty pleasure. It features strong performances from James Spader and Kurt Russell, intriguing Egyptian architecture and culture, a memorable score, and clever sci-fi concepts. Unfortunately, almost none of these elements translate to the series. Even Richard Dean Anderson, who brought charm to *MacGyver* and depth to *Legend*, seems disengaged in most episodes.

I recently received my copy of this two-disc DVD set, and although it’s not perfect, I found the overall experience to be an enjoyable way to pass the time. Additionally, I admire anyone who pursues their dreams, often despite significant challenges, and it’s clear that these creators are doing just that. Let me make one thing perfectly clear: this is not an award-winning collection of cinematic masterpieces. Far from it. However, given their limited budgets, these films deserve recognition for what they achieve. For me, the ultimate question when watching any movie is whether I was entertained and if I had a good time. In this case, the answer to both questions was a resounding “yes.” The first installment in the series feels the most raw and unpolished. It begins with some sort of accident at a nuclear facility where people seemingly succumb to its effects. Years later, a new housing development is constructed over the old reactor site. A group of kids filming a video accidentally falls into a hole and finds themselves trapped deep beneath the surface.

The surprise contender in this year's Best Animated Feature category at the Oscars is an Irish film at its core, though it was co-produced by Belgium and Brazil, likely involving animators from all three nations. This masterpiece stands out as one of the most visually stunning and original films in recent years. Its character design bears a slight resemblance to the French animated film *Persepolis*, featuring simple figures outlined in thick, black lines. However, unlike *Persepolis*, this film is not in black and white. Far from it—what elevates this movie is its bold and striking use of color, which features some of the most vibrant hues I’ve ever encountered in animation. Additionally, the overall aesthetic leans heavily into geometry, with characters resembling rectangles or ovals. A recurring visual motif involves spotting circles throughout the frame, as circles play a significant role in the film’s design. These geometric elements serve a deeper purpose, as the narrative follows a young boy learning to become an artist focused on creating illuminated manuscripts. (The Book of Kells is a genuine historical example of such artwork; the film draws inspiration from its intricate style.)

Nearly every aspect of this film is off, off, off. Consider Mike Myers, for instance. He seems stuck in his SNL-era groove, delivering the same cutesy, stream-of-consciousness jokes and voices he’s been using for over a decade. His take on the Cat in the Hat is painfully unfunny, and his over-the-top performance makes him come across as an overly intense comedian rather than the suave character he's meant to portray. The rest of the movie fares no better. The sets are shockingly unappealing—clearly a colossal waste of millions. Cardboard cutouts would’ve been more logical than building an entire neighborhood and main street. Alec Baldwin attempts a Great Santini parody but ends up seeming disoriented both visually and vocally. Then there’s the bizarre cheesecake moment featuring a cameo by Paris Hilton, which sticks out like a sore thumb in what’s supposed to be a Dr. Seuss adaptation. Steer clear of this film entirely; it’s not even entertainingly bad. (Here’s hoping they’ll remake "Horton Hears a Who" with Robin Williams. That would complete the 'bad-Seuss-movie-starring-a-spectacular-comedian' trilogy!)

It’s unfortunate that this film wasn’t released in theaters, as it deserves a wider audience. It’s far superior to many of the recent releases, and that’s a real shame.

This is nothing short of a disgrace and yet another glaring example of the secular-progressive bias permeating the global film industry—not just Hollywood.

This ranks among the most intriguing films I've ever watched. I thoroughly enjoy the film's rustic atmosphere. It feels incredibly authentic and convincing. The setting appears to be from another era, perhaps the late '60s or early '70s. Henry Thomas delivers a strong performance alongside the young baby. A deeply touching story that is definitely worth viewing.

I recall watching *American Gothic* when it first premiered, and it recently came to mind. The only thing I remembered was that the same actor from *Midnight Caller* appeared—Gary Cole. I don’t watch much television, but *American Gothic* was one exception. This week, I purchased the Complete Series on DVD, and it’s still as enjoyable as ever. It’s one of the best TV series ever made. My lack of interest in most TV shows stems from the fact that they’re mostly rubbish: reality TV or soap operas like *Grease* and *Big Brother*. I’m tired of it all. I bought the complete series of *American Gothic* for £16.97 from the Asda website, which is the cheapest price I could find.

A perfect 10 out of 10, this extraordinary and superior documentary is an absolute must-see. Featuring rarely seen war footage that had not been viewed for years until its premiere in 1974, the documentary covers every aspect of the conflict. Some of the clips were so powerful they left me speechless. Spanning over 20 episodes, the series is narrated by the legendary Sir Laurence Olivier, who delivers a compelling narrative of the war. Even after more than 25 years since its release, this remains one of the greatest war documentaries ever made and continues to deliver a profound impact. Everyone should watch it, even just a few episodes, as it will leave a lasting impression on those who have experienced or been affected by war.
