"Indeed, the combination of drug use, warehouse shoot-'em-ups, 'Matrix'-style bullet dodging, a futuristic city blending various Asian cultures, and a solitary vampire in the same film feels like a narrative that could only have been imagined by a Japanese pop/rock star. And that is precisely what 'Moon Child' is—and then some. While all these elements might suggest the ideal premise for a campy B-movie, the film manages to pull it off with just the occasional predictable misstep.

The movie exudes a gritty, distinctly independent vibe, transitioning between scenes in erratic leaps rather than seamless transitions, offering fleeting glimpses into the characters' lives while skimming the surface of a cohesive plot. Yet the film makes no apologies, transforming its story into one of friendship, love, trust, and betrayal, wrapped in the previously mentioned tropes of futuristic societies, warring gangs, and vampires.

HYDE delivers an outstanding performance as the brooding vampire 'Kei,' infusing depth into the character and tempering the over-the-top acting of Gackt as 'Sho,' an orphan who forms a bond with Kei. Lee-Hom Wang also impresses as the vengeful 'Son,' whose relationship with a grown-up Sho adds another layer of complexity."

This could have been a film centered around Sam and his wife, played by the incomparable Peter Falk and the equally brilliant Olympia Dukakis. That would have been a movie worth watching. Instead, it's a Paul Reiser vehicle, with only a minor appearance from Falk. Elizabeth Perkins, fantastic as always, is also part of this film, yet her presence is almost unnoticeable. It seems Reiser believes himself to be a major movie star in need of the perfect showcase. He’s not. What’s even more frustrating is that Reiser hired some of the finest female character actresses today and proceeded to push them into the background. Dukakis doesn’t appear until the final 15 minutes, but when she does, her presence lights up the screen. The story is truly about Falk and Dukakis, yet we’re forced to endure a pointless, absurd road trip where Reiser gets to demonstrate how unbearably cute, overly precious, and woefully lacking in psychological depth (spoiler: wrong!) he can be. For example, in a restaurant scene meant to echo Cassavetes, Reiser stages a laughably artificial confrontation with Falk that’s so contrived, I felt sorry for Falk.

Over this 4th of July weekend, it’s uplifting to witness the spirit of the Declaration of Independence thriving in the satirical film "War, Inc." Much like our founding fathers stood up to King George III, this movie hilariously exposes the shameless war profiteering engaged in by today’s capitalist opportunists who seek to exploit and privatize even war itself. 

The stellar ensemble cast delivers an impressive performance. John Cusack shines as a dry-witted, morally conflicted corporate hitman, while the captivating Marisa Tomei plays his charming love interest with aplomb. ("George Costanza" wasn’t wrong—Marisa Tomei is stunning!) However, it’s John’s sister, Joan Cusack, who truly commands attention. Her portrayal of a demanding yet obsequious personal assistant is both hilarious and unforgettable, leaving the audience in stitches multiple times with her impeccable comedic timing and expressive face. Dan Aykroyd also makes a brief but impactful appearance as the head of the Tamerlane Corporation, the company orchestrating the war, seated atop...

This is the first installment in the Guinea Pig series and one of the more notorious films within the collection. It took me a while to muster the courage to get my hands on a copy of these infamous movies. I purchased the Guinea Pig Box Set and decided to watch them in the order they were released. So, I put this one in and settled down.

Based on what I’d read online and knowing the content involved, I expected to be thoroughly tested in terms of my nerves. Surprisingly, that wasn’t the case. 

The film revolves around a group of men who abduct a woman and torture her in an attempt to uncover the limits of human endurance and how much pain a person can withstand. Sounds twisted, right? Wrong. The movie falls flat when it comes to delivering shocks. Perhaps I’ve grown desensitized over the years due to my love for horror, but I’d wager that even the most avid gore enthusiasts could breeze through this without much trouble.

On the flip side, someone who isn’t...

This was definitely a low-budget film with noticeable continuity issues, like scenes switching between sunlight and shadows. While I adore Nick Mancuso, his portrayal of the burnt-out character sometimes felt overdone. Some of the supporting actors were subpar, and at least one performer appeared in two roles that were hard to overlook. Still, Richard Grieco stole every scene with his comedic timing—and his hair was worth the price of admission. Steven Ford brought warmth and charm to his role. Mancuso delivered some memorable lines, but oddly enough, Nancy Allen lacked presence entirely. Is it a classic? No. Are there flaws? Definitely. But is it entertaining? Absolutely. Watching them brainstorm Grieco’s hairstyle must have been hilarious. Lines like “Are you fast?” followed by “Y’ain’t THAT fast” remain iconic.

The movie has just one major flaw, unfortunately, and this flaw severely undermines its credibility. The film begins by condemning the Israeli occupation of disputed territories without addressing why the Israelis are there in the first place. It was Egypt, Syria, Iraq, and Jordan who attacked Israel, which is why Israel occupies their land—they won it in a war initiated by those countries.

Additionally, the documentary claims that Israel has defied the United Nations by failing to comply with Resolution 242. However, the Palestinians immediately rejected this resolution when it was proposed, rendering it effectively null and void.

While many films are skillfully assembled and can present compelling footage capable of changing opinions, always keep in mind that you should trust none of what you hear and only half of what you see when consuming media.

Every participant in this film is a known critic of Israel, and several have made numerous antisemitic remarks publicly, eliminating any credibility their statements might have had. All participants would benefit from an objective history lesson—not one skewed by a Palestinian sympathizer.

I typically tune into the MTV Movie Awards to catch a clever and entertaining show with its own unique twist—like Chewbacca receiving a lifetime achievement award. This year was no exception. Although I’m not a fan of Justin Timberlake, Seann William Scott has always struck me as amusing, albeit somewhat ridiculous. I’ve found myself laughing at Stiffler’s antics in both *American Pie* films and even enjoyed him in *Dude, Where's My Car?*. However, this year’s MTV Movie Awards were absolutely terrible. There was nothing coherent, humorous, or entertaining about it. Justin Timberlake should probably stick to singing and dancing because his acting skills leave much to be desired.

I’m genuinely curious about who wrote this year’s script. Last year’s performance by Jack Black and Sarah Michelle Gellar was incredibly funny, particularly the *Lord of the Rings* parody, which made the whole show worthwhile. But this year’s version felt entirely different. What exactly was the point of Timberlake’s comments about Luke Wilson and Kate Hudson (“They’re starring in a movie together, but have never met! Here they are…”)? Where was the punchline? Instead of building on the joke, Kate and Luke just delivered some bland dialogue without referencing Timberlake’s setup. As for Seann William Scott, his talent was completely wasted—he didn’t even manage to make me laugh once.

A highly recommendable masterpiece, not only because of the profound themes explored in the narrative but also due to the unparalleled brilliance and ingenuity of Angelopoulos' cinematography, not to mention the stellar performances by cinematic giants Marcello Mastroianni and Jeanne Moreau, as well as the exceptional characterization delivered by Ilias Logothethis. Gregory Karr’s portrayal might initially appear overshadowed by his more "forceful" co-stars, yet his performance proves impeccable when his character’s true essence emerges in the final scene alongside Khrysikou and Mastroianni (a moment subtly foreshadowed earlier). (Reader beware: this contains a spoiler.)

Approach it with the right mindset! This is an "art film" in every sense of the term and demands focus. It’s not meant for casual entertainment but for experiencing a work of art with the same attentiveness required for reading a book or attending a concert. The cinematographic style benefits from large-screen viewing.

Dialogue is sparse, but the film goes further by incorporating—alongside Greek and English—fragments in Albanian, Kurdish, and Turkish, which will appeal to those captivated by the allure of multilingualism.

Wow, I can’t believe I’m the first and only one to comment on this fantastic movie!  

While the film itself was intriguing enough, what really drew me in was Matt Lillard. Sure, most people might think he’s either overly energetic or just doesn’t measure up, but being the same age and from the same generation, I’ve seen him so many times that he’s now one of my favorite actors. This is one of those rare films where he’s the central figure and leading man, similar to his role in *SLC Punk*, another great Lillard flick.  

Story-wise, it’s your typical heist movie with plenty of twists, which eventually spiral into chaos. Another standout in this film is Vincent D’Onofrio, an incredibly talented yet underrated actor in Hollywood. The female lead is a newcomer, and while she isn’t bad, you can tell she was cast primarily for her accent and the inclusion of a nude scene.  

The plot revolves around a三方博弈 between Jack, Jill, and Bob, each trying to claim the rewards for themselves without sharing with anyone else. As the story unfolds, everyone schemes to come out on top.

Since this movie boasts many excellent entertainment features, I believe it deserves more recognition on IMDb than it has received so far. 

It’s your typical ‘whodunit’ thriller involving sex and murder, but it manages to keep you guessing until the very end. I enjoy这类电影, and I definitely think this one measures up to the standard. 

For me, it was worth watching multiple times, so I would rate it an 8 on IMDb.

Mat Spirogolou (played by Toby Malone), whose family recognizes his football talent, is thrilled when he earns an audition with a major club. They trust that his cousin will take care of him once he moves to the city. 

However, the cousins couldn’t be more different: one is a naïve farm boy, while the other is street-smart but reckless, entangled with drug dealers and gangsters. Mat can expect anything but a quiet evening before his big day. 

After failing to find his cousin George (Damien Robertson) upon arriving in the city, Mat runs into further trouble when a reckless biker takes him for an unexpected and unwanted ride. 

Toby Malone, renowned primarily for his theater work, delivers a commendable performance as the rustic teenager. While the film shows signs of its low budget, it compensates with an infectious sense of fun, spontaneous energy, and charm—qualities often lacking in typical Hollywood blockbusters.

I took some time before writing a review of this documentary because, over a decade ago when I first watched it, I wanted to give careful thought to my thoughts. From a documentary perspective, this is an excellent piece. It achieved its goal of introducing me to something entirely new while keeping me engaged with the world it explored. Prior to watching, I knew nothing about the drag scene or "balls," but learning about them was truly fascinating. The participants' talent and creativity in competing were impressive. The drama—cattiness, complaints (like when someone challenged a judge over a dress being deemed inappropriate), and jealousy—all felt authentic and reminiscent of any competitive environment. This, I believe, was one of the film's key points: showcasing the evolution of the balls and how they've adapted over time.

The documentary also featured older drag queens reflecting on how things used to be compared to the newer generation, who introduced more categories and changes. Watching as others observed the future of the scene unfold was intriguing.

Years ago, a movie-going friend and I went to see a horror film, thinking it would be good because it starred John Cassavetes. For those unfamiliar with him, John Cassavetes was an acclaimed actor, screenwriter, and director (married to actress Gena Rowlands) who was Oscar-nominated three times. He funded his own low-budget films using his acting earnings. Until we watched *The Incubus*, we didn’t realize that he took roles in nearly any project offered to him. Had we known what the film was about beforehand, we might have skipped it entirely. Still, we stayed until the end. At the time, my friend and I jokingly called it the worst movie ever made. That’s not strictly accurate—there are plenty of laughably bad films I’ve seen on Friday nights on Cinemax that are far worse (*did I really just admit that?*). Movies starring Brian Bosworth, for instance, are almost universally worse than *The Incubus*. And let’s not forget *Santa Claus Conquers the Martians*, which is certainly worse. However, I’ve come to use *The Incubus* as a kind of cinematic threshold...

There’s no eloquent way to describe this film because it simply doesn’t warrant it. It’s neither an art film nor some overlooked gem. The kind of movie you might hear about from a friend who stumbled upon an incredible indie flick downtown. Just toss it in with the Christmas decorations and get rid of it as soon as possible.

There is little doubt that H.G. Wells is the most influential writer of the 20th century. While Jules Verne is often credited as the father of science fiction, his stories leaned more toward adventure tales that used marvelous inventions as plot devices. Wells, on the other hand, was profound, weaving complex subtexts into his narratives. His greatest legacy may well be the shift in human thought regarding extraterrestrial life; whereas there was virtually no belief in life on other planets before the 20th century, today many—including prominent figures like Richard Dawkins—consider it almost certain. Of course, there’s no concrete evidence for this, but one cannot help but wonder if Wells was the first to introduce such ideas to human consciousness. Undoubtedly, he planted the seed.

*THINGS TO COME* was adapted by Wells himself from his own novel. However, it quickly becomes apparent that he struggles to distinguish between the technicalities of novel-writing and screenwriting. The dialogue is often heavy-handed, awkward, and unconvincing. For instance, during a conversation between two pilots from opposing sides about the nature of war—"Why must we murder one another. Why?"—the lines feel forced and artificial.

I struggle to recall a murder/mystery film as糟糕 as this one. The movie follows a medical examiner probing his friend’s suspicious death in a car crash, ticking every box for a poor production: terrible acting,乏味的剧情, zero suspense, weak humor, and no dramatic tension. I caught it on PAX, a network known for churning out low-budget, campy made-for-TV movies like this. While TV films naturally lack the grit or suspense of big-screen releases, this one managed to sour everything it touched. The creators missed a chance to turn "Recipe for Murder" into a standout TV movie—the title even hinted at potential intrigue. 

In short, if you're searching for a decent recipe, steer clear of this film. It could ruin your appetite for television altogether.

Grade: F

I found "King Solomon's Mines" to be beautifully executed. My only critique was regarding Alison Doody; while her acting was exceptional, her makeup and hairstyle appeared inconsistent with the period, making her seem somewhat out of place alongside the other actors. Patrick Swayze was an inspired casting choice for Alan Quatermain. It was refreshing to see a seasoned, rugged actor in this role, especially after watching film after film featuring fair-haired, fair-skinned actors like Val Kilmer and Brad Pitt. Swayze was perfectly suited for the part, and I thoroughly enjoyed the movie. This adaptation shouldn't be compared to the 1950s version starring Stewart Grainger, as they belong to different mediums—a big-screen classic versus a made-for-TV production. Both portrayals of the Quatermain character were credible, but the differences between the two should be acknowledged. I’m eager to watch this film again and hope Patrick Swayze considers taking on similar roles in the future.

This art film has an uncertain release year—while the National Film Preservation Foundation lists it as 1969, IMDb states 1972. However, regardless of the precise date, its visual style unmistakably reflects the era, featuring camera work and pop art aesthetics typical of the late 1960s to early 1970s. 

The movie comprises three basic images, each manipulated through unconventional camera techniques. Accompanied only by music, it lacks dialogue or any semblance of a plot. Clearly intended as a form of performance art, it holds interest initially but soon grows monotonous. Frankly, the film is dreadfully dull and would likely appeal only to those involved in its creation, their loved ones, and a niche crowd eager to appear cutting-edge.

While the film had a few entertaining moments, I found it rather disappointing overall. The longer it went on, the weaker it became. Once the action shifted to Monument Valley, I found myself captivated by the stunning landscapes rather than the increasingly ridiculous and unconvincing interactions between the characters. 

The portrayal of the daughter was especially confusing. One moment she’s complicit in the scheme, the next she uncovers the truth and leaves, only to return, then abandon everyone again, and finally reappear once more. Her motivations are completely unclear throughout. Despite some intriguing characters and interesting scenes, there were numerous missed opportunities. In the end, the film felt far less impactful than the sum of its parts. It seems that viewers who enjoyed *Repo Man* might have appreciated this movie as well. However, *Searchers 2.0* doesn’t come close to matching the greatness of *The Searchers*.

Any film where Brooke Shields manages to outshine a Fonda is bound to be both an oddity and a nightmare. While Shields is subpar due to her youth, inexperience, and lack of proper guidance from her co-star, Peter Fonda is simply unconvincing. Although I appreciated him in *Ulee's Gold* years later, he is painfully wooden here. To make matters worse, no one else delivers a decent performance either—there isn't a single noteworthy turn aside from Henry Fonda’s delightful cameo. I’ve never seen a movie with so many糟糕的表演。Luke Askew, who plays the main villain, seems to suffer from weak dialogue and direction, as he has delivered solid performances in the past. His partner, portrayed by Ted Markland, is an over-the-top embarrassment. The writing is atrocious, though the actors deserve little blame for having to deliver such dreadful lines. Yet they manage to do so poorly! Both the editing and direction are abysmal; shots linger unnecessarily long without any dramatic purpose, while others are abruptly cut off before their full impact can register. This film turned out far worse than I anticipated and would likely have been entirely forgotten—or perhaps never made at all—had it not...

Unclaimed letters find their way to an extraordinary world hidden within the post office’s basement. Alice secures a position there in hopes of locating her missing father. Instead, she uncovers the troubled spirit of her enigmatic supervisor, Frank. This quiet Australian gem flew under the radar when it premiered in theaters, now resting unnoticed in the dim recesses of a video store, overshadowed by countless copies of the overrated GODZILLA flick. It’s unfortunate, as this movie delivers a compelling narrative supported by powerful, straightforward imagery and convincing performances from its lead actors. It surpasses Garry Marshall's similarly themed DEAR GOD (1996) and rivals the excellence of He Jianjun's POSTMAN (1995), proving itself a worthy cinematic achievement.

In this 1942 film, Errol Flynn portrays "Gentleman Jim," the story of James J. Corbett, the man who defeated boxing legend John L. Sullivan. Directed with a deft touch by Flynn’s close friend, Raoul Walsh, the movie features an impressive cast including Alexis Smith, Jack Carson, Alan Hale Sr., William Frawley, and Ward Bond. Flynn stars as an ambitious and self-assured young man with a natural aptitude for boxing. Sponsored by San Francisco's prestigious Olympic Club in the late 1800s, his status as a "shanty Irishman" and social climber stirs resentment among its members, many of whom eagerly anticipate his defeat. Despite these challenges, he achieves fame, even dabbling in acting. Eventually, he secures a match with the world champion, John L. Sullivan (played by Ward Bond), who insists on a $10,000 deposit for the $25,000 prize. Desperate for funds, assistance arrives from an unexpected source. 

This is a highly enjoyable film, and the role of Jim Corbett proves to be an ideal fit for Flynn, showcasing his charisma and charm while highlighting his ability to bring depth to complex characters.

Because that's the only way you won't consider this film a complete waste of time and money. A remake of "Heaven Can Wait," which at least had some merit, serves as a poor substitute for a romantic comedy. It mostly functions as a platform for Rock to attempt stand-up comedy, which falls flat on the big screen. The mismatched delivery of jokes, supposedly coming from the character of an old, fat, rich, dead man but visibly performed by Rock himself, creates awkward chemistry. His humor often offends both Black and White audiences, further detracting from the film's appeal. This movie isn't funny, suffers from poor cinematography, and features subpar acting. Save yourself the trouble and rent "Heaven Can Wait" along with one of Rock's live comedy specials instead.

I’ve read several comments about this film and can only conclude that some people have low entertainment thresholds. This movie is forgettable; it’s poorly written, directed, and performed to the point of being unmemorable. The characters spout trite, overused lines, and the scenarios are entirely unrealistic. While such elements might lend the film a campy charm, they fail to do so because everything feels deadened, making the movie tedious. It seems like Lee Rose intended to craft a drama exploring a woman’s struggle with her sexuality, but either studio executives stifled her ability to infuse the narrative with authentic emotion, or she lacked the courage to take creative risks. This film could serve as the quintessential example of a mediocre Lifetime television movie in the encyclopedia.

This film is毫无意义的废话. It’s an unfortunate reflection of the hypocritical and toxic culture of a decade ago. In it, superficial remorse for slavery coexists with colonialist undertones (does the irritating red-haired woman really need to feed Shaka rice?). Historical accuracy is also thrown out the window. Weren’t most Western slaves taken from West Africa? How did an American slaver manage to capture Shaka with just a handful of men? And as for David Hasselhoff, he couldn’t have been more insufferable. One can only wonder how he would have fared in the miniseries (likely meeting an immediate and unfortunate end, such as being impaled). The miniseries was exceptional, and it’s regrettable that Hasselhoff got his hands on something unique and turned it mundane. (I suspect he played a significant role in creating this disaster.)

I don't expect this film to resonate easily with audiences outside Romania. This reflects either the film's specific value or perhaps its lack of universal appeal, but it also underscores the stark differences in the histories and lives of ordinary people in Romania compared to other countries, even within Eastern Europe. 

The movie is an adaptation of a novel by Marin Preda, a controversial writer who passed away under Communist rule shortly after the book’s publication. It follows the story of a philosopher and intellectual whose life is shattered when he is wrongfully imprisoned at the end of the Stalinist era. The first half of the film portrays his struggle for survival in prison, while the second half depicts his attempts to rebuild his life upon release. Even after leaving prison, his survival proves just as challenging on a moral level, as Romania in the 1960s demands various forms of compromise and moral transgression.

The film features outstanding performances from some of Romania's finest actors. Stefan Iordache, who plays the lead role, would have shone in any other time or place.

When I began watching this movie, I recognized the actor from "Buffy," Xander, and thought, "Ah, good to see him still working." Now, I can tolerate strange movies if they're as offbeat as David Lynch's work—like "Twin Peaks" or "Lost Highway"—but you have to be in the right frame of mind for them. This film, however, reminded me of those ridiculous conspiracy theory websites that make absolutely no logical sense. Seriously, Nazi conspiracies with America forming some unholy trinity of evil? They didn’t even mention the hollow Earth, flying saucers, or lizard people. Maybe if you were high on 60 grams of heroin, it might seem coherent, but I don’t condone drugs, and I certainly don’t condone this movie either. It should be burned, shredded, and forgotten so Xander might land another acting gig. His performance was fine, but the script was just nonsensical. Sorry.

Here’s another movie that deserves to be loaded into a satellite, launched into space, and aimed at the Andromeda Galaxy to showcase the best of humanity to distant civilizations. Despite its endearing stupidity and refreshingly honest status as little more than a blatant rip-off of the already underwhelming 1976 KING KONG classic, this film somehow manages to outdo its predecessor in sheer laughable goofiness. It also eerily foreshadowed many of the cringe-worthy elements of Peter Jackson’s 2005 CGI-heavy adaptation, particularly the “romance” between the giant creature—a Yeti—and a stunning human woman (Antonellina Interlenghi, known for her work in Umberto Lenzi’s CITY OF THE LIVING DEAD, whose presence is undeniably captivating). 

Intended for children, the film keeps things mostly innocent, with only mild innuendo involving fish bones and a bizarre nipple pinch during a farewell scene—so forget about anything remotely steamy. The Yeti even sports what appears to be a comically oversized loincloth, making the whole thing even funnier than any semblance of anatomical accuracy would allow. In exchange, viewers are treated to a zany old scientist, two curious kids, and Tony Kendall in a rare role as a morally questionable scoundrel.

I can appreciate why fans of filmmaker Roman Polanski might love this movie—and I also understand how others could absolutely detest it (Ebert was among the rare few who couldn’t fathom why audiences weren’t fleeing the theater). After my first viewing, I’m not entirely sure I’d place myself firmly in either camp. Yet, as someone who adores Kafka and bizarre dark comedies of paranoia, *The Tenant* proves engaging enough within its runtime—or perhaps not. This might be one of those instances where it would’ve been a true masterpiece had it been a half-hour *Twilight Zone* episode, with Serling delivering the closing narration as Trelkovsky (or whoever it may be(?)) writhes in bandages. It mirrors *Repulsion* in its treatment of the doomed protagonist, though it could be argued that the earlier film offered greater ambiguity, a stronger sense of the surreal emerging from the sustained unraveling of character and setting (and, honestly, a superior lead performance).

That said, *The Tenant* does boast an intriguing premise, the sort you enjoy recounting to others: Polanski, a Polish émigré in Paris,

In "Follow the Fleet," an RKO production from 1936, Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers star in a sophisticated romantic comedy. Despite their numerous collaborations in similar films, RKO assisted the duo in crafting another engaging storyline that reflects the social context of its era. The film’s narrative hinges on intertwined plots involving two pairs of central characters, ensuring a satisfying blend of romance and humor.

The movie centers on Bake Baker, a U.S. Navy sailor portrayed by Astaire, and Sherry Martin, Bake's former lover and dance partner, now a singer and dancer played by Rogers. The story kicks off when Bake’s shipmate, Bilge Smith, discovers a photograph of the pair together, prompting Bake to share how he last proposed to her. Inspired, Bilge encourages Bake to reconnect with her when they are on shore, hoping she might introduce him to someone new.

The subsequent key scene introduces the film’s secondary plotline.

Although it's a classic James Arness western, this film is widely regarded as the worst Alamo movie ever made. The storyline was weak, riddled with inaccuracies, and outright falsehoods. Continuity was completely ignored. Did anyone notice the cannon scene? The Mexicans were portrayed as foolishly firing cannons with mud and ramrods clearly still stuck in the barrels. Seriously! And then there’s Brian Keith's absurd hat—clearly, the costume designer either took a day off or lost their mind!

Little Edie and Big Edie are figures who evoke sympathy from anyone who encounters their stories. Despite the squalor of their home, their circumstances are somewhat forgivable given their struggles with mental illness. A poster on the message board aptly noted that "Little Edie has the coping skills of an eight-year-old." This observation resonated with me, especially when recalling Big Edie's words in the 2009 dramatization: "If you're stuck, it's only with yourself!" These women possessed immense beauty, talent, intelligence, and unwavering conviction in their beliefs and actions. Perhaps if Little Edie hadn’t been so harsh on herself after her initial setbacks—losing her hair, her job, and the love of her life—she might have persevered. Her difficulty bouncing back during tough times and recognizing brighter days ahead seems to reflect her mental health challenges. It’s impossible to say how different her life might have been had she heeded her mother's heartfelt plea: "Come home, Edie! Let me take care of you!"

Despite their understandable insecurities, these women remain brilliant, heart-wrenching, and endearing, even in the midst of their filthy surroundings. Their extraordinary nature shines through in their interactions, which often spark moments of humor.

Gédéon and Jules Naudet set out to document the experiences of rookie firefighters in New York City. Instead, they captured the only known video footage inside the World Trade Center on September 11. 

When Jules, who had previously worked with James Hanlon’s ladder company, accompanied the captain to address a gas leak, Gédéon remained at the firehouse. A low-flying airplane caught Jules’ attention, and as he raised his camera to film it, the plane struck Tower One. Deciding to join the captain inside the Towers, Jules witnessed two people on fire, an image he chose not to record. For the following hours, he documented the reactions of firefighters and others present at the scene.

The Naudet brothers exercised sensitivity in editing their footage, avoiding excessive violence or gore. However, the firefighters’ language is occasionally rough, and CBS faced criticism for airing the documentary uncensored. To provide context, the brothers combined their original footage with intimate interviews, allowing the firefighters to articulate their thoughts and emotions during critical moments of the crisis.

Unlike a feature film, this documentary offers an unfiltered look at the events of that day, providing viewers with an authentic portrayal of the chaos and heroism unfolding in real time.

Verhoeven's film was an absolute disaster. He is a talentless director who should be embarrassed by his work. According to his own account, he only read two chapters of the book, lost interest, and proceeded to fabricate the entire story himself. 

If Heinlein were alive at the time, he would have disowned that garbage outright. The movie shamelessly uses the book's title, distorts its political themes (a significant part of the original work), and adds gratuitous nudity to keep the average uninspired American audience entertained.

This anime adaptation may not be flawless, but based on what I know, it remains far more faithful to the source material than Verhoeven's version.

A well-crafted film, notable for its time period, featuring an intense, expansive, and predominantly dark storyline that evokes a sense of John Ford's "The Searchers," albeit without the same level of brutality. The narrative kicks off at a rapid pace and maintains its momentum throughout, highlighted by several memorable exchanges of dialogue involving Jeff Webster, portrayed by Stewart, alongside Ronda Castle and Sheriff Gannon. In certain aspects, this movie mirrors "Bend of the River" (1952), another collaboration between Mann and Stewart, yet it struck me as less sentimental and far more engaging. However, there are a couple of drawbacks: the conclusion feels somewhat rushed and overly sentimental, Corrine Calvert, at just 24 years old, struggles to convincingly portray a naive French teenager, and the setting adheres to the familiar mythic West—a fictional realm where real-world laws and physical realities are suspended. These points are minor issues, though. James Stewart delivers a compelling performance as a brooding, detached character who believes he only cares about himself, and the breathtaking mountain landscapes are unmatched. A solid Western costume drama.

If you ever hear those three words—"Joe Don Baker"—brace yourself...

*Final Justice* is a low-budget action film centered around a sheriff in a Texas town named Geronimo (pronounced "Her-on-ee-mo"). This character is unpleasantly ugly, obnoxious, and crude, chasing a criminal in Malta over the murder of his partner in Texas. Oddly, his partner inexplicably collapses twice, revealing poor editing. Joe Don Baker’s portrayal of Geronimo lands him in jail about four or five times, leaving the story stagnant. Apparently, no one informed him that it’s the 20th century, because he behaves like he’s in the Wild West, shooting everyone in sight. Meanwhile, a female officer is tasked with showing him around Malta; she resembles Elaine from *Seinfeld* and somehow tolerates this Neanderthal. Clearly, she needs therapy! The strip club dancers are far more entertaining, becoming highlights of the movie as their performances provide some semblance of enjoyment compared to watching Geronimo bumble through scenes. The film’s conclusion is both flawed and predictable, rounding out a forgettable experience.

It’s been ages since I watched this comedy, and I had nearly forgotten just how nonsensical it is. It wouldn’t be a stretch to say this ranks among the absolute worst of Elvis Presley’s films—likely in the bottom two or three. In this movie, Elvis portrays Joe Whitecloud, a half-Indian bull rider returning to his roots in Arizona. He finds himself back at his rundown family home, surrounded by friends who seem to party nonstop. Burgess Meredith and Katy Jurado play his parents, while Thomas Gomez portrays his eccentric Native American grandfather. Unfortunately, none of these actors bring any depth or humor to their roles. The U.S. government has invested in the family’s cattle business, but they’re short on bulls. Elvis manages to perform only a couple of forgettable songs, and he’s pursued by both a young woman obsessed with dating and her pistol-wielding mother. Overall, the film feels like an unpolished mess, and the dingy setting reeks of disrepair, which doesn’t help matters. What’s baffling is that despite Elvis’s frustration over being stuck in so many mediocre films, he appears genuinely enjoying himself here.

Don’t let the presence of big names like Burt Reynolds, James Woods, and Anne Archer fool you. They’re essentially glorified extras whose scenes were likely filmed in a single day. Regardless of their reasons for joining this project, if you’ve got an actor like James Woods, you should use him effectively. To me, this feels like a case of poor direction throughout. The plot wasn’t terrible, and the performances from most of the cast were above average. However, Cuba Gooding Jr.’s acting was dreadful. His attempts at drama were so unconvincing that I nearly laughed during his more intense moments—clearly not the reaction intended for a serious film. The action sequences weren’t bad, but they lacked that extra spark to elevate them into something truly thrilling. Better direction was desperately needed here as well. Additionally, the pacing was off for an action-thriller running only 90 minutes; it took the protagonist nearly half an hour to even get into the action, which is far too slow. The sole亮点 is Angie Harmon, who tries her hardest to salvage the film. Unfortunately, the director didn’t give her enough support. Yes, this movie could have been much better.

When young Kevin receives his deceased uncle's boat as a gift, he invites five friends to join him for a weekend trip to Catalina Island. During the voyage, they engage in drinking, intimacy, and games, each revealing their deepest fears along the way. Tragedy strikes when Kevin drowns at sea, the engine fails, and they begin to be tormented—and ultimately killed—by manifestations of their innermost fears.

Yesterday, my family and our friends attempted to watch *Haunted Boat* on DVD. With under 30 minutes elapsed, the group abandoned the film due to its disorganized and monotonous nature. We opted instead to view another movie. Out of curiosity, I finished the rest of *Haunted Boat* later and realized it was better to go to sleep than endure the rest. The convoluted storyline, poor cinematography, and shaky camera work combine poorly with an acting ensemble that appears to still be learning their craft. In the end, this project feels like a subpar exercise from a film school student. The overwrought script includes a laughable twist, leaving the viewer with a thoroughly chaotic and unsatisfying experience.

Nikolai Gogol's tale "Viy" has been adapted into a new film and distributed for home viewing in the US by Faith Films. 

The original story revolves around a priest tasked with guarding the body of a witch, relying solely on his faith for protection. Significantly expanded and relocated to America, though evidently shot in Russia (as evidenced by the inaccurate architecture, attire, and furnishings, despite the presence of English signage), this movie feels disjointed and fails to come together. One issue lies in its peculiar setting, which awkwardly attempts to depict rural America without convincingly pulling it off. Additionally, the film contains strange, deliberately ambiguous moments, particularly concerning the protagonist, who starts as a reporter before abruptly becoming a priest. Even after viewing the DVD's behind-the-scenes featurette, I remain unclear about the reasoning behind this change. Another major flaw is the subpar dubbing; it’s executed in such a way that characters speak only when their lips aren’t visible on screen—or when they are, the audio bears no resemblance to the lip movements. It's unclear whether this is Faith Films' responsibility or the fault of the producers, who likely intended the film for Western audiences, as mentioned in the featurette.

Five Across the Eyes begins with five teenage girls driving home before their curfew. They stop at a store and accidentally hit another car, deciding to flee the scene.不久后，被撞车辆迫使她们停车，一位手持散弹枪的疯狂女子下车怒吼，命令她们脱光衣服并在上面小便，随后又突然开车离开。震惊和慌乱的姑娘们以为噩梦已经结束，但这位疯狂女子再次出现，似乎执意要置她们于死地。此时，这些又迷路又缺油的女孩陷入了极度恐慌……  

由格雷格·斯温森和瑞安·蒂森共同制作并执导，斯温森编剧，蒂森负责摄影与剪辑，我可以毫不夸张地说，《五人对眼》是我看过的最糟糕的电影之一，甚至可能是最差的一部。我实在想不出还有哪部电影比它更令人失望。不过，让我先说明一点：我相信这里的一些电影制作决定是刻意为之，目的是营造氛围、制造紧张感……

At first glance, this documentary/fiction/cartoon is both entertaining and thought-provoking. However, when something prompts deep reflection, it also invites critical examination. The truth is that this film intertwines metaphysics with innuendo and unsupported conclusions. The supposed connection between science and spirituality presented in "What the Bleep..." is, in fact, entirely ungrounded in scientific evidence. The Transcendental Meditation study featured in the film claims that collective meditation can reduce crime in a specific area—in this case, Washington D.C. However, in reality, the HRA (Homicides, Rapes, and Assaults) crime rate was approximately 30% higher in 1993 compared to the average rate between 1988–1992. Notably, there was no reduction in the homicide rate during the study period. Every claim attempting to link metaphysics with science has been thoroughly debunked.

Based on this information, my view is that this movie is either an unsuccessful attempt to indoctrinate viewers or an elaborate jest. In either case, I advise against investing your time in it. 

If you're seeking a thought-provoking, science-focused film, you might consider *Mindwalk* (1990) instead.

Even though Louis B. Mayer supposedly showed little interest in signing the young Greta Garbo to a contract, this actress’s debut American and MGM film turned out to be visually stunning. It’s clear that the production was entrusted to incredibly talented individuals, particularly those responsible for filming and creating matte paintings, as it boasts the high level of polish and artistry typical of the studio’s finest works. The film remains breathtakingly beautiful even 84 years after its release.

Regarding Garbo herself, like her earliest American films, she appears somewhat distinct here. Although she’s unmistakably recognizable, her makeup is notably softer compared to how it would soon evolve—a change that lends her a less harsh appearance and a gentle quality absent from her later performances. Part of me wishes they had maintained this style, but given how iconic her signature look became, who am I to argue against the path that made her so famous? The story revolves around Garbo and her family, who are unjustly driven from their land by the landlord. Landlady Doña Bernarda justifies this by claiming the bank demanded repayment, but in reality, it stems from her son’s infatuation with Garbo—and what better way...

Disturbing dreams, erratic premonitions, sacrilegious themes, and homoerotic fantasies course through Paul Verhoeven's (debatable) magnum opus about a seductive femme fatale who bewitches men only to dispose of them. Packed with violence and sporadic gore, *The Fourth Man* is a masterclass in psychological unease. Viewers may find themselves flinching as Renee brandishes her scissors with dramatic flair.

This film might just earn the title of "The Worst Movie Ever." Without John Hurt's involvement, it might勉强 pass as a children's movie. The true tragedy here is that John Hurt, one of the greatest actors on screen, lowers himself with this project. I gave it two points solely because he appeared at all. I deduct eight points because he stayed with it far longer than he should have. As for the rest of the cast, they are abysmal. Janine Turner, despite her beauty, lacks any acting ability whatsoever. The lead actor is, quite frankly, atrocious. If you can avoid this debacle, do so. It's so bad, it’s almost painful to watch.

Over the years, I’ve watched quite a few of Steven Seagal’s straight-to-video films, and each one offers the same level of entertainment—unfortunately, at a rather low bar. The action sequences were entertaining, but that’s about all they had going for them. Seagal was at his best in movies like *Under Siege*, *Under Siege 2*, and *Executive Decision* (at least from an action perspective). However, over the past decade, his direct-to-video projects haven’t come close to matching his earlier standards. 

On a brighter note, the film made decent use of its runtime, particularly with some of the action scenes and moments of wit. Just when the pacing felt sluggish, a well-executed action sequence would perk things up. I think Seagal’s movies might perform better if he weren’t the sole recognizable face in them. Supporting actors and actresses play a crucial role, and if his recent films featured well-known supporting talent, they might achieve greater popularity.

I stumbled upon this documentary quite accidentally on the UK channel More4, and I must say, it captivated me with its intrigue and depth. I am now eager to track down the book that served as its foundation. Essentially, this is Professor Jared Diamond's exploration of why some regions of Earth's societies thrived while others did not. His argument was novel to me, and his focus on the significance of the right crops and domesticable animals was particularly compelling. The documentary itself is well-produced and engagingly narrated, with a commendable restraint in avoiding excessive recreated scenes that often mar contemporary documentaries. Diamond's approach is refreshingly unpatronizing, a quality lacking in many intellectuals attempting to communicate with the general public. Some have labeled his theory Marxist, but I find it more aligned with socio-geology. It was invigorating to encounter a societal evolution theory devoid of religious influence. Highly recommended viewing.

A few weeks ago, the German broadcaster "SAT1" promoted this movie as the "TV-Event of the year." Sorry, but I’ve seen better offerings on TV this year.

At first, I wasn’t particularly impressed by the film. However, while watching the commercial, I couldn’t help but recall two other dreadful movies: Titanic and Pearl Harbor. The visuals seemed eerily familiar—there was the "heroine" (and I use the term loosely) at the center, flanked by her two "lovers," a scene reminiscent of Pearl Harbor. The love story here feels like a cheap imitation of that one, and even Titanic had more substance! Still, being someone who enjoys dissecting movie structures, I eventually gave it a shot.

The film starts with a doctor leaving his family to join the military operation against Russia toward the end of the Third Reich. He assures his wife he’ll return. Fast-forward to Spring 1948: Germany has lost the war, and the Allies and Russia now occupy the country, each vying for global dominance through their opposing ideologies: capitalism versus communism. If you’re familiar with post-war narratives, you probably see where this is headed—you know the rest.

The Plot: A crime lord is bringing together three distinct mafias for a scheme to purchase an island, which will function as a money-laundering hub for organized crime. To stop this, the FBI attempts to arrest one of the mafia bosses. Things go awry, leading to an improbable series of events, and ultimately result in yet another "buddy cop" movie—this time featuring a feisty female FBI agent and a rugged ex-DEA agent who can’t stand each other.

To be honest, the storyline isn’t exactly brainy. At best, it’s a mediocre joke. Yet, despite its flaws, the film shines thanks to its humor. (The German dubbed version, in particular, is hilariously over-the-top.) The action sequences are solid as well, highlighted by a standout moment involving a shotgun and a rocket launcher. While there’s no deep satire or full-blown slapstick, the blend of comedy hits keeps the laughs coming consistently.

That said, the movie is far from politically correct. It promotes casual drug use casually, without any critique, even portraying it as glamorous. This aspect was particularly frustrating and makes the film inappropriate for younger audiences, in my view. Still, if you're in the mood for mindless fun with a dash of wit, this flick might just do the trick.

This movie is one of numerous "Kung Fu" action films produced in Asia during the late '70s to early '80s, known for their low-budget sound effects, dubbed dialogue, and rapid-fire martial arts sequences. Unlike most movies in this genre, however, it features a solid storyline and plenty of excellent comedy. When employees of a dye factory are driven out of work by oppressive Manchu bullies, they enlist a con artist (Gordon Liu) to scare the bullies away. Unfortunately, his efforts backfire spectacularly. Forced to flee, he dupes his way into a Shaolin temple to genuinely master martial arts. Instead of becoming a traditional Kung Fu student, though, the master assigns him the seemingly mundane task of constructing scaffolding to cover the rooftops of all 36 chambers. As it turns out, while he's busy stacking and tying bamboo poles, he’s actually mastering the techniques needed to become a Kung Fu expert—much like in *The Karate Kid*, where Mr. Miyagi teaches Daniel the fundamentals of karate through everyday chores like "wax on, wax off." The film is filled with hilarious moments throughout and climaxes with thrilling action scenes as Gordon Liu confronts his adversaries once more.

I genuinely believe this movie is fantastic. However, every film has its downside. Some of you might not have seen Hilary Duff’s *Raise Your Voice*, but if you think about it, the two movies share striking similarities. For instance, in *Brave New Girl*, Holly is desperate to join Haverty Conservatory. Similarly, in *Raise Your Voice*, Terri aims to attend a conservatory in L.A. (though I can’t recall its name). Both stories revolve around the music world, and both involve singing competitions at the end of the semester. It’s amusing how these films parallel each other. Personally, I prefer *Brave New Girl* over *Raise Your Voice*.

I recently rewatched *The Convent* for the second time, expecting it to be as enjoyable as my first viewing. I’d remembered it as a fun mix of gore, style, and humor, perfect for a carefree Friday night. However, this time around, I found myself struggling to connect with it. It feels like the filmmakers tried to recapture the cheesy charm of '80s horror classics like *Night of the Demons* but missed the mark on what made those films memorable. To be clear, I’m not a massive fan of *Night of the Demons*, but there were certain aspects I appreciated. While *The Convent* nails the cheesiness, it falls short when it comes to delivering genuine quality.

One of the few bright spots is Joanna Canton’s likable performance as the lead character. The goth girl also stood out, along with a delightful cameo from Adrienne Barbeau. Unfortunately, most of the other characters were painfully unlikable, embodying the worst stereotypes of dim-witted, obnoxious jocks at their absolute worst. This, combined with the film’s glaring lack of gratuitous nudity, made watching it a chore. With terrible dialogue and unappealing characters, it became nearly impossible to overlook the flaws and focus on the film’s positives. On the brighter side, the evil nuns are creatively designed and deliver some standout moments.

"Transylvania 6-5000" is a mildly amusing yet inconsistently funny and charming horror spoof from the mid-1980s, featuring a recognizable cast and occasional witty moments in its script. Two hapless journalists from a sensationalist tabloid are dispatched—reluctantly—to Transylvania to investigate claims of Dr. Frankenstein's return. Along the way, viewers can stumble upon delightful little quirks, such as a miniature guillotine for hard-boiled eggs or lab test tubes repurposed as creamers at the breakfast table. Despite these small charms, the film falls short in delivering consistent humor, with many jokes and parodic scenarios stretching on far too long. In contrast, Roger Corman’s later production, "Transylvania Twist," released four years after this film, is significantly funnier and more enjoyable. This movie primarily pokes fun at the iconic Universal monster films of the early 1930s, so familiarity with those will help appreciate its numerous subtle gags. Interestingly, the film introduces an inventive twist by suggesting that the Frankenstein character only appears mad and evil due to external circumstances.

I’ve always been a big fan of Batman, enjoying both the animated series and *Batman Beyond*. I even occasionally picked up a Batman comic. So, naturally, I was thrilled upon hearing about this series—until I was utterly let down. This show is forgettable at best, failing to hold a candle to the original series. It feels like one extended toy commercial, offering no substance whatsoever. The handling of the Joker was particularly baffling; in my humble opinion, he’s the greatest Batman villain of all time, yet they killed him off. Honestly, I’d almost prefer if his design had been the low point of the series. Unfortunately, there isn’t a single aspect of this show that comes close to being remotely creative or engaging. To sum it up (and trust me, I could go on for much longer), avoid wasting your time and money on this series.

Brooks, working alongside cinematographer Hall, delivers a stark black-and-white recreation of the infamous 1959 Kansas murders, as depicted in Capote's book, lending the film a documentary-like quality. Blake and Wilson deliver strong performances as the killers, while Forsythe shines as the relentless police officer pursuing them. The tense, eerie scenes preceding the murders, shot at the actual crime scene and accompanied by the haunting sound of whistling winds, are particularly gripping. Brooks demonstrates considerable flair in his direction and employs several innovative scene transitions. However, the film is slightly overlong, with the resolution feeling drawn out and somewhat heavy-handed.

This "documentary" (or rather, mockumentary) perfectly illustrates just how absurd people can be when they become fully enthused about something like this. Frankly, I despise Cryptozoology. It’s not science; it undermines legitimate scientific inquiry. That said, one redeeming aspect was the visual effects—those dragons were stunning. However, some of the information presented in this mockumentary was entirely fabricated, which is incredibly disappointing since it came from supposed scientists. For that reason, it only merits a 1 out of 10 instead of a 0. Take, for instance, the hydrogen theory: While it's true that hydrogen can be produced in a creature's stomach according to chemistry, producing it in the quantities needed for flight is implausible. A proper explanation of what actually occurs in a dragon’s stomach is essential. Although there are natural substances containing hydrogen, none exist in sufficient amounts to allow an animal like this to take flight, and hydrogen doesn’t simply materialize out of thin air—it’s impossible. Even worse is the idea of platinum: This element is far rarer than gold, and I struggle to comprehend how...

A touching film with the typically outstanding performance by John Thaw, who recently passed away. A humble man who was undoubtedly among England's top ten actors, especially during my time. He'll always be remembered for his iconic role as Inspector Morse, as well as Jack Regan in the 1970s hit TV series *The Sweeney* and a barrister in *Kavanah QC*. This is a must-watch for the whole family and an excellent addition to any DVD collection. The story evokes nostalgia for those who recall wartime Britain, particularly those evacuated from London to escape the German bombings. The chemistry between the two main characters, Tom and the boy William, was exceptionally portrayed and stayed true to Michelle Magorian's book.

The film was recommended to me as a solid action movie, but I personally wouldn't classify it that way. The plot felt overly complicated and wasn't particularly easy to follow. There isn't much action until the very end, and even then, the dim lighting makes it difficult to fully grasp what's going on. I was hoping for something more engaging, but unfortunately, this wasn't it.

If you have any interest in pirates, pirate films, the history of New Orleans or early 19th-century America, or if you admire Yul Brynner, watch this movie yourself and form your own opinion. Ignore the lukewarm reviews. My take on it was that it’s enjoyable, well-acted (mostly), features clever dialogue, and captures the charm, allure, and enduring fascination of the privateer Jean Lafitte. While not everything in the film is historically precise (can any historical movie claim to be entirely accurate?), I believe it accurately reflects Lafitte's role in New Orleans' history and the complex relationship between the city's "respectable" citizens and this beloved outcast. Focus on what the film achieves rather than what it doesn’t, appreciating its exploration of one of New Orleans' and America's most captivating historical figures.

Alright folks, just look at the title! Haha! I recall watching this movie back in the day during Saturday Late Night Creature Features. It’s a fantastic, campy monster flick with absolutely terrible but entertaining acting. The two hilariously dim-witted hillbillies really up the cheese factor. Those two redneck boat rental guys steal the show—LOL—and don’t miss the boat scene where the English couple is gushing about the stars in broad daylight. Classic! Clearly, they weren’t sweating the details; they just wanted to wrap up filming quickly. In short, if you’re into 70s B-movies, you’ll adore this one!

When this documentary first aired on CBS, I was somewhat skeptical about whether I should watch it. I was among the many people in New York City on that fateful day, attending school at Hunter College. I didn’t want to relive the devastation and destruction, but like so many others, I was curious to see what it was all about. Watching this documentary brought tears to my eyes as all my memories flooded back, and the intensity of the images was overwhelming. I purchased the DVD on the one-year anniversary and watched it several times. The ability of the filmmakers to capture such footage was remarkable. If you haven’t seen this documentary, do yourself a favor and give it a watch. It’s undoubtedly sad and emotional, but it’s an incredible record of one of our nation’s darkest moments.

Perhaps I’m overlooking something, but I’ve encountered mostly positive comments about *The Man Who Cheated Himself*, and yet I can’t seem to connect with it. I enjoy noir films that boast a touch of style, with characters who exude the sophistication of Humphrey Bogart in *The Big Sleep* or Gene Tierney in *Laura*. Unfortunately, none of the individuals in this movie possess that allure or presence. Consider Lee J. Cobb as the lead actor; his disheveled, “just-rolled-out-of-bed” appearance couldn’t be further from the suave, charismatic noir stereotype. Then there’s Jane Wyatt as the femme fatale—a casting choice so misguided that it stands out as one of the worst I’ve seen. She simply doesn’t sell the role.

The plot, too, feels stale, lacking any genuine twists or fresh ideas for the genre. By the five-minute mark, I had guessed how *The Man Who Cheated Himself* would end. Even the climactic cat-and-mouse chase scene falls flat—ten to fifteen minutes of virtually nothing happening completely killed whatever momentum the film might have had.

Comedies frequently carry the unfortunate reputation of lacking substantial depth. However, George Bernard Shaw’s *Arms and the Man* debunks this notion entirely. Shaw’s play brims with comedic drama, blending an engaging storyline with genuine philosophical insight.

At its core, *Arms and the Man* is a successful—and somewhat unconventional—romantic comedy. The story revolves around Raina, a young, idealistic, and superficial woman from a military family deeply entrenched in wartime. Her fiancé and father are both military officers, and her worldview is shaped by traditional notions of heroism and honor. One fateful night, she encounters an enemy soldier who seeks refuge in her home. Despite knowing she must keep this encounter hidden from her family, she helps him escape. When the war ends, the soldier reappears, compelling each character to reassess their values and relationships.

What makes the play remarkable is how Shaw infuses deeper meaning into what could otherwise be a conventional comedic plot. He critiques class structures, satirizes the absurdity of war, and explores the complexities of love. All of this is delivered with Shaw’s characteristic wit while maintaining a captivating narrative. With so much substance woven into the story, it’s easy for readers to overlook its profound themes.

The opening scene is meant to depict the Legion arriving in Paris on November 13, 1918. However, as the troops disembark from the train, they’re still wearing the same uniforms the French Army, including the Legion, had worn when they went to war in 1914. This anachronism is a clear indication that the war film you're about to watch will likely be subpar. (By 1915, the French Army had realized that fighting in red trousers and dark blue overcoats wasn’t practical; metropolitan troops were switched to "horizon blue," while colonial forces were issued khaki uniforms.) At the very least, the Claude Van Damme remake corrected this error with its uniforms. It’s truly unfortunate when directors get other details right but make such glaring historical mistakes.

This mini-series is surprisingly more entertaining than some others with significantly larger budgets and loftier ambitions. *Sword of the Dancing Warrior* (SOTD) sits comfortably between *"Kung-Fu"* and *"H.R. Pufnstuf"* on the entertainment scale. If it weren’t for its lengthy runtime (almost three hours), children might enjoy it quite a bit. It combines adventure, action, and suspenseful cliffhanger moments while avoiding excessive romance or other overly sentimental elements. For younger viewers, flaws like flexing rubber swords, campy acting, and repeated scenes often go unnoticed, as these are reminiscent of classic serials aiming to refresh the story for audiences. Additionally, kids tend to be more forgiving when hearing American accents from Asian actors, not to mention that several key roles are portrayed by non-Asian actors.

I initially intended to rate this film three stars, but the director, producers, and cast deserve credit for completing such an ambitious project. While this movie isn’t art, it required time, effort, and discipline to bring it to life—similar to painting a house.

In conclusion, this isn’t a strong recommendation, but it has its merits.

*Georgia Rule* has to be among – if not the absolute worst – movies I’ve ever seen in my lifetime. The entire film has an incredibly surreal tone that made me audibly exclaim “what?” at least 7-10 times during its excruciating two-hour runtime.

Promoted in its trailer as a story about three generations of women – Jane Fonda as the grandmother, Felicity Huffman as her daughter, and Lindsay Lohan as the rebellious, hyper-sexualized, scantily clad granddaughter – viewers likely expect a clichéd, lightweight, chick-flick centered around growing up and family bonding. 

Boy, was that misleading.

From numerous shots of animals doing "funny" things in the background of pivotal scenes to a shocking five-minute sequence focused on an elderly woman visiting a doctor’s office weekly for a diaper change, *Georgia Rule* takes a dark turn. It turns out the movie is actually about Lindsay Lohan’s character being sexually abused by her stepfather. This bizarre combination of elements establishes its own unique cinematic category: an ungrounded, poorly acted, inappropriate comedy that clumsily tackles deeply serious topics in the strangest, most surreal way possible. If Garry Marshall intended this movie to...

I root for films that bridge subject matter gaps in global cinema. After viewing the trailer for *Water Lilies*, I anticipated enjoying this movie, believing I had discovered something distinctive: a film that authentically depicts teenage lesbian love—a kind of female counterpart to *Beautiful Thing*. 

The central characters are three French teenagers, 15 years old. Marie is slim, reserved, and tomboyishly pretty; Floriane is vivacious, athletic, and stunningly beautiful; and Anne is steadfast, chubby, and emotionally immature. The undercurrent of erotic tension between Marie and Floriane pulses throughout the film, whether subtly hinted at or more overtly present.

However, *Water Lilies* isn’t about the blossoming of same-sex attraction in adolescence—it’s about sexual frustration, suffering, ennui, teenagers at odds with one another, and—tragically—in at least two cases, joyless, mechanical encounters. It also demonstrates how filmmakers and screenwriters can undermine their own work when they rely too heavily on manipulation.  

In the bonus materials accompanying the *Lord of the Flies* DVD, director Peter Brook remarks, “French cynicism begins with the awakening of sexuality,” implying that the French view children as innocent while seeing adolescents and...

This isn’t *Video Nastie* material, but it likely escaped the ban in Britain in 1994 because the creators had presumably grown tired of controversy by then. The film is 75% a retread of *The Boogeyman*, and it probably would have faced the same censorship issues — though the exact reasons remain unclear.

Initially, I was puzzled, thinking Annie (played by Kelly Galindo) might be a different version of Lacey from the first film. However, she’s someone tormented by psychic visions of a boogeyman reminiscent of the character in the original. Fans will quickly realize these actresses are not the same person.

After witnessing a murder in a bathroom and catching a glimpse of the address, Annie, along with her psychiatrist and a para psychology student who looks suspiciously like the guy from cheap romance novel covers and butter commercials, heads to the house. Sure enough, it’s the same bathroom. Twenty-four hours later, a murder unfolds exactly as Annie described. Yet, we’re left clueless about the identity of the alluring woman or the motive behind her killing.

The movie then shifts gears to revisit *The Boogeyman* storyline, featuring additional scenes absent from the original. Notably, this time the boogeyman is visually revealed, unlike in the first film. Unfortunately, the film...

Critics can say what they like about Andy Milligan, but if his family was even remotely as disturbed as the one portrayed in this movie, perhaps his career wouldn’t seem so outlandish by comparison. Sadly, the video version of the film includes sex scene insertions originally filmed by the distributor to enhance its commercial appeal. Throughout the movie, Milligan’s crude cinematography and eerie silent-era soundtrack abruptly halts, only for attractive stand-ins to replace his less visually appealing actors, engaging in psychedelic 60s rock-fueled encounters. These scenes are easy enough to skip if you’re focused on Milligan’s original work, though much of the intended narrative is sacrificed to accommodate these additions. Despite the cuts, what remains is undeniably fascinating. I doubt I’ve ever encountered a more venomous maternal figure in cinema.

I can’t stand most reality shows, and this one is even worse than the one featuring Paris Hilton. And yes, it’s connected to his company. But “you’re fired” or “you’re hired”—how many seasons has this been going on? Watching the show leaves me with zero desire to work for someone with such an inflated ego. Honestly, I find watching paint dry more entertaining.

I’d love to see just one contestant stand up and say, “Donald, I quit, and use some of your money to buy a decent hairdo.” I hear he’s even attempting to buy fame in the WWE. I hope he gets hurt so I never have to look at his pathetic face again. It must be tragic to crave fame so desperately while lacking any real talent and making a fool of yourself trying to purchase it. If I could, I’d rate this show negatively, but it currently gets a 1, and honestly, it doesn’t even deserve that.

I think it's a great movie; I also believe it feels distinctly Romanian in terms of its scenery and atmosphere. I don't think sensuality was the primary goal—it emerged naturally as a result rather than being intentional. I find it incredibly authentic and humane. The story held my interest, and while the performances didn’t remind me of Sean Connery-level icons, they felt genuine—like everyday people capable of giving convincing portrayals. I think the film achieved what it set out to do, evoking emotions within me or perhaps reigniting feelings I've had before. I admit I’m not entirely objective about it. 

That said, I truly enjoyed it—I’m certain of that.

Although the (English) title suggests otherwise, this movie has little to do with devils and is primarily focused on a power-hungry ruler obsessed with the Philosopher’s Stone. This ruler desires to turn lead into gold and collect virgin blood. Jacinto Molina portrays Gilles de Lancre, a character who shows no hesitation in executing those he perceives as threats to his position—or to obtain virgins for their blood. His actions are fueled by the encouragement of his lover and an alchemist in his employ. Greed and madness drive him more than any supposed demonic influence, which is unfortunate. While certain scenes, such as jousting matches and knights using large sticks to knock each other off horses, offer some excitement, the film does possess a visually appealing aesthetic. However, there is little else to praise. The movie lacks significant gore and offers no real scares, which is unusual for a Molina/Naschy production, and surprisingly, there isn’t much unintentional humor either. All things considered, it earns a 4 out of 10.

I wasn’t particularly interested in watching *The Flock*. Andrew Lau, who co-directed the acclaimed *Infernal Affairs* trilogy, was fired from this film and replaced by an emergency director named Niels Mueller. I felt that Lau might have crafted a decent film, but it apparently failed to meet the studio’s expectations, leading to his dismissal. This situation typically doesn’t bode well for a movie (just look at *The Invasion*). Surprisingly, however, *The Flock* turned out to be better than I anticipated. It’s not a masterpiece, but it’s an engaging and entertaining thriller. The character development is excellent, allowing viewers to connect deeply with the characters. The chemistry between the two leads feels authentic and believable. Richard Gere and Claire Danes deliver solid performances. On the downside, one aspect that annoyed me—especially at times when it became outright irritating—was the overuse of flashy editing techniques intended to add “attitude” and style to the film. These gimmicks feel misplaced and gratuitous. Additionally, I believe the movie could have been more ambitious. Despite these flaws, I recommend *The Flock* as a worthwhile thriller. It’s not unforgettable, but it’s enjoyable.

I can't claim that *Wargames: The Dead Code* is the worst film I've ever watched, since it did have a couple of tolerable moments. However, I can confidently say it's the most predictable movie I've ever encountered. From start to finish, every plot twist became apparent to me well over ten minutes before it unfolded. The film lacked any subtlety, offering zero signs of cleverness in its execution. Every spoken or written line felt painfully obvious, making it nearly impossible to immerse myself in the story.

Rather than being engaged, I found myself repeatedly amused by the poorly conceived plot and the clumsy efforts to rekindle the audience's interest. My laughter at these missteps occurred far more frequently than any enjoyment I derived from the movie itself.

Unlike some brief summaries, the female characters in this film are not geisha; they are oiran (prostitutes) residing outside Tokyo's renowned pleasure quarters. Their existence and experiences mirror those of countless women during the Tokugawa period. While the narratives may not be particularly revelatory, their appeal stems from their relatability. The themes—love, friendship, and sacrifice—are timeless and ordinary. 

I thoroughly appreciated the art direction and performances. Watching it felt like catching a rare glimpse into a world I could never experience firsthand. The cast, particularly the four actresses portraying the main oiran, delivered captivating performances. I would only recommend this film to those interested in exploring Japanese culture or appreciating subtle, emotionally resonant storytelling. It serves as an excellent representation of both.

When it comes to horror films, I’m usually happy to overlook subpar production values, forgive plot holes, and set aside disbelief for a decent scare. However, this movie offers none of that. It’s not even enjoyable as camp. The dialogue is atrocious, the acting is terrible, and the direction is abysmal. The kills are predictable and poorly executed, the music is grating, the cinematography is dreadful, and even the costumes are poorly done. I genuinely felt sorry for the actors, who seemed to be giving their all but were stuck with clichéd, contrived dialogue and clearly lacked proper guidance. Rehearsals appear to have been nonexistent. Watching it is embarrassing and excruciatingly boring, requiring immense patience just to reach its contrived “shocking” finale. It’s undoubtedly one of the worst films I’ve ever seen.

I rarely write reviews, but this was so bad that I felt obligated to warn others. This movie is a total waste of time. If you’re curious about it, at least skip ahead to the “Making of” featurette. The writer/director seems to think casting a female killer was some sort of groundbreaking decision. (Trust me, it isn’t.) In it, he and the cast discuss their process, but it only highlights how misguided the entire project was.

Does anyone happen to know the location of the shooting for this film? The aviation scene on the cliff is stunning, and it seems to take place in England. However, Ivy’s apartment building closely resembles the Brill Building, particularly with its intriguing elevators.  

Charles Mendl is credited as playing "Sir Charles Gage." I might have missed it, but I didn’t see him during the film. Perhaps he played the husband’s lawyer, though I don’t recall such a character being explicitly featured, except for a mention about a phone call he made. Could he have been in the aviation scene or the ballroom scene? Did anyone catch a glimpse of him?  

Herbert Marshall was 57 years old at the time of filming.

The highlight of "An American in Paris" is undoubtedly the extended ballet sequence towards the end, where Gene Kelly and Leslie Caron embody various renowned painters. Earlier in the film, Kelly is established as a street artist in Paris, making this sequence a fitting conclusion to a musical brimming with vitality, energy, and timeless Gershwin melodies, alongside memorable performances from Georges Guetary and Oscar Levant. At his peak here, Kelly showcases a side distinct from "Singin' in the Rain." The film's crescendo, capped by the ballet, delivers a remarkable impact. It’s no surprise that this sequence concluded "That's Entertainment," coming after all the other MGM musical highlights!

"A Thief in the Night" is a film that largely flew under the radar for mainstream moviegoers because of its low budget, which was hard to overlook, and its focus on the Rapture of the true Christian church and the fate of those left behind. Despite these factors, it told a captivating story that kept viewers engaged and prompted them to reflect on their relationship with Jesus Christ. The film resonated deeply, even affecting a pastor who preached the Word but didn't truly believe it, illustrating exactly why he was left behind. Both this movie and its sequel, "Distant Thunder," remain essential viewing. Even with the upcoming "Left Behind" series offering a higher-budget retelling of the same story, the impact remains unchanged—“A Thief in the Night” paved the way for this genre and will forever be remembered.

In short, this movie holds no value whatsoever.

The concept is to depict the future as someone from the early 1900s might imagine it. While intriguing in theory, the absence of an engaging plot or memorable characters keeps us from buying into the premise, causing the idea to fall flat.

Evidently, the entire film was shot with actors against green screens, expecting viewers to be impressed. However, as someone familiar with graphics, the excessive softening appeared to be a lazy fix for the tricky issue of blending green screen edges. The colors are overly desaturated with no discernible purpose other than diminishing the visual quality. I fail to see how anyone could deem anything in this movie groundbreaking. Instead, the laughably outdated visuals have set a new low for poor-quality graphics—falling far short even of those in "Jurassic Park." The robot designs were simplistic, bland, and uninteresting. The island also featured bizarre prehistoric creatures, but their presence remains entirely unexplained.

The storyline is abysmal. Frankly, I can't...

Released in 1957—a yes, that’s indeed the accurate year—this J. Arthur Rank production featuring James Robertson Justice, Margaret Rutherford, and Wilfred Hyde White should have been a guaranteed hit, a guaranteed laugh riot, right? Wrong. This film is absolutely dreadful. Its entire premise revolves around a single joke: repeatedly showing people reacting with shock upon seeing a tiny alligator. Music is awkwardly shoehorned in, and it’s as forgettable as it is inappropriate. 

Jeannie Carson, while a vivacious dancer and capable singer, seems out of place here. One can’t help but wonder why she signed up for such a project. Then there’s Diana Dors, who adds some tantalizing scenes meant for promotional purposes, though her acting isn’t terrible. Unfortunately, her role seems to exist solely to give male characters someone to ogle. At least you’re occasionally distracted enough to stop groaning. Nowadays, copies are being sold on eBay. Save your money and time. This comedy offers no laughs, and the musical numbers are forgettable at best.

I’ve always been a fan of Cream’s music, despite their relatively small but incredibly impactful body of work. Even their longer tracks—like “Spoonful” and “Toad” from *Wheels of Fire*, which stretch on for nearly twenty minutes—are nothing short of electrifying compared to most contemporary rock acts. Their ability to captivate an audience remains unmatched, exemplified by the highly anticipated reunion performances at London’s Royal Albert Hall last year. While time has naturally aged both the band members and their fans, their energy remains undiminished. Their masterful reinterpretations of classic blues standards and original compositions alike prove just how timeless their artistry is. Tracks like “White Room,” “Badge,” “Politician,” “Spoonful,” and “Sunshine of Your Love” showcase seamless execution.
