Eric Clapton’s solos during these performances possess a cohesion he rarely achieves in his solo gigs. Ginger Baker’s drumming speaks volumes on its own. Meanwhile, Jack Bruce’s vocal prowess retains a commanding strength that Clapton can’t replicate alone. In short, if you missed out on experiencing what many consider some of the greatest live shows of last year, catching these performances is a must—though some might argue it’s a regrettable oversight.

The Barbarians may not be the best film any of us have seen, but seriously... it's hilarious! I can't put into words how much I laughed when I first watched it. The director intended to create a serious adventure movie, but it's so miserably bad—it's so terrible that it's one of the funniest films I've ever seen. So my advice is: you should watch it, and if you already have, watch it again!!!!!

Before watching this miniseries, I had no idea what *Jane Eyre* was. I’d read and seen numerous classics before, and I thought most of them were dull, overly wordy, and overhyped, with only mildly intriguing plots at best. However, this adaptation of *Jane Eyre* completely transformed my perspective.

Zelah Clarke delivers an exceptional performance as Jane Eyre. Her accent is charming, and her quiet yet resolute demeanor perfectly captures the essence of the young governess. As for Timothy Dalton, he is remarkable as Rochester. His passion and energy bring the character to life, making it feel like he was destined to play the enigmatic master of Thornfield Hall. After viewing this miniseries, I couldn’t sleep that night—the plot is both haunting and inspiring. The performances are masterful, and the story is extraordinary. This is the definitive version of *Jane Eyre* on film.

Later, when I read the book, I was astonished by how faithfully this miniseries adhered to Charlotte Brontë’s original work. *Jane Eyre* is now my favorite film and book. If you want to experience a masterpiece that could change your life, watch the 1983 BBC version of *Jane Eyre*.

Certainly! Here's the rewritten version:

This is a review of the two-disc set that came with the "Wonderland" DVD rental. The two films included, "Wonderland" and the Johnny Wadd documentary, shatter the myth perpetuated by "Boogie Nights." The myth suggests that individuals in the adult film industry were far more than just despicable, self-serving individuals motivated solely by profit, essentially dismissing them as nothing but contemptible characters. This is strikingly similar to how "Wiseguy" and "Goodfellas" debunked the romanticized image of gangsters in "The Godfather" and other related narratives.

What frustrated me the most while watching these films—and what might bother anyone who enjoyed "Boogie Nights"—is how naïve and gullible supposedly intelligent and cultured people can be. "Dirk Diggler" in "Boogie Nights" is undoubtedly based on John Holmes, who, unlike "Diggler," lacked any positive qualities. Holmes was a criminal sociopath who mistreated everyone around him, fixated entirely on his own gratification, and was likely a central figure in the horrific murders on Wonderland Avenue in Los Angeles in 1981. The film exposes the truth about...

This is the kind of film that, if made today, would likely star Sandra Bullock and Hugh Grant. Actually, thinking about it, this movie might even get remade someday. It’s enjoyable but lacks any depth. The casting of James Stewart, who is approximately 20 years older than the character should be, is nearly fatal, resulting in a lack of chemistry between him and the lovely Kim Novak. Ernie Kovacs, playing a small supporting role as an aspiring writer, is the only actor in the film whose performance could be described as witty. (**1/2)

The documentary introduces an innovative theory related to "Guns, Germs and Steel." The series vividly depicts several episodes that strongly back the theory while addressing common criticisms. 

I was quite baffled to read user comments expressing disappointment over the perceived lack of fresh insights in these episodes. They argue that the content feels like basic middle school material, and they're right — it does cover familiar ground. Yet, I thoroughly appreciated the fresh perspective on knowledge I’ve had since my school days and the surprising depth of analysis provided.

So, if you’re someone who enjoys understanding the "why" behind things, has ever taken apart a telephone to figure out how it functions, or visited a farm to learn about its workings and how cows are milked, you’ll likely enjoy this series. It comes highly recommended.

Stacy Peralta has delivered another remarkable documentary following *Dogtown and Z-Boys*, this time exploring the vibrant history of big-wave surfing culture in America. Through a combination of rare archival footage and insightful interviews with legendary surfers, the film takes viewers on a thrilling journey into the daring and liberated world of surfing’s early pioneers. Their unbridled passion for the sport gave rise to an industry that now influences millions worldwide.

The warmth of the film lies in its intimate portrayal of these iconic figures and their compelling stories. Peralta’s deep respect for the community is evident as we learn about Greg Noll, who confidently strode toward 50-foot waves off Hawaii’s North Shore, leaving his fellow surfers in awe. Then there’s Jeff Clark, who single-handedly surfed the perilous Mavericks in Northern California for 15 years before it became a renowned hotspot. The narrative also highlights the legendary career of Laird Hamilton, modern surfing’s epitome, sending shivers down my spine when Greg Noll reverently called him the greatest surfer ever.

(Incidentally, Noll, Clark, and others were present at the Sundance screenings. Noll modestly referred to himself as an "old, over-the-hill surfer," yet he was profoundly touched by ...)

The sole redeeming aspect of "People I Know" is its inadvertent value as a cautionary tale for films Al Pacino should steer clear of. My initial disappointment stemmed from Pacino's attempt at a Georgia accent, which varied from weak and unappealing to overly exaggerated. The dialogue and character interactions were lackluster, and the plot was insipid. The supporting actors failed to inject much life into the film, and even after an hour, there was no sign of a compelling storyline. The story itself is dreadfully dull, and I found myself having to rouse myself several times just to stay engaged.

Avoid this movie at all costs—it’s guaranteed to be a snooze fest.

This movie shouldn't be watched, as it was intentionally made to fail. Ram Gopal Varma initially planned to remake the classic Bollywood film *Sholay*, but after facing issues with the original creators, he proceeded with the project while leaving out all the key elements that make a movie enjoyable—acting, script, songs, music, comedy, action, and more. Essentially, he went ahead with filming just because he had already assembled the crew. A complete waste of money and time. After directing acclaimed films like *Rangeela*, *Satya*, and *Company*, which were inspired by masterpieces like *The Godfather*, this felt like a huge letdown. What were you thinking, RGV? 

The plot, though hard to follow, loosely mirrors *Sholay*. Ajay Devgn plays Heero (originally Beeru), while newcomer Ajay portrays Ajay (originally Jay). These two "bad yet funny" buddies assist a cop in capturing a villain early on. Later, the retired cop hires them as personal bodyguards to protect himself from Bubban, a notorious criminal played by Amitabh Bachchan. If you're unfamiliar with Bollywood, rest assured—the good guys triumph in the end. Consider this review your time-saver; I just spared you three hours of your life!

American playwright Howard W. Campbell, Jr., portrayed with a sense of outdatedness by Nick Nolte, leads a content life in Germany alongside his actress wife, Helga Noth (played by Sheryl Lee), prior to the outbreak of World War II. At the height of his career, Campbell is recruited by an American agent (John Goodman) to serve as a spy for the Allies, despite being warned of the immense risks involved. Tempted by the challenge, he chooses to accept, knowing he stands to lose everything. After his wife’s death and the conclusion of the war, Campbell retreats into solitude in New York City, where his mental state becomes increasingly complex. The central dilemma of both the film and Kurt Vonnegut's original novel—whether Campbell is a hero or a traitor—remains unresolved. Directors Keith Gordon and screenwriter Robert B. Weide provide subtle hints but ultimately leave the decision to the audience, preserving the story’s intrigue. Nolte's portrayal of Campbell evolves from assured intelligence at the start to a more conflicted state by the end, where he grapples with uncertainty or unwavering conviction about his wartime role.

In the 1970s, WPIX aired "The Adventures of Superman" on weekday afternoons for several years. Occasionally, they would surprise viewers by replacing other shows with "Superman and the Mole Men," and those days were always exciting. Watching it recently, I was shocked at just how poorly it held up. 

It wasn’t the special effects—or lack thereof—that made it bad. Sure, George Reeves’ Superman costume was terrible; the foam padding’s edges were clearly visible, attempting to make him appear more imposing. The Mole Men’s outfits were even worse—a supposed fur covering that looked amateurish due to visible zippers, ill-fitting seams, and poor-quality, pilled fabric stitched into loose costumes. These flaws could be overlooked as minor shortcomings.

What truly made the film bad were its contrived plot devices. Over and over again, Superman did little to prevent situations from spiraling out of control. When a lynch mob searched for the creatures, instead of calming the crowd or actively searching for them himself, he idly stood around lecturing Lois about the danger of the situation.

A chemical spill turns people into zombies, and it’s up to two doctors to survive the outbreak. As an Andreas Schnaas film, you can expect the usual—bad acting, terrible special effects, and a nonexistent budget. The dubbing is laughably atrocious, and the worst part is I still feel obligated to write at least ten lines for this IMDb requirement. My initial review was just one word: “Crap.” But that doesn’t meet the guidelines, so here I am, forced to elaborate on how abysmal this film truly is. Honestly, I’m not sure I have enough words to convey just how bad it is. Wait, maybe I do… or maybe not. Anyway, in summary: This movie is dreadful; avoid it at all costs.  

My Grade: F

This film is a reimagining of the 1978 Warren Beatty movie "Heaven Can Wait," adapted to fit the stand-up comedic style of Chris Rock. The core premise remains unchanged: Lance Barton (played by Rock) is prematurely taken to the afterlife and strikes a deal with God's representative, Mr. King, to return to Earth as another person. Like Beatty's version, he selects Charles Wellington, a wealthy white man, simply because he develops an attraction to Sontee Jenkins (Regina King), who happens to visit Wellington’s home during the murder scene. 

However, this remake falters in several areas. The characters of Mrs. Wellington and her lover are diminished compared to their counterparts in the original, and the concept of transforming an elderly white millionaire into a modern-day black comedian attempting to win over Sontee feels forced and doesn’t land well. Additionally, the visual effects used to depict Rock portraying both Wellington and the original “white” Wellington fall flat. While the original Beatty storyline had room for improvement in its depiction of the afterlife, those enhancements were nowhere to be seen in "Down to Earth."

I adore the book *Jane Eyre* and have watched numerous adaptations of it. Each version has its merits and shortcomings, but this one ranks among the poorest I’ve encountered. I found myself indifferent to both Jane and Mr. Rochester. Charlotte Gainsbourg, who portrayed Jane, managed to look appropriately plain, but her delivery lacked depth and emotional resonance. It was hard to understand why Mr. Rochester would be drawn to her.

As for Mr. Rochester himself, William Hurt delivered an even flatter performance, if that’s conceivable. The lack of chemistry between them made their supposed romance feel contrived, failing to engage my interest. One can only wonder if the director, Zeffrelli, nodded off during filming.

On the other hand, the Timothy Dalton version remains truer to the source material, though Ciaran Hinds steals the show as the ideal Mr. Rochester in the 1997 A&E adaptation, which, ironically, deviates more from the book. 

Striving to find some positivity in this film, Geraldine Chaplain delivered a commendable performance.

This movie was absolutely dreadful. Even though Rotten Tomatoes gave it a decent rating, don’t let the positive reviews deceive you. It wasn’t frightening, nor was it funny or witty. Worst of all, it couldn’t keep my attention for more than a few minutes. I completely regret wasting two hours on this mess. The CGI monster was somewhat intriguing at first, but after about 15 minutes, it grew tiresome. The dialogue was atrocious—possibly due to poor translation. Another glaring issue was the portrayal of Americans; there were three, and none of them had depth, intelligence, or good decision-making skills. To meet the required word count, here’s a bit more: I can’t believe I fell for this film’s premise. If the video store staff had seen me holding this box, they might have stopped me from renting it.

Impressed by Sandra Bullock's performance in *Miss Congeniality*, I decided to watch *Murder By Numbers*. Although she excels in lighthearted, self-deprecating roles, her attempts at more serious performances (*Hope Floats*, *Speed 2*, *28 Days*) fall flat. In this film, her character is simultaneously omniscient, confused, and sexually maladjusted, with the subplot about her past feeling like unnecessary filler that fails to deepen her already underdeveloped persona. The two teenage boys delivered decent performances, but their supposed forensic expertise and cocky demeanor are undermined by glaring mistakes that scream "we're guilty." Chris Penn, cast as the overly obvious suspect, is underutilized, as is Ben Chaplin's token partner/romantic interest role.

***Spoilers Ahead*** Beyond the mediocre acting, the film's greatest shortcomings lie in its TV-movie-like plot, which never fully convinces viewers of the murderers' motives. Additionally, numerous contrived elements—such as vomiting after eating rare food at the crime scene, conveniently framing the school janitor, the killers brazenly meeting in public, and a forced romantic subplot—are distracting. These missteps shift the audience's focus from intrigue to boredom.

The bizarre sound you might hear while watching this abysmal adaptation of Jules Verne’s classic “Journey to the Center of the Earth” is likely Verne turning over in his grave. This 80-minute mess shares little more than the title with the original story. Aside from that, everything else in this uninspired production feels entirely disjointed and isn’t worth your time. In fact, the director himself admitted on IMDb.COM that he only directed eight minutes of this film, with the studio later adding parts of Albert Pyun’s sequel to “Alien from L.A.” featuring Kathy Ireland. It seems the producers ran out of funds and, to meet overseas contractual requirements, simply spliced Pyun’s sequel into Lemorande’s movie. Trust us—don’t waste your money or your time on this disaster.

Unlike Henry Levin’s 1959 period piece, starring James Mason and Pat Boone, Lemorande’s version is set in modern-day Hawaii. The story follows two men, a British nanny, and a dog who stumble into an unlikely adventure by sheer happenstance.

I genuinely enjoy what I’ve seen of this cartoon so far. Admittedly, the animation isn’t top-notch, but honestly, I’d much rather see this kind of exaggerated, cartoony style executed quickly and affordably than the older style rushed through in the same way (which was becoming increasingly common—it only looked good with significant time and effort invested). There’s nothing wrong with the angular lines or the simple black-dot eyes—on the contrary, I find them charming. As a child, I never thought Scooby-Doo’s design was especially cute, but now I think I appreciate it more.

Anyway, Shaggy has always been my favorite character, and believe it or not, I believe he holds the most potential for some depth. Sure, the series doesn’t revolve around the classic “mystery-solving” theme, but let’s face it—the original formula had grown stale. Don’t misunderstand; I’m sure there are writers who could infuse more intrigue into Mystery Inc.’s traditional pursuits (which have been somewhat lacking lately). However, for now, this show offers an enjoyable departure from the norm. Shaggy and Scooby are...

I rarely feel compelled to write reviews, but this movie was so unbearably painful that I felt obligated to share my thoughts. The plot was incredibly predictable, the acting lackluster, and I found myself laughing during scenes that were meant to be intense. Most of the audience appeared disinterested and chatty, even during what was supposed to be the film's tensest moment. Among the cast, Molly Ringwald stood out as the only noteworthy performance in an otherwise agonizing production. Surprisingly, the "twist" at the end wasn’t much of one. I’ve heard people say the movie didn’t take itself seriously, but I struggled to find evidence of that within the film itself.

This movie should have stayed on the cutting room floor. Save your time and money—spend them on something better!

I have known the incredible book *Goodnight Mister Tom* for years, and it was only recently that I had the opportunity to watch this adaptation. Having heard numerous positive comments about it, I approached the film with high expectations. However, once it ended, I was thoroughly disappointed.

This movie is far from being good. The adaptation of *Goodnight Mister Tom* was exceptionally poor, with approximately 4.5/10 of the book’s content completely omitted. In particular, many of the characters and several key scenes from the book were entirely absent. The dialogue was minimal, the pacing was rushed, and the story felt far too hurried. What upset me the most, though, was the lack of any meaningful portrayal of the bond and affection between William Beech and Tom—this was a major letdown. Additionally, the casting was underwhelming. I genuinely believe this story could have been powerful, but the film strayed so far from the book that it became unrecognizable. This is one of the poorest adaptations I’ve ever seen. It deserves a proper remake—one that is at least 1000 times better than this disappointing mess.

In recent years, very few chess movies have been produced, but this film stands out as more than just a chess movie—it’s a poignant exploration of the desire for love and the relentless pursuit of victory. John Turturro portrays a psychologically complex character whose world revolves entirely around the 64 squares and 32 pieces of a chessboard. For him, the game is the sole source of validation in his life. Losing a match feels like losing his sense of purpose, and Turturro delivers this emotional depth with remarkable subtlety. Even the affection of a woman proves insufficient to salvage his desolate existence. The film prompts reflection on whether there are others like him—individuals consumed by their obsession with chess. If you’re a chess enthusiast, watching this movie will resonate deeply with you. It’s a thoughtfully crafted and well-executed piece of work that successfully meets its goals. Unfortunately, I doubt we’ll see a sequel.

Like many other reviewers, this movie has remained etched in my memory for 30 years. I remember heading to the library to gather as much information as possible about its true story. I even reached out to the local PBS station for more details. However, despite my efforts, I could only discover that it was originally a newspaper article from the early 1900s.

Fast-forward to 2002—after years of scouring eBay weekly—I finally found a VHS copy of the film. There was another bidder, but I was determined to secure it. Although I won, the losing bidder asked for a copy, which I gladly provided. Even after obtaining a VHS version, I continued my search and eventually found a site selling a DVD edition of the movie. You can purchase it at: [http://www.johntopping.com/Harvey%20Perr/War%20Widow/war_widow.html](http://www.johntopping.com/Harvey%20Perr/War%20Widow/war_widow.html).

Every person we encounter influences our thoughts and alters our behavior, leaving a bit of themselves with us. "The Eighth Day" explores this idea (in contrast to "Rainmaker"). In the film, Harry (played by Daniel Auteuil), an expert in sales psychology, crosses paths with Georges (Pascal Duquenne), a runaway individual with Down syndrome. The standout performances of both actors are the film's greatest asset. The opening scene is particularly strong, as Georges shares his theory about the creation of the world, while the final scene reveals what God supposedly created on the eighth day. Some moments in the story prove frustrating for Harry, such as when Georges, unrestrained, insists on buying expensive shoes despite lacking sufficient funds—a scene that evokes laughter even as it brings tears. I enjoyed the sequence where a group of individuals with Down syndrome goes on an outing to an art gallery, only to escape on a bus and unexpectedly attend the Paradis amusement park. One of the most amusing yet embarrassing moments occurs when Harry and Georges see a horse trailer on the highway and, upon looking back, Georges gives the driver a rude gesture. However, there are also tender scenes throughout the film.

This deserves close to 5 stars purely for the acting, though my opinion is subjective rather than objective, as it should be. However, I understand that these factors are often exploited to boost ratings, particularly for actors whose names can attract audiences. 

I have a significant issue with productions like this. It’s yet another effort—similar to "Untraceable"—to push a propagandistic agenda promoting government interference with personal freedoms. It's ironic that this film arrives at a time when internet service providers are attempting to "prioritize" (read: censor) information, while people in America and Canada are actively resisting such measures. This time, instead of demonizing torrent file transfers, it aims to create a sexually frustrated population en masse. Fearmongering seems to be Hollywood's default mode these days, especially in thrillers, which remain the most popular genre for influencing societal attitudes. The level of violence portrayed is particularly intense.

Everyone who rated this below 5 clearly isn't a fan of witty, tongue-in-cheek humor. Keaton delivers an outstanding performance here, as she often does. This film isn't a loud, larger-than-life blockbuster; instead, it offers campy, slapstick comedy brought to life by some of Hollywood's most talented and versatile actors. Piscopo was equally impressive as the aspiring top dog in his role. 

If you're looking for the funniest scene involving creative attempts to avoid cursing, you must watch Dimitri’s portrayal of Morone. 

I gave it a 7.

I watched this movie at the Toronto Film Festival with fairly high expectations. With its stellar cast and status as the closing night film, it had to be worth it, right? Boy, was I mistaken.  

Even before the credits rolled, things took a turn for the worse. During the pre-film Q&A, the director gushed about meeting an unknown actor named Kevin Spacey while working on *Wiseguy*. Honestly, the fact that this *Edison* director seems to have some connection to Spacey is the only explanation I can come up with for why any of these talented people signed on. The whole endeavor feels like a career low point for everyone involved—including Spacey, if the rumors about him being blackmailed hold any weight.  

This film is downright atrocious! It’s a mishmash of every cop-movie stereotype imaginable. There’s nothing remotely original here. The acting was subpar, and the direction made it feel like an old episode of *Wiseguy*. In fact, it might as well have been straight-to-video—it’s the most polished DTV flick I’ve ever seen.  

Let me give you a few examples of just how laughably bad this movie is: Morgan Freeman gyrating around his apartment to rock-and-roll music for no apparent reason… Justin Timberlake trying (and failing miserably) to channel his inner artiste. These scenes are so absurdly out of place that they almost feel intentional. Almost.  

Overall, *Edison* is a complete trainwreck—a total waste of talent, time, and potential. Avoid it at all costs.

With the exception of approximately 10 sublime minutes featuring HB Warner aboard the celestial train, this film amounted to 94 minutes of cringe-worthy horror! While the acting was abysmal, the story was what truly left me appalled. The performances were stiff and unnatural, even by the standards of early talkies (though Lee Tracy and HB Warner stood out as the sole exceptions—neither of them ever disappoints). Rose Hobart was painfully wooden and uninspired as Julie, a portrayal that mirrored her lackluster performance in the otherwise excellent 1932 film *Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde*. The rest of the cast fared even worse; their performances defied adequate description. 

But the acting pales in comparison to the narrative. For reasons inexplicable, Julie adores Liliom, a womanizing cad devoid of any positive qualities. Despite his neglect—he refuses to provide for her, lounges in bed all day, or cavorts with his lowlife friend (played by Lee Tracy)—and frequent verbal cruelty and physical abuse, Julie remains devoted to him. She continuously makes excuses for his behavior, seemingly encouraging his increasingly aggressive tendencies. Worse still, the film presents this toxic relationship as if it’s romantic or morally justifiable. It’s sickening how the story frames this abusive dynamic as something worthy of admiration.

To me, *A Matter of Life and Death* is exactly that—simply the greatest film ever made. From start to finish, it exudes elegance. It's engaging, thought-provoking, and a reflection of the post-war world and human relationships.

The cinematography is breathtaking, and the seamless blending of black-and-white with Technicolor to highlight two distinct worlds is masterful. The characters and plot progression are nearly flawless, and the meticulous attention to detail lends authenticity to its fantastical elements.

No matter how many times I revisit this film—and I’ve watched it countless times—it never ceases to move me. It brings a smile, laughter, deep thought, and even tears. It remains as vibrant today as it was in 1946.

If I could only save one film to watch again, *A Matter of Life and Death* would undoubtedly be that film.

This is a visually stunning movie, created using just six or seven colors. When it was released over 15 years ago, its unique color palette left audiences in awe, standing out dramatically from anything else ever seen on film. For me, those colors make this an endlessly captivating film to watch. There are countless scenes I'd love to pause and turn into paintings to study their artistic brilliance.

While the characters and story aren’t quite as impressive as the cinematography, they’re all larger-than-life, particularly the villains. The renowned actors portraying "Flatop," "Pruneface," "Lips," "Mumbles," and others must have thoroughly enjoyed hamming it up on set.

Warren Beatty and Glenne Headly deliver solid performances as Dick Tracy and his sweetheart, Tess Truehart. She embodies the sweetness her name suggests. Charlie Korsmo also shines as the troubled young boy taken in by Dick and Tess. The vivid supporting cast includes familiar faces like Al Pacino, Dustin Hoffman, Dennis Hopper, Paul Sorvino, Mandy Patinkin, and Madonna. Their colorful portrayals add immense charm to the film. To discover more, check it out!

Any potential intrigue in this material is quickly buried within the first few seconds by a disclaimer stating that the events we're about to see can never be truly known, and that "this is the whisper [rumor] most often told" regarding one of Hollywood's most sensational "mysteries." Fair enough. So we're not getting anything groundbreaking here—E!'s "Mysteries & Scandals" covers the specific incident with slightly more depth, which isn’t exactly high praise. But what does this film offer instead?

We discover that Hollywood is a cesspool of vipers and hedonists—hardly revelatory information. More compellingly, it explores how a washed-up director will stoop to extreme lengths to reclaim his influence in either the entertainment world or the political sphere. This raises the intriguing possibility that Peter Bogdanovich may be drawing from his own experiences through these characters. However, what unfolds is so cynical, ugly, and convoluted that we end up feeling tainted for watching what amounts to fabricated history masquerading as fact.

The film’s tone possesses an oddly manic quality that I found more frustrating than entertaining. We don’t feel any empathy for the characters, and the iconic “Citizen Kane” style ultimately overshadows the relationship between Davies and Heartswood.

If you possess even an ounce of empathy for others, this film is difficult to watch, particularly in its latter half. During this portion, we witness a sweet little boy being beaten, which triggers a violent outburst from a mentally-challenged man who witnesses the brutality. The subject matter is unsettling.

Nevertheless, it’s a well-crafted movie with strong performances. The storyline lingers with you long after it ends. 

Tom Hulce plays "Dominick," the intellectually disabled character, and delivers what may be his finest performance. Dominick is cared for by a medical student named "Eugene," portrayed by Ray Liotta, who gained fame the next year starring alongside Kevin Costner in "Field of Dreams." 

Dominick is a kind-hearted garbage collector who enjoys reading "Hulk" comics and watching wrestling. He's the sort of gentle soul you can't help but cheer for as he seeks a fulfilling life. His meltdown stems from legitimate reasons—watch the film to uncover the full narrative. While it’s worth your time, brace yourself for an intense emotional journey that may leave you deeply moved.

This film stands apart from anything else I've seen; the only comparison I can draw is to a Woody Allen movie. However, while Woody Allen often explores the quirks of humanity, Bret Carr seems focused on grappling with the one crippling insecurity that shapes us, for better or worse. In "Lou," this insecurity is tied to his stutter, which stems from a single childhood trauma gradually unveiled through flashbacks.

The world is full of uniquely neurotic individuals, and I believe each deserves a chance at redemption. After all, the diversity of human nature is what makes life so fascinating—perhaps we shouldn’t strive to “fix” our neuroses any more than we’d want to alter our noses or breasts.

Despite being made on a tight budget, this indie film boasts impressive production values and a compelling scope. It feels like a quirky gem for the self-help genre. I’m eagerly anticipating what this filmmaker will do next—I can easily envision a career similar to Woody Allen’s or Albert’s.

This is absolutely one of the best movies I’ve ever watched. It takes me on an emotional roller-coaster. I laugh, cry, feel disgusted, experience happiness, and even fall in love—all within just over two hours! 

The performances are exceptional! The leading actor, Michael Nyqvist, delivers a remarkable performance. I must also highlight the actor who plays Tore. He portrays a mentally challenged young man with incredible authenticity, reminiscent of Leonardo DiCaprio’s role in *What’s Eating Gilbert Grape*. And then there’s the most beautiful song in the world: "Gabriella's Sång."

I highly recommend this film to everyone—it’s a must-watch!

This specific Joe McDoakes short was clearly inspired by the all-star Warner Bros. extravaganza *Thank Your Lucky Stars*, one of those wartime morale-boosting spectacles from the era. In that film, Eddie Cantor played himself as well as a would-be comedian eager to break into movies but held back by his resemblance to Cantor.

In the McDoakes series, George O'Hanlon, who stars as Joe McDoakes, portrays both himself and the titular character, a man simply trying to make it in the film industry. Similar to *Thank Your Lucky Stars*, a handful of Warner Bros. contract players make cameo appearances here.

O'Hanlon is sent by central casting for a minor one-liner role in a World War I movie, but the lookalike McDoakes ends up receiving the message instead. Nervous about his big moment, McDoakes contemplates how best to deliver his single line, even considering adopting a "movie star" tone. After 86 takes, much to the frustration of director Ralph Sanford and patient co-star Clyde Cook (who plays a British Cockney soldier), they discover a place for the hapless McDoakes in the film world. This hilarious short subject, which earned an Oscar nomination, is definitely worth watching.

This was an appalling waste of time. There was no discernible plot, and the acting was so dreadfully subpar that it should serve as a cautionary example in acting classes for what not to do. It’s simply a shameless cash-grab sequel to the earlier *Universal Soldier*, which also features painfully poor performances. It's disheartening to see Van Damme (VD) feel the need to stroke his ego every few years, and even more disappointing that audiences are willing to shell out money to endure this. This kind of low-quality work tarnishes the reputation of martial arts films. Compared to this, Segal, Norris, and even Arnold come off as nearly gifted.

Maybe VD should follow Leslie Nielsen's lead and poke fun at his own genre. At least then, we could laugh with him rather than at him.

The direction in this comedy is exceptional. Many scenes have a comic book aesthetic, and the visuals are much darker than anticipated, though the storyline remains light-hearted. While it may not be the funniest film ever, particularly compared to raunchy comedies like *Something About Mary* or *American Pie*, it contains fewer crude, sexist jokes. On repeat viewings, certain jokes grow funnier. Fans of comic books or comic-inspired movies like *Batman* or *X-Men* will appreciate the subtle humor贯穿始终. Those who don’t enjoy such themes might still find the respectful satire engaging. For viewers who liked the film, the DVD offers some enjoyable bonus features. (8/10)

As a child, I found the murderer's weapon somewhat intriguing, but I was young and admittedly naive. Even at that age, though, I could tell the movie's plot was lackluster and dull whenever the killer wasn't wielding his glowing blade. What's puzzling is that the film boasts an impressive cast. What screenplay did they sign up for? It’s undeniably tedious, functioning more like a glorified lightsaber showcase on a miniature scale. The storyline occasionally makes no sense, and the ending feels utterly chaotic. The entire movie seems fixated on aliens and their singular weapon. The plot follows two children and a man experiencing an alien encounter, then jumps forward in time where something akin to a recurrence occurs. Dead animals and other elements are thrown in, and somehow the protagonist acquires the alien weapon, proceeding to embark on a minimalistic killing spree. Honestly, you have to question why this film was made. If the goal was to...

Dolph Lundgren delivers a brooding and scowling performance in this convoluted mystery/thriller, which falls far short of the coolness promised by its packaging. Despite his strong performance, the story is a jumbled mess of B-movie tropes, including detectives, revenge plots, wealthy tycoons, prostitutes, and S&M elements, as if it were written on the fly. While the film improves slightly in its second half, those seeking a better Lundgren movie should opt for *Red Scorpion* instead.

The movie was outstanding, except for some scenes featuring Esposito. I loved how it gathered every detective from the series and tied up loose ends left unresolved by NBC. It was fantastic to see Pembleton and Bayliss portrayed in their most relatable and genuine forms. Braugher and Secor delivered incredible performances, as always, yet they’ll likely go unnoticed. It was heartbreaking to realize this marked the conclusion of *Homicide*. While memories, tapes, and reruns on CourtTV can’t replicate the experience of watching it air live every Friday, the film succeeded beautifully, offering a poignant portrayal of life post-Al’s retirement and the familial bonds within the unit. I thoroughly enjoyed it.

CREEP is a straight-up serious horror film set in real-time, with the sole focus of showing people being attacked by a mutant on an abandoned subway platform for 85 minutes. And that’s exactly what it delivers—no frills, no extras. Director Christopher Smith maximizes tension by introducing characters who have legitimate reasons to be in the subway after hours, while keeping the origins of the titular Creep intentionally ambiguous (with hints of unlawful 1960s experiments beneath the city). This mysterious approach mostly pays off. Unfortunately, Smith undermines his own effort towards the end by hesitating to deliver on a twist ending involving additional genetic anomalies, which were also subtly foreshadowed. Surprisingly, I would have preferred a clichéd twist! Franka Potente, known for *Run Lola Run*, gives a solid performance as the terrified protagonist, and the supporting cast is competent overall.

WOW! Why would anyone create a sequel to a film that was already dreadful? "Half Past Dead" wasn't great, but at least it had some sense of direction. "HPD2," on the other hand, is utterly clueless about its purpose. It exists on screen for reasons I can’t even begin to comprehend. Spoiler alert: The entire movie revolves around Twitch (played by Kurupt of Tha Dogg Pound), who gets moved to another prison where there may be a box containing gold bricks buried. While there, a riot erupts between rival inmates, one of whom is shot by a man named Cortez. Cortez then begins planning his escape. During a conjugal visit, Twitch's fiancée and Burke's (played by Bill Goldberg) daughter are kidnapped by Cortez and held in an execution room. Reluctantly, Burke teams up with Twitch, and together they find themselves entangled with the dim-witted inmates while uncovering Cortez’s plan to hold their loved ones hostage.

Opinion: This is one of the most unnecessary sequels since "Universal Soldier: The Return." The script is atrocious, the acting is abysmal, the dialogue is laughable, and every character in this film feels like a caricature. I understand it was a low-budget project, but that doesn’t justify the poor quality.

This is an extremely bizarre film... I couldn't quite figure out what it was trying to say. A group of lowlifes from North London discovers a mute boy in the woods, whom they all believe is some sort of oracle. Somehow, this convinces them each, in their own way, to make changes in their lives—changes that typically lead to disaster. The movie wraps up after roughly 90 minutes, leaving me thoroughly dissatisfied, even irritated by its apparent lack of purpose. I found myself indifferent to all the characters—they never manage to become likable or relatable.

What was the takeaway? Am I missing something? It was just so strange. What happens to Runner? And why does Emilio shoot the kid? That moment made absolutely no sense—it felt completely arbitrary and pointless. Can anyone explain this confusing mess of a film to me?

Curious viewers drawn in by the promise of cannibals will likely feel disappointed. Instead of focusing on actual cannibals, the documentary follows a peculiar man named Tobias Schneebaum, who revisits a Papua New Guinea village inhabited by native people, one of whom was once his lover decades earlier. As a quintessentially New York Jewish man, Schneebaum makes numerous appearances throughout the film, complete with his yarmulke. 

The documentary doesn’t feature real cannibals but relies on stories shared by the villagers and Schneebaum himself. While it’s not a bad film overall, it offers an intriguing narrative and impressive cinematography. Schneebaum remains likable, providing a captivating look into a lifestyle vastly different from Western civilization.

However, it fails to deliver on its promised subject matter. 

Rating: 4 out of 10.

I generally don’t care much for remakes, or as they’re called nowadays, “reimaginings,” but this movie really rubbed me the wrong way. The original *Prom Night*, though far from a cinematic marvel in my opinion, at least understood its purpose: to deliver horror. There are a few basic rules to keep in mind when making a horror film. Maintaining suspense is key to keeping the audience engaged. Unfortunately, this film failed spectacularly on that front. It wasn’t edge-of-your-seat material by any stretch. The scares were cheap and overly predictable. For instance, the overused trope of a cat leaping out of a closet, followed shortly by an unconvincing jump scare from the villain, felt like a tired retread. If the filmmakers couldn’t even execute something as routine as that effectively, how could I expect them to handle any other horror conventions? A likable protagonist is essential, yet this film lacks one entirely. The character I found most relatable was the lead detective. His composed yet logical reaction to the unfolding chaos—staying calm while pursuing a murderer—was exactly the kind of grounded, common-sense approach that more movies like this should adopt. After all, if you’re running from a psychopath wielding an axe, you don’t stand around waiting—you run in the opposite direction!

Viggo Mortensen plays a new inmate at a haunted prison where the warden, skillfully portrayed by Lane Smith, harbors a gruesome secret that might explain why both prison guards and inmates are being murdered by a supernatural force. Lincoln Kilpatrick portrays the lifer who knows the secret and fears for his life. When I think of prison movies, I usually picture action films featuring Stallone or Van Damme or intense dramas like *The Shawshank Redemption* or *The Green Mile*. However, this film takes an unexpected turn with its ghost story, reminiscent of *Exorcist III*. Despite its genre, *Prison* is atmospheric and stands as Renny Harlin’s strongest work. The movie is eerie and features solid performances from an ensemble of then-unknown actors. Lane Smith delivers the most compelling performance, as his warden is not the stereotypical embodiment of evil but instead portrayed as nervous and twitchy, adding depth to a film that surpasses expectations.  
*** out of 4 (Good).

What a delightful surprise—this is exactly what a true thriller should be. I walked into the video store, picked up a movie on impulse without fully reading the synopsis, and hoped for the best. I couldn’t have been more thrilled with my choice. The performances were outstanding; each actor brought their character to life in a convincing and engaging way. The plot was cleverly crafted, expertly written, and beautifully directed, maintaining interest from beginning to end without a single dull moment.

For fans of thrillers, especially those who appreciate well-paced stories that hold your attention, I highly recommend this film. It’s an absolute 10 out of 10 in my book.

As a horror movie enthusiast, I make it a point to watch all major releases within the genre, particularly those from my country's cinema. However, "The Power of Fear," known in Russian as "Vedma," ranks among the poorest efforts in this category. First and foremost, it fails to evoke even the slightest scare; its pacing is painfully slow and entirely predictable, leaving no room for genuine horror. To be honest, it falters in every aspect. The plot is absurdly weak—transforming a classic tale of Ukrainian witchcraft into a trite modern-day American thriller was clearly a poor decision. As the previous reviewer noted, it doesn’t excite or thrill in the least. Even worse is the subpar acting. Every actor, including lead performers Valeri Nikolayev and Yevgeniya Kryukova, who are well-known in Russia, delivers wooden performances that feel lifeless. It seems they put minimal effort into their roles, reciting their English lines with zero emotion. Lastly, I find it baffling that the filmmakers chose to shoot this movie in English with Russian actors. This choice strikes me as a significant misstep.

At first glance, this movie seemed promising, but it failed to deliver on its initial promise. While the director showcases talent with impressive camera work and creative ideas—traits common among Asian filmmakers—the narrative lacked substance and coherence. The story meandered aimlessly, veering off in numerous directions without establishing a clear, engaging focus. Ultimately, the film did not align with the hype from its promotional materials. Despite this, the acting was commendable. All the performers delivered strong performances, particularly Jude Law, whose talent shone through even in this weaker project. It’s unfortunate that he chose to star in such a flawed film.

What starts as a moderately clever farce centered around a somewhat dubious security monitoring company quickly transforms into an uninspired and utterly absurd murder mystery. David Arquette and the exceptional Stanley Tucci put forth a valiant effort to salvage this cinematic train wreck, but some narrative flaws are simply beyond redemption.

For instance, what prompts Gale to abruptly shift from her warm, motherly demeanor to becoming a belligerent drunk at Tommy's parents' house? Why would Heinrich, despite his slimy nature, jeopardize the business he has dedicated his life to by robbing and potentially murdering his clients? How can Tommy, who seems rational, suspect Heinrich of murder based almost solely on a dream, and even if we accept that, why wouldn’t he report it to the authorities? Additionally, why doesn’t Gale set off the alarm upon returning home, especially after admonishing Howie about leaving it off? These plot points, though essential to the story (and I use that term quite loosely), are glaringly contrived. It might be excusable if they produced even a modicum of humor, but from Howie’s disturbing recounting of his date rape to the coroner’s baffling misidentification of Gale, to the absurd conclusion—every moment feels forced and nonsensical.

What can I say? I guess I need to start with a "Spoiler alert" and then reveal that the F-word was used constantly in this movie—pretty much in every other sentence. Honestly, I didn’t enjoy it at all. There were way too many suggestive hints about sexual perversions, inappropriate side stories, and cheating. The excessive swearing was just over the top. I rated this movie a "3," but two of those points go to Mira Sorvino’s attractive dancing scenes.

The previous reviewer was quite generous. While I somewhat enjoyed the first movie, I must admit I didn’t find this one particularly enjoyable. It starts off tolerable, but it quickly takes a nosedive in quality. I simply can’t picture Jon Bon Jovi as a "tough vampire hunter," and the vampire princess comes across as neither alluring nor intimidating. Many of the scenes lack coherence, and it’s hard to believe that anyone—let alone an experienced hunter—would overlook the obvious red flags when a mysterious woman suddenly appears to seduce them. The relationship between Una and Jovi feels arbitrary and is never properly explained. If the film had been entertaining despite its flaws, that might have been forgivable, but even entertainment was too much to hope for here. This has to rank among the worst vampire movies I’ve ever seen.

The late Dudley Moore delivered the most iconic performance of his tragically brief career in the 1981 classic *Arthur*, a riotously funny yet deeply touching story that evokes warm smiles, hearty laughter, and even the occasional tear if you're in the right frame of mind. Moore earned a Best Actor Oscar nomination for his portrayal of Arthur Bach, a charming yet perpetually drunk playboy who enjoys "racing cars, playing tennis, fondling women," but insists on having "weekends off" and being "his own boss." Arthur faces an impending dilemma when he's set to inherit $750 million upon marrying Susan Johnston (played by Jill Eikenberry), a haughty socialite and the daughter of an undercover gangster. Complications arise when Arthur encounters Linda Marolla (Liza Minnelli), a resourceful waitress and aspiring actress from Queens who shoplifts ties for her father's birthday. Moore shines brightly onscreen in what stands as one of the funniest performances of the past five decades. The late Sir John Gielgud won a Best Supporting Actor Oscar for his impeccable performance as Arthur's sharp-tongued butler and confidant, Hobson, whose outward disapproval of Arthur's antics masks deeper paternal affection. Other comedic highlights include Barney Martin as Linda's father, Stephen Elliott as Susan's father, and Geraldine Fitzgerald as Arthur's eccentric grandmother. The film was skillfully directed by...

As we all know, the subgenre of sex comedies is quite saturated. Just being extremely crude isn't enough to grab my attention anymore. I've encountered countless disgusting jokes and scenes, so these days a sex comedy needs to offer more than just shock value to interest me. 

Entering *The 40-Year-Old Virgin*, I had a general idea of what to expect—after all, I'd seen the advertisements featuring lines like, "Is it true that if you don’t use it, you lose it?" What I didn’t anticipate was discovering a heartfelt story with genuine attempts at character growth. While the film still features the quirky, eccentric characters common in Adam Sandler’s movies and includes enough crude language to make Noah blush, it surprisingly boasts a meaningful love story and even an underlying message.

The protagonist, Andy, is (much to my chagrin) someone I can identify with. From the very first scene, I noticed that he shares my enthusiasm for *Mystery Science Theater 3000*—his wall features a poster for one of its movies—and throughout the film, we learn about his impressive collection of antiques. Andy also enjoys gaming and demonstrates a deep understanding of various video games.

This disappointing misuse of film stock only needs Count Floyd appearing every sixty seconds to complete the disaster. Somehow, they managed to bring together Steve Railsback, Susan Anspach, John Vernon, and Joe Flaherty on a set but couldn’t get anywhere near producing an actual movie. THIS THING IS AWFUL. From the unoriginal opening sequence to the mind-numbing finale, not a single line, idea, shot, or effect stands out. Susan Anspach, who dazzled in *Five Easy Pieces*, is dull here. Steve Railsback? Dull. John Vernon? Dull. Even the giant bug? Dull. If this counts as a horror film, then the *Buttercream Gang* is a gritty crime doc. 

Seriously, every bad movie telegraphs its flaws—usually via the opening credits with “Written, Directed, and Produced by” all under one name. Or there’s some talentless bimbo front and center, revealing the project’s sole purpose. In this case, the truth hides in the closing credits, where gratitude is expressed to about a dozen Canadian government departments. 

Right now, I’m watching MST’s riff on *Beast of Yucca Flats* to cleanse my palate.

This movie is poorly executed, from its conception to its execution. The acting is subpar, the writing lacks depth, and the overall result is disappointing.

Jon Heder is irritating and stuck in his "Napoleon Dynamite" persona, making him self-absorbed and ignorant.

Diane Keaton reprises a similar role here as she did in "Because I Said So," portraying an overbearing, contradictory mother figure who is both overly involved and disinterested in her children's lives.

Anna Faris, whom I usually enjoy, delivers a forgettable performance as a shallow caricature in this film.

Jeff Daniels gives an average performance at best, failing to bring any distinction to his role.

In short, avoid this movie if you wish to preserve your faith in cinema.

“All the world’s a stage and its people actors”—or something along those lines. Who on earth decided that theater ends at the orchestra pit—or even at the theater doors? Why aren’t audiences active participants in the theatrical experience, part of the story itself?  

This film was a bold experiment, proclaiming: “Hey! The story is you, and it demands more than just your attention—it requires your active involvement.” “Sometimes we bring the story to you; other times, you must seek out the story.”  

Alas, few heeded the call, but that doesn’t mean it wasn’t worth saying.

I had high expectations for this movie, especially since it was a Yashraj Film.

Jimmy works at a call center when he's invited by Pooja Singh to tutor her boss, Lakhan Singh, also known as Bhaiyyaji. They fall in love and plan to elope, but Pooja reveals she can't leave due to a debt owed to Bhaiyyaji. Despite this, they steal money from him, and only then does Jimmy learn that Bhaiyyaji is a crime lord. Meanwhile, Bhaiyyaji employs a man named Bachchan Pandey to track down Jimmy and Pooja.

Starring Saif Ali Khan, Kareena Kapoor, Anil Kapoor, and Akshaye Kumar, the film is directed by debutante Viay Krishna Acharya and produced by Aditya Chopra and Yash Chopra.

"Tashan" is undoubtedly one of the worst movies I've seen. While the cinematography is visually appealing and Kareena Kapoor (with her widely discussed weight loss) looks great, the plot is painfully weak and lacks coherence between scenes – which is why I have...

(Without spoilers, just plot details) I struggle to comprehend the negative reactions to this episode. If you're looking for a poor installment of *Smallville*, try "Subterranean"—now that's a weak episode. Tom Welling delivers a solid performance here, which doesn’t happen frequently, and Michael Rosenbaum shines as usual. The alternate reality feels disturbingly plausible. In this episode, the Martian Manhunter, who was last seen in "Static," reappears and informs Clark that the asylum director is actually a Phantom from the Phantom Zone. To return to his world, Clark must kill him. Overall, it’s a strong episode with commendable acting and a well-paced storyline.

This goes beyond the delightful story of a middle-aged man rediscovering the joys of ballroom dancing (though it certainly includes that). It’s the inspiring journey of someone rekindling their passion for life, transcending the stresses of work and finances to find happiness again. One of the film's standout features is its intriguing portrayal of evolving attitudes in modern Japan towards activities like ballroom dancing and physical touch. You’ll laugh out loud in some scenes, feel inspired to dance in others, and walk away with an overall sense of warmth and positivity. 

For those who believe Japanese cinema is solely heavy and difficult to access, this is an excellent entry point into contemporary filmmaking.

Believe it or not, at just 12 minutes long, this film (for 1912) qualifies as a full-length movie. Back then, very few films exceeded that runtime, but that’s definitely *not* what makes this quirky little production stand out! What sets it apart is that all the actors—save for one frog—are bugs... yes, actual bugs! This straightforward domestic comedy might easily have been mistaken for a Chaplin, Laurel and Hardy, or Max Linder production. However, this Russian filmInstead, uses bugs—or, I suspect, models designed to resemble them. Since Chaplin and Laurel and Hardy hadn’t yet been discovered and Linder was likely occupied, perhaps this was their creative workaround! Using stop-motion animation, the bugs move, dance, and fight in an impressively realistic way—far more convincingly than the effects in "King Kong," made 21 years later! 

The story begins with Mr. Beetle sneaking out for a night of fun, leaving his wife supposedly waiting at home. Unbeknownst to him, he’s captured on film by a local cinephile. Meanwhile, Mrs. Beetle is secretly seeing someone herself—a free-spirited grasshopper.

I genuinely can't believe what qualifies as entertainment these days. Death (and mocking death), violence, suggestive humor, adults intimidating children, crude behavior, underage drinking, drug theft, dysfunctional parents, a nightmare babysitter, stereotypes about African Americans, police officers, and overweight individuals, along with kids sneaking out late at night — yes, absolutely, this sounds like a perfect kids' movie. Not! Throw in the darker, scarier aspects — a deceased woman possessing a house and imprisoning her devoted husband for over two decades while terrifying an entire neighborhood — and it’s just heartwarming for children. PARENTS, is this really what you want your kids exposed to? Is this how you wish to shape their understanding of life?

This film is far too frightening for young children, and I worry that teenagers might already be experiencing scenarios like those portrayed. So why emphasize these themes further? For adult viewers, the movie isn’t scary or entertaining; instead, it's dull, forced, and predictable. The characters don’t fare much better either: clueless parents, inept police, foolish and irritating friends, and mean-spirited manipulators abound.

Melissa Joan Hart is outstanding! This show is incredible—there's no comparison. Maybe not even to her role in "Clarissa Explains it All," where she was equally fantastic. This series absolutely outshines "Buffy, the Vampire Slayer." This show is truly wonderful!

I encountered this film many years after the television series premiered, and at first, it didn’t resonate with me. However, as my memory of the show faded over time, I revisited it and discovered just how hilariously funny it is. Adapted from Neil Simon’s stage play, the movie hasn’t been overly “opened up” for the big screen, which is actually one of its strongest qualities. Walter Matthau and Jack Lemmon deliver outstanding performances as Oscar and Felix, and the supporting cast is equally impressive, especially John Fielder as ‘Vinnie.’ To this day, certain scenes still have the power to bring me to tears of laughter—the moment Felix interrupts Oscar during a baseball game to ask about dinner, Oscar losing his temper and chasing Felix around their apartment, the downtrodden Pigeon Sisters succumbing to Felix’s tearful tales, and, of course, the iconic cafeteria scene (later echoed in Nora Ephron’s *When Harry Met Sally*). The dialogue is razor-sharp as well. When the guys believe Felix may have overdosed, Oscar quips, “They could be vitamins! He could be the healthiest one in the room!” Simply fantastic!

I can't comprehend how so many people are praising this film in comparison to the first. It was so disappointing that I felt compelled to leave a comment. This sequel is nothing more than a blatant attempt to capitalize on the success of the original. The dialogue is dreadful and lacks the authenticity and intrigue of the first movie.

The plot is absurd, the depiction of the French police is laughable, and Doyle's characterization bears little resemblance to what we saw in the first film.

Seriously, how often do drug lords personally visit the docks to oversee shipments? Doyle's effortless discovery of the antagonist is ridiculous. It's as if all the French police were idle until Doyle arrived from America and started doing some "real" police work. Give me a break. Trying to uncover major criminals in a foreign city using just a travel map and tourist brochures is beyond absurd. Pathetic.

This sequel is utterly terrible, and anyone who disagrees is clearly out of their mind.

Following World War I, an expedition from the Allied nations travels to Cambodia to thwart Count Mazovia’s efforts in building a zombie-like army of soldiers and laborers. Hoping to avoid a potential outbreak of war due to Mazovia's actions, the group ventures through the jungle toward Angkor Wat, despite the dangers involved. Among them is Armand, whose motives conflict with the group’s objectives, as noted on the DVD sleeve’s synopsis. 

Be warned: the zombie makeup team staged a revolt before filming began. 

Furthermore, this "Revolt of the Zombies" bears little resemblance to its supposed precursor, the classic "White Zombie" (1932) ****, featuring Bela Lugosi. If the original zombies failed to impress, these certainly won’t. A youthful Dean Jagger (as Armand Louque) plays a man consumed by obsession with blonde Dorothy Stone (as Claire Duval). While a couple of supporting performances shine—devilish Roy D'Arcy (as Mazovia) and subservient Teru Shimada (as Buna)—neither receive sufficient material to salvage the film.  

** *Revolt of the Zombies* (1936) – Directed by Victor Halperin; starring Dean Jagger, Dorothy Stone, Roy D'Arcy.

While "The Fluffer" may contain some elements of truth about the porn industry, its poor direction, subpar acting, and uninspired script are hard to overlook. From beginning to end, it feels like a low-grade production. It would be mortifying to imagine mainstream audiences seeing this as representative of cutting-edge gay filmmaking. 

Let’s hope it has a short run on the gay film festival circuit and fades quietly away on home video. This movie kicks off the Queer Film Weekend in Brisbane on April 10, 2002. Its success there might depend on how much alcohol is flowing at the pre-screening cocktail party—viewers might need a drink or two just to get through it.

It seems the talented team behind Shonda Rhimes may have handed off the writing of this series to a less impressive source, perhaps even landing in MediocreLand. "Private Practice" brings to mind the many uninspired yet initially promising but ultimately predictable projects from David E. Kelley (such as *Picket Fences*, *Ally McBeal*, and *Boston Legal*). The absurd cases they encounter are so over-the-top that they fail to elicit much sympathy or emotional impact. What truly drives compelling medical dramas is the ability to create scenarios that feel terrifyingly real—cases that trigger an "This could happen to me" reaction. These stories here lack both tension and humor.

While the performances are solid, the plots feel stagnant and beyond revival. As a therapist myself, I must point out that Amy Brennen’s portrayal of a therapist is alarmingly incompetent, unethical, and unrealistic. The writers clearly didn’t pass their ethics or transference/counter-transference courses at Stanford. Someone needs to hand them a copy of the official code of ethics—especially regarding episodes like the one with the nose-bleeding wife and the therapist’s inappropriate involvement. Real-life therapists simply don’t act this way.

The trope of women pining for men who’ve moved on has long since worn thin; we’ve graduated from *Sex and the City*. Addison’s aggressive pursuit of the guy she likes feels contrived and out of touch.

Diane and I watched an incredible film today in Fremantle, and we both agreed it stood head and shoulders above other pastiche movies. I believe this is because we were captivated by the brief, five-to-ten-minute segments that made up the film, and the fact that each segment was crafted around a central theme—love in all its forms. 

The movie ostensibly took place in various Parisian arrondissements, lending each segment a distinct flavor. Although I’ve only been to Paris a few times and wasn’t familiar enough with the locations to identify them, I’m certain Europeans, especially those from France, would easily recognize them. Regardless, the viewer is drawn into each story due to the high production quality, making the cityscapes feel secondary to the narrative. 

The film flows at a brisk pace, leaving the audience processing one scene while another unfolds onscreen. The stories themselves are not overly explicit or sensational, like some shallow Hollywood fare; instead, they are subtle, thought-provoking, and gentle—much like life itself, unburdened by the overblown hype that often drowns out meaningful storytelling.

Brian Yuzna is often criticized as a director for his over-the-top gore-filled films, but the reality is that his movies aren't half bad. While the "Re-Animator" sequels don't quite measure up to the original, they're still solid entries in the realm of horror sequels. "Return of the Living Dead 3" stands out as the best in its series, and "Society" comes close to being a surrealist horror classic. This thriller might not be a masterpiece, but it showcases Yuzna's talent for horror effectively, with a plot that remains consistently thrilling and engaging. It’s surprising that a horror film centered on dentistry didn’t emerge until 1996, given how going to the dentist taps into a primal fear—akin to running from a tiger in the modern age. Dentistry doesn’t scare me, but I seem to be in the minority. The story follows Dr. Feinstone, a perfectionist dentist who has everything most people dream of: a nice home, a thriving career, and a beautiful wife. But his life takes a dark turn when he discovers his wife’s affair with the pool cleaner—and his life isn’t the only one affected by this revelation.

I rented this film in DVD format without any prior knowledge of its content, as part of a winter marathon where I watched a movie every night. Following several disappointing American action-adventure films ("Ballistic," "Daredevil," and "Cradle of Life"), *Zhu Warriors* stood out as a refreshingly original piece of filmmaking. While the plot is nonsensical, the film's sincerity, earnestness, and complete absence of irony were invigorating. Additionally, the visuals were stunning. True, the special effects aren’t on par with those crafted by Hollywood in terms of technical precision, but the filmmakers cleverly prioritize color, composition, and movement over realism. Many of the shots are visually striking. In one scene, two superhuman characters stand atop jagged rock spires with a massive moon looming before them, creating an image that feels exquisitely balanced. Another moment shows a warrior-princess soaring through the sky, her glowing sword trailing behind her like a heat-seeking missile. The colors burst across the screen in each frame, used to convey emotion rather than replicate reality.

The characters share the same straightforward, iconic quality as those in comic books—simple yet emblematic archetypes that resonate more profoundly than individual depth. Physically, some of the actors are incredibly impressive.

I've been working my way through the AFI's list of the top 100 comedies, and I have to say, this film ranks among the worst I've encountered—not just among the 90 movies on the list I've viewed, but among all the movies I've ever seen. While drunks can be humorous at times, Dudley’s attempts fall flat. Liza almost salvaged the experience, but ultimately, it was disappointing. If you’re looking to see her in something genuinely entertaining, check out *Arrested Development*. Honestly, is Dudley’s laughter and drinking supposed to be comedic? I’d strongly suggest nearly any other film from the AFI’s top 100 comedies for better laughs. For a funnier portrayal of a “drunk,” *The Thin Man* is a far superior choice. And if you want an overall funnier movie, any Marx Brothers film will leave you rolling (especially if you imagine Arthur as one of them).

I recently watched this film at TIFF (Toronto International Film Festival), and fans of Hal Hartley are sure to love it! Even if you're unfamiliar with this director's body of work, it doesn’t matter—this movie stands on its own perfectly. I’m heading to the second screening; it was incredible, and I need to see it again—fast! 

This film is incredibly humorous, with sharp and witty dialogue. Parker Posey delivers an outstanding performance in the titular role of Fay Grim. "Fay Grim" is the latest installment exploring the universe and characters first introduced in *Henry Fool* (2000). Stylistically, the film prominently features the frequent use of the canted (or Dutch) angle, a hallmark of Hartley’s previous works, including those found in the *Possible Films: Short Works by Hal Hartley 1994–2004* collection and *The Girl from Monday* (2005).

I watched this film particularly fittingly on September 11th. Thematically, the narrative unfolds against the backdrop of the world transformed post-September 11, 2001. Without delving into spoilers, this work and its story-world boldly tackle political themes and challenges the status quo.

I believe many people dismissed *Vanilla Sky* as just another eccentric Tom Cruise film (*Magnolia*, *Eyes Wide Shut*), but this movie stands on its own. Critics often called it weird, but it wasn’t—different and confusing, yes, but not weird. "Weird" belongs to Stanley Kubrick or Pauly Shore. "Different" is more like *The Truman Show*. "Confusing" is *The Matrix* or *The Game*. Unlike Kubrick, this film has a resolution. Everything ties together eventually—perhaps not right away, or even today, but it does. *Vanilla Sky* is confusing because David Aames (Cruise) is himself confused. That’s the crux: the so-called "weirdness" that put off critics stemmed from this very idea. Had they paid attention, like the characters are urged to do in the original 1997 Spanish version, they’d have realized it. But if that’s not enough reason to watch, the music alone makes it worth seeing. Cameron Crowe delivers a fantastic soundtrack, using it to establish the elusive "feel" that many films struggle to achieve. Songs like The Beach Boys’ "Good Vibrations" heighten the drama and emotion, creating an offbeat yet perfectly suited atmosphere. A wonderful film overall, *Vanilla Sky* deserves recognition for its unique storytelling and emotional depth.

The entire Biker Movie genre must surely comprise some of the worst films in cinematic history. This particular film is packed with fights, copious amounts of blood, bikers clashing with Native Americans, and a shantytown being demolished one shack at a time. The performances are abysmal. Whatever became of Robert Walker, Jr.? He once starred in major studio productions but seemingly vanished over time. While this movie is dreadful, it's worth watching if you haven't seen a Biker film in ages. By the end, you'll likely feel somewhat guilty for having watched it!

"The Thief of Baghdad" is remarkable for the portrayal of the menacing magician Jaffar (Conrad Veidt), who uses deceit and magical incantations to seize the throne from the rightful ruler, young King Ahmad, and to claim a beautiful princess from her father... 

Ultimately, Jaffar meets his downfall, as all oppressors do (in literature and folklore), succumbing to love and the resilience of ordinary people, here represented by the resourceful little thief (Sabu). 

The opposing forces of good and evil, depicted in stark black-and-white imagery, are masterfully crafted both visually and narratively... 

The screenplay is poetic, simple yet breathtakingly beautiful... The magician’s attire, flowing and undulating like the wings of dark birds, signals an impending assault under cover of darkness, spreading chaos and fear... 

In contrast, the noble hero sports pristine white turbans and robes, while his princess is adorned in soft hues of pink and pale blue... 

This cinematic masterpiece matches the grandeur of its predecessors in terms of spectacle, while its innovative use of color brings an enchanted realm vividly to life... 

With its flying carpets, winged white horses, and a towering genie (played exceptionally by Rex Ingram), alongside menacing sorcerers, the film weaves a timeless tale of heroism and magic...

The very first encounter when studying fascism is ostracism, as this pseudo-philosophy requires scapegoats to validate its ideology. Ettore Scola’s film, possibly his magnum opus, centers on those who were cast aside by the regime—its outcasts and scapegoats. 

The historical event of Hitler and Mussolini’s alliance takes a backseat here, with only fleeting glimpses shown: some military parades, garlands, and distant voices. Our protagonists are not part of this celebration of masculinity. “Genius is essentially masculine,” reads the golden rule embroidered by Antonietta (a superb performance by Sophia Loren). For Antonietta, her world revolves around her kitchen, and her pride lies in her children. At the start of the film, she is a victim of this hyper-masculine society but remains oblivious to it, believing herself to be content. Gabriel, on the other hand, is politically conscious, aware of the rot consuming his nation. However, as a gay man, he has been alienated from it all and is on the verge of arrest.

Forgetting their differences, they discover shared experiences and consummate their relationship. This act of intimacy is rebellious, especially for Antonietta, whose moral code would traditionally condemn such behavior. Embracing infidelity in a land where politics and religion collude to suppress women propels her toward a newfound awareness of the political implications of her actions.

Settling in to watch the 14th season of "The Bachelor," titled *"On the Wings of Love,"* I anticipated an experience that would be equal parts captivating and questionable. I’d dabbled in previous seasons here and there, catching a couple of episodes before losing interest for weeks at a time. While the show holds a certain allure, its moral standing and overall quality tend to fall short.  

In *"On the Wings of Love,"* viewers follow Jake, a 31-year-old commercial pilot from Dallas, Texas, on his quest to find genuine love within the confines of a season-long reality dating drama. Jake meets 25 stunning women from across the nation. Though he attempts to form connections, their interactions remain largely surface-level—how much depth can truly be achieved in brief five-minute conversations? From the outset, Jake makes his intentions clear to the audience: he isn’t merely seeking romance or entertainment; he’s aiming for a fiancée or wife. One must presume he conveyed similar sentiments to the contestants themselves. If...

After paying homage to classic film noir with *Chinatown*, Roman Polanski revisited the themes that had made him famous in the 1960s with this unsettling psychological horror. Like *Repulsion* and *Rosemary's Baby*, the film explores the paranoia and claustrophobia inherent in apartment living.

Polanski excels at creating suffocating environments, and *The Tenant* stands as his most confined and oppressive work. The emphasis on side walls and distant vanishing points is more pronounced than ever, and even in the few exterior scenes, the sky is barely visible. Yet *The Tenant* is not just constrained spatially; it also immerses viewers in the intense focus on its protagonist. Played by Polanski himself, Trelkovsky appears in nearly every scene and shot. When he is off-screen, the camera frequently adopts his perspective. Moreover, almost everything he observes reflects back at him through mirrors.

I can’t think of another film that delves so deeply into the internal struggles and isolation of a single character. While psychological thrillers like *M* or *Peeping Tom* engage audiences by manipulating their emotions, *The Tenant* draws viewers inward, compelling them to experience the protagonist's descent into madness.

This was my favorite film during my childhood, and I've even participated in the stage production a few times, which means it will always hold a special place as my favorite musical. I seriously doubt anyone could ever remake the story of *Oliver Twist* on screen as well as this version did.

My all-time favorite "villain" has to be Oliver Reed as Bill Sikes. Not only did he terrify me when I watched it at age six, but now, as an adult, I find myself empathizing more with Nancy’s character—the barmaid/prostitute who helps Oliver secure the life he deserves.

Jack Wilde was brilliant as the Artful Dodger, and I don’t think anyone could surpass his portrayal of the clever pickpocket and Fagin’s loyal sidekick. The music is incredible, especially Fagin’s songs. I’m also grateful they didn’t give Bill Sikes a musical number; it wouldn’t have suited his sinister nature.

Carol Reed did an excellent job with Nancy’s tragic fate, keeping the film family-friendly by subtly implying her beating without showing graphic violence, yet still conveying Bill’s brutality toward her.

This movie is...

This is the essence of the musical genre—humor, talent, romance, and action all combined into one unforgettable experience.  

Frank Sinatra delivered a remarkable performance, speaking volumes without uttering an extra word. Although Marlon Brando wasn’t a singer, his portrayal of Sky Masterson captivated audiences and endeared him to many. Interestingly, his inability to sing enhanced his character’s authenticity. While the female leads were solid, it was the male actors who truly shone in this film.  

A timeless classic, it appeals to viewers of all ages and resonates with every audience, leaving them smiling and laughing.  

Undoubtedly, a must-watch and enjoy classic!

Although I generally respect personal preferences and avoid dismissing others' tastes, I must say this movie was truly dreadful, and there’s no denying it. I’m not a big fan of Ani DiFranco, but I acknowledge her talent as a guitarist and songwriter. However, I cannot find even a single positive aspect about this film. Some argue that it accurately depicts the challenges faced by high school students, and perhaps it does, but everything feels exaggerated to the point of absurdity. The film attempts a “Naked Gun”-style comedy, but the timing is completely off. Each actor pauses so long between lines, as though expecting laughter (which never came). The screenplay is all over the place, cramming numerous controversial topics into one movie without adequately exploring any of them—particularly the unsettling scenario of a student being impregnated by a teacher. Not once did I laugh during this film. Instead, I felt insulted by its poorly executed humor and satire, leaving me no choice but to roll my eyes repeatedly.

I watched this film just once, around 25 years ago, but ever since, I’ve always told people it might be the best movie I’ve ever seen. Despite having no spoken dialogue—only internal thoughts—the film captivated me, to the point that I even held my breath at times to avoid making any noise. I highly recommend this movie; I wish it were available on DVD.

"WINCHESTER 73" tells the tale of a man, played by Jimmy Stewart, whose sole obsession is reclaiming his cherished Winchester repeating rifle, which has been stolen from him. As the rifle changes hands throughout the film, Stewart relentlessly pursues it. Directed by Anthony Mann in 1950, this black-and-white gem leans more toward being a crime drama than a conventional Western.
