The portrayal of cowboys often resembles that of modern-day gangsters rather than traditional Western archetypes. Shelley Winters delivers a nuanced performance as a woman of ambiguous morals who sets out for a ranch intending to marry another man (Charles Drake). However, she ultimately falls for Stewart, though not without experiencing some questionable encounters first. Winters' character stands out as the most multifaceted among a cast full of eccentric personalities. Keep an eye out for a young Dan Duryea as a deranged killer and Tony Curtis in a brief yet memorable role. Will Geer's casting as Wyatt Earp is notably ill-fitted.

I’ll keep this brief. In my opinion, this is an exceptional film. Some reviewers have criticized it for being poorly written, amateurishly shot, and having a subpar soundtrack, while others claim its depiction of life feels unrealistic. While it might not be entirely convincing throughout, this movie conveys a powerful message of hope that some seem to have overlooked. It offers the belief that it’s not too late to help those affected by the widespread violence in so many lives. Gang-related violence is indeed real, but that doesn’t make it acceptable. This film delivers an important social message that, despite being disliked by cynics, deserves praise rather than criticism. I’ve watched this movie at least eight times with immense enjoyment, each viewing reaffirming my belief that the world can improve and is not beyond redemption (well, at least not until 2008). I give it a 9 out of 10; it’s nearly flawless in my eyes. JMV

Did the filmmakers even screen this before releasing it? The script jumps erratically between scenes without providing much context. It’s unclear whether this is a prequel or not, starting with Superman's origins on Earth only to leap forward to a point after the previous film without properly signaling the shift. This is incredibly confusing. Superman himself feels weak and emotionally unstable, resembling someone who could use some help. He’s portrayed as a potential home-wrecker, a stalker, and someone who seems deeply depressed and confused. Such a characterization rarely makes for an engaging protagonist. The ending is utterly absurd. Seeing Superman end up in the hospital made me wish he would just disappear. Honestly, I’m waiting for a Saturday Night Live sketch where Superman shows up on Maury Povich, and Maury announces, “You ARE the father!” In summary, decent performances from this Superman and Kevin Spacey can’t save the movie, which suffers from a horrible script. This film is practically unwatchable.

This is a peculiar little film, and I must say there’s some quirky acting on display as well.  

It chronicles the escapades of a young man who sets out to become a renowned Las Vegas illusionist. The story is partly about chasing his dream, partly about the aspirations of others, and entirely about the challenges of show business. I found the movie delightful, with a couple of genuinely magical moments that make the entire experience worthwhile.  

Alan Arkin delivers a fantastic performance as the failed magician turned mentor, and his bond with Max is both humorous and heartwarming.  

While it may not appeal to everyone, if you enjoy films centered around the journey, I believe you’ll appreciate this one.

Wow, my initial review of this movie was so negative that it wasn’t accepted. I’ll try to tone this one down. Let’s be honest! No one wants to see a Chuck Norris movie where he isn’t the central figure. There was a decent fight scene at the end, but the rest of the film was lackluster. I can’t help but wonder if Chuck is struggling to keep up with his past achievements. Has he become so slow that he has to resort to making low-quality films like this, hoping his reputation will save the day? Chuck is an incredible martial artist and, as demonstrated by *Walker, Texas Ranger*, a reasonably talented actor. The key is to merge both skills effectively in his movies, which this one fails to do. This is extremely disappointing for us Norris fans. Chuck, stick to being the main character in your films, because this approach clearly doesn’t suit you. — Gary

This movie is not porn, nor was it ever intended to be. And unless my uncle becomes president of the world, it should never be labeled as such. 

With that matter settled, I can confidently say that I highly recommend this film. Its themes remain relevant today, and it’s both humorous and thought-provoking. The acting is excellent, and it raises intriguing questions.

I don’t fully grasp why this movie faced such harsh criticism, which is partly why I’ve decided never to visit the U.S. Lena is truly a pioneer of the modern riot-grrrl movement, embodying confusion, curiosity, and wit. Though she can be fiery at times, isn’t that just human nature?

Spoilers:

I was deeply disappointed with "Love's Abiding Joy." After waiting a long time to watch it, I finally caught it when it re-aired on Hallmark last Thursday. While I thoroughly enjoyed the first three "Love" films, this one fell short of my expectations. The entire movie was melancholic and disheartening, filled with numerous mistakes, and the editing was subpar, with too many scenes appearing out of context. Additionally, the death of baby Kathy occurred much earlier than anticipated, and Clark’s inclusion felt forced and unnatural. It seemed as though the actors lacked enthusiasm, with minimal emotional depth and little chemistry between Missie and Willie.

I believe the screenwriters should have stayed truer to the source material. Each adaptation thus far has drifted further from Janette Oke's original stories. For instance, the movie failed to mention key plot points such as the mine incident involving the two boys or Clark’s injury due to it. Furthermore, Missie and Willie’s reactions to Kathy's death felt inconsistent with what fans would expect based on the book.

This is a highly entertaining film that you can easily enjoy without much thought as the storyline becomes increasingly twisted—and hilariously so. With Sally Field, Teri Hatcher in her prime, Kevin Kline, Elisabeth Shue, and Robert Downey Jr., all these talented actors deliver performances as if they were soap opera stars or producers. If you’ve ever watched a soap opera and wondered, “How did they come up with this?” then you’ll absolutely adore this movie. I’ve seen it several times, and with each viewing, I notice more subtle humor and appreciate just how skillfully it’s acted. Don’t expect an Oscar-worthy film; this is purely meant for fun, not a deep philosophical exploration. So sit back, unwind, and laugh!

The opening sequences left me marveling at their ingenuity—the reimagined version of the Archers' logo, the clever introductory disclaimer, and the smooth camera movement panning across the cosmos. It’s odd to consider that *It’s a Wonderful Life* was released in the same year. While not coincidental—given the 1940s were saturated with celestial-themed films—the heavenly cotton-candy nebulae and saccharine angelic imagery of the competition now seem dated and pale in comparison to Alfred Junge’s visionary work. 

The film maintains its visual splendor throughout, unveiling increasingly inventive concepts one after another. Generally, I’m not a fan of blending color with black and white, as one scheme often diminishes the appeal of the other. Yet, here, Powell seamlessly transitions between the two as though it’s the most natural progression imaginable, simply shifting palettes. Both the color cinematography and the black-and-white sequences stand beautifully on their own.

As for the story… this might just be Pressburger’s finest screenplay, though the conclusion feels somewhat illogical, which prevents it from reaching its full potential.

I apologize to everyone—this was meant to be an "art" film, but honestly, they should’ve given out guns at the screening so viewers could end their misery rather than endure it. While the scene design and cinematography were impressive, the story itself was excruciating to watch. The lack of a soundtrack was punishing, and the excessively long takes dragged on far too long. How many minutes can you stare at two people just sitting and talking, especially when their conversation amounts to constant complaining? It was a struggle to make it through this entire movie. The performances were strong, but the relentless gloom, monotony, and lack of inspiration became unbearable. The only highlight for me was Maureen Stapleton’s red dress and her captivating dance scene. Otherwise, this felt like a poor imitation of Bergman, and I’m no fan of his work either. If someone claims they enjoyed 1 1/2 hours of this, I’d say they’re probably lying.

I've long been impressed by Chavez's opposition to globalization, but it wasn't until I watched the film at the Amsterdam International Documentary Film Festival that I truly grasped what he had accomplished. The documentary recounts the coup attempt and conspiracy orchestrated by Venezuela's elite, oil companies, and corrupt Western governments eager for oil, all aimed at ousting the democratically elected President Chavez and reinstating a brutal dictatorship. This film is essential viewing for anyone who values freedom and justice, and serves as a vital lesson for the rest of the world! I applaud the people of Venezuela for taking matters into their own hands and safeguarding their nation from forces like Halliburton and the Bush administration.

If you're seeking a definitive biography of boxer James Corbett's life, this movie may not be the one for you. His life gets a 1940s "Hollywood-style" treatment, making the story far more entertaining than reality. Still, thanks to strong performances—especially from Errol Flynn—and an engaging script, the film's creative liberties can be overlooked.

Errol Flynn portrays James "Gentleman Jim" Corbett, a boxer from the Gay Nineties who became world champion in 1892. The film traces his journey from humble beginnings to his victory over John L. Sullivan. While it could have centered on the fights, most matches are brief (save for the final championship bout), with greater focus on Corbett's bold personality and his relationship with the character played by Alexis Smith. The supporting cast, featuring familiar faces like Alan Hale, delivers excellent performances, and the script effectively brings these characters to life.

One standout aspect of the film is witnessing Flynn's athletic prowess.

"The Muppets Take Manhattan" stands out from other Muppet films in several ways. First, it remains the only Muppet movie not owned by Disney; as of 2008, it still belonged to 20th Century Fox (then CBS Fox at the time of its release), despite Disney owning the rights to the Muppets. Additionally, the film features a nonlinear storyline with unpredictable events. 

While it’s challenging to surpass the original "Muppet Movie" from 1979, which had more iconic songs, "The Muppets Take Manhattan" excels in another area: its surprisingly realistic scenarios. In the first film, the Muppets effortlessly secure a "Rich & Famous" contract just by walking into an agent's office. In contrast, this movie portrays the reality that success requires hard work, particularly in the entertainment industry. This message, while easy to overlook, is both significant and impactful when viewed through the lens of suspension of disbelief.

Last November, I had the opportunity to watch this film at the Reno Film Festival. It was such a delightful experience. Despite a few technical glitches, I thoroughly enjoyed it. The writing and acting, particularly from the actor who portrayed the lead role, were outstanding. This movie is filled with heart and wit. After the screening, I had the chance to chat with some of the filmmakers, and they came across as genuinely pleasant individuals. Overall, the entire film was a positive experience, and I would highly recommend it. The storyline was engaging and relatable; as a woman, I’ve encountered many of the same challenges as the protagonist, which made his struggles easier for me to empathize with. The film excels at creating characters we can easily connect with. The supporting characters are also exceptionally well-developed—they feel authentic. I recognize people like them in real life, though I wish my own conversations with friends could be as witty! The movie has a laid-back, cool vibe, and I wish there were more films like it available.

For those interested in gaining insight into the Soviet perspective on modern Russian history, this epic film is invaluable. The narrative begins at the turn of the 20th century (1900) in the sepia tones of old photographs, transitioning to black and white during the mid-century, and culminating in vibrant color as it nears contemporary times (the 1960s).

The story centers on a boy from a remote Siberian village, whose life is profoundly affected by the arrival and arrest of an anarchist during the czarist era. As an adult, he joins the Bolsheviks following the revolution and introduces Soviet communism to his community. His son, born to the village beauty, serves in World War II and later returns home as the oil industry takes root, showcasing Soviet economic ideals.

Though lengthy and slow-paced, the film is highly coherent and exceptionally well-crafted. It can be viewed in three distinct parts.

I suppose this could be considered a great film for someone who wholeheartedly embraces organized Christian dogma, but for anyone with an open mind—believing in free will, rational thought, the separation of church and state, and quality science fiction—it’s nothing short of a dreadful joke!  

Some recognizable actors appear to have either been desperate for work or felt compelled to impose their personal beliefs on the rest of us non-believers.  

Still, I found myself amused by this movie in much the same way I was entertained by *Reefer Madness*. The latter tried to educate about drugs using scare tactics, while this film attempts to impart “Christian” values through threats of hell and suffering for decent individuals who don’t subscribe to its worldview.  

It had me laughing uncontrollably while simultaneously frightening me at just how many people genuinely think our society should return to the moral standards of the 19th century!

Here's a hidden treasure for those of you who may not have heard of or seen this film. In the 1980s, Dennis Quaid was a major star, but by the early '90s, he seemed to vanish from the spotlight. Then, in 1993, he made a comeback with three movies, all of which unfortunately flopped. Out of those three, I genuinely enjoyed two, and today I want to talk about one of them.

"Wilder Napalm" is a quirky film about two brothers, Wallace (played by Quaid) and Wilder (Arliss Howard), who happen to be... fire starters. Yes, they possess pyrokinetic abilities. 

Wilder has chosen to abandon his powers—well, at least the less practical ones—after a tragic event in his youth when he and his brother accidentally caused a fatal explosion while setting fire to an abandoned house. Since then, Wilder has become a firefighter and is now married to Vida (Debra Winger), who is currently under house arrest for—yep—arson. Oh, and they haven’t spoken to each other in five years because Wallace once set Wilder’s hair on fire at his bachelor party.

Wallace, on the other hand, revels in his pyro abilities and uses them...

I wouldn’t go so far as to say this film merits the harsh criticism some reviewers have bestowed upon it. While it does suffer from an excessively padded runtime, heavy-handed editing, and an overuse of cheesy special effects, it also lacks the energy most comedies need to keep the average viewer engaged. 

That said, the movie has its share of genuinely funny moments, a capable and committed cast, and the familiar yet endearing underdog storyline. Macy, Stiller, and Azaria deliver standout performances as the central trio, while Garofalo and Studi add depth and intrigue to the ensemble. Although Reubens and Mitchell didn’t make a significant impact overall, they did have moments that highlighted their talent. 

As for the plot, it follows the tried-and-true "underdog succeeds" trajectory, which isn’t exactly groundbreaking since the outcome is predictable. However, what sets it apart isn’t the exaggerated heroes and villains but rather the sharp dialogue and the interactions among the characters. At its core, the film portrays individuals with childlike hearts, striving to do what’s right. The most memorable scenes tap into this sentiment, giving the film its emotional resonance.

The performances by Fishbourne, who is oddly humorous in an inexplicable way, and Ed Harris, who has a brief but notable role, stand out. Conversely, Connery’s portrayal feels disjointed, as if he struggles to grasp the essence of his character, culminating in movements that resemble those of an 80-year-old man. The screenplay is deeply flawed; it reads more like an accidental assembly than a coherent narrative, with a 60-minute happy-ending plot abruptly tacked on alongside a superfluous appendix that lacks any meaningful connection to the characters or their arcs. This mishmash might serve as a cautionary example in screenwriting classes. The more one reflects on the details, the clearer this becomes. Capital punishment, despite being introduced early on as a central theme, gradually vanishes without resolution or commentary. While the subject matter and setting hold potential, they are squandered due to the poorly executed script.

"Harman and Ising's 'Old Mill Pond'" stands as a true masterpiece within the art of animation. The exceptional skill and craftsmanship evident in their work shine most brightly in this short film. It’s unfortunate that many now perceive offense in what was, and was always meant to be, a lighthearted piece of entertainment—not in any way intended to disparage Black people. If anything, it pays homage to the infectious humor and musicality of the Black community. For years, I've been unable to watch this gem due to "race commissars" in England deeming it too offensive for display in multicultural Britain. If anyone knows where I might acquire a copy, I’d greatly appreciate the opportunity to revisit this classic. Those who incessantly search for meanings and intentions never meant in these cartoons—works that are, after all, six decades old—should perhaps adopt a lighter perspective. While the world has evolved significantly since then, no one has the authority to impose censorship on past creations simply because they don’t align with contemporary sensitivities.

Look, this is the third installment, so you already know it’s bound to be a mess. And “Maniac Cop” wasn’t strong enough to justify a sequel, so you can bet this one is even worse. But just how bad is it? Awful, bordering on downright God-awful.

When Maniac Cop goes on a killing spree, a reporter dramatically declares, “What happened here can ONLY be described as a black rainbow of death.”

1. Rainbows are never black, nor can they ever be.  
2. Rainbows are inherently harmless and cannot cause pain or death.  
3. A competent news reporter might find a more fitting way to describe the aftermath of such carnage. “A black rainbow of death” is far from the only possible description.  

This is what you’re in for.

I rewatched this film and was struck by how closely it adheres to the novel, particularly if we overlook the portion about Cary's [Leslie Howard] upbringing. Despite the era's limitations on what could be depicted on screen—though the book itself doesn't delve deeply into these scenes—the character's fixation on Mildred [Bette Davis] is effectively communicated to viewers. I highly recommend this film to anyone who has ever been smitten with someone only to have the other party exploit their feelings. I’ve heard that Maugham was once asked to record the novel for commercial sale, but as soon as he began in the studio, he became overwhelmed and couldn't get past a few lines, leading to the project being abandoned. It’s clear that the novel was crafted with deep personal emotion, and this film serves as a solid adaptation of at least part of it.

I gave this movie a one-star rating, and if there were an option for zero stars, I would have chosen that instead. When I inserted the DVD into my TV and settled onto the couch, I expected it to deliver the worst filmmaking possible. Checking its rating on IMDb confirmed it as one of the lowest-rated movies, so I approached it with a critical eye. However, nothing could have prepared me for the sheer mediocrity that unfolded before my eyes.

The box art might lead you to believe the movie is somewhat decent, but don’t be fooled—it should be removed from every shelf globally. The best description I can offer is that it feels like porn without any sex scenes. The acting (and I use the term loosely), the "plot" (which is full of more holes than Swiss cheese), and the special effects are all abysmal.

Do not make the same mistake I did by renting this movie thinking it will be amusing. In the end, I’m not saying I could make a better film than this, but...

I incorporated this film into a religion class I taught. In the story, a golden fish swims cheerfully in its bowl on an upper-floor apartment. A young boy and his mother are temporarily away from home. The boy has been entrusted with money to purchase milk. While returning, he halts at a carnival to try his luck at a game. Standing beside him is a man in a black suit who appears somewhat intimidating. The boy accidentally drops the milk bottle; it shatters. The man in black offers him money to replace the broken milk. Simultaneously, at home, a black cat ascends the fire escape and enters the apartment. The cat spots the fish bowl and observes it closely. The fish swims vivaciously and leaps out of the bowl. By this point, several teenagers in my class and I have developed a fondness for the fish. The cat picks up the fish in its mouth, and everyone holds their breath. To our relief, the cat gently places the fish back into the bowl. The narrative follows two parallel storylines: one involving the suspicious man in black and the other concerning the mysterious black cat. Both characters evoke initial prejudice but ultimately prove to be harmless and innocent. This film served as an excellent conversation starter in my class.

When a film boasts no fewer than FIVE distinct titles, it often indicates various issues, and almost invariably suggests significant problems within the movie itself. *Necromancy* is undeniably flawed and outright poor. I watched the version titled *Rosemary's Disciples*. While I acknowledge that other editions may vary slightly, I doubt any version—with its potential extra few minutes—will fare significantly better. The story presents the most glaring issue: the film begins with Laurie awakening and her husband bringing her to a town where he secured a job at a toy factory run by occultists (yes, it nosedives from here). This town, named Lillith, features a man with a rifle guarding the bridge, ensuring entry is restricted to individuals approved by the town’s “owner.” It soon becomes clear that every resident of Lillith is a witch, adhering to the commands of Mr. Cato—the leader of this eerie coven—who seeks to resurrect his deceased son (hence the title *Necromancy*). The townsfolk engage in witch-like activities—

*Prix de Beauté* was produced during the transition from silent films to talkies, a shift that occurred slightly later in Europe than in Hollywood. Initially intended as a silent film, it was released in France with a dubbed soundtrack featuring a French actress voicing Louise Brooks' lines. However, it was distributed as a silent in Italy and other parts of Europe. I had the privilege of watching the Cineteca di Bologna’s impeccable new restoration of an Italian silent print at the Tribeca Film Festival. While I haven’t yet seen the sound version, it’s reasonable to assume that the silent edition is far more engaging, given widespread criticism of the poor dubbing—Louise Brooks’ English speech clearly doesn’t align with lip movements. Additionally, the film adheres strictly to the silent style, using minimal intertitles and relying little on dialogue. *Prix de Beauté* unfolds visually through dynamic, inventive cinematography. The opening sequence immediately immerses viewers in fast-paced city life and beach scenes, capturing movement and action with precision. Across the film, there is a strong focus on visual elements, including costumes, machinery, decor, and symbolic imagery like a caged bird and a pile of...

This is a truly awful movie, with only a handful of redeeming moments or positive aspects.

The film begins with pregnant Linda Blair sprinting down a hallway, seemingly fleeing either monsters or a mob wielding pitchforks—though it’s hard to tell for sure. She leaps through a window, only to wake up and reveal that she is heavily pregnant. Interestingly, her level of pregnancy seems inconsistent throughout the movie.

Linda teams up with an obnoxious and possibly intellectually disabled young boy—who I initially assumed was her son—as they journey to an abandoned hotel located on an island. It’s no surprise that Italian horror directors always manage to cast the most grating child actors in their films! Joining them on the island are David Hasselhoff and his German-speaking virgin girlfriend (you know, given the stereotype about Germans adoring Hasselhoff...). Hasselhoff is busy taking photos, while his girlfriend is deciphering an obscure German text about witchcraft, I believe.

Meanwhile, an elderly couple who’ve bought the island, along with a real estate agent and another woman I initially mistook for their daughter, are also en route to the island. Apparently, the latter is an architect, and it turns out that Linda Blair and the boy are actually the children of the older couple. Though they’re technically part of the same group, it feels like Linda and the boy are wandering the island alone.

I watched "Brother's Shadow" at the Tribeca Film Festival and found myself still reflecting on it two days later. This story of a prodigal son (played by Scott Cohen) returning to his family’s custom furniture business following time in prison is a solid drama with all the required elements: memorable characters, sharp and insightful dialogue, and a filmmaker who uses the camera with visual intelligence.

Beyond these attributes, however, it offers something increasingly scarce in today’s multiplexes: the unyielding vision of a mature perspective. Director-screenwriter Todd S. Yellin’s talent feels fully formed, yet it’s clear he, like his protagonist, has paid his dues. He understands how real people grapple with life, and he captures our desire to witness—or at least vicariously live—success. Still, Yellin respects his audience enough not to offer false promises or empty triumphs. Ultimately, we realize that Jake’s victory isn’t measured by commissions or his family’s approval, but by “the work” he couldn’t leave behind even if he tried.

This is a vital theme in a world—and particularly in a movie industry—that often can’t look beyond “the bottom line.”

What’s wrong with the actors involved in this mess? Michael Dorn should stick to Star Trek merchandise. John Diehl—does anyone recall his role in Miami Vice? He was decent there... Anyway, what can you expect from a movie featuring one of the lifeguards from Baywatch in the lead role? Nothing, and that’s exactly what we end up with. None of the characters is remotely likable, and the special effects are laughable—not in a good way. The plot is a (terrible) joke, lacking any semblance of logic. It feels like the filmmakers were attempting something along the lines of *Attack of the Killer Tomatoes*. This is especially evident in the scene where key officials discuss national security in what looks like a closet. 

If you come across this film on TV, flip the channel—it’ll save your TV set from embarrassment.

I typically enjoy sci-fi and Bigfoot-themed films, but this one was a disappointment. The abundance of cheese was overwhelming, and even the effects and dialogue left much to be desired. This is one to avoid at all costs. I only rented it by mistake, as I was searching for the Sasquatch film featuring Lance Henriksen (which I still haven’t watched). The concept had potential, but the execution fell flat. It's baffling how such a project turned out this way. You could find better scripts written by high school students interested in film, arts, or English.

I was captivated by just how dreadfully bad this movie actually was. Were viewers meant to learn something, or engage in any form of reflection while watching it? What was the deal with the pumpkins? Was I expected to be wowed by the motel scenes? Does it hold significance that there are trash bags visible on a rooftop across from a hotel? Why does the narrator awkwardly mock those he interviews, given how evident it is that he edited out the more insightful portions of the conversations to create that effect? The highlight of the film was the interview with the film professor, who candidly informed us about how terrible the movie would be even before it concluded.

I’m genuinely astounded. It seems the creator is either striving to establish themselves as an intellectual or attempting to win over the academic community.

This Kiyoshi Kurosawa-directed ghost movie is quite erratic, and it did manage to deliver at least one jump scare that caught me off guard. However, overall, the film is incredibly nonsensical. It follows a detective who is tasked with tracking down a suspected serial killer, only to discover that he might be responsible for one of the murders. He then starts being haunted by a beautiful Asian ghost woman, though neither he nor the audience understands why. As additional murders occur, the detective grows increasingly confused, as the actual killers are quickly identified, yet the ghost continues to haunt him for no clear reason. The plot is thoroughly absurd, and the ghostly presence is more comedic than terrifying—especially when she inexplicably zips across the city like Wonder Woman. The ending is baffling, and honestly, the entire film makes very little sense. I cannot recommend it at all. If the filmmakers hadn't taken themselves so seriously, I'd suspect it was meant to be a black comedy. Aside from "Bright Future," this is the weakest Kurosawa film I've encountered so far.

This film, *Evil Breed: The Legend of Samhain*, offers minimal thought or effort. It relies heavily on rapid "slasher"-style killings and crude depictions of violence. The acting receives a grade of D, as the performers display limited talent, and their questionable decisions throughout the movie raise eyebrows. Their portrayal of characters does not align with their supposed age group, creating a jarring disconnect. Although there are brief moments that could be considered respectable, they are swiftly overshadowed by grotesque, stomach-turning scenes of death. For instance, one particularly graphic sequence involves a character being disemboweled from the anus, lasting around five minutes. It's painfully evident that the victims offer little resistance. This movie is best suited for those who enjoy watching disturbing deaths and near-torture sequences.
This movie is a terrible waste of time with poor acting, a weak plot, and糟糕的导演。这是有史以来最无聊的电影！有些糟糕的电影还是有趣的（比如《弗雷迪对杰森》），但有些电影真的很烂，这部属于后者。总结来说：千万别浪费时间在这上面。

This is without a doubt the worst movie I’ve ever watched! 

I can confidently say I’ve never seen anything worse than this film! 

And I mean *never*! 

I’m a huge fan of “B” horror movies, so I’ve seen some real stinkers over the years. But this movie? It’s in a league of its own. 

The title drew me in—I mean, come on, who wouldn’t be intrigued by something called “Vampires vs. Zombies”? I imagined undead creatures duking it out for eternity. I was sold before I even pressed play! 

But here’s the truth: I wish I’d skipped this mess entirely. 

The title is incredibly misleading. There’s not even a hint of vampires versus zombies—there’s barely a plot to speak of! Honestly, if someone asked me what this movie is about, I’d have to admit I don’t know. 

No plot. No story. Just pure nonsense from start to finish. 

By the time it ended, I felt bad—not for myself, but for the people involved in making it.

I had heard numerous positive reviews (both orally and in print) about *Weeds*, and I was eagerly anticipating becoming engrossed in yet another exceptional cable series, similar to *Entourage*, *The Sopranos*, or *Mad Men*. However, my excitement gradually faded with each episode of Season One that I watched—by the time I reached the sixth episode, I had lost interest entirely. 

The writing felt uninspired, overly predictable, and the depiction of Black characters was cringe-worthy. The dialogue seemed forced, as if the writers were desperately striving for wit and modernity. It was a rare occasion when I genuinely chuckled out loud. 

None of the characters evolved to the point where I could feel invested in their stories; they were self-centered and unlikable. The introduction of the brother-in-law was particularly grating—he came across as such a repulsive figure that I wondered why he hadn’t been arrested sooner. Sending the Hodes’ daughter Quinn to boarding school in Mexico felt trite and clichéd, making me suspect the writers were intentionally pushing viewers' patience. 

With every episode, my dislike for the characters grew stronger, and I found it increasingly difficult to overlook the numerous narrative inconsistencies. Adding fuel to the fire, I also learned that Season Two received even worse reviews.

A childless couple, played by Brooke Adams and Jeff Hayenga, visits a doctor, portrayed by James Karen, in hopes of starting a family. To their surprise, the procedure succeeds, but Adams gradually realizes that something is deeply amiss with the developing child. 

The premise shows promise but falls victim to a weak script—while the core concept is decent, the ending grows increasingly predictable, with every twist feeling inevitable. The directing is lackluster, lacking any sense of cohesion or purpose in staging even the simplest scenes. Production values are subpar, bordering on amateurish, further detracting from the experience. Additionally, the graphic scenes, such as a pregnant woman self-harming, are gratuitously distressing, and the special effects are poorly executed. By the conclusion, it’s painfully evident that the filmmakers lacked a coherent plan for wrapping up the story.

Despite these flaws, the performances offer some亮点. Adams, Hayenga, and Karen deliver commendable work, maintaining viewer engagement through their talent. However, this obscure 1991 release has largely remained forgotten for good reason. I rate it a 4 out of 10.

Will Smith delivers a captivating performance in *Seven Pounds*, a film that tugs at your heartstrings with even more force than a rock guitarist mid-solo. It surpasses the director’s earlier collaboration with Smith, *The Pursuit of Happiness*, a movie I also thoroughly enjoyed. Keep an eye on Gabriele Muccino, as his work might go overlooked if the attached talent isn’t as high-profile. 

Unfortunately, I deduced Will Smith’s plan early on—when he fakes his own suicide in the opening scene and introduces Rosario Dawson’s character as someone with an incurable heart condition. Still, I believe the writer/director made the correct decision in structuring the bookends this way; they’re the source of urgency and tension throughout the film. Watching the gradual unfolding of how a person could reach such an extreme sacrifice was gut-wrenching, especially as Smith’s and Dawson’s characters’ relationship blossomed despite the inevitable tragedy looming over them. 

One of my friends who watched it with me...

When will the pain end? I never want to watch another adaptation of "A Christmas Carol" again. They just keep remaking the same story, competing frantically to outdo one another, yet inevitably falling short. Sadly, it's not because the tale itself is compelling; it's moralistic, outdated, and steeped in conservative optimism, as though anyone truly learns from it. The countless versions of this film only confirm that we haven't.

When even John Cassavetes delivers a lackluster performance at half his usual intensity, it’s a clear sign that a film is heading for trouble. "The Incubus" is a prime example of a talented actor phoning it in just to make ends meet, and it’s easy to sympathize with him given the over-the-top script and the overly ornate art direction by John Hough. The story revolves around a string of rape-murders plaguing a small town, with plenty of supernatural nonsense thrown into the mix. Despite the premise, the uninspired direction drains every scene of tension and engagement, leaving Cassavetes visibly frustrated at times. The titular Incubus finally makes an appearance in the final moments, but its design, while commendable, isn’t enough to salvage the movie from its mediocrity. 

1/10

Before watching this film, I read a review here claiming it might be one of the greatest movies ever!? Ha ha. Scene by scene, the tension builds—but from the irritating characters in this movie. From the little girl speaking nonsense and attempting to drown the boy, to the killer wandering around unnoticed (and who was the guy at the beach talking to the boy!?), events occur randomly and remain unresolved. As I watched, it felt like the story was heading in one direction, only to shift unexpectedly—and keep shifting—without resolution.

The acting is excellent, but the writing is terrible. Every character’s actions and dialogue feel contrived, unrealistic, and out of place, while the supporting actors’ reactions are bizarre. The film introduces issues that never get resolved, leaving viewers confused and feeling as though they’ve wasted their time.

What an episode! Last week, when Melissa kept popping up in cameos emphasizing the friendship between Annie and Brandi, I nearly lost my lunch. But that was just the beginning compared to the chaos of her meltdown after being fired. Watching her hobble around on crutches while ranting obscenities and demanding someone fetch her purse was hands down the funniest moment in reality TV history. She went on to scream at crew members off-camera, insisting they pack all her clothes, as if anyone else would willingly wear her tacky outfits. Seriously, Melissa, you're almost 40, and you're still throwing toddler-like tantrums? Then Joan joined the drama, hurling insults at Annie and Brandi before storming off the show. Clearly, both Rivers are entitled divas who stayed on longer than deserved, solely to boost ratings. Melissa’s tears and refusal to participate in an exit interview only confirmed what everyone already knew—you’re a pampered brat who throws fits when things don’t go your way. Meanwhile, Annie admitted manipulating Melissa to see her point of view, which she promptly did. Melissa is undoubtedly the sharpest contestant and unquestionably deserves to take home the grand prize. WAH WAH I didn’t get my way!

This movie was created by a group of white guys who attended the same school. There’s nothing inherently wrong with that, but it feels like it was made by exactly that—a group of white guys from the same school. The majority of the cast consists of white males around the same age, reminiscent of a bunch of guys at summer camp turning the camera on themselves. The film lacks a coherent plot; it’s essentially a series of repetitive bloodbaths strung together. While there are a few humorous moments and comedic elements, they fail to break the monotony of the flat narrative.

The graphic cartoon sequences seem to compensate for the filmmakers' limited budget or resources, but they aren’t executed particularly well. Whenever practical effects weren't feasible, the filmmakers resorted to cheap animations. 

I watched this movie based on the trailer, which gave the impression of being a Tarantino-inspired piece. Unfortunately, the trailer scenes represent the film’s high point. The rest plays out as a tedious mix of mundane, uninspired comedy. Some parts work, but overall, it becomes monotonous and dull.

I had to watch this film due to its outrageously absurd plot, and it didn’t disappoint. In fact, it can be quite uncomfortable at times. Unlike other Meyer movies, the sexual content is kept to a bare minimum. Some of the violent scenes are gratuitously unnecessary and offensive. The plot is chaotic, and several of the performances and dialogue lines are terrible.

The movie awkwardly blends a sado-masochistic fantasy with a depiction of the brutality and immorality of slavery, failing on every level. It seems Meyer was attempting to compensate for his usual sexploitation/blackploitation themes by adding a pseudo-moral message. We’re made to feel slightly guilty about being aroused by the early scene of Lady Susan wielding a whip in a provocative outfit. Meyer then tries to redirect us toward a more righteous narrative about good overcoming evil. However, these conflicting elements cancel each other out, leaving the film with no clear purpose.

Despite its numerous flaws, which make it genuinely awful, the film is surprisingly worth watching for those who enjoy dissecting poorly made movies.

Once upon a time, in the enchanting land of France, its people lived happily, where the women were carefree and the men found solace in their cherished pastime: war, the sole diversion of kings that the common folk could partake in. This particular conflict was the Seven Years' War, and when the grim reality set in that there were more graves than soldiers, recruiters were dispatched to refill the ranks.  

Thus it happened that Fanfan (played by Gérard Philipe), caught romancing a farmer’s daughter in a haystack, dodged marriage by joining the prestigious Regiment d'Aquitane—but only after he had embraced the prophecy of a gypsy, who claimed he would achieve fame, wealth, and even the hand of the king’s daughter. Little did he know that Adeline (portrayed by Gina Lollobrigida), dressed in revealing blouses, was no gypsy but the recruiting sergeant's daughter.  

As Fanfan charged heroically with his saber drawn to save an attacked carriage, he found himself face-to-face with none other than the Marquise du Pompadour—and the king’s daughter herself. This encounter only reinforced his belief in his destined rise. Meanwhile, Adeline, too, began to realize her growing affection for Fanfan. And so, we find ourselves ensnared in the whirlwind of romance, ambition, and destiny in this tale of love and war.

"New York, I Love You" is a collaborative effort comprising eleven short films, each approximately 10 minutes long. Although the segments don’t follow a cohesive narrative, they share a common theme: love. Whether it’s between couples or casual conversations between strangers, every story revolves around the search for connection. The ensemble cast includes notable actors such as Shia LaBeouf, Natalie Portman, Hayden Christensen, Orlando Bloom, Chris Cooper, Andy Garcia, Christina Ricci, Irrfan Khan, Robin Wright Penn, Julie Christie, Ethan Hawke, Bradley Cooper, Rachel Bilson, and Anton Yelchin. Given the impressive lineup and intriguing concept, expectations were high for this film. However, "New York, I Love You" ultimately feels like the sum of its parts rather than a unified whole. While some segments are witty, inventive, and captivating, others—like the ones featuring Orlando Bloom/Christina Ricci and Ethan Hawke/Maggie Q—are disappointingly shallow. The movie suffers from inconsistency and adopts an experimental style that can feel amateurish at times. From a storytelling perspective, it resembles something crafted by fledgling filmmakers. Despite these issues, there are standout moments, particularly the touching segment with Eli Wallach and Cloris Leachman as an elderly couple taking a walk.

This film is little more than a rehash of a dozen superior movies, particularly Steve Martin's "LA Story," which at least had the decency to embrace its fictional nature, even if it starred his real-life girlfriend as his on-screen counterpart.

Yes, naive viewers, "20 Dates" is a mockumentary, though I'm not entirely sure that was Myles Berkowitz's original intention. My sense is that he began the project somewhat earnestly but soon recognized that it would feel pitiful and unfunny unless he exaggerated the scenarios to absurd levels. Consequently, the entire production exudes an uncomfortable, amateurish, and disingenuous vibe.

As one astute observer noted, the film features two of the "dates" suing Myles and obtaining restraining orders against him, yet they still appear in the movie—a logistical impossibility without signed consent forms. Additionally, it seems to me that most of the women cast as "the dates" are professional actresses (with the exception of Tina Carrere), albeit not well-known ones—they're far too strikingly attractive, refined, slim, and at ease in front of the camera to pass for ordinary civilians.

Mr. Berkowitz commits a common mistake by limiting his casting to such conventionally beautiful individuals.

Likely inspired by the acclaim for her earlier work, "Orlando," Potter takes on multiple roles in this film—writing, directing, starring, and even co-writing the music, which includes a sentimental love song. The movie feels like a high school or college project by a young filmmaker who believes her personal romances and dramatic fixations are as captivating to viewers as they are to her. However, Potter’s character is unappealing, while the subject of her romantic fixation is equally unlikable, making the entire film an uncomfortable showcase of self-indulgence disguised as a tribute to the tango. It’s possible the project could have succeeded had she not starred in it; her acting, whether portraying herself or another role, falls flat. The film is pretentious, overly ambitious, tedious, and nonsensical.

What feels distinctly French about this film is the deliberate effort it takes to develop the two main characters. This may demand a touch of patience, particularly since neither fits the conventional Hollywood standard of attractiveness. Yet, as soon as the heist begins, the movie hurtles forward at a rapid pace, possibly moving too swiftly at times. Still, it's an exhilarating thrill ride, and if you suspend disbelief, it all feels quite plausible. The sort of film that Hollywood likely would have ruined.

Kate Beckinsale shines in this adaptation! Bravo! It’s a shame that Knightly isn’t as attractive as Jeremy Northam. Mark Strong delivers an outstanding performance. Bernard Hepton perfectly embodies Emma’s father. I adore the closing scene (an addition to the novel but well crafted), where the harvest is complete and Knightly shares a meal with both his workers and high society friends. This moment shows Emma accepting the new dynamic, highlighting her transformation. While the change feels abrupt, I’m willing to accept it. Samantha Bond brings depth to Emma’s former governess and confidante, embodying the character exactly as I envisioned her. I truly believe that when the UK adapts Jane Austen, it results in the finest versions. American adaptations of British literature often prioritize profit over quality. Watch this one—it’s exceptional!

Admittedly, the casting in this film is quite unusual—part of it stems from the storyline itself, but I still found it challenging to fully buy Pierce Brosnan in the lead role, despite his solid performance. 

The movie is based on the true story of an Englishman who moved to live among the Canadian Indians in the early 1900s. He claimed to be of mixed Native American descent. Surprisingly, he became highly respected and successful, attracting people from far and wide to attend his lectures and join his wilderness expeditions—despite the fact that he wasn’t actually of Native heritage, and all his knowledge was either learned from books or fabricated. The film focuses on this deception and the events that unfolded when the truth was revealed.

The performances and settings were impressive, and I thoroughly enjoyed the movie once I accepted Brosnan’s portrayal. It didn’t receive wide distribution likely because it’s quite intellectual—not your typical Bond film or romantic drama, but rather an intriguing story about an extraordinary individual.

Following *Highlander 2*—a film I’m still struggling to accept—I believed it was impossible for a sequel to make me cry, though not out of emotion but due to its poor quality. I was mistaken. While I adored the original *WarGames*, this sequel gets several details about computers and the first movie wrong. At the very least, the original *WarGames* featured functional hacks. The person who wrote this sequel apparently knew nothing about computers beyond using a word processor. They likely didn’t even watch the first film. The acting isn’t even believable. Save yourself: under no circumstances should you watch this movie. Even if your TV is stuck on this channel and you can’t turn it off, *this film will ruin your life*.

This is an awful movie. The cast seems fully aware of just how poor it is. It begins badly and by the end is downright terrible. The acting is dismal, and the script might as well have been improvised on the spot. Despite being labeled a horror film, it lacks any genuinely frightening moments. A miserable 1 out of 10.

"Diagnosis Murder" has been airing on most weekday afternoons on BBC1 ever since I watched it during my school days whenever I was ill. Even though I know I probably shouldn’t enjoy it as much as I do—similar to how I shouldn’t enjoy "Murder, She Wrote"—I’m completely hooked on both shows and even own the DVD box sets... okay, so maybe that’s a little embarrassing! 

Dick Van Dyke anchors the series with his portrayal of Dr. Mark Sloan, a doctor at Community General Hospital in Los Angeles who also serves as a police consultant for the LAPD. His son, Steve (played by Barry Van Dyke, Dick’s real-life son), is a police officer who often seeks his father’s expertise in suspicious death cases.

Joining them is Dr. Amanda Bentley (played by Victoria Bryant), the hospital’s resident pathologist. For the first few seasons, Scott Baio played Dr. Jack Stewart, until he left the show in 1995 to pursue bigger opportunities. Unfortunately, those didn’t pan out; his acting career never took off afterward. In fact, his only notable role in recent years was in "Baby Geniuses 2: Superbabies." Yikes! 

Dr. Jack Stewart was later replaced by the younger Dr. Jesse.

If you enjoy films about school bullies, courageous kids, funny toddlers, and the occasional worm feast, *How to Eat Fried Worms* will surely capture your attention.

The movie follows Billy, a boy who, on his very first day at a new school, finds out that some of his classmates have played a prank on him by sneaking worms into his lunch. The school’s resident bully, Joe, and his group of friends mock Billy, dubbing him “worm boy.”

Determined not to let their teasing get to him, Billy confidently claims that he regularly eats worms. Although skeptical, Joe accepts Billy’s challenge to eat ten worms in one day—on penalty of showing up to school with worms in his pants. 

The boys agree to the bet, forcing the queasy Billy to embark on a quest to earn his classmates’ respect by consuming worms in various forms—cooked, fried, or straight out of the ground.

While the premise might sound bizarre, the film delivers meaningful lessons. It highlights the importance of genuine friendships and accepting others for who they are, while also exploring the reasons behind bullying behavior.

I believe this covers most of what I needed to express. Still, I feel compelled to clarify my stance. Frankly, I’ve rarely encountered a production so amateurish, and I use the term comprehensively. While the physical camerawork, boom microphone operation, and other technical elements are laughable, the issues extend far beyond that.

Unlike some classic independent films that were salvaged by strong scripts, compelling characterizations, and engaging plots, this unfortunately suffers from a terrible script, poor acting, and, worst of all, insufferably annoying characters.

It’s a tragedy that for every indie film like *Haiku Tunnel* that finds distribution, ten others quietly fade away. I can only assume the Kornbluth brothers have connections at Sony because there’s no other explanation for how this amateur family project ever saw the light of day. It baffles me why they chose to distribute it.

The sole intriguing aspect of this film is its title. However, even that proves disappointing upon closer inspection. Hopefully, this review will spare a few curious souls tempted by the title from wasting their time on it.

I believe most people were thoroughly disappointed with this sci-fi film. Firstly, it was directed by Tim Burton, and secondly, it’s a remake of what’s considered a classic. I found it dull, repulsive, and absurd. If you’ve watched it, you’ll understand exactly what I mean. Almost everyone on IMDb agrees it’s terrible, and they’re absolutely correct! If you haven’t seen it yet, steer clear—it’s incredibly boring. My rating: 1 out of 10.

"Justice" is one of those films that initially leaves you puzzled about its harsh critical reception upon release—it’s not groundbreaking but solid enough, with a standout performance from Ed Harris. However, as you progress into the final act, the story becomes progressively absurd. By the end, you’re faced with a deranged killer wielding a flashlight on his head, menacingly threatening to harm Sean Connery’s wife (the predictably stiff and unconvincing Kate Capshaw) and their child (a notably young Scarlett Johansson) inside an alligator trapper’s cabin. This is the sort of movie best suited for a flight, and even then, it’s worth watching only once.

"Dressed to Kill" is one of the greatest thrillers ever made. Its handling of sex and violence cements it as a film for mature audiences. Brian De Palma once again demonstrates why no other director matches his ability to convey stories through cinematography. He directs numerous scenes without dialogue, using visuals and Pino Donaggio's exceptional score to drive the narrative. Filmed in Panavision, the movie demands to be viewed in widescreen, as De Palma utilizes the full width of the frame to craft his tale. When cropped for video, the essence of "Dressed to Kill" is lost. The strong performances, masterful direction, and possibly the greatest film score ever composed elevate this movie to a must-see status.

I simply want to point out that this production is highly one-sided and undermines the impartiality necessary for being taken seriously. 

There are no credits provided for the people they interviewed, so it's impossible to determine whether their perspectives are credible.

The documentary presents the story from only one point of view, which is risky because future generations may adopt harmful ideas as a result, contributing to the continuation of conflicts. While this is not the sole cause of wars, it certainly does not help. 

You can watch this documentary, but make sure to do extensive research online first. The Balkans, like human history itself, are incredibly complex.

This film serves as an eye-opener for those who only see the glamorous lives of celebrities. It highlights how individuals who want to do good often can't. Additionally, the bomb blast scene feels very authentic.

What you read and learn doesn’t always align with reality!!!

It might increase your blood pressure by 10%.

All the actors delivered impressive performances.

Some scenes could have been omitted to make it suitable for teenagers.

The movie is quite mature in theme.

Not suitable for watching with the family.

The casting is fantastic!!!

Steve McQueen undoubtedly has a devoted fanbase, and for good reason—he was undoubtedly a magnetic presence, one of the screen’s most captivating figures. However, even McQueen can’t salvage this poorly made film, which appears to have been shot with what looks like a Brownie camera in real locations around St. Louis. 

In the movie, McQueen plays a newcomer with no criminal history who is recruited by another member of the gang to help plan a bank heist. There’s a strong implication of a romantic connection between McQueen’s character and David Clarke, further straining relations with the rest of the crew, who resent him due to his lack of criminal experience. 

Adding to the tension, McQueen’s girlfriend, Molly McCarthy, begins to suspect something is amiss when he starts spending time with Crahan Denton and James Dukas, both of whom exude a rougher, more suspicious vibe. It’s the kind of situation that would raise anyone’s alarm bells.

"The Great St. Louis Bank Robbery" was directed by Charles Guggenheim and John Stix. Guggenheim primarily worked on documentaries, while Stix had an undistinguished career. Apparently, one of them decided that McQueen’s performance should include a poor imitation of Marlon Brando, a choice that only adds to the film’s overall awkwardness.

According to the DVD sleeve’s synopsis, a trio of treasure hunters sets sail through the West Indies in search of a hidden fortune. As they draw closer to the treasure’s location, the promise of gold intensifies the tension among the group. Hoping to locate the coveted gold, the deep-sea divers soon discover that greed and hatred lead to violence. The boat they sail on is called *Manfish*—not a monster. A convincing skeleton presents Captain John Bromfield (played by Brannigan) with his half of the treasure map, while veteran actor Victor Jory (as Professor) contributes the other half. First mate Lon Chaney Jr. (as Swede) feigns ignorance, and Tessa Prendergast (as Alita), who guards the rum, does so rather ineffectively. Despite its promising premise, the film suffers from significant editing and continuity issues, which detract from what could have been a more compelling story. *** *Manfish* (2/56) — W. Lee Wilder ~ John Bromfield, Victor Jory, Lon Chaney Jr.

This is the worst movie I’ve ever paid to watch, and aside from *They Saved Hitler's Brain*, it’s the worst movie I’ve seen overall. When this film came out, I was a huge fan of *SNL* and *SCTV*, so I was eagerly expecting what I thought would be the funniest movie possible, assuming it wouldn’t face the same creative limitations as their TV formats. 

The writers seem to have thought, “Let’s add some grossness, flatulence jokes, and cheap sexual humor—voila, instant edgy comedy.” But their attempt at humor falls flat. The game show sketches are nothing but uninspired rip-offs of *Let’s Make a Deal*, filled with cringe-worthy grossness. The sitcom parody featuring the single woman and her boyfriend is pure high school-level humor. The stun gun ad sketch might as well have been written for *Sesame Street*. The LA subway scene offers bland, tasteless blood humor. And the French chef blindly wandering around muttering “There is no difference” in a stereotypical accent? You get the idea.

The only remotely funny moment was a Chevy Chase sketch, which lasted all of one minute. That’s 60 seconds of entertainment in an otherwise painful experience.

I thoroughly enjoyed this film. Tobey Maguire delivers an outstanding performance as Jake, and he ranks among the finest actors I've seen. I was pleasantly surprised by the numerous humorous lines throughout the movie; his comedic timing was exceptional, despite never having seen him in a comic role before. The film effectively draws you into the characters' world, leaving you eager to discover their fates. While I wasn't sure what to anticipate from Jewel's performance, she acquitted herself admirably. The movie features plenty of thrilling moments, making it an immensely entertaining experience. I'm now a devoted fan of Maguire's. Be sure to watch *The Cider House Rules*; it's one of the greatest films ever made.

What truly amazes me is that this film even got made. The director, writer, and actor must be incredibly charismatic in person. I can’t think of any other way it would have passed the script stage. Here’s something to consider: while watching the movie, I found myself feeling sorry for the actors. It felt like being in a comedy club where the performer is struggling on stage, and all you can do is feel bad for them because they’re clearly trying so hard. I’d love to know the budget for this film—it must have been low, given how poor the production quality is. I wanted to say, “The jokes didn’t resonate with me,” but the truth is, for them to work, you’d have to be either the person who wrote them or someone who doesn’t quite get humor. Imagine that same script getting greenlit—that’s pretty impressive, isn’t it?

Truly an appalling mess of a film! 

Predictable, excruciatingly slow-paced, and utterly soul-crushing, this movie makes self-harm with a blunt object seem like a reasonable response. 

The performances are overly dramatic given the sparse dialogue, each scene dragging on far longer than necessary. The tedious minutiae of careers crumbling or flourishing is mind-numbingly dull. Even the soundtrack, which might otherwise be enjoyable, feels insufficient compensation for enduring such an agonizing viewing experience. Three decent songs simply don’t justify the effort.

As I watched, I desperately wished for either narcolepsy or divine intervention to end my suffering. 

I will never subject myself to this cinematic torment again—never, ever, ever.

The U.S. State Department might not want us to watch this movie due to tensions with the Iranian government. Yet, it beautifully highlights the sophistication of Iranian society, even as its narrative focuses on the fight for women's rights in straightforward terms: the right to attend a soccer match at the stadium, a privilege exclusively reserved for men. The film is delightfully humorous, and by its very existence, serves as evidence of free speech and expression in Iran. I thoroughly enjoyed this movie. It follows five young women attempting to sneak past security at a soccer match between Iran and Bahrain. The ensuing comedic events, from their bus ride to the stadium to their detention by police, are impossible to fully describe but are incredibly entertaining. This is a must-see classic and one of the finest foreign films I’ve watched in years.

I must confess that I’ve always struggled to watch an Antonioni film from beginning to end on my first attempt, and even with this one, I ended up viewing it in three segments over multiple sittings. In hindsight, I think that approach turned out to be for the best, as it pushed me to stop focusing on conventional plot structures and simply appreciate each scene individually. 

The initial segment feels quite fragmented, which isn’t necessarily a flaw—it just demands more attention to follow seamlessly. However, when it shifts to the desert scenes, every bit of effort pays off tenfold. While the breathtaking cinematography is undoubtedly part of its allure, what truly elevates these moments is how the landscape becomes an almost tangible presence. Its silence, vastness, and bittersweet yet liberating quality merge beautifully with the two young protagonists. The desert may appear lifeless, but it somehow feels closer and more relatable than the sterile urban settings depicted earlier. The interplay between the plane flying overhead and the girl’s car creates some striking visuals. The unfolding romance...
